  • Lines 41–44: .NET 10 incorporates LINQ for asynchronous streams (class [System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable], previously available in the NuGet and [System.Linq.Async] packages): [Where], [Select], [Take], [FirstAsync], [ToListAsync]… apply to a [IAsyncEnumerable<T>]. Methods that produce a stream ([Where], [Select]) return another stream; those that produce a value ([ToListAsync], [CountAsync], [FirstAsync]) return a task that is pending;
  • Line 76: The method [ToString] of [record] and [Mesure] is redefined for a more compact display.

docs.title: 9.10.1. ValueTask<T>
docs.text:
A task is an object: each call to a method that returns a [Task<T>] (generally) allocates an object on the heap, which the garbage collector will have to reclaim. This is negligible for I/O that lasts milliseconds, but not for a method called millions of times per second that, most of the time, already has the result (a cache, a pre-filled buffer). For this case, .NET offers the [ValueTask<T>] structure (C# 7, 2017): it contains either the result directly (no allocation) or a true task when the operation is truly asynchronous. The program [async-18.cs] uses it for a cached exchange rate service:

// ValueTask<T>: an asynchronous method that, in most cases, already has the result
using System.Diagnostics;

var service = new ServiceTaux();
var chrono = Stopwatch.StartNew();
foreach (string code in new[] { "EUR", "USD", "EUR", "EUR", "USD", "GBP", "EUR" })
{
    long debut = chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds;
    decimal taux = await service.LireTauxAsync(code);
    Console.WriteLine($"{code} : {taux,6} lu en {chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds - debut,3} ms");
}
Console.WriteLine($"accès au serveur : {service.NbAccesServeur}, réponses du cache : {service.NbAccesCache}");

class ServiceTaux
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, decimal> cache = [];
    public int NbAccesServeur { get; private set; }
    public int NbAccesCache { get; private set; }

     // ValueTask<decimal>: no task allocation when the result is in the cache
    public ValueTask<decimal> LireTauxAsync(string code)
    {
        if (cache.TryGetValue(code, out decimal taux))
        {
             // fast, synchronous path: the result is already known
            NbAccesCache++;
            return ValueTask.FromResult(taux);
        }
         // slow, asynchronous path: the server must be queried
        return new ValueTask<decimal>(LireTauxServeurAsync(code));
    }

    private async Task<decimal> LireTauxServeurAsync(string code)
    {
        NbAccesServeur++;
         // simulates querying a remote server
        await Task.Delay(300);
        decimal taux = code switch
        {
            "EUR" => 1m,
            "USD" => 1.17m,
            "GBP" => 0.87m,
            _ => throw new ArgumentException($"devise inconnue : {code}"),
        };
        cache[code] = taux;
        return taux;
    }
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-18.cs
EUR :      1 lu en 323 ms
USD :   1,17 lu en 301 ms
EUR :      1 lu en   0 ms
EUR :      1 lu en   0 ms
USD :   1,17 lu en   0 ms
GBP :   0,87 lu en 301 ms
EUR :      1 lu en   0 ms
accès au serveur : 3, réponses du cache : 4

Comments:

  • Lines 21–30: The method is not [async]. If the rate is in the cache, it returns a [ValueTask<decimal>] that directly contains the result ([ValueTask.FromResult]): no object is created. Otherwise, it wraps the task of the [async] method—which queries the server—in a [ValueTask<decimal>];
  • lines 33–45: the simulated server query (300 ms), which stores the result in the cache. A method [async] can also directly return a [ValueTask<T>];
  • line 9: for the caller, nothing changes: it waits for the [ValueTask] with [await]. The results show the 3 server accesses (300 ms each) and the 4 immediate responses from the cache.

[ValueTask<T>] has constraints: it must be waited for only once (no two [await] on the same [ValueTask], no simultaneous waiting from multiple locations), and it cannot be passed directly to [Task.WhenAll]: it must first be converted to a task using [AsTask()]. The rule of thumb is simple: use [Task] and [Task<T>] by default, and [ValueTask] only in code that has been measured to be heavily loaded and often synchronous. You’ll mostly encounter [ValueTask] as the return type for methods of .NET: [Stream.ReadAsync(Memory<byte>)], [DisposeAsync], [ChannelWriter.WriteAsync]…

docs.title: 9.10.2. ConfigureAwait and the synchronization context
docs.text:
The [async-05.cs] program demonstrated that, in the console, the remainder of a method following a [await] is executed by any thread in the pool. This is not the case in a graphical application (Windows Forms, WPF, MAUI). A graphical component can only be manipulated by the UI thread: the 2008 course had to use [listBoxEvts.Invoke(...)] from its callback methods to have the update executed by that thread. With [await], this is no longer necessary: the interface thread has a synchronization context ([SynchronizationContext.Current] is not [null]), which [await] stores; at the end of the wait, the rest of the method is returned to this context and thus executed by the interface thread. We can write:

private async void BoutonTelecharger_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    labelEtat.Text = "téléchargement en cours…";          // interface thread
    string page = await client.GetStringAsync(adresse);     // the interface remains responsive while waiting
    textBoxPage.Text = page;                                 // returns to the interface thread
}

This return to the original context has a cost and a risk: if code blocks the interface thread while waiting for a task ([tache.Result]), and that task needs that same thread to execute its remaining code, the two will wait for each other indefinitely (“deadlock”). This is the main reason for the “no [.Result]” rule.

The method [ConfigureAwait(false)] instructs [await] not to return to the original context: [await flux.ReadAsync(tampon).ConfigureAwait(false);]. The rest of the code is then executed by a thread from the pool. The recommendations are as follows:

  • In the code of a general-purpose library (which does not handle a graphical user interface and does not know who will call it), use *[ConfigureAwait(false)] for each *[await]: this is slightly more efficient and prevents deadlocks if a careless caller uses *[.Result]*;
  • in application code (graphical user interface, console program, ASP.NET Core application), it is not written. Console programs and ASP.NET Core applications do not have a synchronization context anyway: [ConfigureAwait(false)] makes no difference there.

The examples in this course, which are applications, do not use [ConfigureAwait].

docs.title: 9.10.3. TaskCompletionSource<T>: Converting an Event into a Task
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to use a API that signals the end of its operations via an event (the EAP model, or any class that publishes events), while the rest of the code is written using [await]. The [TaskCompletionSource<T>] class allows you to create a task that you terminate yourself at the desired time:

  • its [Task] property is an unfinished [Task<T>], which is returned to the caller;
  • [SetResult(valeur)] / [TrySetResult(valeur)] successfully completes the task;
  • [SetException(exception)] / [TrySetException(exception)] terminates it with a failure;
  • [SetCanceled()] / [TrySetCanceled()] cancels it.

The [TryXxx] methods return [false] instead of throwing an exception if the task has already completed. In fact, it was a [TaskCompletionSource<int>] that was used by the simplified state machine of the [CompterSucresAsync] method presented above. The [async-19.cs] program waits for a thermometer, which publishes its measurements via an event, to reach a certain temperature:

// TaskCompletionSource<T>: Convert an event-driven API into a task
using System.Diagnostics;

var chrono = Stopwatch.StartNew();
var thermometre = new Thermometre();
thermometre.Demarrer();

// 1 - wait, without blocking the thread, for the first reading greater than or equal to 21 °C
double mesure = await AttendreTemperatureAsync(thermometre, 21, CancellationToken.None);
Console.WriteLine($"{chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms : 1 - température atteinte : {mesure} °C");

// 2 - the same wait, limited to one second: the task is canceled
using (var delai = new CancellationTokenSource(1000))
{
    try
    {
        mesure = await AttendreTemperatureAsync(thermometre, 30, delai.Token);
        Console.WriteLine($"{chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms : 2 - température atteinte : {mesure} °C");
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms : 2 - 30 °C non atteints dans le délai d'une seconde");
    }
}
thermometre.Arreter();

// converts the MesureFaite events from the thermometer into a task
static Task<double> AttendreTemperatureAsync(Thermometre thermometre, double seuil, CancellationToken token)
{
     // the source of a task that you terminate yourself
    var source = new TaskCompletionSource<double>(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);
     // registration with the cancellation token, to be released when the task is complete
    CancellationTokenRegistration inscription = default;
     // The event handler terminates the task when the threshold is reached
    void SurMesure(object? sender, double temperature)
    {
        if (temperature >= seuil && source.TrySetResult(temperature))
        {
            thermometre.MesureFaite -= SurMesure;
            inscription.Dispose();
        }
    }
    thermometre.MesureFaite += SurMesure;
     // A cancellation request terminates the task with the status "Canceled"
    inscription = token.Register(() =>
    {
        if (source.TrySetCanceled(token))
        {
            thermometre.MesureFaite -= SurMesure;
        }
    });
     // The task is returned immediately; it will terminate later
    return source.Task;
}

// A thermometer that publishes a measurement every 200 ms via an event (API “old-style”)
class Thermometre
{
    public event EventHandler<double>? MesureFaite;
    private Timer? minuterie;
    private double temperature = 19;

    public void Demarrer()
    {
        minuterie = new Timer(_ =>
        {
            temperature += 0.5;
            Console.WriteLine($"          mesure : {temperature} °C");
            MesureFaite?.Invoke(this, temperature);
        }, null, 200, 200);
    }

    public void Arreter()
    {
        minuterie?.Dispose();
    }
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-19.cs
          mesure : 19,5 °C
          mesure : 20 °C
          mesure : 20,5 °C
          mesure : 21 °C
  805 ms : 1 - température atteinte : 21 °C
          mesure : 21,5 °C
          mesure : 22 °C
          mesure : 22,5 °C
          mesure : 23 °C
          mesure : 23,5 °C
 1812 ms : 2 - 30 °C non atteints dans le délai d'une seconde

Comments:

  • Lines 57–75: The thermometer, an “old-school” class: A timer ([System.Threading.Timer], which executes a method at regular intervals on a thread from the pool) increases the temperature by 0.5 °C every 200 ms and publishes it via the event [MesureFaite], of type [EventHandler<double>] (events were discussed in Chapter 7);
  • lines 28–53: the method that converts events into a task. It is not [async]: it creates a [TaskCompletionSource<double>], subscribes a handler to the event, and immediately returns the source task, which is not yet complete;
  • Line 31: This option specifies that the remaining code awaiting the task should not be executed by the thread calling [TrySetResult] (in this case, the timer thread, in the middle of emitting the event), but by a thread from the pool. This is the recommended option in almost all cases;
  • lines 35–40: At each measurement, the handler checks the threshold. When it is reached, the handler terminates the task with the temperature as the result, then unsubscribes from the event and releases the registration with the cancellation token;
  • lines 45–47: [token.Register(action)] registers an action to be executed if cancellation is requested. Here, it cancels the task (status [Canceled]) and unsubscribes the handler. Without this, a task waiting for a threshold that is never reached would never terminate;
  • lines 9–22: For the caller, waiting for a temperature is an asynchronous method like any other: it is awaited using [await] and time-limited with a cancellation token.

[Task.Factory.FromAsync], mentioned above, plays the same role for the API instances of the APM model ([BeginXxx] / [EndXxx]).

docs.title: 9.11.1. Parallel.ForEachAsync
docs.text:
[Task.WhenAll] launches all operations at the same time. This is not always desirable: to download 10,000 web pages, you don’t want to open 10,000 simultaneous connections to the same server. The previous chapter introduced [Parallel.ForEach], which distributes the processing of a collection across multiple threads; its asynchronous version, [Parallel.ForEachAsync] (.NET 6), processes the elements of a collection using an asynchronous function, limiting the number of concurrent operations. The program [async-20.cs] downloads nine pages, no more than three at a time:

// Parallel.ForEachAsync: Process a collection with a limited number of concurrent operations
using System.Diagnostics;

var chrono = Stopwatch.StartNew();
string[] pages = [.. Enumerable.Range(1, 9).Select(i => $"page{i}.html")];
int enCours = 0;

// no more than 3 downloads at the same time
var options = new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 3 };
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(pages, options, async (page, token) =>
{
     // counter shared by concurrent operations: it is modified atomically
    int n = Interlocked.Increment(ref enCours);
    Afficher($"début de {page} ({n} en cours)");
     // Simulated download of a page
    await Task.Delay(1000, token);
    Interlocked.Decrement(ref enCours);
    Afficher($"fin de {page}");
});
Afficher($"les {pages.Length} pages sont téléchargées");

void Afficher(string message)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms [thread {Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId,2}] : {message}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-20.cs
   12 ms [thread  4] : début de page1.html (1 en cours)
   12 ms [thread  6] : début de page2.html (2 en cours)
   29 ms [thread  6] : début de page3.html (3 en cours)
 1024 ms [thread  6] : fin de page1.html
 1025 ms [thread  6] : début de page4.html (3 en cours)
 1028 ms [thread  4] : fin de page3.html
 1028 ms [thread  6] : fin de page2.html
 1029 ms [thread  4] : début de page5.html (2 en cours)
 1029 ms [thread  6] : début de page6.html (3 en cours)
 2023 ms [thread  6] : fin de page4.html
 2023 ms [thread  6] : début de page7.html (3 en cours)
 2028 ms [thread  6] : fin de page6.html
 2028 ms [thread  6] : début de page8.html (3 en cours)
 2030 ms [thread  4] : fin de page5.html
 2030 ms [thread  4] : début de page9.html (3 en cours)
 3025 ms [thread  8] : fin de page9.html
 3026 ms [thread  8] : fin de page7.html
 3025 ms [thread  4] : fin de page8.html
 3026 ms [thread  4] : les 9 pages sont téléchargées

Comments:

  • line 5: the nine page names, constructed using a collection expression with the spread operator [..];
  • line 9: the property [MaxDegreeOfParallelism] of [ParallelOptions] sets the maximum number of concurrent operations (by default, the number of processors). A rollback token ([CancellationToken]) can also be set here;
  • Lines 10–18: [Parallel.ForEachAsync] receives the collection, the options, and an asynchronous function (a lambda [async]) that is called for each element with the element and a cancellation token, to be passed to the function’s asynchronous operations. [Parallel.ForEachAsync] returns a task that completes when all elements have been processed;
  • lines 13–17: the functions run simultaneously on multiple threads: the counter [enCours] that they share is modified atomically using the [Interlocked] class from the previous chapter;
  • The results show three waves of three pages: as soon as one page is finished, another begins, and the number of downloads in progress never exceeds 3. The entire process takes 3 seconds instead of 9. When two threads write at nearly the same time, the order of the lines may vary from one execution to another, and a displayed time may even be slightly earlier than that of the previous line;
  • only two or three threads executed all the functions: during wait periods, no thread is busy.

docs.title: 9.11.2. Producer/Consumer: System.Threading.Channels
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced the producer/consumer pattern using the [BlockingCollection<T>] collection: producer threads enqueue elements into a queue, and consumer threads dequeue them; [Take] (or the enumeration [GetConsumingEnumerable]) blocks a consumer as long as the queue is empty, while [Add] blocks a producer as long as a bounded queue is full. These waits block threads. Channels in the [System.Threading.Channels] namespace (.NET Core 3.0) provide the same service with asynchronous waits:

  • [Channel.CreateBounded<T>(capacité)] creates a bounded channel, [Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>()] creates an unbounded channel;
  • the [Writer] property ([ChannelWriter<T>]) is used by producers: [WriteAsync] publishes an item (waiting asynchronously for space to become available), [TryWrite] attempts to add it immediately, [Complete] indicates that there will be no more elements;
  • The property [Reader] ([ChannelReader<T>]) is used by consumers: [ReadAsync] retrieves an element, while [ReadAllAsync] returns an asynchronous stream of all elements, which ends when the channel is closed by [Complete] and is empty.

The program [async-21.cs] processes commands, generated every 50 ms, using two consumers that each take 400 ms to process a command:

// producer/consumers with a channel (System.Threading.Channels)
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Threading.Channels;

var chrono = Stopwatch.StartNew();
// A bounded channel: it contains at most 2 commands awaiting processing
Channel<int> canal = Channel.CreateBounded<int>(2);

// The producer and two consumers are working simultaneously
Task producteur = ProduireAsync(canal.Writer, 8);
Task consommateur1 = ConsommerAsync("C1", canal.Reader);
Task consommateur2 = ConsommerAsync("C2", canal.Reader);
await Task.WhenAll(producteur, consommateur1, consommateur2);
Afficher("toutes les commandes ont été traitées");

// The producer: one order every 50 ms
async Task ProduireAsync(ChannelWriter<int> ecrivain, int nbCommandes)
{
    for (int i = 1; i <= nbCommandes; i++)
    {
        await Task.Delay(50);
         // TryWrite places the order immediately if there is space in the channel
        if (ecrivain.TryWrite(i))
        {
            Afficher($"P  : commande {i} déposée");
        }
        else
        {
             // Channel full: WriteAsync waits (without blocking a thread) for space to become available
            Afficher($"P  : canal plein, la commande {i} attend");
            await ecrivain.WriteAsync(i);
            Afficher($"P  : commande {i} déposée");
        }
    }
     // nothing more will be written: the consumers will exit their loop
    ecrivain.Complete();
    Afficher("P  : fin de la production");
}

// one consumer: processing a command takes 400 ms
async Task ConsommerAsync(string nom, ChannelReader<int> lecteur)
{
     // ReadAllAsync returns an asynchronous stream that ends when the channel is closed and empty
    await foreach (int commande in lecteur.ReadAllAsync())
    {
        Afficher($"{nom} : traitement de la commande {commande}");
        await Task.Delay(400);
    }
    Afficher($"{nom} : plus de commandes");
}

void Afficher(string message)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms : {message}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-21.cs
   63 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 1
   63 ms : P  : commande 1 déposée
  130 ms : P  : commande 2 déposée
  130 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 2
  181 ms : P  : commande 3 déposée
  233 ms : P  : commande 4 déposée
  284 ms : P  : canal plein, la commande 5 attend
  479 ms : P  : commande 5 déposée
  479 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 3
  530 ms : P  : canal plein, la commande 6 attend
  530 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 4
  530 ms : P  : commande 6 déposée
  583 ms : P  : canal plein, la commande 7 attend
  879 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 5
  879 ms : P  : commande 7 déposée
  930 ms : P  : canal plein, la commande 8 attend
  930 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 6
  930 ms : P  : commande 8 déposée
  935 ms : P  : fin de la production
 1277 ms : C1 : traitement de la commande 7
 1330 ms : C2 : traitement de la commande 8
 1679 ms : C1 : plus de commandes
 1731 ms : C2 : plus de commandes
 1731 ms : toutes les commandes ont été traitées

Comments:

  • line 7: an integer queue (containing the order numbers) that holds at most 2 pending orders;
  • Lines 10–13: The producer and the two consumers are three asynchronous methods launched simultaneously; the program waits for all three to finish;
  • lines 23–31: the producer attempts to submit each order using [TryWrite]. If the channel is full, it signals this and waits for space to become available with [WriteAsync]: the producer is throttled to the consumers’ pace (lines 8–9), without any thread being blocked. This is the benefit of a bounded channel: a producer that is too fast cannot fill up the memory;
  • line 36: production is complete. The consumers will empty the channel and then exit their loop;
  • lines 44–49: Each consumer processes the asynchronous stream [ReadAllAsync]. An order is delivered to only one consumer: orders are distributed between C1 and C2 based on their availability;
  • As in the previous example, two lines displayed at nearly the same time may appear out of order (the displayed timestamps are therefore not always in ascending order).

Channels are the modern tool for the producer-consumer pattern, both between asynchronous methods and between threads.

docs.title: 9.12. Time: PeriodicTimer and TimeProvider
docs.text:
Two recent classes round out the time-related tools:

  • [PeriodicTimer] (.NET 6) is a timer used with [await]: its method [WaitForNextTickAsync] returns a task that completes at the next “top.” Unlike [System.Threading.Timer] (used in [async-19.cs]), which calls a callback method on a thread from the pool—possibly while the previous call is still in progress— [PeriodicTimer] is written as a simple loop and never overlaps two executions;
  • [TimeProvider] (.NET 8) is an abstract class that represents the clock: the current time ([GetUtcNow], [GetLocalNow]), timing ([GetTimestamp], [GetElapsedTime]), and the creation of timers. [TimeProvider.System] is the system clock. A class that depends on the time receives a [TimeProvider] instead of using [DateTime.Now] directly: it can then be tested with a controlled clock.

The program [async-22.cs] uses both:

// Time: PeriodicTimer and TimeProvider
// 1 - PeriodicTimer: one action every 500 ms, stopped after 2.2 seconds
TimeProvider horloge = TimeProvider.System;
long debut = horloge.GetTimestamp();
using (var minuterie = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500)))
using (var arret = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2.2)))
{
    int nbTops = 0;
    try
    {
         // WaitForNextTickAsync sets to true on every tick, false if the timer is stopped by Dispose
        while (await minuterie.WaitForNextTickAsync(arret.Token))
        {
            nbTops++;
            Console.WriteLine($"{horloge.GetElapsedTime(debut).TotalMilliseconds,6:F0} ms : top n° {nbTops}");
        }
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{horloge.GetElapsedTime(debut).TotalMilliseconds,6:F0} ms : minuterie arrêtée après {nbTops} tops");
    }
}

// 2 - TimeProvider: a class that depends on the time receives its own clock instead of reading from DateTime.Now
var matin = new HorlogeFixe(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 10, 3, 9, 30, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
var soir = new HorlogeFixe(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 10, 3, 19, 45, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
Console.WriteLine(new Accueil(matin).Saluer("Pierre"));
Console.WriteLine(new Accueil(soir).Saluer("Pierre"));

// a class that depends on the current time
class Accueil(TimeProvider horloge)
{
    public string Saluer(string nom)
    {
        DateTimeOffset maintenant = horloge.GetLocalNow();
        string formule = maintenant.Hour < 18 ? "Bonjour" : "Bonsoir";
        return $"[{maintenant:dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm}] {formule} {nom}";
    }
}

// a stopped clock, for testing: it always shows the same time (in Coordinated Universal Time)
class HorlogeFixe(DateTimeOffset instant) : TimeProvider
{
    public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => instant;
    public override TimeZoneInfo LocalTimeZone => TimeZoneInfo.Utc;
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-22.cs
   507 ms : top n° 1
  1003 ms : top n° 2
  1505 ms : top n° 3
  2001 ms : top n° 4
  2227 ms : minuterie arrêtée après 4 tops
[03/10/2026 09:30] Bonjour Pierre
[03/10/2026 19:45] Bonsoir Pierre

Comments:

  • Lines 5–20: a 500-ms timer and a 2.2-second cancel source. [WaitForNextTickAsync(jeton)] returns [true] on each clock pulse and [false] if the timer has been cleared ([Dispose]); here, the reset stops the loop after 4 clock cycles;
  • line 4: [GetTimestamp] and [GetElapsedTime] from [TimeProvider] measure a duration, just like the methods of the same name in [Stopwatch];
  • Lines 31–37: The class [Accueil] says “Hello” or “Good evening” depending on the time. It receives its clock in its primary constructor instead of reading from [DateTime.Now]: this is an injected dependency, just as the [dao] layer is injected into the [metier] layer in Chapter 6;
  • Lines 42–45: A stopped clock, derived from [TimeProvider], which redefines universal time and the time zone. It allows you to verify the behavior of [Accueil] in the morning and evening without having to wait until nightfall. The NuGet and [Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing] package provides a more comprehensive test clock, [FakeTimeProvider], which can be advanced at will, including for delays and timers ([Task.Delay(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)], [new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)]).

docs.title: 9.13. Application: Tax Calculation with Asynchronous I/O
docs.text:
The program [async-23.cs] brings together several tools from this chapter related to the tax calculation covered in the main thread. It reads the tax brackets from the file [DataImpot.txt] (which has already been used) and reads a list of taxpayers from the file [contribuables.txt]:

o 2 60000
o 3 60000
n 0 60000
n 2 25000
o 5 120000
x 1 20000
o 1 -5

(each line contains: married [o/n], number of children, annual salary), calculates each taxpayer’s tax, and writes the results to the file [resultats.txt]. All I/O operations are asynchronous, and the entire process is limited to 10 seconds.

// application: tax calculation with asynchronous input/output
// - tax brackets are read from [DataImpot.txt], taxpayers from [contribuables.txt]
// - the results are written to [resultats.txt]
using System.Globalization;

using var annulation = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));
try
{
    TrancheImpot[] tranches = await ChargerTranchesAsync("DataImpot.txt", annulation.Token);
    int nbResultats = await CalculerImpotsAsync(tranches, "contribuables.txt", "resultats.txt", annulation.Token);
    Console.WriteLine($"{nbResultats} lignes écrites dans [resultats.txt] :");
    Console.Write(await File.ReadAllTextAsync("resultats.txt", annulation.Token));
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("traitement abandonné : délai dépassé");
}
catch (Exception e) when (e is IOException or FormatException)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"erreur : {e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
}

// reads the tax brackets (range: coeffR:coeffN, decimal point)
static async Task<TrancheImpot[]> ChargerTranchesAsync(string fichier, CancellationToken token)
{
    string[] lignes = await File.ReadAllLinesAsync(fichier, token);
    return [.. lignes.Where(l => l.Trim() != "").Select(TrancheImpot.Parse)];
}

// reads the taxpayers (married with children, salary), calculates their tax, and writes the results
static async Task<int> CalculerImpotsAsync(TrancheImpot[] tranches, string entree, string sortie, CancellationToken token)
{
    int nbLignes = 0;
    await using var ecrivain = new StreamWriter(sortie);
    await foreach (string ligne in File.ReadLinesAsync(entree, token))
    {
        string[] champs = ligne.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
        string resultat = champs switch
        {
            [var m, var e, var s] when m is "o" or "n" && int.TryParse(e, out int enfants) && enfants >= 0
                                       && int.TryParse(s, out int salaire) && salaire >= 0
                => $"impôt = {CalculerImpot(tranches, m == "o", enfants, salaire)} €",
            _ => "ligne incorrecte",
        };
        await ecrivain.WriteLineAsync($"{ligne,-12} : {resultat}");
        nbLignes++;
    }
    return nbLignes;
}

// tax calculation (2004 tax schedule based on 2003 income, retained for the fiscal year)
static int CalculerImpot(TrancheImpot[] tranches, bool marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire)
{
    decimal nbParts = marie ? nbEnfants / 2m + 2 : nbEnfants / 2m + 1;
    if (nbEnfants >= 3)
    {
        nbParts += 0.5m;
    }
    decimal revenu = 0.72m * salaire;
    decimal quotient = revenu / nbParts;
     // the first tax bracket whose threshold exceeds the family quotient; otherwise, the last one
    TrancheImpot tranche = tranches.FirstOrDefault(t => quotient <= t.Limite, tranches[^1]);
    return (int)(tranche.CoeffR * revenu - tranche.CoeffN * nbParts);
}

// a tax bracket
readonly record struct TrancheImpot(decimal Limite, decimal CoeffR, decimal CoeffN)
{
    public static TrancheImpot Parse(string ligne)
    {
        string[] champs = ligne.Split(':');
        return new TrancheImpot(decimal.Parse(champs[0], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture),
                                decimal.Parse(champs[1], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture),
                                decimal.Parse(champs[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture));
    }
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-23.cs
7 lignes écrites dans [resultats.txt] :
o 2 60000    : impôt = 4282 €
o 3 60000    : impôt = 2959 €
n 0 60000    : impôt = 11519 €
n 2 25000    : impôt = 792 €
o 5 120000   : impôt = 11109 €
x 1 20000    : ligne incorrecte
o 1 -5       : ligne incorrecte

Comments:

  • line 6: a cancellation source that limits the entire process to 10 seconds. Its token is passed to all asynchronous methods;
  • Lines 24–27: Reading the brackets. The collection expression with spreading [[.. séquence]] converts the sequence LINQ into an array;
  • Lines 31–48: processing of taxpayers. The rows are read one by one using the asynchronous stream [File.ReadLinesAsync], and the results are written using [WriteLineAsync] into a [StreamWriter] released by [await using];
  • Lines 38–43: Validation of a line using a [switch] expression with a three-element list pattern ([[var m, var e, var s]]) and a [when] clause that checks the three fields;
  • lines 52–63: the tax calculation. The [FirstOrDefault] method of LINQ, with a default value, returns the first bracket whose limit is greater than or equal to the family quotient, or the last bracket if none applies (without modifying the data, unlike the 2008 code);
  • lines 14–20: Possible errors are handled in a single location within the main program: time-limit violations, and I/O or format errors (missing file, incorrectly entered number), filtered by [when] with a reason code of [or];
  • The results provide the benchmark values: €4,282 for a married couple with 2 children and a combined income of €60,000; €2,959 with 3 children; and €11,519 for a single person without children.

The calculation itself is synchronous: it performs no I/O and takes a few microseconds. It would be pointless—and even harmful—to make it asynchronous. Only operations that involve waiting are made asynchronous.

docs.title: 9.14. The Golden Rules
docs.text:
Let’s summarize the rules of asynchronous programming with .NET:

  • async all the way: a method that waits for an asynchronous operation becomes asynchronous itself ([async Task]), and so do its callers, all the way back to the entry point ([Main] asynchronous, event handler, controller action ASP.NET Core). Mixing asynchronous code with blocking waits negates the benefits of asynchrony;
  • do not use [.Result], [.Wait()], or [Task.WaitAll] on an unfinished task: use [await], [Task.WhenAll], [Task.WhenAny], or [Task.WhenEach] instead. These blocking forms freeze a thread and can cause permanent deadlocks in graphical applications;
  • Do not use [Thread.Sleep] in asynchronous code: use [await Task.Delay(...)] instead;
  • Do not use the [async void] method, except in GUI event handlers; an asynchronous method should use [Task] or [Task<T>] (in exceptional cases, [ValueTask<T>]);
  • The name of an asynchronous method ends with [Async]: [CalculerImpotsAsync], [LireTauxAsync];
  • A cancelable asynchronous method receives a [CancellationToken] as its last parameter and passes it to all the asynchronous operations it calls; a canceled operation ends with a [OperationCanceledException];
  • [Task.Run] is reserved for calculations that you want to execute in the background (to avoid blocking a GUI thread, for example). Do not wrap a synchronous I/O operation in [Task.Run] to “make it asynchronous”: use the [XxxAsync] version of the operation;
  • start first, then wait: to run multiple independent operations simultaneously, start them all and then wait for them using [Task.WhenAll]; to limit the number of operations, use [Parallel.ForEachAsync] or a channel;
  • [ConfigureAwait(false)] is used in libraries, not in applications;
  • a launched task must be waited for (or explicitly ignored using [_ =], while handling its exceptions): a forgotten task hides its exceptions and may be interrupted by the end of the program.

The following table summarizes the equivalences between the world of threads (previous chapter, 2008 course) and that of tasks:

Threads, blocking waitsTasks, asynchronous waits[Thread.Sleep(1000)][await Task.Delay(1000)][thread.Start()] followed by [thread.Join()][var t = MethodeAsync();] then [await t]Wait for multiple threads ([Join] in a loop, [Task.WaitAll])[await Task.WhenAll(...)][Thread.Abort()] (obsolete), [BackgroundWorker.CancelAsync][CancellationTokenSource.Cancel()] and [CancellationToken][BackgroundWorker.ReportProgress] / [ProgressChanged][IProgress<T>.Report][BackgroundWorker.RunWorkerCompleted]The code following [await][BeginXxx] / [EndXxx] and recall methods (APM)[await XxxAsync(...)][Control.Invoke] to return to the interface thread[await], which automatically returns to the synchronization context[BlockingCollection<T>] ([Add] / [GetConsumingEnumerable])[Channel<T>] ([WriteAsync] / [ReadAllAsync])[System.Threading.Timer][PeriodicTimer]

The following chapters will apply these rules: asynchronous database access with ADO.NET (Chapter 10) and Entity Framework Core (Chapter 11), asynchronous multi-client TCP server and [HttpClient] client (Chapter 12), ASP.NET Core web services and their [HttpClient] clients (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 4.1.1. Overview
docs.text:
We will now explore object-oriented programming through examples. An object is an entity that contains data defining its state (referred to as fields, attributes, etc.) and functions (referred to as methods). An object is created based on a template called a class:

public class C1
{
    Type1 p1;          // field p1
    Type2 p2;          // field p2
    ...
    Type3 M3(...)      // method M3
    {
        ...
    }
    Type4 M4(...)      // method M4
    {
        ...
    }
    ...
}

Starting from the previous class [C1], you can create many objects such as [O1], [O2], … All of them will have the fields [p1], [p2], … and the methods [M3], [M4], … However, they will have different values for their [pi] fields, thus each having its own unique state. If [o1] is an object of type [C1], [o1.p1] refers to the field [p1] of [o1], and [o1.M3] refers to the method [M3] of [o1].

Let’s consider an initial object model: the [Personne] class.

docs.title: 4.1.2. Creating the C# Project
docs.text:
In the examples from the previous chapter, a program fit into a single source file. From now on, a program may consist of multiple source files: one class per file, plus the main program. These files are grouped together in a project. The 2008 course created projects using the Visual Studio 2008 wizards; here we use the command-line tool [dotnet], which works the same way on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Chapter 2 showed how to open the same project in VS Code or Visual Studio.

In a terminal, navigate to the [04-classes] folder and create a console project named [Personnes]:

> dotnet new console -n Personnes
Le modèle « Application console » a bien été créé.

Traitement des actions postérieures à la création en cours... Merci de patienter.
Restauration de .../04-classes/Personnes/Personnes.csproj :
  Identification des projets à restaurer...
  Restauration effectuée de .../04-classes/Personnes/Personnes.csproj (en 126 ms).
Restauration réussie.

The command creates a folder named [Personnes] containing two files. The file [Personnes.csproj] describes the project:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>
  • Line 4: The project produces an executable;
  • line 5: the target program is .NET 10;
  • line 6: a set of common namespaces ([System], [System.IO], [System.Collections.Generic], [System.Linq], …) is implicitly imported into all source files in the project. This is why we can write *[Console.WriteLine] without the ***[using System;]** clause;
  • Line 7: Nullable reference types are enabled. The compiler issues a warning for any reference-type variable (a string, an object) that might take on the value [null] without the program expecting it. We’ll return to this in the section dedicated to these types; for now, just keep in mind that our programs must compile without any warnings.

The second file, [Program.cs], contains the main program. All [*.cs] files in the project folder (and its subfolders) are part of the project: to add a [Personne] class, simply create the file [Personne.cs] in the [Personnes] folder. To run the project, type [dotnet run] in its folder: the command compiles the project, if it has changed, and then runs it.

All the projects in this chapter are grouped into a solution—a file that references a set of projects—which VS Code or Visual Studio can open all at once. The [.slnx] (XML) format, supported by the [dotnet] command since .NET 9 and the default format since .NET 10, replaces the old [.sln] format:

> dotnet new sln --format slnx -n 04-classes
Le modèle « Fichier solution » a bien été créé.

> dotnet sln 04-classes.slnx add Personnes/Personnes.csproj
Projet 'Personnes/Personnes.csproj' ajouté à la solution.

The [dotnet build 04-classes.slnx] command then compiles all projects in the solution.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Definition of the Person class
docs.text:
The definition of the [Personne] class in the source file [Personne.cs] will be as follows:

namespace Personnes;

public class Personne
{
     // attributes (fields)
    private string prenom = "";
    private string nom = "";
    private int age;

     // method
    public void Initialise(string p, string n, int age)
    {
        this.prenom = p;
        this.nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // method
    public void Identifie()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{prenom}, {nom}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • Line 1: The class belongs to the [Personnes] namespace (the project name). This form, [namespace Personnes;]—known as “file scope”—places all types in the file within the namespace. Namespaces are discussed at the end of the chapter;
  • Lines 6–8: The class’s three fields. The two strings are initialized with the empty string; otherwise, they would be set to [null] when the object is created, and the compiler—which has nullable types enabled—would issue a warning;
  • lines 11–15: a method that sets the object’s state;
  • lines 19–21: a method that sets the object’s state;

Here we have the definition of a class, and thus a data type. When we create variables of this type, we call them objects or class instances. A class is therefore a template from which objects are constructed.

The members of a class can be data (fields), methods (functions), or properties. Properties are special methods used to retrieve or set the value of an object’s fields. These members can be accompanied by one of the following keywords:

KeywordAccess[private]A private member is accessible only by the class’s internal methods. This is the default access level[public]A public member is accessible by any method, whether or not it is defined within the class[protected]A protected member is accessible only through the internal methods of the class or a derived class (see the concept of inheritance below)[internal]An internal member is accessible by any method within the same assembly (the same project)

In general, a class’s data is declared private, while its methods and properties are declared public. This means that the user of an object (the programmer):

  • will not have direct access to the object’s private data;
  • can call the object’s public methods, including those that provide access to its private data.

The syntax for declaring a class [C] is as follows:

public class C
{
    private donnée ou méthode ou propriété privée;
    public donnée ou méthode ou propriété publique;
    protected donnée ou méthode ou propriété protégée;
}

The order in which the members [private], [protected], and [public] are declared is arbitrary.

docs.title: 4.1.4. The Initialize method
docs.text:
What is the purpose of the [Initialise] method? Because [nom], [prenom], and [age] are private members of the [Personne] class, the statements:

Personne p1;
p1.prenom = "Jean";
p1.nom = "Dupont";
p1.age = 30;

are invalid. We need to initialize an object of type [Personne] using a public method. This is the purpose of the [Initialise] method. We’ll write:

Personne p1;
p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);

The notation [p1.Initialise] is valid because [Initialise] is publicly accessible.

docs.title: 4.1.5. The new operator
docs.text:
However, the previous sequence of statements is incorrect. The statement

Personne p1;

declares [p1] as a reference to an object of type [Personne]. This object does not yet exist, and therefore [p1] is not initialized. When we then write [p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30)], we call the method [Initialise] of the object referenced by [p1]. However, this object does not exist, and the compiler reports the error: the local variable [p1] has not been assigned a value. If we write:

Personne? p1 = null;
p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);

we explicitly indicate with the keyword [null] that the variable [p1] does not yet reference any object (the question mark in [Personne?] indicates that the variable may be set to [null]). The compiler then issues only a warning (dereferencing a null reference), and at runtime, the method call throws a [NullReferenceException] exception. For [p1] to reference an object, you must write:

Personne p1 = new Personne();

This creates an object of type [Personne] that has not yet been initialized: its fields have their default values, in this case the empty string for [nom] and [prenom], and 0 for [age] (a numeric field without an explicit initial value is 0; a reference-type field is [null]). Now that [p1] references an object, the initialization statement for that object, [p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30)], is valid.

docs.title: 4.1.6. The this keyword
docs.text:
Let’s look at the code for the [Initialise] method:

    public void Initialise(string p, string n, int age)
    {
        this.prenom = p;
        this.nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

The statement [this.prenom = p] means that the field [prenom] of the current object ([this]) is assigned the value [p]. The keyword [this] refers to the current object—the one on which the method is being executed. How do we know this? Let’s look at how the object referenced by [p1] is initialized in the calling program:

p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);

It is the method [Initialise] of the object [p1] that is called. When, within this method, the object [this] is referenced, it actually refers to the object [p1]. The method [Initialise] could also have been written as follows:

public void Initialise(string p, string n, int age)
{
    prenom = p;
    nom = n;
    this.age = age;
}

When a method of an object references a field [A] of that object, the notation [this.A] is implied. It must be used explicitly when there is a conflict of identifiers. This is the case with the statement [this.age = age;], where [age] refers to both a field of the current object and the parameter [age] received by the method. In this case, the ambiguity must be resolved by referring to the field [age] as [this.age].

docs.title: 4.1.7. A Test Program
docs.text:
Here is a short test program. It is written in the source file [Program.cs] of the project:

using Personnes;

// a Person object
Personne p1 = new Personne();
p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
p1.Identifie();
  • Line 1: The main program is written using high-level statements that do not belong to any namespace. To refer to the class [Personne] by its name alone, you must import its namespace [Personnes] using the clause [using];
  • Line 4: Creation of a [Personne] object referenced by [p1];
  • Line 5: Initialize the object;
  • Line 6: Display its status.

Results:

> dotnet run
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.8. Single-file applications
docs.text:
For a short example, a project is unnecessarily cumbersome. Since version 10, a standalone source file can be executed directly by NET, without a [.csproj] file: this is a single-file application, which we used in the previous chapter. The project options (nullable types enabled, implicit [using]) are the same as those for a console project. We’ll use this format whenever the example contains only one or two classes.

The file then contains the top-level directives followed by the class declarations: the compiler enforces this order, as the top-level directives must precede any type declarations (class, structure, interface, etc.) in the file. Classes declared in this way do not belong to any namespace, which is irrelevant in a single-file program.

docs.title: 4.1.9. Another Method: Overloading
docs.text:
Let’s continue with the class *[Personne] and add a second method, *[Initialise], to it. The program *[classes-01.cs]* is as follows:

// overload of the Initialize method
Personne p1 = new Personne();
p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
p1.Identifie();
Personne p2 = new Personne();
p2.Initialise(p1);
p2.Identifie();

// The Person class is declared after the top-level statements
public class Personne
{
     // attributes
    private string prenom = "";
    private string nom = "";
    private int age;

     // initialization using three values
    public void Initialise(string p, string n, int age)
    {
        prenom = p;
        nom = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // initialization based on another person
    public void Initialise(Personne p)
    {
        prenom = p.prenom;
        nom = p.nom;
        age = p.age;
    }

     // person's identity
    public void Identifie()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{prenom}, {nom}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • lines 2–7: the high-level instructions, i.e., the main program;
  • Line 10: The class [Personne] is declared after the high-level statements;
  • lines 18–22: the method [Initialise] from the previous paragraph;
  • lines 26–30: a second method, [Initialise].

We now have two methods named [Initialise]: this is valid as long as they accept different parameters (in number or type). The method [Initialise] is said to be overloaded. The compiler chooses which method to call based on the actual parameters: [p1.Initialise("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] (line 3) calls the first one, and [p2.Initialise(p1)] (line 6) calls the second one.

The parameter of the second method is a reference ([p]) to a person. The fields of the person ([p]) are then assigned to the current object ([this]). Note that the method [Initialise] has direct access to the fields of the object [p] even though they are private (lines 28–30). This is always true: a method of a class [C] has access to the private members of all objects of the same class [C].

Results:

> dotnet run classes-01.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.10. Constructors of the Person class
docs.text:
A constructor is a method that bears the name of the class and is called when the object is created. It is generally used to initialize the object. It is a method that can accept parameters but does not return a value. Its declaration is not preceded by any type (not even [void]).

If a class [C] has a constructor that accepts n parameters, the declaration and initialization of an object of this class can be done as follows:

C objet = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);

or

C objet;
...
objet = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);

When a class [C] has one or more constructors, one of these constructors must be used to create an object of that class. If a class [C] has no constructors, it has a default constructor, which is the parameterless constructor [public C()]. The object’s fields then retain their initial values. This is what happened in the previous programs, where we had written [new Personne()].

The program [classes-02.cs] provides three constructors for the class [Personne]:

// constructors of the Person class
Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
p1.Identifie();
Personne p2 = new Personne(p1);
p2.Identifie();
Personne p3 = new Personne();
p3.Identifie();

public class Personne
{
     // attributes
    private string prenom;
    private string nom;
    private int age;

     // main constructor
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // copy constructor: it calls the primary constructor
    public Personne(Personne p) : this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age)
    {
    }

     // parameterless constructor: it also calls the primary constructor
    public Personne() : this("?", "?", 0)
    {
    }

     // person's identity
    public void Identifie()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{prenom}, {nom}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • lines 17–21: the “main” constructor initializes the three fields. Since its parameters have the same names as the fields, the fields are distinguished using [this];
  • line 25: the copy constructor. The notation [: this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age)] means that before executing the (empty) body of the constructor, the constructor of the same class that accepts three parameters—[string], [string], [int]. This is referred to as chained constructors. The initialization code is thus written only once;
  • line 30: the parameterless constructor, which is also chained to the main constructor. Since the class has declared constructors, it no longer has a default constructor: if we want to be able to write [new Personne()], we must declare it;
  • Lines 11–14: The two strings are no longer initialized upon declaration. This is no longer necessary: all constructors, either directly or through chaining, assign a value to them, and the compiler verifies this.

The 2008 course had constructors call the [Initialise] method. Chaining with [this(...)] is preferable: with nullable types enabled, the compiler does not inspect the contents of methods called by a constructor and would flag that the fields [prenom] and [nom] could be set to [null] at the end of construction.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-02.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[?, ?, 0]

docs.title: 4.1.11. Object references
docs.text:
We use the [Personne] class from the previous program, omitting its parameterless constructor but including the [Initialise(string, string, int)] method from the beginning of the chapter. The test program becomes the following [classes-03.cs] (we do not reproduce the class):

// object references
// p1
Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Console.Write("p1="); p1.Identifie();
// p2 refers to the same object as p1
Personne p2 = p1;
Console.Write("p2="); p2.Identifie();
// p3 refers to an object that is a copy of the object referred to by p1
Personne p3 = new Personne(p1);
Console.Write("p3="); p3.Identifie();
// The state of the object referenced by p1 is changed
p1.Initialise("Micheline", "Benoît", 67);
Console.Write("p1="); p1.Identifie();
// Since p2 = p1, the object referenced by p2 has changed state
Console.Write("p2="); p2.Identifie();
// p3 does not reference the same object as p1: the object referenced by p3 has not changed
Console.Write("p3="); p3.Identifie();
// Are p1 and p2 the same reference? What about p1 and p3?
Console.WriteLine($"p1 == p2 : {p1 == p2}, p1 == p3 : {p1 == p3}");

Results:

> dotnet run classes-03.cs
p1=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p2=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p2=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1 == p2 : True, p1 == p3 : False

When the variable [p1] is declared as [Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);] (line 3), [p1] refers to the object [Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] but is not the object itself. In C, this would be referred to as a pointer—that is, the address of the created object. If we then write [p1 = null;], it is not the object [Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] that is modified; rather, it is the reference [p1] that changes its value. The object will be “lost” if it is not referenced by any other variable: the memory it occupies will later be reclaimed by the garbage collector for .NET.

When we write [Personne p2 = p1;] (line 6), we initialize the reference [p2]: it “points” to the same object (it refers to the same object) as the reference [p1]. Thus, if the object “pointed to” (or referenced) by [p1] is modified, the object referenced by [p2] is also modified (lines 5–6 of the results).

When [Personne p3 = new Personne(p1);] is written (line 9), a new object, [Personne], is created. This new object will be referenced by [p3]. If the object referenced by [p1] is modified, the object referenced by [p3] (line 7) remains unchanged.

Finally, on line 19, the operator [==], applied to two object references, indicates whether they refer to the same object: [p1] and [p2] refer to the same object, while [p1] and [p3] refer to two different objects, although they have the same content (line 8).

docs.title: 4.1.12. Passing Object Reference Parameters
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we examined how function parameters are passed when they are simple types ([int], [double], …). Let’s see what happens when the parameter is an object reference. For this, we’ll use the class [StringBuilder] from .NET. A [string] object cannot be modified: an operation such as [s.ToUpper()] returns a new [string] object. An object [StringBuilder], on the other hand, is a mutable string: its method [Append] adds characters to the string without creating a new object.

The program [classes-04.cs] is as follows:

using System.Text;

// passing parameters of the object reference type
StringBuilder sb0 = new StringBuilder("essai0"), sb1 = new StringBuilder("essai1"), sb2 = new StringBuilder("essai2");
Console.WriteLine($"Dans fonction appelante avant appel : sb0={sb0}, sb1={sb1}, sb2={sb2}");
ChangeStringBuilder(sb0, sb1, ref sb2, out StringBuilder sb3);
Console.WriteLine($"Dans fonction appelante après appel : sb0={sb0}, sb1={sb1}, sb2={sb2}, sb3={sb3}");

// The called function
static void ChangeStringBuilder(StringBuilder sbf0, StringBuilder sbf1, ref StringBuilder sbf2, out StringBuilder sbf3)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Début fonction appelée : sbf0={sbf0}, sbf1={sbf1}, sbf2={sbf2}");
    sbf0.Append("*****");
    sbf1 = new StringBuilder("essai1*****");
    sbf2 = new StringBuilder("essai2*****");
    sbf3 = new StringBuilder("essai3*****");
    Console.WriteLine($"Fin fonction appelée : sbf0={sbf0}, sbf1={sbf1}, sbf2={sbf2}, sbf3={sbf3}");
}
  • line 1: the class [StringBuilder] belongs to the namespace [System.Text], which is not part of the implicitly imported namespaces;
  • line 4: three [sb0, sb1, sb2] references to objects of type [StringBuilder];
  • line 6: These are passed to the function [ChangeStringBuilder] with different modes: [sb0] and [sb1] with the default mode, [sb2] with the keyword [ref], and a fourth reference, [sb3], declared within the call itself ([out StringBuilder sb3]), with the keyword [out];
  • lines 10–17: a local function with the formal parameters [sbf0, sbf1, sbf2, sbf3]. The relationships between the formal parameters [sbfi] and the actual parameters [sbi] are as follows:
    • [sbf0] and [sb0] are, when the function starts, two distinct references that point to the same object (references are passed by value);
    • the same applies to [sbf1] and [sb1];
    • [sbf2] and [sb2] are one and the same reference (keyword [ref]);
    • [sbf3] and [sb3] are also the same reference (key [out]), which the function must initialize.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-04.cs
Dans fonction appelante avant appel : sb0=essai0, sb1=essai1, sb2=essai2
Début fonction appelée : sbf0=essai0, sbf1=essai1, sbf2=essai2
Fin fonction appelée : sbf0=essai0*****, sbf1=essai1*****, sbf2=essai2*****, sbf3=essai3*****
Dans fonction appelante après appel : sb0=essai0*****, sb1=essai1, sb2=essai2*****, sb3=essai3*****

Explanations:

  • [sb0] and [sbf0] are two distinct references to the same object. This object was modified via [sbf0] (line 13). This modification is visible via [sb0] (line 5);
  • [sb1] and [sbf1] are two distinct references to the same object. [sbf1] is assigned a new value within the function and now points to a new object (line 14). This does not change the value of [sb1], which continues to point to the original, unmodified object;
  • [sb2] and [sbf2] are the same reference. [sbf2] now points to a new object (line 15). Since [sbf2] and [sb2] are one and the same entity, [sb2] also points to this new object;
  • before the function call, [sb3] had no value. After the call, [sb3] refers to the object created by the function (line 16).

docs.title: 4.1.13. Temporary Objects
docs.text:
In an expression, you can explicitly call an object’s constructor: the object is created, but there is no variable to access it later (to modify it, for example). This temporary object is created for the purpose of evaluating the expression and is then discarded. The memory space it occupied will be automatically reclaimed later by the garbage collector, whose role is to reclaim memory space occupied by objects that are no longer referenced by the program’s data.

Consider the following program, [classes-05.cs], where the constructors of the [Personne] class display a message:

// Temporary objects
new Personne(new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)).Identifie();

public class Personne
{
     // attributes
    private string prenom;
    private string nom;
    private int age;

     // constructors
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Constructeur Personne(string, string, int)");
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public Personne(Personne p)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Constructeur Personne(Personne)");
        prenom = p.prenom;
        nom = p.nom;
        age = p.age;
    }

     // person's identity
    public void Identifie()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{prenom}, {nom}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • Line 2: The object [Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] is constructed and then passed to the copy constructor, which constructs a second object; the method [Identifie] is then called on that object. Neither of the two objects is referenced by a variable.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-05.cs
Constructeur Personne(string, string, int)
Constructeur Personne(Personne)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

The results show the successive creation of the two temporary objects.

docs.title: 4.1.14. Methods for Reading and Writing Private Fields
docs.text:
We add the necessary methods to the [Personne] class to read or modify the state of the fields in the [classes-06.cs] objects:

// methods for reading (getters) and writing (setters) private attributes
Personne p = new Personne("Jean", "Michelin", 34);
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.GetPrenom() + "," + p.GetNom() + "," + p.GetAge() + ")");
p.SetAge(56);
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.GetPrenom() + "," + p.GetNom() + "," + p.GetAge() + ")");

public class Personne
{
     // attributes
    private string prenom;
    private string nom;
    private int age;

     // constructor
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

     // getters
    public string GetPrenom()
    {
        return prenom;
    }

    public string GetNom()
    {
        return nom;
    }

    public int GetAge()
    {
        return age;
    }

     // mutators
    public void SetPrenom(string prenom)
    {
        this.prenom = prenom;
    }

    public void SetNom(string nom)
    {
        this.nom = nom;
    }

    public void SetAge(int age)
    {
        this.age = age;
    }
}
  • lines 22–35: the read methods, called getters;
  • lines 38–51: the write methods, called setters.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-06.cs
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)

This approach is typical of the Java language. C# offers a more elegant mechanism: properties.

docs.title: 4.1.15. Properties
docs.text:
There is another way to access a class’s fields: by creating properties. These allow us to manipulate private fields as if they were public.

A property allows you to read ([get]) or set ([set]) the value of a field. A property is declared as follows:

public Type Propriété
{
    get { ... }
    set { ... }
}

where [Type] is generally the type of the field managed by the property. It may have two methods named [get] and [set]. The method [get] is usually responsible for returning the value of the field it manages (it could return something else; there’s nothing preventing it from doing so). The [set] method receives a parameter named [value], which it normally assigns to the field it manages. It can use this opportunity to verify the validity of the received value and, if necessary, throw an exception if the value is invalid.

Consider the program [classes-07.cs], where the previous accessors and mutators have been replaced by read-write properties:

// properties
Personne p = new Personne("Jean", "Michelin", 34);
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.Prenom + "," + p.Nom + "," + p.Age + ")");
p.Age = 56;
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.Prenom + "," + p.Nom + "," + p.Age + ")");
try
{
    p.Age = -4;
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}
// object initializer: parameterless constructor followed by property assignment
Personne p2 = new Personne { Age = 7, Prenom = "Arthur", Nom = "Martin" };
Console.WriteLine($"p2=({p2.Prenom},{p2.Nom},{p2.Age})");
try
{
    Personne p3 = new Personne { Prenom = "Paul", Nom = " " };
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}

public class Personne
{
     // attributes
    private string prenom = "";
    private string nom = "";
    private int age;

     // constructors
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
         // We use the properties to take advantage of their validation checks
        Prenom = prenom;
        Nom = nom;
        Age = age;
    }

    public Personne()
    {
    }

     // properties
    public string Prenom
    {
        get { return prenom; }
        set
        {
             // Is the first name valid?
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"prénom ({value}) invalide");
            }
            prenom = value;
        }
    }

    public string Nom
    {
        get { return nom; }
        set
        {
             // Is the last name valid?
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"nom ({value}) invalide");
            }
            nom = value;
        }
    }

    public int Age
    {
        get { return age; }
        set
        {
             // Is the age valid?
            if (value < 0)
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"âge ({value}) invalide");
            }
            age = value;
        }
    }
}

The [set] methods for the three properties validate the received value (lines 52–57, 66–71, 80–85).

  • Lines 53–55: The method [string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace] returns [true] if the string is [null], empty, or consists solely of spaces. The exception thrown is of type [ArgumentException], the exception defined by .NET to signal an invalid parameter. The 2008 version threw an exception of the general type [Exception], which requires the caller to catch all exceptions;
  • lines 34–39: the constructor initializes the object via properties rather than fields. This allows it to take advantage of the validations performed by the [set] methods, which are implemented in only one place.

How are the methods [get] and [set] called? In the statement on line 3, the program attempts to retrieve the values of the properties [Prenom], [Nom], and [Age] for the person [p]. The [get] method for these properties is then called, and it returns the value of the field they manage. In the [p.Age = 56;] statement (line 4), we want to set the value of the [Age] property. The [set] method of this property is then called. It receives 56 as its [value] parameter.

A property [P] of a class [C] that defines only the method [get] is said to be read-only. If [c] is an object of class [C], the operation [c.P = valeur] will be rejected by the compiler.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-07.cs
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)
âge (-4) invalide
p2=(Arthur,Martin,7)
nom ( ) invalide

Line 4 of the results shows that the assignment [p.Age = -4] (line 8) was rejected by the method [set] of the property [Age].

docs.title: 4.1.16. Object initializers
docs.text:
Properties can be used in conjunction with a constructor using the following syntax:

Classe objet = new Classe(...) { Propriété1 = val1, Propriété2 = val2, ... };

This syntax, known as an object initializer, is equivalent to the following code:

Classe objet = new Classe(...);
objet.Propriété1 = val1;
objet.Propriété2 = val2;
...

The order of the properties does not matter. In the previous program [classes-07.cs], the class [Personne] has a parameterless constructor that does not initialize anything. Let’s return to the end of the main program:

// object initializer: parameterless constructor followed by property assignment
Personne p2 = new Personne { Age = 7, Prenom = "Arthur", Nom = "Martin" };
Console.WriteLine($"p2=({p2.Prenom},{p2.Nom},{p2.Age})");
try
{
    Personne p3 = new Personne { Prenom = "Paul", Nom = " " };
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}

Line 15: The parameterless constructor is used to create a person, which is then initialized by its properties. We could have written [new Personne() { Age = 7, ... }], but parentheses are not required for the parameterless constructor in this syntax. The [set] methods are indeed called: on line 19, the name containing a space is rejected (line 6 of the results).

docs.title: 4.1.17. Automatic properties
docs.text:
In many cases, the methods [get] and [set] of a property simply read from and write to a private field without any further processing. In such cases, you can use an automatic property declared as follows:

public Type Propriété { get; set; }

The private field associated with the property is not declared; it is automatically generated by the compiler and can only be accessed through its property. Thus, instead of writing the field [prenom] and the property [Prenom] for the program [classes-07.cs], you can write:

public string Prenom { get; set; } = "";

without declaring the private field [prenom]. The expression [= ""] following the property is the initial value of the hidden field. The difference between the two properties is that the first one validates the first name in [set], while the second one performs no validation.

Is using the automatic property [Prenom] equivalent to declaring a public field [public string Prenom;]? For the user of the class, the syntax is the same. However, declaring a class field as public is not recommended: it violates the concept of encapsulation of an object’s state, which should be private and exposed through public methods. With an automatic property, checks can be added later in [set] without changing the code of the class’s users.

Automatic properties have several variants, as demonstrated by the program [classes-08.cs]:

// automatic, read-only, init, required properties
var p = new Personne("Dupont", 30) { Prenom = "Jean", Ville = "Angers" };
Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
// FirstName is read/write
p.Prenom = "Jacques";
// Age can only be modified within the class
p.Vieillir();
Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
// The following lines are rejected by the compiler
// p.Nom = "Durand";      // Last Name is read-only
// p.Age = 40;            // The Age set is private
// p.Ville = "Paris";     // City can only be set when the object is created

// required property
var c = new Contact { Email = "jean.dupont@exemple.fr" };
Console.WriteLine($"Contact : {c.Email}, {c.Telephone}");
// var c2 = new Contact();    // rejected: the required Email property is not initialized

public class Personne
{
     // constructor
    public Personne(string nom, int age)
    {
        Nom = nom;
        Age = age;
    }

     // automatic read/write property, with an initial value
    public string Prenom { get; set; } = "";
     // automatic read-only property: set by the constructor
    public string Nom { get; }
     // automatic property whose write access is restricted to the class
    public int Age { get; private set; }
     // init property: set by the constructor or by an object initializer
    public string Ville { get; init; } = "?";
     // read-only computed property (expression-bodied member)
    public string Identite => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {Age}, {Ville}]";

     // method with an expression body
    public void Vieillir() => Age++;
}

public class Contact
{
     // The property must be initialized when the object is created
    public required string Email { get; init; }
     // optional property
    public string Telephone { get; init; } = "inconnu";
}
  • line 29: a read-write automatic property with an initial value;
  • line 31: a read-only automatic property—it has no [set] and can only be set by a constructor (line 24);
  • line 33: the [set] method may have more restricted access than the property: here, the [Age] property is readable by everyone but can only be modified by the class’s methods, such as [Vieillir] (line 40);
  • line 35: a [init] property (C# 9): it can be set by a constructor or an object initializer (line 2), but not afterward. This is a way to create immutable objects while taking advantage of the object initializer syntax;
  • line 37: a read-only property whose value is computed. The notation [=> expression] is a shorthand form of [get { return expression; }]. It also applies to methods (line 40): these are referred to as expression-bodied members;
  • line 46: a required property (C# 11): the keyword [required] requires the code that creates a [Contact] object to initialize the [Email] property in an object initializer (line 15). The compiler rejects line 17 if it is uncommented;
  • lines 10–12: three statements that the compiler rejects, for the reasons given in the comments.

Recall that with the keyword [var] (line 2), the variable’s type is inferred from the expression that initializes it, in this case [Personne].

Results:

> dotnet run classes-08.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30, Angers]
[Jacques, Dupont, 31, Angers]
Contact : jean.dupont@exemple.fr, inconnu

Finally, an automatic property can be declared virtual ([public virtual string Prop { get; set; }]) and overridden in a derived class, for example, to add a validation in [set]. The keywords [virtual] and [override] are introduced with inheritance.

docs.title: 4.1.18. The field keyword (C# 14)
docs.text:
Between the automatic property, which does not perform any validation, and the full property in the [classes-07.cs] program, which requires a field to be declared, C# 14 offers an intermediate option: in a property’s accessors, the keyword [field] refers to the field created by the compiler. This allows you to write a validation without declaring a field:

// the `field` keyword (C# 14)
var p = new Personne { Prenom = "  jean ", Nom = "Dupont", Age = 30 };
Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
try
{
    p.Nom = "";
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}
try
{
    p.Age = -4;
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}
Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);

public class Personne
{
     // Properties with validations, without a declared field:
     // [field] refers to the field created by the compiler
    public string Prenom
    {
        get;
        set => field = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)
            ? throw new ArgumentException($"prénom ({value}) invalide")
            : value.Trim();
    } = "";   // initial value of the hidden field

    public string Nom
    {
        get;
        set => field = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)
            ? throw new ArgumentException($"nom ({value}) invalide")
            : value.Trim();
    } = "";

    public int Age
    {
        get;
        set
        {
            if (value < 0)
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"âge ({value}) invalide");
            }
            field = value;
        }
    }

     // identity
    public string Identite => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {Age}]";
}
  • Lines 26–31: The property [Prenom]. Its method [get] is automatic ([get;]): it returns the value of the hidden field. Its method [set] checks the received value and assigns it—with leading and trailing spaces removed—to the hidden field designated by [field]. The expression [condition ? throw ... : valeur] uses a throw statement: if the condition is true, an exception is thrown; otherwise, the expression evaluates to [value.Trim()];
  • line 32: the initial value of the hidden field;
  • lines 42–51: a [set] written using a block of statements.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-09.cs
[jean, Dupont, 30]
nom () invalide
âge (-4) invalide
[jean, Dupont, 30]

The first name “jean,” provided surrounded by spaces (line 2), was stored without them (line 2).

docs.title: 4.1.19. Class Methods and Attributes
docs.text:
Suppose we want to count the number of [Personne] objects created in an application. We could manage a counter ourselves, but we risk overlooking temporary objects that are created here and there. It seems safer to include a statement in the constructors of the [Personne] class that increments a counter. This counter cannot be a regular field, since each object has its own fields: it is a field of the class itself, not of a particular instance of that class. We declare it using the keyword [static]:

private static long nbPersonnes;

To refer to it, we write [Personne.nbPersonnes] to indicate that it is a field of the [Personne] class itself. Here, we have created a private field that cannot be accessed directly from outside the class. We therefore create a public property to provide access to the class field [nbPersonnes]. To return the value of [nbPersonnes], the [get] method of this property does not require a specific [Personne] object: so we also need a property declared as [static], which will be called from the outside using the syntax [Personne.NbPersonnes]. Here is an example of [classes-10.cs]:

// class members (static)
Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Personne p2 = new Personne(p1);
new Personne(p1);
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre de personnes créées : {Personne.NbPersonnes}");
// a class method
Personne p3 = Personne.Inconnue();
p3.Identifie();
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre de personnes créées : {Personne.NbPersonnes}");

public class Personne
{
     // class attribute
    private static long nbPersonnes;

     // class property
    public static long NbPersonnes
    {
        get { return nbPersonnes; }
    }

     // class method
    public static Personne Inconnue()
    {
        return new Personne("?", "?", 0);
    }

     // instance attributes
    private string prenom;
    private string nom;
    private int age;

     // constructors
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
        nbPersonnes++;
    }

    public Personne(Personne p) : this(p.prenom, p.nom, p.age)
    {
    }

     // person's identity
    public void Identifie()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{prenom}, {nom}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • line 14: the class field. Like any numeric field, it is initialized to 0;
  • lines 17–19: the read-only class property. It could have been written more simply as [public static long NbPersonnes { get; private set; }];
  • lines 23–25: a class method. It is called using the class name: [Personne.Inconnue()] (line 7). A class method has no current object: the keyword [this] has no meaning here, and it can only directly access the class members [static];
  • Line 39: The primary constructor increments the counter. The copy constructor, which is chained to the primary constructor, therefore increments it as well.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-10.cs
Nombre de personnes créées : 3
[?, ?, 0]
Nombre de personnes créées : 4

The program correctly counted the temporary object created on line 4. We have been using class members from the start: [Console.WriteLine], [int.Parse], and [Math.Sqrt] are methods of [static]. [Console] and [Math] are even static classes ([static class]): they contain only members of type [static], and no instances of them can be created.

docs.title: 4.1.20. An array of people
docs.text:
An object is a piece of data like any other, and as such, multiple objects can be grouped together in an array [classes-11.cs]:

// an array of people
Personne[] amis = new Personne[3];
amis[0] = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
amis[1] = new Personne("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52);
amis[2] = new Personne("Neil", "Armstrong", 66);
// display
foreach (Personne ami in amis)
{
    ami.Identifie();
}
  • Line 2: creates an array of 3 elements of type [Personne]. These 3 elements are initialized here with the value [null], meaning they do not reference any objects. Technically speaking, we refer to this as an “array of objects,” even though it is merely an array of object references. The creation of the array—which is itself an object (as indicated by [new])—does not create any objects of the same type as its elements; this must be done subsequently.
