Note that the compiler does not flag the fact that the elements of an array of type [Personne[]] are equal to [null] immediately after its creation: this is a limitation of nullable type analysis;
  • Lines 3–5: Create 3 objects of type [Personne];
  • lines 7–9: display the contents of the table [amis].

The class [Personne], declared below, is derived from the program [classes-03.cs], reduced to its three-parameter constructor and its method [Identifie]. Results:

> dotnet run classes-11.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]

docs.title: 4.1.21. new() expressions with a target type
docs.text:
When the type of the object to be created is known from the context, C# 9 allows the class name to be omitted after [new]. The program [classes-12.cs] demonstrates this:

// object initializers and `new()` expressions with target type
// The type of the created object is inferred from the variable's type
Personne p1 = new("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Personne p2 = new() { Prenom = "Arthur", Nom = "Martin", Age = 7 };
// an array initialized by a collection expression
Personne[] amis =
[
    p1,
    p2,
    new("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52),
    new() { Prenom = "Neil", Nom = "Armstrong", Age = 66 },
];
foreach (Personne ami in amis)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ami.Identite);
}
// `new()` with a target type in a method call: the type is that of the parameter
Affiche(new("Pauline", "Leduc", 12));

// a local function
static void Affiche(Personne p)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Affiche : {p.Identite}");
}

public class Personne
{
     // constructors
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        Prenom = prenom;
        Nom = nom;
        Age = age;
    }

    public Personne()
    {
    }

     // automatic properties
    public string Prenom { get; set; } = "";
    public string Nom { get; set; } = "";
    public int Age { get; set; }
     // identity
    public string Identite => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {Age}]";
}
  • Line 3: The type of the object created by [new(...)] is that of the variable that receives it, [Personne]. This syntax is the opposite of [var]: with [var], the type of the variable is inferred from the expression; with [new()], the type of the object is inferred from the variable;
  • line 4: [new()] with an object initializer;
  • lines 6–11: an array created and populated by a collection expression (C# 12): the elements are enclosed in square brackets and separated by commas. The type of the elements, [Personne], is known: [new(...)] is sufficient to create them;
  • line 18: the type of the created object is that of the parameter of the [Affiche] function.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-12.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Arthur, Martin, 7]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]
Affiche : [Pauline, Leduc, 12]

docs.title: 4.2.1. Overview
docs.text:
Here we discuss the concept of inheritance. The purpose of inheritance is to “customize” an existing class so that it meets our needs. Suppose we want to create a class named [Enseignant]: a teacher is a specific type of person. They have attributes that other people do not have: the subject they teach, for example. But they also have the attributes common to all people: first name, last name, and age. A teacher is therefore a full member of the class [Personne] but has additional attributes. Rather than creating a class [Enseignant] from scratch, we prefer to build upon the existing class [Personne] and adapt it to the specific characteristics of teachers. The concept of inheritance allows us to do this.

To indicate that the class [Enseignant] inherits the properties of the class [Personne], we write:

public class Enseignant : Personne

[Personne] is called the parent (or base) class, and [Enseignant] is called the derived (or child) class. A [Enseignant] object has all the characteristics of a [Personne] object: it has the same fields and methods. These fields and methods from the parent class are not repeated in the definition of the child class; we simply specify the fields and methods added by the child class. A C# class can be derived from only one parent class.

The examples in this section are two console projects, [Heritage1] and [Heritage2], from the [04-classes.slnx] solution. In the [Heritage1] project, the [Personne] class is defined as follows: [Personne.cs]:

namespace Heritage1;

public class Personne
{
     // class property: the number of people created
    public static long NbPersonnes { get; private set; }

     // constructor
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        Prenom = prenom;
        Nom = nom;
        Age = age;
        NbPersonnes++;
        Console.WriteLine("Constructeur Personne(string, string, int)");
    }

     // properties
    public string Prenom
    {
        get;
        set => field = Verifier(value, "prénom");
    } = "";

    public string Nom
    {
        get;
        set => field = Verifier(value, "nom");
    } = "";

    public int Age
    {
        get;
        set => field = value >= 0 ? value : throw new ArgumentException($"âge ({value}) invalide");
    }

     // person's identity
    public string Identite => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {Age}]";

     // validation of a required string
    private static string Verifier(string valeur, string libelle)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(valeur))
        {
            throw new ArgumentException($"{libelle} ({valeur}) invalide");
        }
        return valeur;
    }
}
  • line 6: the person counter from the previous paragraph, this time written as an automatic class property whose definition is reserved for the class;
  • lines 9–15: the constructor initializes the object using its properties and displays a progress message;
  • lines 19–34: three properties that validate their values using the keyword [field]. The validations for the first name and last name, which are identical, are factored into the private class method [Verifier] (lines 41–47);
  • line 38: the [Identifie] method from the previous examples has been replaced by the read-only property [Identite], which returns the person’s identity instead of displaying it.

We are creating a class named [Enseignant] that inherits from the classes [Personne] and [Enseignant.cs]:

namespace Heritage1;

public class Enseignant : Personne
{
     // constructor
    public Enseignant(string prenom, string nom, int age, int section)
        : base(prenom, nom, age)
    {
         // the section is stored via the Section property
        Section = section;
         // tracking
        Console.WriteLine("Constructeur Enseignant(string, string, int, int)");
    }

     // Section property
    public int Section { get; set; }

     // Identity property: it overrides (new) that of the parent class
    public new string Identite => $"Enseignant[{base.Identite},{Section}]";
}

The [Enseignant] class adds to the methods and properties of the [Personne] class:

  • line 3: the class [Enseignant] derives from the class [Personne];
  • line 16: a property [Section], which is the section number to which the teacher belongs within the teaching staff (roughly one section per subject);
  • lines 6–12: a constructor used to initialize all of a teacher’s properties;
  • line 19: a new property, [Identite], which will be discussed in more detail later.

docs.title: 4.2.2. Creating a Teacher Object
docs.text:
A child class does not inherit constructors from its parent class. It must define its own constructors. The constructor for the [Enseignant] class is as follows:

    public Enseignant(string prenom, string nom, int age, int section)
        : base(prenom, nom, age)
    {
         // The section is stored via the Section property
        Section = section;
         // tracking
        Console.WriteLine("Constructeur Enseignant(string, string, int, int)");
    }

The declaration on lines 6–7 specifies that the constructor takes four parameters: [prenom], [nom], [age], [section], and passes three ([prenom], [nom], [age]) to its base class, in this case the class [Personne]. We know that this class has a constructor, [Personne(string, string, int)], which will allow us to create a person using the passed parameters. Once the construction of the [Personne] part is complete, the construction of the [Enseignant] object continues with the execution of the constructor’s body (line 10).

Note that on the left side of the = sign, the [Section] property is used. If this property performed validity checks, the constructor would benefit from them. This avoids having to place these checks in two different places: the constructor and the property.

In summary, the constructor of a derived class:

  • passes to its base class the parameters it needs to construct itself;
  • uses the remaining parameters to initialize its own members.

We could have chosen to write:

public Enseignant(string prenom, string nom, int age, int section)
{
    this.prenom = prenom;
    this.nom = nom;
    this.age = age;
    Section = section;
}

This is impossible, for two reasons. First, the class *[Personne] does not have a parameterless constructor: in the absence of ***[: base(...)], the compiler attempts to call this constructor and reports an error. Second, even if the private fields [prenom], [nom], and [age] existed (here, these are the hidden fields of the properties), only objects of the class [Personne] have direct access to them. All other objects, including objects of derived classes as in this case, must access them through public (or protected) members. This would have been different if the class *[Personne] had declared these fields as protected (*[protected]*): it would then have allowed derived classes to access them directly. Using the parent class’s constructor is therefore the correct solution and the standard approach: when constructing a child object, first call the parent object’s constructor, then complete the initializations specific to the child object ([Section]* in our example).

If the class [Enseignant] did not define a property [Identite], the expression [e.Identite]—where [e] is a teacher—would refer to the property [Identite] inherited from the class [Personne]: it is public and, through inheritance, becomes a public property of the class [Enseignant]. This would then yield the identity of the [Personne] part of the teacher, without its section.

docs.title: 4.2.3. Hiding a property or method: the new keyword
docs.text:
To obtain a teacher’s full identity, the class [Enseignant] defines its own property [Identite]:

     // Identity property: it overrides (new) that of the parent class
    public new string Identite => $"Enseignant[{base.Identite},{Section}]";

The property [Identite] of class [Enseignant] relies on the property [Identite] of its parent class, designated as [base.Identite], to obtain the “Person” portion ” and then supplements it with the section, which is specific to the class [Enseignant].

Consider a teacher object [E]. This object contains a [Personne] object:

The property [Identite] is defined in both the class [Enseignant] and its parent class [Personne]. In the child class [Enseignant], the property [Identite] is preceded by the keyword [new] to indicate that a new property, [Identite], is intentionally defined for the class [Enseignant] (without [new], the compiler issues a warning). The class [Enseignant] now has two properties, [Identite]:

  • one inherited from the parent class [Personne];
  • its own.

If [E] is a [Enseignant] object, [E.Identite] refers to the property [Identite] of the class [Enseignant]. It is said that the property [Identite] of the child class masks (hides) the property [Identite] of the parent class. Generally speaking, if [O] is an object and [M] is a method, to execute the method [O.M], the compiler searches for a method [M] in the following order:

  • in the class of the object [O];
  • in its parent class, if it has one;
  • in the parent class of its parent class, if it exists;
  • and so on.

Inheritance therefore allows the child class to redefine methods and properties with the same names as those in the parent class. This is what enables the child class to be adapted to its own needs.

The test program [Program.cs] for project [Heritage1] is as follows:

using Heritage1;

// a teacher
Enseignant e = new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
// the Identity property of the Teacher class
Console.WriteLine(e.Identite);
// the Identity property of the Person class is still there
Console.WriteLine(((Personne)e).Identite);
// a person
Personne p = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
// the `Display` method accepts a `Person` or an object of a derived class
Affiche(e);
Affiche(p);
// the ToString method inherited from the `object` class
Console.WriteLine(e.ToString());
Console.WriteLine(p.ToString());
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre de personnes créées : {Personne.NbPersonnes}");

// displays the identity of p
static void Affiche(Personne p)
{
    Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
}
  • line 4: creates a teacher;
  • line 6: displays its identity, that of the class [Enseignant];
  • line 8: the conversion operator [(Personne)] treats the object [e] as a [Personne]: the property [Identite] of the class [Personne] is then used;
  • lines 12–13: call to the function [Affiche] (lines 20–22) with a teacher followed by a person. We’ll return to this in the next paragraph;
  • lines 15–16: call to the [ToString] method on both objects. We’ll also come back to this.

Results:

> dotnet run
Constructeur Personne(string, string, int)
Constructeur Enseignant(string, string, int, int)
Enseignant[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
Constructeur Personne(string, string, int)
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Heritage1.Enseignant
Heritage1.Personne
Nombre de personnes créées : 2

We can see that:

  • an object [Personne] (line 2) was created before the object [Enseignant] (line 3);
  • [e.Identite] provided the teacher's full identity (line 4), and [((Personne)e).Identite] provided the identity of the party associated with [Personne] (line 5).

docs.title: 4.2.4. Polymorphism
docs.text:
Consider a class hierarchy: C0 ← C1 ← C2 ← … ← Cn, where Ci ← Cj indicates that class Cj is derived from class Ci. This implies that class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Let Oi be objects of type Ci. It is valid to write [Oi = Oj] with j > i. Indeed, by inheritance, class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Therefore, an object Oj of type Cj contains an object of type Ci. The operation [Oi = Oj] causes Oi to be a reference to the object of type Ci contained within the object Oj.

The fact that a variable Oi of class Ci can actually reference not only an object of class Ci but any object derived from class Ci is called polymorphism: the ability of a variable to reference different types of objects.

Let’s take an example and consider the function [Affiche] from the previous program:

static void Affiche(Personne p)
{
    Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
}

We can pass it either a *[Personne]* or a *[Enseignant]: In the latter case, the formal parameter [p], which is of type [Personne], receives a value of type [Enseignant]. Since the type [Enseignant] is derived from the type [Personne]*, this is valid.

The property [p.Identite] returns a string identifying the object [Personne] as [p]. What happens if the parameter passed to the [Affiche] function is an object of type [Enseignant]? The previous results show that: the [p.Identite] statement executed the [Identite] property of a [Personne] each time, first the person contained in the teacher [e] (line 7), then the person [p] itself (line 8). It did not adapt to the object actually passed as a parameter to [Affiche]. We would have preferred to have the full identity of the teacher [e]. For that to happen, the notation [p.Identite] would have had to refer to the property [Identite] of the object actually pointed to by [p], rather than the property [Identite] of the “Person” part of that object. With masking ([new]), the property is selected at compile time, based on the declared type of the variable ([Personne]).

docs.title: 4.2.5. Redefinition and Polymorphism: virtual and override
docs.text:
It is possible to achieve the desired result by declaring [Identite] as a virtual property ([virtual]) in the base class [Personne]. This is what the [Heritage2] project does; its [Personne] class is the same as the one in the [Heritage1] project, with two changes:

     // Person's identity: virtual property
    public virtual string Identite => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {Age}]";

     // override of the ToString method from the `object` class
    public override string ToString() => Identite;
  • Line 38: The keyword [virtual] makes [Identite] a virtual property. This keyword can also be applied to methods. Child classes that override a virtual property or method must then use the keyword [override] instead of [new] to qualify their overridden property or method;
  • line 41: a redefinition of the method [ToString], discussed in the following paragraph.

In the class [Enseignant], the property [Identite] is redefined as follows:

namespace Heritage2;

// A sealed class: cannot be derived from
public sealed class Enseignant : Personne
{
     // constructor
    public Enseignant(string prenom, string nom, int age, int section)
        : base(prenom, nom, age)
    {
        Section = section;
        Console.WriteLine("Constructeur Enseignant(string, string, int, int)");
    }

     // Section property
    public int Section { get; set; }

     // Identity property: it overrides that of the parent class
    public override string Identite => $"Enseignant[{base.Identite},{Section}]";
}
  • Line 18: The property [Identite] overrides the one in the parent class;
  • Line 4: The class is sealed ([sealed]), which we’ll explain in more detail later.

With a virtual property or method, the choice of which property is executed by [p.Identite] is made at runtime, based on the actual type of the object referenced by [p]. The program [Program.cs] from the project [Heritage2] is as follows:

using Heritage2;

// a teacher
Enseignant e = new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
Affiche(e);
// a person
Personne p = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Affiche(p);
// Console.WriteLine(object) displays the result of the object’s ToString method
Console.WriteLine(e);
Console.WriteLine(p);
// an array of people of different types
Personne[] personnes = [p, e];
foreach (Personne personne in personnes)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{personne.GetType().Name} : {personne}");
}

// displays the identity of p
static void Affiche(Personne p)
{
    Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
}

Results:

> dotnet run
Constructeur Personne(string, string, int)
Constructeur Enseignant(string, string, int, int)
Enseignant[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Constructeur Personne(string, string, int)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Enseignant[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Personne : [Jean, Dupont, 30]
Enseignant : Enseignant[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]

This time, on line 4, the function [Affiche] correctly displayed the teacher’s full name.

docs.title: 4.2.6. The ToString method
docs.text:
The class [object] (the C# alias for class [System.Object]) is the “parent” class of all C# classes. So when you write:

public class Personne

you are implicitly writing:

public class Personne : object

The [object] class defines a virtual method, [ToString], which by default returns the full class name of the object. This is what the last two lines of output from the [Heritage1] project displayed, with the calls to [e.ToString()] and [p.ToString()]: [Heritage1.Enseignant] and [Heritage1.Personne]. Although we did not override the [ToString] method in the [Personne] and [Enseignant] classes, the [ToString] method of the [object] class was able to display the object’s actual class name.

In the [Heritage2] project, the [Personne] class redefines the [ToString] method (see above):

public override string ToString() => Identite;

Let’s return to the program [Program.cs] in the project [Heritage2]:

// Console.WriteLine(object) displays the result of the ToString method of the object
Console.WriteLine(e);
Console.WriteLine(p);
// a table of people of different types
Personne[] personnes = [p, e];
foreach (Personne personne in personnes)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{personne.GetType().Name} : {personne}");
}

In Line 10, the method [WriteLine] of class [Console] has no variant that accepts a parameter of type [Personne]. Among the various variants of [WriteLine], there is one that accepts a parameter of type [object]. The compiler will use this method, [WriteLine(object o)], because this signature means that the parameter [o] can be of type [object] or a derived type. Since [object] is the superclass of all classes, any object can be passed as a parameter to [WriteLine]—including an object of type [Personne] or [Enseignant]. The [WriteLine(object o)] method writes [o.ToString()] to the console. Since the [ToString] method is virtual, the [ToString] method of the actual object is used—in this case, that of the [Personne] class. This method returns [Identite], which is also a virtual property: For the teacher [e], it is therefore the property [Identite] of the class [Enseignant] that is used, as shown in line 7 of the results. It is therefore unnecessary to redefine [ToString] in the class [Enseignant], unlike in the 2008 course.

The same mechanism applies to string interpolation: in [$"{personne}"] (line 16), the object [personne] is converted to a string by its method [ToString]. The loop on lines 14–16 iterates over an array of references to [Personne], which actually point to objects of different types: the method [GetType] (which is also inherited from [object]) returns the actual type of the object, whose property [Name] is the name.

docs.title: 4.2.7. Sealed classes
docs.text:
The class [Enseignant] in the [Heritage2] project is declared as [public sealed class Enseignant : Personne]. The keyword [sealed] (sealed) prevents classes from being derived from the class [Enseignant]: the declaration [class EnseignantChercheur : Enseignant] would be rejected by the compiler. A class is sealed when it is not intended to be derived from; the compiler and the runtime can also optimize calls to its virtual methods. The keyword also applies to a redefined method or property: [public sealed override string Identite] would prevent derived classes from redefining it again, without prohibiting derivation from the class.

Conversely, a method or property that is not declared as [virtual], [abstract] (see below), or [override] cannot be overridden with [override]: in C#, unlike in Java, methods are not virtual by default.

docs.title: 4.3. Redefining the meaning of an operator for a class
4.3.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Consider the expression [op1 + op2], where [op1] and [op2] are two operands. It is possible to redefine the meaning of the operator [+]. If the operand [op1] is an instance of class [C1], a static method must be defined in class [C1] with the following signature:

public static Type operator +(C1 operande1, C2 operande2)

When the compiler encounters the expression [op1 + op2], it translates it to [C1.operator +(op1, op2)]. The type returned by the method [operator] is important. In fact, consider the operation [op1 + op2 + op3]. It is translated by the compiler as [(op1 + op2) + op3]. Let [res12] be the result of [op1 + op2]. The next operation performed is [res12 + op3]. If [res12] is of type [C1], it will also be translated to [C1.operator +(res12, op3)]. This allows operations to be chained together.

Unary operators with only one operand can also be redefined. Thus, if [op1] is an object of type [C1], the operation [op1++] can be redefined by a static method of the [C1] class:

public static C1 operator ++(C1 operande1)

What has been stated here applies to most operators, with a few exceptions:

  • Operators [==] and [!=] must be redefined together, as must [<] and [>], [<=] and [>=];
  • the operators [&&], [||], [=], [.], [?:], [??], and [new] cannot be redefined;
  • up to C# 13, the compound assignment operators ([+=], [-=], …) could not be overridden: [a += b] was always compiled to [a = a + b]. C# 14 allows them to be overridden, as we will see.

docs.title: 4.3.2. An example
docs.text:
The [Listes] project in the solution defines a class named [ListeDePersonnes], which is a list of people. The classes [Personne] and [Enseignant] in this project are the same as those in the [Heritage2] project, but without their tracking messages and the person counter. The 2008 course had the class *[ListeDePersonnes] derived from the class *[ArrayList]*, a list of objects of type *[object], which is now obsolete. We use the generic list [List<Personne>] (generic classes are discussed later in this chapter; the class [List<T>] is covered in the next chapter) and, rather than inheriting from it, we place it in a private field of the class. This is referred to as using composition rather than inheritance: the class [ListeDePersonnes] thus exposes only the operations it has chosen. From the class [List<Personne>], we use only the following elements:

  • the method [L.Add(p)], which adds the person [p] to the list [L], and the method [L.AddRange(L2)], which adds all the elements of the list [L2] to it;
  • the property [L.Count], which returns the number of elements in the list [L];
  • The notation [L[i]], which refers to item No. i in the list [L].

The definition of class [ListeDePersonnes] is as follows: [ListeDePersonnes.cs]:

namespace Listes;

public class ListeDePersonnes
{
     // the people on the list
    private readonly List<Personne> personnes = [];

     // number of people in the list
    public int Count => personnes.Count;

     // + operator: returns a new list containing the people in l and the person p
    public static ListeDePersonnes operator +(ListeDePersonnes l, Personne p)
    {
        ListeDePersonnes resultat = new ListeDePersonnes();
        resultat.personnes.AddRange(l.personnes);
        resultat.personnes.Add(p);
        return resultat;
    }

     // compound assignment operator += (C# 14): adds p to the current list
    public void operator +=(Personne p)
    {
        personnes.Add(p);
    }

     // position-based iterator, read-write
    public Personne this[int i]
    {
        get { return personnes[i]; }
        set { personnes[i] = value; }
    }

     // name-based indexer, read-only: returns the position of the person or -1
    public int this[string nom]
    {
        get
        {
             // Searching for a person
            for (int i = 0; i < personnes.Count; i++)
            {
                if (personnes[i].Nom == nom)
                {
                    return i;
                }
            }
            return -1;
        }
    }

     // ToString: returns (person1, person2, ...)
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return "(" + string.Join(",", personnes) + ")";
    }
}
  • line 6: the list of people. The keyword [readonly] indicates that the field can only be assigned at the time of its declaration or within a constructor: the list itself may change in content, but the field will always refer to the same list. [] is an empty collection expression: the type of the created collection, [List<Personne>], is inferred from the field’s type;
  • line 9: the number of people, a read-only property;
  • lines 12–17: definition of the operator [+] for the operation [l + p], where [l] is of type [ListeDePersonnes] and [p] is of type [Personne] or a derived type. The operator creates a new list (line 14), copies the people from [l] into it (line 15), and then adds the person [p] (line 16). As with the [+] operator for numbers or strings, the operands are not modified. Since the list [l] is of the same class, the operator has access to its private field [l.personnes]. The resulting list is of type [ListeDePersonnes], which allows the [+] operators to be chained together as in [l + p1 + p2], interpreted (operator precedence) as [(l + p1) + p2];
  • Lines 21–23: definition of the operator [+=] (C# 14). Unlike the other operators, this is not a static method but an instance method with no return value ([void]): it modifies the current object, in this case by adding the person [p] to it;
  • lines 51–53: we redefine the method [ToString] to display a list of people in the form (person1, person2, ...), where personi is itself the result of the person’s [ToString] method. The static method [string.Join(séparateur, éléments)] concatenates the textual representations of the elements, separating them with the separator. The 2008 course built this string manually using a [StringBuilder] object.

Note that the [ListeDePersonnes] class has no constructor. It therefore uses the default constructor [public ListeDePersonnes()], which does nothing other than initialize the [personnes] field with the value specified in its declaration. Lines 26–46 are discussed in the following section.

The test program [Program.cs] begins as follows:

using Listes;

// --- the + operator
// a list of people
ListeDePersonnes l = new ListeDePersonnes();
// add people
l = l + new Personne("jean", "martin", 10) + new Personne("pauline", "leduc", 12);
// display
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
// l + p returns a new list: l remains unchanged
ListeDePersonnes l2 = l + new Personne("louis", "durand", 8);
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
Console.WriteLine("l2=" + l2);

// --- the += operator (C# 14)
ListeDePersonnes l3 = l;
// += adds the teacher to the list referenced by l, without creating a new list
l += new Enseignant("camille", "germain", 27, 60);
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
// l and l3 always refer to the same object
Console.WriteLine($"l3=l : {ReferenceEquals(l, l3)}");
  • line 5: creation of an empty list of people [l];
  • line 7: adds two people using the [+] operator;
  • line 11: [l + p] creates a new list [l2]; the list [l] remains unchanged;
  • line 18: adds a teacher using the [+=] operator;
  • Lines 9–13: Concatenating a string and an object uses the [ToString] method, which is redefined from the [ListeDePersonnes] class.

Results:

> dotnet run
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12])
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12])
l2=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12],[louis, durand, 8])
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12],Enseignant[[camille, germain, 27],60])
l3=l : True

docs.title: 4.3.3. Compound assignment operators (C# 14)
docs.text: Why define the operator [+=] when [l = l + p] produces the same output? If the class does not define [+=], the compiler translates [l += p] to [l = l + p]: a new list is created, all the people from [l] are copied into it, then [l] refers to this new list, and the old one is discarded by the garbage collector. With the operator [+=] defined by the class, the person is added to the existing list without being copied. Line 16 stores a second reference, [l3], to the list [l]; after the [l += ...] statement, both references still point to the same object (line 6 of the results), which proves that the list was not recreated. For a large list, or in a loop, the difference in performance is significant.

docs.title: 4.4. Defining an indexer for a class
docs.text:
Here, we continue to use the class [ListeDePersonnes]. If [l] is an instance of [ListeDePersonnes], we want to be able to use the notation [l[i]] to refer to person number i in the list [l], both for reading ([Personne p = l[i]]) and writing ([l[i] = new Personne(...)]).

To be able to write [l[i]], where [l[i]] refers to an object [Personne], we need to define a specific property named [this] in the [ListeDePersonnes] class:

     // position-based indexer, read and write
    public Personne this[int i]
    {
        get { return personnes[i]; }
        set { personnes[i] = value; }
    }

     // name-based indexer, read-only: returns the person’s position or -1
    public int this[string nom]
    {
        get
        {
             // Searching for the person
            for (int i = 0; i < personnes.Count; i++)
            {
                if (personnes[i].Nom == nom)
                {
                    return i;
                }
            }
            return -1;
        }
    }

The property [this[int i]] is called an indexer because it gives meaning to the expression [obj[i]], which resembles array notation, whereas [obj] is not an array but an object. The method [get] of theindexer of the object [obj] is called when [variable = obj[i]] is written, and the method [set] is called when [obj[i] = valeur] is written.

  • Lines 27–30: The position-based indexer. The method [get] returns person No. i from the private list [personnes], and the method [set] assigns person [value] to it. The 2008 course, whose class was derived from [ArrayList], had to mask the parent class’s indexer with the keyword [new] and convert the element of type [object] that it returned to [Personne]. With a generic list, no more conversion is needed;
  • lines 34–46: we also want to be able to write [int i = l["nom"]], that is, to index the list [l] not by an element number but by a person’s name. The result of [l[nom]] is an integer: the position in the list of the person with the name [nom], or -1 if that person is not in the list. Only the method [get] is defined, thereby preventing the syntax [l["nom"] = valeur], which would have required the definition of a method [set]. A class can have multiple indexers, provided their parameters differ.

The test program continues as follows:

// --- the indexers
// change element #1
l[1] = new Personne("franck", "gallon", 5);
// display element #1
Console.WriteLine("l[1]=" + l[1]);
// displaying list l
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
// search for people by name
string[] noms = ["martin", "germain", "xx"];
foreach (string nom in noms)
{
    int inom = l[nom];
    if (inom != -1)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Personne({nom})={l[inom]}");
    }
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Personne({nom}) n'existe pas");
    }
}
  • line 25: call to the method [set] of the indexer [this[int]];
  • line 27: call to its method [get];
  • Line 34: Call to the [this[string]] indexer;
  • line 37: call to the [this[int]] indexer.

Results:

l[1]=[franck, gallon, 5]
l=([jean, martin, 10],[franck, gallon, 5],Enseignant[[camille, germain, 27],60])
Personne(martin)=[jean, martin, 10]
Personne(germain)=Enseignant[[camille, germain, 27],60]
Personne(xx) n'existe pas

docs.title: 4.5.1. Value and Reference
docs.text:
The C# structure is analogous to the C language structure and is very similar to the concept of a class. A structure is defined as follows:

struct NomStructure
{
     // fields
    ...
     // Properties
    ...
     // constructors
    ...
     // methods
    ...
}

Despite similarities in their declarations, there are significant differences between classes and structures. For example, the concept of inheritance does not exist with structures (a structure can, however, implement interfaces, which are discussed later). If we are writing a class that is not meant to be derived from, what are the differences between a structure and a class that will help us choose between the two? Let’s use the following example to find out: [classes-13.cs]:

// structure and class: value copy, reference copy
// a structure sp1
SPersonne sp1;
sp1.Nom = "paul";
sp1.Age = 10;
Console.WriteLine("sp1=SPersonne(" + sp1.Nom + "," + sp1.Age + ")");
// a structure sp2
SPersonne sp2 = sp1;
Console.WriteLine("sp2=SPersonne(" + sp2.Nom + "," + sp2.Age + ")");
// sp2 is modified
sp2.Nom = "nicole";
sp2.Age = 30;
// Checking sp1 and sp2
Console.WriteLine("sp1=SPersonne(" + sp1.Nom + "," + sp1.Age + ")");
Console.WriteLine("sp2=SPersonne(" + sp2.Nom + "," + sp2.Age + ")");

// an op1 object
CPersonne op1 = new CPersonne();
op1.Nom = "paul";
op1.Age = 10;
Console.WriteLine("op1=CPersonne(" + op1.Nom + "," + op1.Age + ")");
// an op2 object
CPersonne op2 = op1;
Console.WriteLine("op2=CPersonne(" + op2.Nom + "," + op2.Age + ")");
// op2 is modified
op2.Nom = "nicole";
op2.Age = 30;
// Verification of op1 and op2
Console.WriteLine("op1=CPersonne(" + op1.Nom + "," + op1.Age + ")");
Console.WriteLine("op2=CPersonne(" + op2.Nom + "," + op2.Age + ")");

// structure SPersonne
struct SPersonne
{
    public string Nom;
    public int Age;
}

// class CPersonne
class CPersonne
{
    public string Nom = "";
    public int Age;
}
  • lines 33–36: a structure with two public fields: [Nom], [Age];
  • lines 40–43: a class with two public fields: [Nom], [Age]. Public fields, which are generally discouraged, make this example more readable.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-13.cs
sp1=SPersonne(paul,10)
sp2=SPersonne(paul,10)
sp1=SPersonne(paul,10)
sp2=SPersonne(nicole,30)
op1=CPersonne(paul,10)
op2=CPersonne(paul,10)
op1=CPersonne(nicole,30)
op2=CPersonne(nicole,30)

This structure does not have a constructor here. It could have one, as we will show later. By default, it always has a parameterless constructor—in this case, [SPersonne()]—which sets all its fields to zero ([null] for the references).

The declaration on line 3 creates a structure ([Nom], [Age]), and the value of [sp1] is this structure itself. Its fields do not yet have values: the compiler requires that they all be assigned (lines 4–5) before the structure is used (line 6). In the case of a class, the object ([Nom], [Age]) must be created explicitly using the [new] operator (line 18). The statement creates a [CPersonne] object (roughly equivalent to our structure), and the value of [op1] is then the address (the reference) of that object.

To summarize:

  • in the case of the structure, the value of [sp1] is the structure itself;
  • in the case of the class, the value of [op1] is the address of the created object.

When [SPersonne sp2 = sp1;] is written in the program (line 8), a new structure [sp2] ([Nom], [Age]) is created and initialized with the value of [sp1], which is the structure itself:

The structure of [sp1] is duplicated in [sp2] (left side of the diagram). This is a value copy. Now let’s consider the instruction [CPersonne op2 = op1;] (line 23). In the case of classes, the value of [op1] is copied to [op2], but since this value is actually the object’s address, the object itself is not duplicated (right side of the diagram).

In the case of the structure, changing the value of [sp2] does not change the value of [sp1], as shown by the program (lines 4–5 of the results). In the case of the object, if you modify the object pointed to by [op2], the one pointed to by [op1] is also modified since they are the same (lines 8–9).

We can therefore conclude from these explanations that:

  • the value of a variable of type structure is the structure itself;
  • the value of a variable of type class is the address of the object it points to.

It is said that structures are value types and classes are reference types. The simple types in C# ([int], [double], [decimal], [bool], [char], …) are structures of type .NET ([System.Int32], [System.Double], …), whereas [string] and arrays are reference types. A structure is suitable for representing a small piece of data (a point, a color, a date, an amount…) that is treated as a value. A structure is not allocated individually on the garbage collector’s heap: a local variable of type structure is generally placed on the stack, and an array of structures contains the structures themselves rather than references to them.

docs.title: 4.5.2. A Structure with Properties and Constructors
docs.text:
Once the fundamental difference between a value and a reference is understood, a structure proves to be very similar to a class, as shown in the following example [classes-14.cs]:

// a structure with constructors, properties, and a method
// a person p1
SPersonne p1 = new SPersonne();
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1}");
p1.Nom = "paul";
p1.Age = 10;
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1}");
// a person p2
SPersonne p2 = p1;
Console.WriteLine("p2=" + p2);
// p2 is modified
p2.Nom = "nicole";
p2.Age = 30;
// verification of p1 and p2
Console.WriteLine("p1=" + p1);
Console.WriteLine("p2=" + p2);
// a person p3
SPersonne p3 = new SPersonne("amandin", 18);
Console.WriteLine("p3=" + p3);
// a person p4
SPersonne p4 = new SPersonne { Nom = "x", Age = 10 };
Console.WriteLine("p4=" + p4);
// the default value of a structure: all fields set to zero (null for references)
SPersonne p5 = default;
Console.WriteLine("p5=" + p5);
// equality of two structures: comparison of field values
SPersonne p6 = new SPersonne("nicole", 30);
Console.WriteLine($"p1.Equals(p2) : {p1.Equals(p2)}, p2.Equals(p6) : {p2.Equals(p6)}");

// structure SPersonne
struct SPersonne
{
     // constructors
    public SPersonne(string nom, int age)
    {
        Nom = nom;
        Age = age;
    }

    public SPersonne() : this("?", 0)
    {
    }

     // properties
    public string? Nom { get; set; }
    public int Age { get; set; }

     // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"SPersonne({Nom},{Age})";
    }
}
  • lines 34–37: a constructor with two parameters. The 2008 course explained that a struct constructor could not initialize fields via properties: this restriction has been removed (C# 11);
  • line 40: Since C# 10, a struct can declare its own parameterless constructor, which is chained to the previous one here. It is called by [new SPersonne()] (line 3) and by the object initializer on line 21, which then modifies the two properties;
  • lines 45–46: two automatic properties. The property [Nom] is declared as type [string?] (a string that could be [null]) because a struct can always be created without using a constructor: this is the case for its default value (line 24), where all fields are set to zero and the name is therefore [null], as well as for the elements of a newly created array of structures;
  • lines 49–51: redefinition of the method [ToString]. A structure implicitly derives from the class [System.ValueType], which itself derives from [object];
  • line 28: The [Equals] method, inherited from [ValueType], compares two structures field by field. The [==] operator, on the other hand, is not defined for a structure unless it is overridden.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-14.cs
p1=SPersonne(?,0)
p1=SPersonne(paul,10)
p2=SPersonne(paul,10)
p1=SPersonne(paul,10)
p2=SPersonne(nicole,30)
p3=SPersonne(amandin,18)
p4=SPersonne(x,10)
p5=SPersonne(,0)
p1.Equals(p2) : False, p2.Equals(p6) : True

At the end of the program, the structures [p1] and [p2] are different (lines 5–6): with a class, [p1] and [p2] would have referred to the same object.

docs.title: 4.5.3. Immutable Structures and Record Structures
docs.text:
A structure whose state can be modified can lead to unexpected results: since it is copied with every assignment or parameter pass, one often modifies a copy while believing one is modifying the original. Therefore, it is recommended to make structures immutable: once created, they can no longer be modified. The program [classes-15.cs] demonstrates both ways to do this:

// immutable structures (read-only structs) and record structures (record structs)
Point a = new Point(1, 2);
// a.X = 5;    // rejected: the properties of a read-only struct cannot be modified
Point b = a.Deplacer(3, 4);
Console.WriteLine($"a={a}, b={b}");

// a record struct: ToString; Equals, ==, and != are generated by the compiler
PointR r1 = new PointR(1, 2);
PointR r2 = new PointR(1, 2);
Console.WriteLine($"r1={r1}, r2={r2}");
Console.WriteLine($"r1 == r2 : {r1 == r2}");
// A record struct (not read-only) is modifiable
r2.Y = 20;
Console.WriteLine($"r2={r2}, r1 == r2 : {r1 == r2}");
// The `with` expression creates a modified copy
PointR r3 = r1 with { X = 10 };
Console.WriteLine($"r3={r3}");

// A read-only record struct is immutable
Couleur rouge = new Couleur(255, 0, 0);
Couleur rose = rouge with { V = 128, B = 128 };
Console.WriteLine($"rouge={rouge}, rose={rose}");
// rose.V = 0;    // rejected: the structure is read-only

// an immutable structure
readonly struct Point
{
    public Point(int x, int y)
    {
        X = x;
        Y = y;
    }

    public int X { get; }
    public int Y { get; }

     // The point is not modified: a new one is returned
    public Point Deplacer(int dx, int dy) => new Point(X + dx, Y + dy);

    public override string ToString() => $"({X},{Y})";
}

// a “positional” record structure: X and Y are public properties
record struct PointR(int X, int Y);

// an immutable record structure
readonly record struct Couleur(byte R, byte V, byte B);
  • lines 26–40: a structure declared as [readonly] (C# 7.2). The compiler verifies that all its fields and properties are read-only. To “move” a point, the method [Deplacer] returns a new point (line 38);
  • line 44: a record structure (C# 10). This single line declares a structure whose constructor has two parameters, [X] and [Y], and which has two public read-write properties, [X] and [Y]. The compiler also generates a method named [ToString] that displays the structure’s name and its properties, the equality methods and operators [==] and [!=] (line 11), as well as support for the expression [with], which creates a copy of the structure by modifying certain properties (line 16);
  • line 47: an immutable record structure: its properties are read-only (more precisely, [init]: they can only be set at creation), while the expression [with] remains valid (line 21).

Results:

> dotnet run classes-15.cs
a=(1,2), b=(4,6)
r1=PointR { X = 1, Y = 2 }, r2=PointR { X = 1, Y = 2 }
r1 == r2 : True
r2=PointR { X = 1, Y = 20 }, r1 == r2 : False
r3=PointR { X = 10, Y = 2 }
rouge=Couleur { R = 255, V = 0, B = 0 }, rose=Couleur { R = 255, V = 128, B = 128 }

The records ([record]) also exist as classes: we’ll examine them in detail a little later. For now, let’s just note that a [readonly record struct] is the most concise way to declare a small, immutable value-type data item: this is the type we’ll use for the tax brackets in this chapter’s example application.

docs.title: 4.6.1. A First Example
docs.text:
An interface is a set of method or property declarations that forms a contract. A class (or structure) that chooses to implement an interface commits to providing an implementation of all the methods and properties defined in the interface. The compiler verifies this implementation.

For example, here is the definition of the [System.Collections.IEnumerator] interface from .NET:

public interface IEnumerator
{
     // properties
    object Current { get; }
     // methods
    bool MoveNext();
    void Reset();
}

The properties and methods of the interface are defined only by their signatures. They are not implemented (they have no code). It is the classes that implement the interface that provide code for the interface’s methods and properties:

public class C : IEnumerator
{
    ...
    public object Current { get { ... } }
    public bool MoveNext() { ... }
    public void Reset() { ... }
}
  • Line 1: The class [C] implements the interface [IEnumerator]. Note that the symbol [:] used for implementing an interface is the same as the one used for deriving a class;
  • Lines 4–6: The implementation of the methods and properties of the [IEnumerator] interface. They must be public.

By convention, an interface name begins with the letter I. The following examples make up the [Statistiques] project in the solution. Consider the following interface, [IStats.cs]:

namespace Statistiques;

public interface IStats
{
     // mean of a series of values
    double Moyenne { get; }

     // standard deviation of the series
    double EcartType();
}

The [IStats] interface has:

  • a read-only property [Moyenne]: to calculate the average of a series of values;
  • a method [EcartType]: to calculate the standard deviation.

Note that it is not specified anywhere which set of values is being referred to. It could be the average grades of a class, the monthly average sales of a particular product, the average temperature in a given location… This is the principle behind interfaces: they assume the existence of methods in the object but not that of specific data.

A first implementation class for the [IStats] interface could be a class used to store the grades of students in a class for a given subject. A student is characterized by the following [Eleve] structure: [Eleve.cs]:

namespace Statistiques;

// a student
public readonly record struct Eleve(string Prenom, string Nom);

The student is identified by their first and last names. The 2008 course defined a structure with two automatic properties; an immutable record structure, as shown in the previous paragraph, is represented in a single line. A grade is characterized by the following structure: [Note] [Note.cs]:

namespace Statistiques;

// a student's grade
public readonly record struct Note(Eleve Eleve, double Valeur)
{
    public override string ToString() => $"[{Eleve.Prenom},{Eleve.Nom},{Valeur}]";
}

The grade is defined by the student being graded and the grade itself. The structure redefines the method [ToString] generated by the compiler to display a grade in the form [prénom,nom,valeur].

The grades of all students in a given subject are grouped in the following class [TableauDeNotes]: [TableauDeNotes.cs]:

namespace Statistiques;

public class TableauDeNotes : IStats
{
     // properties
    public string Matiere { get; }
    public Note[] Notes { get; }
    public double Moyenne { get; }
     // field
    private readonly double ecartType;

     // constructor
    public TableauDeNotes(string matiere, Note[] notes)
    {
         // data storage
        Matiere = matiere;
        Notes = notes;
         // calculating the average of the grades
        double somme = 0;
        foreach (Note note in Notes)
        {
            somme += note.Valeur;
        }
        Moyenne = Notes.Length != 0 ? somme / Notes.Length : -1;
         // calculating the standard deviation
        double carres = 0;
        foreach (Note note in Notes)
        {
            carres += Math.Pow(note.Valeur - Moyenne, 2);
        }
        ecartType = Notes.Length != 0 ? Math.Sqrt(carres / Notes.Length) : -1;
    }

     // Implementation of the EcartType method of the IStats interface
    public double EcartType()
    {
        return ecartType;
    }

     // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"matière={Matiere}, notes=({string.Join(",", Notes)})";
    }
}
  • Line 3: The class [TableauDeNotes] implements the interface [IStats]. It must therefore implement the property [Moyenne] and the method [EcartType]. These are implemented on line 8 ([Moyenne]) and lines 35–37 ([EcartType]);
  • lines 6–8: three read-only automatic properties: the subject for which the object stores grades, the grade array, and the grade average;
  • line 10: a field storing the standard deviation of the grades;
  • lines 13–31: the constructor. Here, we assume that the grades passed to the constructor will not change afterward. Therefore, we use the constructor to immediately calculate the average and standard deviation of these grades and store them. A read-only property such as [Moyenne] can be assigned a value in the constructor (line 24); it cannot be assigned a value afterward. The expressions [condition ? valeur1 : valeur2] set the mean and standard deviation of an empty array to -1;
  • lines 41–43: the method [ToString] uses [string.Join] to concatenate the grades, each of which is converted to a string by the method [ToString] of the structure [Note].

In the previous class, grades were stored in an array. It was not possible to add a new grade after the [TableauDeNotes] object was created. We now offer a second implementation of the [IStats] interface, called [ListeDeNotes], where this time the notes are stored in a list [List<Note>], with the ability to add notes after the initial creation of the [ListeDeNotes] and [ListeDeNotes.cs] objects:

namespace Statistiques;

public class ListeDeNotes : IStats
{
     // properties
    public string Matiere { get; }
    public List<Note> Notes { get; }
     // stored mean and standard deviation (null: not yet calculated)
    private double? moyenne;
    private double? ecartType;

     // constructor
    public ListeDeNotes(string matiere, List<Note> notes)
    {
        Matiere = matiere;
        Notes = notes;
    }

     // Add a note
    public void Ajouter(Note note)
    {
        Notes.Add(note);
         // The mean and standard deviation will need to be recalculated
        moyenne = null;
        ecartType = null;
    }

     // Average of scores: calculated on the first request
    public double Moyenne
    {
        get
        {
            moyenne ??= CalculerMoyenne();
            return moyenne.Value;
        }
    }

     // Standard deviation of scores: calculated upon the first request
    public double EcartType()
    {
        ecartType ??= CalculerEcartType();
        return ecartType.Value;
    }

    private double CalculerMoyenne()
    {
        if (Notes.Count == 0)
        {
            return -1;
        }
        double somme = 0;
        foreach (Note note in Notes)
        {
            somme += note.Valeur;
        }
        return somme / Notes.Count;
    }

    private double CalculerEcartType()
    {
        if (Notes.Count == 0)
        {
            return -1;
        }
        double m = Moyenne;
        double carres = 0;
        foreach (Note note in Notes)
        {
            carres += Math.Pow(note.Valeur - m, 2);
        }
        return Math.Sqrt(carres / Notes.Count);
    }

     // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"matière={Matiere}, notes=({string.Join(",", Notes)})";
    }
}
  • Line 3: The class [ListeDeNotes] implements the interface [IStats];
  • line 7: Notes are now stored in a list rather than an array;
  • lines 20–25: You can now add a grade to those already stored. The mean and standard deviation are no longer calculated in the constructor but on demand, within the interface members themselves: [Moyenne] (lines 29–34) and [EcartType] (lines 39–42). Once calculated, these values are stored so they aren’t recalculated with every request: they are said to be cached. Adding a score invalidates the cache;
  • lines 9–10: the cache. The type [double?] (C# 2) is a nullable value type: a variable of this type contains a [double] or [null], which here means “not yet calculated.” The 2008 course used the value -1 for this;
  • line 33: the [??=] operator (C# 8) only assigns a value to the left-hand variable if it is [null]. The method [CalculerMoyenne] is therefore called only if the average has not yet been calculated. The property [Value] of a variable [double?] returns the value [double] that it contains.

A test program could look like this: [Program.cs]:

using Statistiques;

// a few students and their English grades
Eleve[] eleves = [new Eleve("Paul", "Martin"), new Eleve("Maxime", "Germain"), new Eleve("Berthine", "Samin")];
Note[] notes = [new Note(eleves[0], 14), new Note(eleves[1], 16), new Note(eleves[2], 18)];
// which are stored in an object TableauDeNotes
TableauDeNotes anglais = new TableauDeNotes("anglais", notes);
// displaying the mean and standard deviation
AfficheStats(anglais);
// the same grades in an object ListeDeNotes
ListeDeNotes francais = new ListeDeNotes("français", new List<Note>(notes));
AfficheStats(francais);
// a score is added
francais.Ajouter(new Note(new Eleve("Jérôme", "Jaric"), 10));
AfficheStats(francais);
// A variable can have an interface as its type
IStats stats = anglais;
Console.WriteLine($"Moyenne d'anglais : {stats.Moyenne}");
stats = francais;
Console.WriteLine($"Moyenne de français : {stats.Moyenne}");

// Displaying the mean and standard deviation of an object that implements IStats
static void AfficheStats(IStats valeurs)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{valeurs}, Moyenne={valeurs.Moyenne}, Ecart-type={valeurs.EcartType()}");
}
  • line 4: creates an array of students;
  • line 5: creation of an array of grades;
  • line 7: a [TableauDeNotes] object, whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 9;
  • line 11: an object [ListeDeNotes], whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 12. The class [List<Note>] has a constructor that accepts a collection of grades, in this case the array [notes];
  • line 14: a new grade is added, followed by a new display;
  • lines 23–25: The function [AfficheStats] takes a [IStats] type as a parameter, which is an interface type. This means that the actual parameter can be any object that implements the [IStats] interface. When using a data object of an interface type, only the methods of the interface implemented by that object are used. The rest is ignored. This property is similar to the polymorphism we saw with classes. If a set of classes Ci that are not related to each other through inheritance (and therefore cannot use inheritance-based polymorphism) share a set of methods with the same signature, it may be useful to group these methods into an interface I that all the relevant classes would implement. Instances of these classes Ci can then be used as actual parameters of functions that accept a formal parameter of type I—that is, functions that use only the methods of the Ci objects defined in the interface I, and not the specific fields and methods of the various Ci classes;
  • lines 17–19: A variable can be of the type of an interface. It can then refer to any object of a class that implements the interface. The compiler allows access only to the members of the interface: the property [Moyenne] and the method [EcartType].

Results:

> dotnet run
matière=anglais, notes=([Paul,Martin,14],[Maxime,Germain,16],[Berthine,Samin,18]), Moyenne=16, Ecart-type=1,632993161855452
matière=français, notes=([Paul,Martin,14],[Maxime,Germain,16],[Berthine,Samin,18]), Moyenne=16, Ecart-type=1,632993161855452
matière=français, notes=([Paul,Martin,14],[Maxime,Germain,16],[Berthine,Samin,18],[Jérôme,Jaric,10]), Moyenne=14,5, Ecart-type=2,958039891549808
Moyenne d'anglais : 16
Moyenne de français : 14,5

Finally, note that interfaces can have multiple implementations; that is, you can write:

public class ClasseDerivee : ClasseDeBase, I1, I2, ..., In
{
    ...
}

where the Ij are interfaces: a class inherits from only one class, but can implement as many interfaces as it wishes.

docs.title: 4.6.2. Default Interface Methods
docs.text:
Starting with C# 8, an interface can provide a default implementation for some of its methods. A class that implements the interface can then use this implementation or provide its own. This makes it possible, for example, to add a method to an already published interface without requiring all classes that implement it to be modified. The program [classes-16.cs] provides an example:

// default interface methods (C# 8)
IForme[] formes = [new Carre(2), new Cercle(1)];
foreach (IForme forme in formes)
{
    Console.WriteLine(forme.Description());
}
// The default method is accessible only through the interface type
Carre carre = new Carre(3);
// Console.WriteLine(carre.Description());    // rejected: Carre does not define Description
Console.WriteLine(((IForme)carre).Description());

public interface IForme
{
     // method to be implemented
    double Surface();

     // method with a default implementation
    string Description() => $"{GetType().Name} de surface {Surface():F2}";
}

// Carre uses the default implementation of Description
public class Carre : IForme
{
    private readonly double cote;

    public Carre(double cote)
    {
        this.cote = cote;
    }

    public double Surface() => cote * cote;
}

// Circle provides its own implementation of Description
public class Cercle : IForme
{
    private readonly double rayon;

    public Cercle(double rayon)
    {
        this.rayon = rayon;
    }

    public double Surface() => Math.PI * rayon * rayon;

    public string Description() => $"Cercle de rayon {rayon} et de surface {Surface():F2}";
}
  • Lines 12–18: The [IForme] interface declares a method, [Surface], to be implemented, and a method, [Description], with a default implementation. This method can use the other members of the interface ([Surface]) and those of [object] ([GetType]). The [{Surface():F2}] format displays the area with two decimal places;
  • lines 22–31: The class [Carre] implements only [Surface]; it uses the method [Description] by default;
  • lines 35–46: The class [Cercle] provides its own method, [Description];
  • line 10: the default method belongs to the interface, not to the [Carre] class: it can only be called through a reference of type [IForme]. The call to [carre.Description()] is rejected by the compiler.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-16.cs
Carre de surface 4,00
Cercle de rayon 1 et de surface 3,14
Carre de surface 9,00

Finally, starting with C# 11, an interface can declare abstract static members that the types implementing it must provide. These are used only with generics: we’ll cover them at the end of the section on generics.

docs.title: 4.7. Abstract Classes
docs.text:
An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated. You must create derived classes, which can be instantiated. Abstract classes can be used to refactor the code of a class hierarchy. Let’s examine the following example, which forms the [Utilisateurs] project within the [Utilisateur.cs] solution:

namespace Utilisateurs;

public abstract class Utilisateur
{
     // fields
    private readonly string login;
    private readonly string motDePasse;
    private readonly string role;

     // constructor
    protected Utilisateur(string login, string motDePasse)
    {
         // The information is saved
        this.login = login;
        this.motDePasse = motDePasse;
         // Identify the user
        string? role = Identifie();
         // Identified?
        if (role == null)
        {
            throw new ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu($"[{login},{motDePasse}]");
        }
        this.role = role;
    }

     // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"Utilisateur[{login},{motDePasse},{role}]";
    }

     // Identification: returns the user's role or null if the user is not recognized
    protected abstract string? Identifie();
}
  • line 3: the class is declared abstract using the keyword [abstract];
  • Lines 11–23: the constructor for the [Utilisateur] class. This class stores information about a web application’s user. The application has various types of users who are authenticated via a username and password (lines 6–7). These two pieces of information are verified against a directory (LDAP) for some users, against a database for others, and so on. The constructor is [protected]: it can only be called by the constructors of derived classes;
  • lines 14–15: the authentication information is stored;
  • line 17: it is verified by a method named [Identifie]. Because the authentication method is not known at this level, it is declared abstract (line 33) using the keyword [abstract]. An abstract method has no body: derived classes will provide one. A class that has an abstract method must itself be declared abstract. The method [Identifie] returns a string specifying the user’s role (basically, what they are authorized to do), or [null] if the user is not recognized: its return type is therefore [string?];
  • lines 19–21: if the user is not recognized, an exception is thrown;
  • lines 27–29: the method [ToString], which identifies an instance of the class.

We assume here that the developer wants to have control over the construction of instances of the class [Utilisateur] and its derived classes, perhaps because they want to ensure that an exception of a certain type is thrown if the user is not recognized. Derived classes can rely on this constructor. To do so, they must provide the method [Identifie]. Note that the constructor here calls a method overridden by the derived classes even though those classes have not yet executed their own constructors: the method [Identifie] must therefore not use any fields of the derived class, which have not yet been initialized. This is a practice that should be used with caution.

The [ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu] class is as follows:

namespace Utilisateurs;

public class ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu : Exception
{
    public ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu(string message) : base(message)
    {
    }
}
  • Line 3: It derives from the [Exception] class;
  • line 5: it has only one constructor that takes an error message as a parameter. This parameter is passed to the parent class, which has the same constructor.

We now derive the class [Utilisateur] from the child class [Administrateur]:

namespace Utilisateurs;

public class Administrateur : Utilisateur
{
     // constructor
    public Administrateur(string login, string motDePasse)
        : base(login, motDePasse)
    {
    }

     // identification
    protected override string? Identifie()
    {
         // Identification LDAP
        // ...
        return "admin";
    }
}
  • lines 6–7: the constructor simply passes the parameters it receives to its parent class;
  • Lines 12–16: The [Identifie] method of the [Administrateur] class. Suppose an administrator is identified by a directory LDAP. This method overrides the abstract method [Identifie] of its parent class: the keyword [override] is required (an abstract method is implicitly virtual). The 2008 course incorrectly stated the opposite. It retains the access specifier [protected] of the method it overrides.

We now derive the class [Utilisateur] from the child class [Observateur]:

namespace Utilisateurs;

public class Observateur : Utilisateur
{
     // constructor
    public Observateur(string login, string motDePasse)
        : base(login, motDePasse)
    {
    }

     // identification
    protected override string? Identifie()
    {
         // database identification
        // ...
        return "observateur";
    }
}
  • Lines 12–16: the [Identifie] method of the [Observateur] class. We assume that an observer is identified by verifying their identification data in a database.

Ultimately, the objects [Administrateur] and [Observateur] are initialized by the same constructor, that of the parent class [Utilisateur]. This constructor uses the method [Identifie] provided by these classes.

A third class, [Inconnu], also derives from the [Utilisateur] class:

namespace Utilisateurs;

public class Inconnu : Utilisateur
{
     // manufacturer
    public Inconnu(string login, string motDePasse)
        : base(login, motDePasse)
    {
    }

     // Identification
    protected override string? Identifie()
    {
         // user unknown
        // ...
        return null;
    }
}
  • Line 16: The [Identifie] method returns the pointer [null] to indicate that the user was not recognized.

A test program for [Program.cs] might look like this:

using Utilisateurs;

Console.WriteLine(new Observateur("observer", "mdp1"));
Console.WriteLine(new Administrateur("admin", "mdp2"));
try
{
    Console.WriteLine(new Inconnu("xx", "yy"));
}
catch (ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu e)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Utilisateur non connu : " + e.Message);
}
// User u = new User("x", "y"); // rejected:   the User class is abstract

Note that in lines 3 and 4, the method [Utilisateur.ToString()] is called by the method [WriteLine]. On line 7, the constructor throws a [ExceptionUtilisateurInconnu] exception, which is caught on line 9: the object is not created, and nothing is displayed by [WriteLine]. Line 13, if uncommented, is rejected by the compiler: you cannot create an object of an abstract class.

Results:

> dotnet run
Utilisateur[observer,mdp1,observateur]
Utilisateur[admin,mdp2,admin]
Utilisateur non connu : [xx,yy]

An abstract class is similar to an interface: both declare members that other classes must implement. However, an abstract class can have fields, constructors, and code common to its derived classes; conversely, a class can derive from only one abstract class, whereas it can implement multiple interfaces. The two are often combined: an interface defines the contract, and an abstract class that implements it factors out the code common to multiple implementations. This is what the example application in this chapter will do.

docs.title: 4.8.1. Generic Classes and Methods
docs.text:
Suppose we want to write a method that swaps two integers. This method could look like this:

public static void Echanger1(ref int value1, ref int value2)
{
     // Swap the values of value1 and value2
    int temp = value2;
    value2 = value1;
    value1 = temp;
}

Now, if we wanted to swap two references to [Personne] objects, we would write:

public static void Echanger2(ref Personne value1, ref Personne value2)
{
     // Swapping the references for value1 and value2
    Personne temp = value2;
    value2 = value1;
    value1 = temp;
}

What distinguishes the two methods is the type T of the parameters: [int] in [Echanger1], and [Personne] in [Echanger2]. Generic classes, interfaces, and methods address the need for code that differs only in the type of certain data. They were introduced with C# 2: prior to that, the type [object] was used, which accepts any type, at the cost of type conversions at runtime and errors detected only at runtime. This is what the [ArrayList] class, mentioned in the section on operators, did.

The program [classes-17.cs] features a generic class, a generic method, and a second, more realistic generic class:

// Generic classes and methods
// --- a generic class Generic1<T>
// int
int i1 = 1, i2 = 2;
Generic1<int>.Echanger(ref i1, ref i2);
Console.WriteLine($"i1={i1},i2={i2}");
// string
string s1 = "s1", s2 = "s2";
Generic1<string>.Echanger(ref s1, ref s2);
Console.WriteLine($"s1={s1},s2={s2}");
// Person
Personne p1 = new Personne("jean", "clu", 20), p2 = new Personne("pauline", "dard", 55);
Generic1<Personne>.Echanger(ref p1, ref p2);
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1},p2={p2}");

// --- a generic method Generic2.Echanger<T>
Generic2.Echanger<int>(ref i1, ref i2);
Console.WriteLine($"i1={i1},i2={i2}");
// the compiler infers T from the type of the actual parameters
Generic2.Echanger(ref s1, ref s2);
Console.WriteLine($"s1={s1},s2={s2}");
Generic2.Echanger(ref p1, ref p2);
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1},p2={p2}");

// --- a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type T
Pile<Personne> pile = new Pile<Personne>();
pile.Empiler(p1);
pile.Empiler(p2);
Console.WriteLine($"La pile contient {pile.Count} personnes");
Personne sommet = pile.Depiler();
Console.WriteLine($"Personne dépilée : {sommet}, il en reste {pile.Count}");
// pile.Empiler("x");    // rejected: the stack only accepts Person objects

// a generic class
class Generic1<T>
{
    public static void Echanger(ref T value1, ref T value2)
    {
         // we swap the values of `value1` and `value2`
        T temp = value2;
        value2 = value1;
        value1 = temp;
    }
}

// a non-generic class with a generic method
class Generic2
{
    public static void Echanger<T>(ref T value1, ref T value2)
    {
        T temp = value2;
        value2 = value1;
        value1 = temp;
    }
}

// a stack of elements of type T
class Pile<T>
{
     // the elements in the stack
    private readonly List<T> elements = new List<T>();

     // number of elements
    public int Count => elements.Count;

     // adding an element to the top of the stack
    public void Empiler(T element)
    {
        elements.Add(element);
    }

     // removing the element at the top of the stack
    public T Depiler()
    {
        if (elements.Count == 0)
        {
            throw new InvalidOperationException("pile vide");
        }
        T element = elements[^1];
        elements.RemoveAt(elements.Count - 1);
        return element;
    }
}

// a person
class Personne
{
    private readonly string prenom;
    private readonly string nom;
    private readonly int age;

    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public override string ToString() => $"[{prenom}, {nom}, {age}]";
}
  • lines 35–42: The class *[Generic1] is parameterized by a type denoted as *[T]. You can name it whatever you want. This type, [T], is then used within the class just like any other type: for the two parameters to be swapped and for the temporary variable [temp]. The class [Generic1] is said to be a generic class;
  • Line 5: When using a generic class parameterized by the types T1, T2, …, these types must be “instantiated.” Here, we use the static method [Echanger] of type [Generic1<int>] to indicate that the references passed to the method [Echanger] are of type [int]. Lines 9 and 13: the same applies to the types [string] and [Personne];
  • Lines 47–49: The class [Generic2] is not generic, but its static method [Echanger] is;
  • line 17: the method [Echanger] is called, specifying the type of the parameters between [<>]. In fact, the compiler is able to deduce, based on the type of the actual parameters, which variant of the method [Echanger] to use. Therefore, the code on lines 20–22 is valid;
  • lines 58–81: a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type [T]. Elements are pushed onto the top of the stack and popped from the top. The elements are stored in a generic list of type [List<T>] (line 61), which is itself parameterized by the stack’s type, [T]. The expression [elements[^1]] (line 79) refers to the last element of the list;
  • line 26: a stack of people. The compiler guarantees that it will contain only people: the statement on line 32 would be rejected. The method [Depiler] returns an object of type [Personne], without conversion.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-17.cs
i1=2,i2=1
s1=s2,s2=s1
p1=[pauline, dard, 55],p2=[jean, clu, 20]
i1=1,i2=2
s1=s1,s2=s2
p1=[jean, clu, 20],p2=[pauline, dard, 55]
La pile contient 2 personnes
Personne dépilée : [pauline, dard, 55], il en reste 1

Note that, to swap two variables, C# 7 now offers a more concise syntax based on tuples: [(a, b) = (b, a);].

docs.title: 4.8.2. Constraints on Generic Parameters
docs.text:
You can place constraints on generic parameters using the keyword [where]. The main ones are as follows:

ConstraintMeaning[where T : struct]T must be a value type (structure), excluding nullable types such as [int?][where T : class]T must be a reference type (class, interface, array, delegate)[where T : notnull]T must be a non-nullable type (value or reference)[where T : new()]T must have a public constructor with no parameters. This constraint comes last[where T : ClasseDeBase]T must be the specified class or a derived class[where T : IInterface]T must implement the specified interface. Multiple interfaces may be specified[where T : U]T must be the type U or a type derived from U, where U is another generic parameter[where T : unmanaged]T must be a value type that contains no references

The program [classes-18.cs] uses two of them:

// constraints on generic parameters
// --- constraint where T : class
string s1 = "s1", s2 = "s2";
Generic3.Echanger(ref s1, ref s2);
Console.WriteLine($"s1={s1},s2={s2}");
int i1 = 1, i2 = 2;
// Generic3.Echanger(ref i1, ref i2);    // error CS0452: int is not a reference type
Console.WriteLine($"i1={i1},i2={i2}");

// --- constraint where T : IValeur
// swap instances of type Random
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    Aleatoire c1 = new Aleatoire(), c2 = new Aleatoire();
    Console.Write($"Avant échange --> c1={c1},c2={c2}");
    Generic4.Ordonner(ref c1, ref c2);
    Console.WriteLine($"   Après échange --> c1={c1},c2={c2}");
}
// Exchange instances of type String
Chaine c3 = new Chaine("xxxxxxxxxxxxxx"), c4 = new Chaine("xx");
Console.WriteLine($"Avant échange --> c3={c3},c4={c4}");
Generic4.Ordonner(ref c3, ref c4);
Console.WriteLine($"Après échange --> c3={c3},c4={c4}");

// T must be a reference type
class Generic3
{
    public static void Echanger<T>(ref T value1, ref T value2) where T : class
    {
        T temp = value2;
        value2 = value1;
        value1 = temp;
    }
}

// Type T must implement IValeur
class Generic4
{
    public static void Ordonner<T>(ref T element1, ref T element2) where T : IValeur
    {
         // If the first element is greater than the second, swap the elements
        if (element1.Valeur() > element2.Valeur())
        {
            T temp = element2;
            element2 = element1;
            element1 = temp;
        }
    }
}

// An object with an integer value
interface IValeur
{
    int Valeur();
}

// an object with a random value
class Aleatoire : IValeur
{
     // a random number generator shared by all instances
     // (initialized with a fixed seed so that results are reproducible)
    private static readonly Random generateur = new Random(2026);
     // value of the object
    private readonly int valeur = generateur.Next(100);

    public int Valeur() => valeur;

    public override string ToString() => valeur.ToString();
}

// an object whose value is the length of a string
class Chaine : IValeur
{
    private readonly string s;

    public Chaine(string s)
    {
        this.s = s;
    }

    public int Valeur() => s.Length;

    public override string ToString() => s;
}
  • lines 26–28: the generic method [Echanger] requires that the type [T] be a reference type (constraint [where T : class]);
  • line 7: if this line is uncommented, the compiler reports an error because the type [int] is not a class or an interface—it is a structure.

Here is the error message received when compiling the program after line 7 is uncommented:

> dotnet build classes-18.cs
classes-18.cs(7,10): error CS0452: Le type 'int' doit être un type référence afin d'être utilisé comme paramètre 'T' dans le type ou la méthode générique 'Generic3.Echanger<T>(ref T, ref T)'

The compiler message is displayed in the system language—in this case, French (on a computer configured for English, it would be in English). It lists the filename, the line and column numbers of the error, and the error code ([CS0452]), which can be looked up in the documentation.

Let’s return to the program [classes-18.cs]:

  • Lines 37–39: The type [T] must implement the interface [IValeur] (lines 52–54). This interface has a method named [Valeur], used on line 42, which returns the value of the object of type [T]. Without this constraint, the compiler would reject the call to [element1.Valeur()]: any object of type [T] does not have a method named [Valeur]. The two references [element1] and [element2] are swapped only if the value of [element1] is greater than the value of [element2]: the method [Ordonner] sorts the two elements in ascending order by value;
  • lines 58–68: the class [Aleatoire] implements the interface [IValeur]. The value of an instance is a random number between 0 and 99 (line 64), provided by a random number generator in the [Random] class shared by all instances (line 62). This generator is initialized with a fixed “seed”: it therefore always produces the same sequence of numbers, making the results reproducible. The 2008 course created a generator for each object, initialized with the current time, and had to wait one millisecond between creations to obtain different numbers. Since reproducibility is not required, we now use the shared generator [Random.Shared];
  • lines 72–83: the [Chaine] class also implements the [IValeur] interface: the value of an instance is the length of the string passed to the constructor;
