  • lines 12–17: Instances of type [Aleatoire] are sorted;
  • lines 20–23: instances of type [Chaine] are sorted.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-18.cs
s1=s2,s2=s1
i1=1,i2=2
Avant échange --> c1=15,c2=28   Après échange --> c1=15,c2=28
Avant échange --> c1=91,c2=99   Après échange --> c1=91,c2=99
Avant échange --> c1=91,c2=7   Après échange --> c1=7,c2=91
Avant échange --> c1=66,c2=85   Après échange --> c1=66,c2=85
Avant échange --> c1=62,c2=36   Après échange --> c1=36,c2=62
Avant échange --> c3=xxxxxxxxxxxxxx,c4=xx
Après échange --> c3=xx,c4=xxxxxxxxxxxxxx

docs.title: 4.8.3. A generic interface: IComparer<T>
docs.text:
To illustrate the concept of a generic interface, we will sort an array of people first by their names, then by their ages. The method that allows us to sort an array is the static method [Sort] of the class [Array]. It has different signatures (it is overloaded). We will use the following signature:

public static void Sort<T>(T[] tableau, IComparer<T>? comparateur)

[Sort] is a generic method where [T] denotes any type. The method takes two parameters:

  • [T[] tableau]: the array of elements of type [T] to be sorted;
  • [IComparer<T>? comparateur]: a reference to an object that implements the [IComparer<T>] interface.

[IComparer<T>] is a generic interface defined as follows (simplified definition):

public interface IComparer<in T>
{
    int Compare(T? x, T? y);
}

The [IComparer<T>] interface has only one method. The [Compare] method:

  • takes two parameters, [x] and [y], of type [T]. The type [T?] indicates that their values can be [null] (the keyword [in] is a technical detail that we will not explain here);
  • returns a positive number if x > y, 0 if x == y, and a negative number if x < y. It is up to the developer to define the meaning of the operators <, ==, and >. For example, if [p1] and [p2] are two [Personne] objects, we can say that p1 > p2 if the name of [p1] comes after the name of [p2] in alphabetical order. This will result in an ascending sort based on the people’s names. If we want to sort by age, we’ll say that p1 > p2 if the age of [p1] is greater than the age of [p2];
  • to sort in descending order, simply reverse the sign of the results.

We now know enough to sort an array of people. The program [classes-19.cs] is as follows:

// the generic interface IComparer<T>: sort an array of people
Personne[] personnes = [new Personne("claude", "pollon", 25), new Personne("valentine", "germain", 35), new Personne("paul", "germain", 32)];
// display
Affiche("Tableau à trier", personnes);
// sorting by first and last name
Array.Sort(personnes, new CompareNoms());
Affiche("Tableau après le tri selon les nom et prénom", personnes);
// Sorting by age
Array.Sort(personnes, new CompareAges());
Affiche("Tableau après le tri selon l'âge", personnes);

// displaying a table of people
static void Affiche(string texte, Personne[] personnes)
{
    Console.WriteLine(texte.PadRight(50, '-'));
    foreach (Personne p in personnes)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(p);
    }
}

// one person
class Personne
{
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        Prenom = prenom;
        Nom = nom;
        Age = age;
    }

    public string Prenom { get; }
    public string Nom { get; }
    public int Age { get; }

    public override string ToString() => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {Age}]";
}

// comparison of the first and last names of two people
class CompareNoms : IComparer<Personne>
{
    public int Compare(Personne? p1, Personne? p2)
    {
         // Excluding cases with null references
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p1);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p2);
         // Comparing names
        int i = string.Compare(p1.Nom, p2.Nom, StringComparison.CurrentCulture);
        if (i != 0)
        {
            return i;
        }
         // Name equality: comparing first names
        return string.Compare(p1.Prenom, p2.Prenom, StringComparison.CurrentCulture);
    }
}

// comparison of two people's ages
class CompareAges : IComparer<Personne>
{
    public int Compare(Personne? p1, Personne? p2)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p1);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p2);
         // comparing ages
        return p1.Age.CompareTo(p2.Age);
    }
}
  • Line 2: the array of people;
  • line 6: sorting the table of people by last name and first name. The second parameter of the generic method [Sort] is an instance of the class [CompareNoms], which implements the generic interface [IComparer<Personne>];
  • lines 40–54: the class [CompareNoms]. Its method [Compare] implements the method [int Compare(T? x, T? y)] of the interface [IComparer<T>], where [T] = [Personne]:
    • lines 45–46: Since the parameters are declared as type [Personne?], the compiler requires that a null reference be handled before using [p1] and [p2]. The static method [ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull] throws an exception if its parameter is [null]; the compiler knows that after it is called, the parameter is not null;
    • line 48: the method [string.Compare] compares two strings in alphabetical order according to the current culture, in this case French;
  • line 9: sorting the array of people by age, using an instance of the [CompareAges] class from lines 59–66. The [CompareTo] method for numeric types returns a negative, zero, or positive number depending on whether the number is less than, equal to, or greater than its parameter: this is exactly what the [Compare] method expects.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-19.cs
Tableau à trier-----------------------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[paul, germain, 32]
Tableau après le tri selon les nom et prénom------
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[claude, pollon, 25]
Tableau après le tri selon l'âge------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]

We will see in Chapter 7, which covers delegates, that we can also pass a simple comparison function to [Array.Sort] without writing a class: [Array.Sort(personnes, (p1, p2) => p1.Age.CompareTo(p2.Age));].

docs.title: 4.8.4. Abstract Static Members and Generic Mathematics
docs.text:
Can we write a generic method that sums the elements of an array of numbers, regardless of their type ([int], [double], [decimal]…)? We would need to be able to write [somme + valeur] and have the zero element of type [T]. However, the operator [+] is a static method, and a standard interface constraint only allows the use of instance methods. Since C# 11, an interface can declare abstract static members ([static abstract]), which every type that implements it must provide. .NET 7 has derived “generic mathematics” from this: All numeric types implement the [INumber<T>] interface in the [System.Numerics] namespace, which declares the type’s zero ([T.Zero]), arithmetic operators, and so on. The program [classes-20.cs] demonstrates this:

using System.Numerics;

// Abstract static interface members (C# 11) and generic math
Console.WriteLine($"Somme d'entiers : {Somme([1, 2, 3])}");
Console.WriteLine($"Somme de réels : {Somme([1.5, 2.25])}");
Console.WriteLine($"Somme de décimaux : {Somme([10.5m, 0.25m])}");
// Our own interface
Decrire<Chat>();
Decrire<Chien>();

// Sum of the elements in an array of numbers of type T
// INumber<T> declares abstract static members: T.Zero, the + operator, ...
static T Somme<T>(T[] valeurs) where T : INumber<T>
{
    T somme = T.Zero;
    foreach (T valeur in valeurs)
    {
        somme += valeur;
    }
    return somme;
}

// the method uses a static member of type T
static void Decrire<T>() where T : IAnimal
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{typeof(T).Name} : {T.Cri}");
}

interface IAnimal
{
     // static member that every class must implement
    static abstract string Cri { get; }
}

class Chat : IAnimal
{
    public static string Cri => "miaou";
}

class Chien : IAnimal
{
    public static string Cri => "ouaf";
}
  • lines 13–20: The generic method *[Somme] requires that *[T] implement *[INumber<T>]. It can then use the static member [T.Zero] (line 15) and the operator [+] of type [T]* (line 18);
  • lines 4–6: the same method adds together [int], [double], and [decimal]. Collection expressions create arrays of the expected type;
  • lines 29–32: a custom interface that declares an abstract static property [Cri];
  • lines 35–42: two classes implement the static property;
  • Lines 24–26: The generic method [Decrire] uses the static member [T.Cri] of type [T], without requiring an instance of that type. [typeof(T)] returns the description of the type [T], whose property [Name] is the name.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-20.cs
Somme d'entiers : 6
Somme de réels : 3,75
Somme de décimaux : 10,75
Chat : miaou
Chien : ouaf

docs.title: 4.9. Namespaces
docs.text:
To write a line on the screen, we use the [Console.WriteLine(...)] statement. If we look at the definition of the class [Console] in the documentation for .NET, we find that it is part of the namespace [System]. This means that the class [Console] should be referred to as [System.Console], and we should actually write [System.Console.WriteLine(...)]. We avoid this by using a [using] clause:

using System;
...
Console.WriteLine(...);

This means that the [System] namespace is imported along with the [using] clause. When the compiler encounters a class name (in this case, [Console]), it searches for it in the various namespaces imported by the [using] clauses. Here, it finds the class [Console] in the namespace [System]. In a recent .NET project, we don’t even need to write [using System;]: this namespace is included in the project’s implicit **using** statements, as we saw at the beginning of the chapter.

The documentation provides a second piece of information about the [Console] class: the assembly that contains it, the [System.Console.dll] file. An assembly is the result of compiling a project: a [.dll] file (library) or an executable. To use the classes in an assembly, the compiler must be aware of it. The 2008 course demonstrated how to pass these references to the [csc] compiler via the command line ([csc /r:fic1.dll /r:fic2.dll prog.cs]). Today, we no longer call the compiler directly: the assemblies of the .NET framework are referenced automatically, and the [.csproj] file references the other libraries, either as packages ([PackageReference]), or as projects ([ProjectReference]), as we will see in Chapter 6, which is devoted to layered architectures.

When creating a class, you can create it within a namespace. The purpose of these namespaces is to avoid name conflicts between classes, for example, when they are distributed. Consider two companies, E1 and E2, distributing packaged classes in the assemblies [e1.dll] and [e2.dll], respectively. Suppose a client C purchases these two sets of classes, in which both companies have defined a class named [Personne]. If the client’s program uses the class [Personne], the compiler will not know whether to use the class [Personne] from [e1.dll] or the one from [e2.dll]. It will report an error. If the company E1 creates its classes in a namespace named [E1] and the company E2 creates its classes in a namespace named [E2], the two classes named [Personne] will then be named [E1.Personne] and [E2.Personne]. The client must use either [E1.Personne] or [E2.Personne] (or an alias) in its classes, but not [Personne]. The namespace resolves this ambiguity.

To create a class in a namespace, the 2008 course stated:

namespace EspaceDeNoms
{
     // class definition
}

This format remains valid (it allows you to include multiple namespaces in a single file), but since C# 10, the file-scope namespace—[namespace EspaceDeNoms;]—placed at the beginning of the file is preferred, as it saves one level of indentation. This is the format we have been using since the beginning of this chapter.

The [EspacesDeNoms] project in the solution illustrates these concepts. It contains two classes, [Personne], in two different namespaces. The first, [E1/Personne.cs]:

// the classes in this file belong to the E1 namespace
namespace E1;

public class Personne
{
    private readonly string prenom;
    private readonly string nom;

    public Personne(string prenom, string nom)
    {
        this.prenom = prenom;
        this.nom = nom;
    }

    public override string ToString() => $"E1.Personne[{prenom}, {nom}]";
}

The second, *[E2/Personne.cs]*:

// The classes in this file belong to the E2 namespace
namespace E2;

public class Personne
{
    public Personne(string nom)
    {
        Nom = nom;
    }

    public string Nom { get; }

    public override string ToString() => $"E2.Personne[{Nom}]";
}

Note that a source file’s folder does not determine its namespace; only the declaration *[namespace]* matters. However, it is a useful convention to organize files from a single namespace into a folder with the same name.

The file [GlobalUsings.cs] contains the following clauses [global using] (C# 10):

// imports valid for all source files in the project
global using E1;
global using System.Text;

A [global using] directive applies to all source files in the project. This is how implicit using statements are implemented: during compilation, the SDK file generates a [obj/Debug/net10.0/EspacesDeNoms.GlobalUsings.g.cs] file that contains the lines [global using System;], [global using System.Collections.Generic;], [global using System.IO;], [global using System.Linq;], [global using System.Net.Http;], [global using System.Threading;], and [global using System.Threading.Tasks;]. You can also add a global "using" statement in the file [.csproj]: [<Using Include="E1" />].

The main program, [Program.cs], is as follows:

// namespace aliases and type aliases
using PersonneE2 = E2.Personne;
using Point = (int X, int Y);

// No one refers to E1.Personne: the namespace E1 is imported into GlobalUsings.cs
Personne p1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont");
// PersonneE2 is an alias for E2.Personne
PersonneE2 p2 = new PersonneE2("Durand");
// The full name of a class eliminates any ambiguity
E2.Personne p3 = new E2.Personne("Martin");
Console.WriteLine($"{p1} {p2} {p3}");
// full names of the types and the assembly that contains them
Console.WriteLine($"{typeof(Personne).FullName}, {typeof(PersonneE2).FullName}");
Console.WriteLine($"{typeof(Console).FullName} est dans l'assemblage {typeof(Console).Assembly.GetName().Name}");
// StringBuilder is known via the global `using` statement for System.Text
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("abc");
Console.WriteLine(sb.Append("def"));
// Point is an alias for the tuple type (int X, int Y)
Point origine = (0, 0);
Console.WriteLine($"origine=({origine.X},{origine.Y})");
  • line 2: an alias: in this file, [PersonneE2] refers to the class [E2.Personne];
  • line 3: Starting with C# 12, an alias can refer to any type; here, it refers to a tuple with two fields named [X] and [Y];
  • line 6: [Personne] refers to the class [E1.Personne], thanks to the clause [global using E1;]. If the namespace [E2] were also imported, the name [Personne] would be ambiguous and the compiler would reject it;
  • line 8: use of the alias;
  • line 10: the fully qualified class name resolves any ambiguity;
  • line 13: the property [FullName] of a type returns its full name, prefixed by its namespace;
  • line 14: the property [Assembly] of a type refers to the assembly that contains it;
  • line 16: the class [System.Text.StringBuilder] is defined via the clause [global using System.Text;];
  • line 19: use of the alias for the tuple type.

Results:

> dotnet run
E1.Personne[Jean, Dupont] E2.Personne[Durand] E2.Personne[Martin]
E1.Personne, E2.Personne
System.Console est dans l'assemblage System.Console
abcdef
origine=(0,0)

docs.title: 4.10. Records
docs.text:
Many classes serve only to carry data: a person, a grade, a tax bracket… For these, we always write the same code: a constructor that copies its parameters into properties, a [ToString] method that displays these properties, and often comparison methods. C# 9 introduced records: the compiler generates this code from a single-line declaration. We’ve already encountered the structure version ([record struct]); here’s the class version ([classes-21.cs]):

// records (C# 9)
Personne r1 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Personne r2 = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
// ToString generated by the compiler
Console.WriteLine(r1);
// Equality by value: r1 and r2 are two different objects but are equal
Console.WriteLine($"r1 == r2 : {r1 == r2}, même objet : {ReferenceEquals(r1, r2)}");
// properties are read-only (init)
// r1.Age = 31;    // rejected
// The `with` expression creates a modified copy
Personne r3 = r1 with { Age = 31 };
Console.WriteLine(r3);
Console.WriteLine($"r1 == r3 : {r1 == r3}");
// Destructuring into variables
var (prenom, nom, age) = r1;
Console.WriteLine($"prénom={prenom}, nom={nom}, âge={age}");

// the same thing with a class
PersonneC c1 = new PersonneC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
PersonneC c2 = new PersonneC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Console.WriteLine(c1);
Console.WriteLine($"c1 == c2 : {c1 == c2}");

// a derived record
Enseignant e = new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
Console.WriteLine(e);
Console.WriteLine(e.Identite);
// Equality takes type into account: a Person is not equal to a Teacher
Personne pe = new Personne("Lucile", "Dumas", 56);
Console.WriteLine($"pe == e : {pe == e}");

// a positional record: FirstName, LastName, Age are public properties { get; init; }
record Personne(string Prenom, string Nom, int Age)
{
     // Members can be added
    public virtual string Identite => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {Age}]";
}

// A record can be derived from another record
record Enseignant(string Prenom, string Nom, int Age, int Section) : Personne(Prenom, Nom, Age)
{
    public override string Identite => $"Enseignant[{base.Identite},{Section}]";
}

// An equivalent class... or almost
class PersonneC
{
    public PersonneC(string prenom, string nom, int age)
    {
        Prenom = prenom;
        Nom = nom;
        Age = age;
    }

    public string Prenom { get; init; }
    public string Nom { get; init; }
    public int Age { get; init; }
}
  • Lines 33–36: a positional record. The declaration [record Personne(string Prenom, string Nom, int Age)] generates:
    • a constructor with three parameters;
    • three read-only public properties: [Prenom], [Nom], and [Age] ([{ get; init; }]);
    • a method [ToString] that displays the type name and its public properties (line 5);
    • the methods [Equals] and [GetHashCode] and the operators [==] and [!=], which compare property values rather than references;
    • a method [Deconstruct] that breaks the object down into variables (line 15);
    • the expression [with];
    • a record can also, like a class, have additional members; here, the property [Identite];
  • Line 7: [r1] and [r2] are two distinct objects ([ReferenceEquals] is a reference to [false]) but they are equal in the sense of [] because their properties have the same values. For an ordinary class, [] compares the references (line 22);
  • line 11: Since a record is, in principle, immutable, it is not modified (line 9): the expression [with] creates a copy of [r1] in which certain properties have been changed;
  • lines 40–42: A record can be derived from another record (not from an ordinary class). The parameters [Prenom], [Nom], and [Age] are passed to the parent record’s constructor. The property [Identite], declared as [virtual] in [Personne], is redefined;
  • line 30: record equality takes into account the actual type of the objects: a [Personne] is never equal to a [Enseignant], even if their common properties are equal;
  • Lines 46–57: A class that resembles the record [Personne]… except that the constructor and properties had to be written, and equality between [ToString] and [with] is not provided.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-21.cs
Personne { Prenom = Jean, Nom = Dupont, Age = 30, Identite = [Jean, Dupont, 30] }
r1 == r2 : True, même objet : False
Personne { Prenom = Jean, Nom = Dupont, Age = 31, Identite = [Jean, Dupont, 31] }
r1 == r3 : False
prénom=Jean, nom=Dupont, âge=30
PersonneC
c1 == c2 : False
Enseignant { Prenom = Lucile, Nom = Dumas, Age = 56, Identite = Enseignant[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61], Section = 61 }
Enseignant[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
pe == e : False

Note that the generated method [ToString] also displays the calculated property [Identite] (line 2), whereas the class method [PersonneC] simply displays the class name (line 7).

Let’s summarize the differences between a class and a record:

ClassRecordEquality: [==], [Equals]same object (equal references)same property values, same type[ToString]type nametype name and public propertiesconstructor and propertiesto be writtenGenerated by the positional declaration, properties [init]modified copyto be writtenexpression [with]inheritancefrom a classfrom a record

A record is used for data defined by its value (a person retrieved from a database, a message exchanged over a network, a tax bracket), and a class is used for an object with an identity and behavior (a computing service, a connection, an editable list). A record is written as [record] (or [record class], which is identical) for a reference type, and [record struct] for a value type.

docs.title: 4.11. Primary constructors
docs.text:
Positional records declare their constructor parameters immediately after their name. Since C# 12, ordinary classes and structures can do the same: this is the primary constructor. The program [classes-22.cs] illustrates this:

// primary constructors (C# 12)
Personne p = new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
p.Vieillir();
Console.WriteLine(p.Identite);
// another constructor
Personne inconnu = new Personne("Martin");
Console.WriteLine(inconnu.Identite);
// a derived class
Enseignant e = new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
Console.WriteLine(e.Identite);
// a struct
Point pt = new Point(3, 4);
Console.WriteLine($"pt=({pt.X},{pt.Y}), distance à l'origine : {pt.Distance()}");

// a class with a default constructor
class Personne(string prenom, string nom, int age)
{
     // The first_name and last_name parameters are used to initialize properties
    public string Prenom { get; } = prenom;
    public string Nom { get; } = nom;
     // The `age` parameter is used by methods: it is stored in a hidden field
    public int Age => age;

     // Any other constructor must call the primary constructor
    public Personne(string nom) : this("?", nom, 0)
    {
    }

    public void Vieillir() => age++;

    public virtual string Identite => $"[{Prenom}, {Nom}, {age}]";
}

// A derived class: it passes three of its parameters to the primary constructor of the parent class
class Enseignant(string prenom, string nom, int age, int section) : Personne(prenom, nom, age)
{
    public int Section { get; } = section;

    public override string Identite => $"Enseignant[{base.Identite},{Section}]";
}

// a struct with a primary constructor
readonly struct Point(double x, double y)
{
    public double X { get; } = x;
    public double Y { get; } = y;

    public double Distance() => Math.Sqrt(X * X + Y * Y);
}
  • line 17: the class [Personne] has a primary constructor with three parameters. Unlike those of a record, these parameters do not become public properties: they are parameters, visible throughout the entire body of the class;
  • lines 20–21: the parameters [prenom] and [nom] are used to initialize two read-only properties;
  • line 23: the parameter [age] is used by members of the class: the property [Age], the method [Vieillir] (line 30), and the property [Identite]. The compiler then stores it in a hidden field, which can be modified ([age++]). It is recommended not to mix these two uses for the same parameter (initializing a property and using it directly), as this may result in two copies of the same data;
  • line 26: a class with a primary constructor may have other constructors, but these must call the primary constructor using [this(...)];
  • line 36: A derived class passes some of the parameters from its primary constructor to the constructor of its parent class: [: Personne(prenom, nom, age)]. This is equivalent to [: base(prenom, nom, age)] in a traditional constructor;
  • line 44: A structure can also have a primary constructor.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-22.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 31]
[?, Martin, 0]
Enseignant[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
pt=(3,4), distance à l'origine : 5

The primary constructor eliminates repetitive code from constructors that merely store their parameters. It is widely used for classes that receive services during construction, as we will see with dependency injection (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 4.12. Extension Methods and Members
docs.text:
How do you add a method to a class that cannot be modified, such as the class [string] derived from .NET? C# 3 introduced extension methods: static methods that are used as instance methods of the extended type. C# 14 extends this mechanism to properties and static members with extension blocks. The program [classes-23.cs] demonstrates both:

// extension methods (C# 3) and extension members (C# 14)
Personne p = new Personne("jean", "dupont", 30);
// classic extension methods: they are used like instance methods
Console.WriteLine(p.Initiales());
Console.WriteLine("jean".PremiereMajuscule());
// The previous call is translated by the compiler into the following static method call
Console.WriteLine(ExtensionsClassiques.PremiereMajuscule("jean"));
// extension properties (C# 14)
Console.WriteLine($"{p.NomComplet} est majeur : {p.EstMajeur}");
Console.WriteLine($"\"il fait beau\" a {"il fait beau".NbMots} mots");
// Static extension member (C# 14): It is used with the type name
Personne inconnue = Personne.Inconnue;
Console.WriteLine($"{inconnue.NomComplet} est majeur : {inconnue.EstMajeur}");

// a person
record Personne(string Prenom, string Nom, int Age);

// traditional extension methods: static methods of a static class,
// whose first parameter is preceded by the keyword `this`
static class ExtensionsClassiques
{
    public static string Initiales(this Personne p)
    {
        return $"{char.ToUpper(p.Prenom[0])}.{char.ToUpper(p.Nom[0])}.";
    }

    public static string PremiereMajuscule(this string s)
    {
        return s.Length == 0 ? s : char.ToUpper(s[0]) + s[1..];
    }
}

// extension blocks (C# 14)
static class ExtensionsCs14
{
     // instance members added to the Person type: p refers to the extended object
    extension(Personne p)
    {
        public bool EstMajeur => p.Age >= 18;

        public string NomComplet => $"{p.Prenom.PremiereMajuscule()} {p.Nom.ToUpper()}";
    }

     // static members added to the Person type
    extension(Personne)
    {
        public static Personne Inconnue => new Personne("?", "?", 0);
    }

     // a property added to the `string` type
    extension(string s)
    {
        public int NbMots => s.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Length;
    }
}
  • lines 20–29: Traditional extension methods are static methods of a static class. Their first parameter, preceded by the keyword [this], specifies the extended object:
    • [Initiales(this Personne p)] extends the type [Personne]: it is called [p.Initiales()] (line 4);
    • [PremiereMajuscule(this string s)] extends the type [string]: it is called ["jean".PremiereMajuscule()] (line 5). The expression [s[1..]] refers to the substring starting at character #1;
  • line 7: an extension method remains an ordinary static method: the compiler translates ["jean".PremiereMajuscule()] into this call. The method has access only to the public members of the extended object;
  • lines 34–53: the C# 14 extension blocks, also declared within a static class:
    • lines 37–41: the block ***[extension(Personne p)] adds the instance members it contains to the type *[Personne]. *[p]* refers to the extended object. Properties can now be added ([EstMajeur], [NomComplet]), which was not possible with traditional extension methods;
    • lines 45–47: the block [extension(Personne)], with no parameter names, adds static members to the type [Personne]: [Personne.Inconnue] (line 12) is written as if the property had been declared in the record [Personne];
    • Lines 51–53: An extension property of type [string], used on line 10.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-23.cs
J.D.
Jean
Jean
Jean DUPONT est majeur : True
"il fait beau" a 3 mots
? ? est majeur : False

Extension methods are ubiquitous in .NET: the operators of LINQ ([Where], [Select], [OrderBy]…), discussed in the next chapter, are extension methods of the [IEnumerable<T>] interface. For an extension to be usable, the namespace of its static class must be imported.

docs.title: 4.13. Pattern Filtering on Objects
docs.text:
The expression [switch] and pattern filtering are not limited to simple values (numbers, strings); they also apply to objects. You can test an object’s type, check the values of its properties, and retrieve the object converted to the correct type—all in a single expression. The program [classes-24.cs] uses a hierarchy of three records:

// pattern matching on objects
object?[] objets =
[
    new Personne("Jean", "Dupont", 30),
    new Personne("Lise", "Morel", 12),
    new Enseignant("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61),
    new Enseignant("Marc", "Petit", 44, 27),
    new Etudiant("Paul", "Martin", 19, "informatique"),
    "une chaîne",
    42,
    null,
];

// 1 - the pattern of type: is Variable Type
foreach (object? o in objets)
{
    if (o is Personne p)
    {
         // Here, p is a Person (or an object of a derived class)
        Console.WriteLine($"{p.Prenom} est de type {p.GetType().Name}");
    }
}

// 2 - the property pattern: { Property: pattern }
foreach (object? o in objets)
{
    if (o is Personne { Age: >= 18 } adulte)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{adulte.Prenom} est majeur");
    }
}

// 3 - the switch expression based on the object’s type and properties
foreach (object? o in objets)
{
    Console.WriteLine(Decrire(o));
}

static string Decrire(object? o) => o switch
{
    Enseignant { Section: 27 } e => $"{e.Prenom} enseigne l'informatique",
    Enseignant e => $"{e.Prenom} enseigne dans la section {e.Section}",
    Etudiant(var prenom, _, _, var filiere) => $"{prenom} étudie {filiere}",
    Personne { Age: < 18 } p => $"{p.Prenom} est mineur",
    Personne p => $"{p.Prenom} a {p.Age} ans",
    string s => $"une chaîne de {s.Length} caractères",
    int n and > 0 => $"l'entier positif {n}",
    null => "la référence null",
    _ => "un objet inconnu",
};

record Personne(string Prenom, string Nom, int Age);
record Enseignant(string Prenom, string Nom, int Age, int Section) : Personne(Prenom, Nom, Age);
record Etudiant(string Prenom, string Nom, int Age, string Filiere) : Personne(Prenom, Nom, Age);
  • lines 52–54: a [Personne] record and two derived records, [Enseignant] and [Etudiant];
  • lines 2–11: an array of objects of various types (the type [object?] also accepts [null]);
  • line 17: the pattern of type [o is Personne p] is true if [o] references an object of type [Personne] or a derived type; in this case, the variable [p], of type [Personne], references this object. This avoids the sequence from the 2008 course: testing the type with [is], then converting with [(Personne)o]. The pattern is false if [o] is equal to [null];
  • line 27: the property pattern [{ Age: >= 18 }] (C# 8) tests the value of a property of the object, in this case using a relational pattern [>= 18] (C# 9). Multiple properties can be tested by separating them with commas;
  • lines 39–49: the expression [switch] tries the patterns in order and returns the value associated with the first one that matches:
    • line 41: a teacher from section 27;
    • line 42: any other teacher. The order is important: if placed before the previous one, this pattern would have made it inaccessible, which the compiler would have flagged as an error;
    • line 43: a positional pattern: it uses the method [Deconstruct] of the record [Etudiant] to extract its properties in the order they were declared; [_] ignores a property;
    • line 44: a minor;
    • line 47: a positive integer, using the [and] combinator (C# 9); there are also [or] and [not];
    • line 48: the pattern [null];
    • line 49: the pattern [_] accepts everything. Without it, the compiler would report that the expression [switch] does not cover all cases.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-24.cs
Jean est de type Personne
Lise est de type Personne
Lucile est de type Enseignant
Marc est de type Enseignant
Paul est de type Etudiant
Jean est majeur
Lucile est majeur
Marc est majeur
Paul est majeur
Jean a 30 ans
Lise est mineur
Lucile enseigne dans la section 61
Marc enseigne l'informatique
Paul étudie informatique
une chaîne de 10 caractères
l'entier positif 42
la référence null

Note that the type pattern also matches derived types: the type pattern loop (lines 2–6) captured the teachers and the student, who are people. Pattern matching is a useful alternative to cascading [if (o is ...)]; however, it should not replace polymorphism: when behavior depends on the object’s type and you have control over the class hierarchy, a virtual method redefined in each class remains the object-oriented solution.

docs.title: 4.14. Nullable reference types
docs.text:
Since the beginning of this chapter, our projects have had nullable reference types enabled ([<Nullable>enable</Nullable>] in [.csproj], an option enabled by default in single-file applications). The principle is as follows:

  • A variable, field, parameter, or reference-type result declared without a question mark—for example, of type [Personne]—is never supposed to be equal to [null];
  • if it can be [null], it is declared with a question mark: [Personne?];
  • the compiler analyzes the program flow and issues a warning whenever a potentially null value is used without verification, or assigned to a non-nullable variable.

The language does not prohibit anything at runtime: these are compilation warnings, but a program that compiles without warnings is much less prone to the [NullReferenceException] exception, the most common runtime error. The 2008 course, which predates this feature (C# 8, 2019), obviously did not cover it. The program [classes-25.cs] demonstrates the operators associated with nullable types:

// nullable reference types applied to objects
Personne[] personnes = [new Personne("Jean", "Dupont") { SecondPrenom = "Marie" }, new Personne("Paul", "Martin")];
foreach (Personne p in personnes)
{
     // ?. : returns null if the left-hand object is null; otherwise, accesses the member
    int? longueur = p.SecondPrenom?.Length;
     // ??: returns the right-hand operand if the left-hand operand is null
    Console.WriteLine($"{p.Prenom} : second prénom={p.SecondPrenom ?? "(aucun)"}, longueur={longueur?.ToString() ?? "null"}");
}

// a method that can return null: its return type is Person?
Personne? trouvee = Chercher(personnes, "Durand");
Console.WriteLine(trouvee?.Prenom ?? "Durand : personne non trouvée");
// After a check, the compiler knows that the reference is not null
trouvee = Chercher(personnes, "Martin");
if (trouvee is not null)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Martin : {trouvee.Prenom}");
}
// ??=: assigns a value only if the variable (or property) is null
personnes[1].SecondPrenom ??= "Pierre";
personnes[0].SecondPrenom ??= "Pierre";
Console.WriteLine($"{personnes[0].SecondPrenom}, {personnes[1].SecondPrenom}");
// C# 14: conditional assignment: it only occurs if the object is not null
Chercher(personnes, "Dupont")?.SecondPrenom = "Louise";
Chercher(personnes, "Durand")?.SecondPrenom = "Louise";
Console.WriteLine(personnes[0].SecondPrenom);
// ! : tells the compiler that the reference is not null
Personne martin = Chercher(personnes, "Martin")!;
Console.WriteLine(martin.Prenom);
// The following lines trigger compiler warnings
// Console.WriteLine(new Person("Lise", "Morel").SecondPrenom.Length);   // warning
// Person dupond = Search(people, "Dupond"); // wa  rning
// people[0] = null; /  / warning

// searching for a person by name
static Personne? Chercher(Personne[] personnes, string nom)
{
    foreach (Personne p in personnes)
    {
        if (p.Nom == nom)
        {
            return p;
        }
    }
    return null;
}

class Personne
{
    public Personne(string prenom, string nom)
    {
        Prenom = prenom;
        Nom = nom;
    }

     // non-nullable properties: they must never be null
    public string Prenom { get; }
    public string Nom { get; }
     // nullable property: null means “no middle name”
    public string? SecondPrenom { get; set; }
}
  • lines 58–61: The class [Personne] has two non-nullable properties, initialized by the constructor, and one nullable property, [SecondPrenom]: [null] means “no middle name”;
  • line 6: the [?.] operator (C# 6) returns [null] if the object on its left is [null], and accesses the member otherwise. The result is of type [int?];
  • line 8: the operator [??] returns its left operand if it is not [null], and its right operand otherwise;
  • lines 37–46: the function [Chercher] returns the person being searched for or [null]; its return type is [Personne?];
  • line 13: the two operators are combined;
  • lines 16–18: After the [is not null] check, the compiler knows that [trouvee] is not equal to [null]: [trouvee.Prenom] can be written without a warning;
  • lines 21–22: the operator [??=] only assigns a value to the property if it is [null]: Jean’s middle name, “Marie,” is not replaced;
  • lines 25–26: C# 14 allows [?.] on the left side of an assignment: the assignment is performed only if the object is not null. Dupont exists and is given a new middle name; Durand does not exist, and the statement does nothing;
  • line 29: the [!] operator (a “null-forgiving” operator) tells the compiler that we know the value is not null: it does not issue a warning. It’s up to the developer to be sure of this: if the value is null at runtime, an error will occur later on. Use sparingly;
  • lines 32–34: three statements that trigger warnings.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-25.cs
Jean : second prénom=Marie, longueur=5
Paul : second prénom=(aucun), longueur=null
Durand : personne non trouvée
Martin : Paul
Marie, Pierre
Louise
Paul

Let’s uncomment the last three lines of the main program and compile:

> dotnet build classes-25.cs
classes-25.cs(32,19): warning CS8602: Déréférencement d'une éventuelle référence null.
classes-25.cs(33,19): warning CS8600: Conversion de littéral ayant une valeur null ou d'une éventuelle valeur null en type non-nullable.
classes-25.cs(34,16): warning CS8625: Impossible de convertir un littéral ayant une valeur null en type référence non-nullable.
  • Warning [CS8602]: The property [SecondPrenom] of a newly created person may be [null]: You cannot use its property [Length] without verification;
  • Warning [CS8600]: The function [Chercher] may return [null], a value that is assigned to a non-nullable variable of type [Personne];
  • Warning [CS8625]: The constant [null] is assigned to an element of type [Personne], which is non-nullable.

The program would run despite these warnings, but the first line would throw a [NullReferenceException] exception. In this course, all programs compile without any warnings: we correct the code (by declaring the type as nullable, checking the value, or providing a default value using [??]) rather than ignoring the warning or suppressing it with [!].

docs.title: 4.15. Sample Application - V2
docs.text:
We’ll revisit the tax calculation we covered in the previous chapter (Version 1) and implement it using classes and interfaces. Let’s review the problem. We aim to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. We’ll consider the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only a single salary to report (using the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, kept as-is: this is an exercise):

  • we calculate the employee’s number of tax brackets: nbParts = nbEnfants / 2 + 1 if they are unmarried, nbEnfants / 2 + 2 if he is married, where nbEnfants is the number of his children;
  • if he has at least three children, he receives an additional half-share;
  • his taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.72 × S, where S is his annual salary;
  • his family quotient is calculated as QF = R / nbParts;
  • his tax I is calculated using the following table:
thresholdcoeffRcoeffN49620083820.068291.0914,7530.1911,322.9223,8880.2832,668.3938,8680.3744,846.9847,9320.4266,883.6600.4819,505.54

Each row has three fields. To calculate tax I, find the first row where QF ≤ the limit. For example, if QF = 5,000, the row (8,382; 0.068; 291.09) will be found. Tax I is then equal to 0.068 × R - 291.09 × nbParts. If QF is such that the condition QF ≤ limit is never satisfied, then the coefficients of the last row are used, resulting in tax I = 0.481 × R - 9,505.54 × nbParts.

The application generates the [ImpotsV2] project from the solution:

ImpotsV2/
  TrancheImpot.cs      une tranche du barème
  IImpot.cs            l'interface du calcul de l'impôt
  AbstractImpot.cs     une classe abstraite implémentant IImpot
  HardwiredImpot.cs    une classe dérivée, avec des données écrites en dur
  Program.cs           le programme de dialogue avec l'utilisateur
  ImpotsV2.csproj

First, we define a type capable of encapsulating a row from the previous array [TrancheImpot.cs]:

namespace ImpotsV2;

// a tax bracket
public readonly record struct TrancheImpot(decimal Limite, decimal CoeffR, decimal CoeffN);

The 2008 course used a structure with three automatic read-write properties. We use an immutable record structure ([readonly record struct]):

  • a structure because a slice is a small piece of data without an identity, defined solely by its value: an array of slices directly contains the slices, without a separate object in memory for each one. With three [decimal] (48 bytes), the structure exceeds the size of approximately 16 bytes usually recommended for a structure; this is not a problem here: there are few segments, and they are copied only when they are read;
  • immutable ([readonly]) because there is no reason for a tax bracket segment to be modified once it has been created. The 2008 course, incidentally, modified the limit of the last tax bracket segment during the calculation—a side effect that we are eliminating;
  • a record ([record]) because the compiler generates the constructor, the properties, [ToString], and the equality operator from a single line.

Then we define an interface [IImpot] capable of calculating the tax [IImpot.cs]:

namespace ImpotsV2;

public interface IImpot
{
     // calculation of a taxpayer’s tax
    int Calculer(bool marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire);
}
  • Line 6: The method for calculating the tax based on three pieces of data: the taxpayer’s marital status, the number of children, and annual salary. It returns the tax rounded down to the nearest euro.

Next, we define an abstract class that implements this interface [AbstractImpot.cs]:

namespace ImpotsV2;

public abstract class AbstractImpot : IImpot
{
     // The tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
     // known only to derived classes
    protected abstract TrancheImpot[] TranchesImpot { get; }

     // tax calculation
    public int Calculer(bool marie, int nbEnfants, int salaire)
    {
         // Calculation of the number of shares
        decimal nbParts = (decimal)nbEnfants / 2 + (marie ? 2 : 1);
        if (nbEnfants >= 3)
        {
            nbParts += 0.5m;
        }
         // Calculation of taxable income and the family quotient
        decimal revenu = 0.72m * salaire;
        decimal quotient = revenu / nbParts;
         // Determination of the tax bracket: the last one is used if no other bracket applies
        TrancheImpot[] tranches = TranchesImpot;
        TrancheImpot tranche = tranches[^1];
        for (int i = 0; i < tranches.Length - 1; i++)
        {
            if (quotient <= tranches[i].Limite)
            {
                tranche = tranches[i];
                break;
            }
        }
         // tax calculation
        return (int)(revenu * tranche.CoeffR - nbParts * tranche.CoeffN);
    }
}
  • Line 3: The class [AbstractImpot] implements the interface [IImpot];
  • line 7: the scale data, in the form of a protected abstract property. The class [AbstractImpot] does not know where this data comes from (written in the code, read from a file, a database, etc.). It leaves this up to the derived classes. This is why it is declared abstract, which prevents it from being instantiated. The 2008 course used a protected field that derived classes had to initialize; the abstract property requires derived classes to provide it: the compiler verifies this;
  • lines 10–33: the implementation of the [Calculer] method of the [IImpot] interface. Derived classes will not need to rewrite this method. The [AbstractImpot] class thus serves as a factorization class for the derived classes: it contains what is common to all of them;
  • line 13: the number of shares. The conversion [(decimal)nbEnfants] is essential: without it, [nbEnfants / 2] would be an integer division (3 / 2 = 1). The expression [marie ? 2 : 1] equals 2 for a married taxpayer, 1 otherwise;
  • Lines 19–20: taxable income and the family quotient. All calculations are performed using [decimal], a type adapted to the amounts: the suffix [m] of [0.72m] denotes a constant of this type;
  • Lines 22–29: Determining the tax bracket. By default, this is the last bracket ([tranches[^1]], line 23). The loop iterates through all brackets except the last one and stops ([break]) at the first bracket whose limit is greater than or equal to the family quotient;
  • line 33: tax calculation. The conversion [(int)] truncates the result [decimal] to its integer part.

A class that implements the [IImpot] interface can be created by deriving it from the [AbstractImpot] class. This is what we will now do with [HardwiredImpot.cs]:

namespace ImpotsV2;

public class HardwiredImpot : AbstractImpot
{
     // tax calculation data (2004 tax schedule for 2003 income), hard-coded
    private static readonly decimal[] limites = [4962m, 8382m, 14753m, 23888m, 38868m, 47932m, 0m];
    private static readonly decimal[] coeffR = [0m, 0.068m, 0.191m, 0.283m, 0.374m, 0.426m, 0.481m];
    private static readonly decimal[] coeffN = [0m, 291.09m, 1322.92m, 2668.39m, 4846.98m, 6883.66m, 9505.54m];

     // Tax brackets
    private readonly TrancheImpot[] tranchesImpot;

     // generator
    public HardwiredImpot()
    {
         // Creation and population of the tax bracket table
        tranchesImpot = new TrancheImpot[limites.Length];
        for (int i = 0; i < tranchesImpot.Length; i++)
        {
            tranchesImpot[i] = new TrancheImpot(limites[i], coeffR[i], coeffN[i]);
        }
    }

     // Implementation of the parent class’s abstract property
    protected override TrancheImpot[] TranchesImpot => tranchesImpot;
}
  • Lines 6–8: The class [HardwiredImpot] hard-codes the data needed to calculate the tax. These are class fields ([static]) that are read-only ([readonly]): they are shared by all instances and cannot be replaced by other arrays;
  • lines 14–20: the constructor uses this data to build the tax bracket table;
  • line 25: the parent class’s abstract property is implemented: it returns the tax bracket table.

The next chapter will add other classes derived from [AbstractImpot], which will read the tax brackets from a text file or JSON: they will only need to provide the [TranchesImpot] property.

A test program might look like the following [Program.cs]:

using ImpotsV2;

// Interactive tax calculation program
// The user enters three pieces of data via the keyboard: married nbEnfants salary
// The program then displays the tax due

const string syntaxe = """
    syntaxe : Marié NbEnfants Salaire
    Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
    NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants
    Salaire : salaire annuel en euros
    """;

// creation of an object IImpot
IImpot impot = new HardwiredImpot();

// input loop
while (true)
{
     // The program prompts for the tax calculation parameters
    Console.Write("Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : ");
    string parametres = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "").Trim();
     // Is there anything to do?
    if (parametres == "")
    {
        break;
    }
     // Checking the number of fields in the entered row
    string[] champs = parametres.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
    if (champs.Length != 3)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntaxe);
        continue;
    }
     // Checking parameter validity
     // Married
    string marie = champs[0].ToLower();
    if (marie != "o" && marie != "n")
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntaxe + "\nArgument marié incorrect : tapez o ou n");
        continue;
    }
     // nbEnfants
    if (!int.TryParse(champs[1], out int nbEnfants) || nbEnfants < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntaxe + "\nArgument NbEnfants incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
        continue;
    }
     // salary
    if (!int.TryParse(champs[2], out int salaire) || salaire < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntaxe + "\nArgument salaire incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul");
        continue;
    }
     // The parameters are correct: calculate the tax
    Console.WriteLine($"Impôt={impot.Calculer(marie == "o", nbEnfants, salaire)} euros");
}

The program above allows the user to perform repeated tax calculation simulations.

  • lines 7–11: the help message is written as a raw string literal (C# 11), delimited by three quotation marks: the string can span multiple lines, and the common indentation of the lines, determined by the position of the closing quotation marks, is removed;
  • Line 15: Creation of a [impot] object that implements the [IImpot] interface. This object is obtained by instantiating a type [HardwiredImpot], a type that implements the [IImpot] interface. Note that the variable [impot] was not assigned the type [HardwiredImpot] but rather the type [IImpot]. By writing this, we indicate that we are only interested in the [Calculer] method of the [impot] object and not in the rest. To use data from a file, simply change this single line;
  • lines 18–56: the loop for tax calculation simulations;
  • line 22: the three parameters required for the [Calculer] method are requested in a single line entered via the keyboard. [Console.ReadLine] returns [null] if standard input is closed: the operator [??] then replaces [null] with an empty string, which terminates the program;
  • line 29: the method [Split] splits the line into words separated by spaces, with the option [StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries] removing empty words caused by consecutive spaces;
  • lines 44–50: the method [int.TryParse] verifies that the last two fields are integers; the declaration [out int nbEnfants] creates the variable that receives the number. The 2008 course used [int.Parse] within a [try / catch] block;
  • line 56: call to the [Calculer] method of the [impot] object implementing the [IImpot] interface.

Here is an example of the program in action:

> dotnet run
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : q s d
syntaxe : Marié NbEnfants Salaire
Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants
Salaire : salaire annuel en euros
Argument marié incorrect : tapez o ou n
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : o 2 d

Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié
NbEnfants : nombre d'enfants

Argument salaire incorrect : tapez un entier positif ou nul

Marié : o pour marié, n pour non marié

Salaire : salaire annuel en euros

Impôt=4282 euros
