Console.WriteLine($"Take(2)=[{string.Join(", ", noms.Take(2))}], Skip(5)=[{string.Join(", ", noms.Skip(5))}]");
Console.WriteLine($"Skip(2).Take(2)=[{string.Join(", ", noms.Skip(2).Take(2))}], TakeWhile(longueur 6)=[{string.Join(", ", noms.TakeWhile(n => n.Length == 6))}]");

// Chunk: division into fixed-size chunks (pagination)
int page = 1;
foreach (Personne[] paquet in personnes.Chunk(3))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"page {page++} : {string.Join(", ", paquet.Select(p => p.Nom))}");
}

record Personne(string Nom, string Prenom, int Age, string Ville);

Results:

> dotnet run linq-03.cs
Any(mineur)=True, All(mineur)=False, Any()=True
Count()=7, Count(Angers)=3
Sum(âge)=221, Average(âge)=31,57
Min(âge)=15, Max(âge)=52
MinBy(âge)=moreau, MaxBy(âge)=simon
First()=dupont, First(Paris)=martin, Last()=laurent
FirstOrDefault(Brest)=null
Single(Lyon)=laurent
Single(Angers) : InvalidOperationException : Sequence contains more than one matching element
First(Brest) : InvalidOperationException : Sequence contains no matching element
Distinct(villes)=[Angers, Paris, Nantes, Lyon]
DistinctBy(ville)=[dupont, martin, leroy, laurent]
Take(2)=[dupont, martin], Skip(5)=[simon, laurent]
Skip(2).Take(2)=[durand, leroy], TakeWhile(longueur 6)=[dupont, martin, durand]
page 1 : dupont, martin, durand
page 2 : leroy, moreau, simon
page 3 : laurent

Comments:

  • Line 15: [Any] returns [true] if at least one element satisfies the condition, and [All] if all of them satisfy it. Without parameters, [Any] indicates whether the sequence is non-empty;
  • Lines 18–20: The aggregates [Count], [Sum], [Average], [Min], [Max] calculate a value based on the entire sequence. [Count] accepts a condition (a list also has a property [Count], which is preferred over the method when there is no condition); [Sum], [Average], [Min], and [Max] accept a lambda that specifies the value to be considered for each element;
  • Line 22: [MinBy] and [MaxBy] (.NET 6) return the element (in this case, the person) for which the key is the minimum or maximum, not the key value itself. For an empty sequence of objects (reference type), they return [null], hence the operator [?.];
  • line 25: [First] returns the first element of the sequence, or the first one that satisfies a condition; [Last] returns the last one;
  • Line 26: If no element matches, [First] throws an exception (line 11 of the results), whereas [FirstOrDefault] returns the default value for the type, in this case [null];
  • Line 28: [Single] returns the single element that satisfies the condition and throws an exception if there are zero or more such elements (line 10). This is used when uniqueness is a rule of the data, such as searching for an element by its key. [SingleOrDefault] returns the default value if there are no elements;
  • line 32: the result of the call is not used; it is assigned to the ignored element [_] (C# 7) to flag it;
  • line 49: [Distinct] removes duplicates; [DistinctBy] (.NET 6) keeps the first element of each key value;
  • lines 57–58: [Take(n)] keeps the first n elements, [Skip(n)] skips them. Combined, they extract a “page” of results. [TakeWhile] keeps the elements as long as a condition is met and stops at the first element that does not meet it;
  • line 62: [Chunk] (.NET 6) splits the sequence into arrays of 3 elements, the last of which may be shorter;
  • line 64: the variable [page] is incremented after being used in the interpolation.

docs.title: 5.5.4. Anonymous Types, Groupings, Joins
docs.text:
The program [linq-04.cs] introduces anonymous types and more complex operations:

// LINQ: anonymous types, groupings, joins, conversions

List<Personne> personnes =
[
    new("dupont", "jean", 45, "Angers"),
    new("martin", "marie", 17, "Paris"),
    new("durand", "paul", 32, "Angers"),
    new("leroy", "sophie", 28, "Nantes"),
    new("moreau", "luc", 15, "Paris"),
    new("simon", "julie", 52, "Angers"),
    new("laurent", "marc", 32, "Lyon"),
];
List<Ville> villes =
[
    new("Angers", "Maine-et-Loire"),
    new("Nantes", "Loire-Atlantique"),
    new("Paris", "Paris"),
    new("Brest", "Finistère"),
];

// 1 - An anonymous type: an object whose nameless type is created by the compiler
var p1 = new { Nom = "dupont", Age = 45 };
Console.WriteLine($"[type anonyme] {p1}, p1.Nom={p1.Nom}");
// SELECT into an anonymous type: only the useful properties are retained
var resumes = personnes.Where(p => p.Age > 40).Select(p => new { p.Nom, Decennie = p.Age / 10 * 10 });
foreach (var r in resumes)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {r.Nom} a plus de {r.Decennie} ans");
}

// 2 - GroupBy: grouping people by city
Console.WriteLine("[GroupBy]");
foreach (IGrouping<string, Personne> groupe in personnes.GroupBy(p => p.Ville))
{
     // A group has a key and is itself a sequence of people
    Console.WriteLine($"  {groupe.Key} : {groupe.Count()} personne(s), âge moyen {groupe.Average(p => p.Age):F1} ({string.Join(", ", groupe.Select(p => p.Nom))})");
}

// 3 - Join: associating people and cities based on the city name
Console.WriteLine("[Join]");
var jointure = personnes.Join(villes,
    p => p.Ville,                                    // key on the people side
    v => v.Nom,                                      // key on the city side
    (p, v) => new { p.Nom, v.Departement });         // what we retain from a pair
foreach (var j in jointure)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {j.Nom} habite le département {j.Departement}");
}
// the same join in query syntax: Lyon, which is not on the list of cities, also disappears
var jointure2 = from p in personnes
                join v in villes on p.Ville equals v.Nom
                where p.Age >= 18
                select $"{p.Nom}/{v.Departement}";
Console.WriteLine($"[join en syntaxe de requête] {string.Join(", ", jointure2)}");

// 4 - conversions: ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary
List<string> nomsMajeurs = personnes.Where(p => p.Age >= 18).Select(p => p.Nom).ToList();
Dictionary<string, int> agesParNom = personnes.ToDictionary(p => p.Nom, p => p.Age);
Console.WriteLine($"[ToList] {nomsMajeurs.Count} majeurs ; [ToDictionary] agesParNom[\"leroy\"]={agesParNom["leroy"]}");

// 5 - .NET 9: CountBy, AggregateBy, Index
Console.WriteLine("[CountBy]");
foreach (KeyValuePair<string, int> paire in personnes.CountBy(p => p.Ville))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {paire.Key}={paire.Value}");
}
Console.WriteLine("[AggregateBy : somme des âges par ville]");
foreach (var (ville, total) in personnes.AggregateBy(p => p.Ville, 0, (somme, p) => somme + p.Age))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {ville}={total}");
}
Console.WriteLine("[Index]");
foreach (var (index, personne) in personnes.Where(p => p.Age < 30).Index())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {index} : {personne.Nom}");
}

record Personne(string Nom, string Prenom, int Age, string Ville);
record Ville(string Nom, string Departement);

Results:

> dotnet run linq-04.cs
[type anonyme] { Nom = dupont, Age = 45 }, p1.Nom=dupont
  dupont a plus de 40 ans
  simon a plus de 50 ans
[GroupBy]
  Angers : 3 personne(s), âge moyen 43,0 (dupont, durand, simon)
  Paris : 2 personne(s), âge moyen 16,0 (martin, moreau)
  Nantes : 1 personne(s), âge moyen 28,0 (leroy)
  Lyon : 1 personne(s), âge moyen 32,0 (laurent)
[Join]
  dupont habite le département Maine-et-Loire
  martin habite le département Paris
  durand habite le département Maine-et-Loire
  leroy habite le département Loire-Atlantique
  moreau habite le département Paris
  simon habite le département Maine-et-Loire
[join en syntaxe de requête] dupont/Maine-et-Loire, durand/Maine-et-Loire, leroy/Loire-Atlantique, simon/Maine-et-Loire
[ToList] 5 majeurs ; [ToDictionary] agesParNom["leroy"]=28
[CountBy]
  Angers=3
  Paris=2
  Nantes=1
  Lyon=1
[AggregateBy : somme des âges par ville]
  Angers=129
  Paris=32
  Nantes=28
  Lyon=32
[Index]
  0 : martin
  1 : leroy
  2 : moreau

Comments:

  • Line 22: an anonymous type (C# 3): the expression [new { Nom = ..., Age = ... }] creates an object whose nameless class is generated by the compiler with two read-only properties, [Nom] and [Age]. Since this type has no name, the variable must be declared as [var]. The compiler, however, is fully aware of this type: [p1.Nom] is validated at compile time, and the editor suggests the properties of [p1] in autocomplete;
  • line 25: the main use of anonymous types: in a [Select], keep only the useful data without having to declare a class for it. [p.Nom] is an abbreviation for [Nom = p.Nom];
  • Line 33: [GroupBy] groups elements with the same key. The result is a sequence of groups [IGrouping<TKey,TElement>]: each group has a property [Key], the common value of the key, and is itself the sequence of the group’s elements, to which we can apply [Count], [Average], [Select]… (line 36);
  • lines 41–44: [Join] associates each person with the city of the same name. Its parameters are the second sequence, the join key on each side, and a lambda that constructs the result from a pair (person, city). Like a join SQL, [Join] retains only the pairs that match: Laurent, who lives in Lyon—which is absent from the list of cities—does not appear, nor does Brest, which has no residents;
  • lines 50–53: the join in query syntax, which is more readable: [join ... in ... on ... equals ...]. A filter, [where], is added to it. The query syntax also includes a clause, [group ... by ...], for groupings;
  • line 57: [ToList] (and [ToArray]) executes the query and stores its results in a list (an array);
  • line 58: [ToDictionary] constructs a dictionary: the first lambda provides the key for each element, the second its value. A duplicate key causes an exception;
  • Line 63: [CountBy] (.NET 9) counts the elements of each key value. It returns a sequence of [KeyValuePair<string,int>] pairs. This is a shortcut for [GroupBy(p => p.Ville).Select(g => (g.Key, g.Count()))];
  • Line 68: [AggregateBy] (.NET 9) accumulates a value for each key value: starting from 0, for each person, their age is added to the sum of their city. The returned tuples are decomposed in the loop [foreach];
  • line 73: [Index] (.NET 9) associates each element with its position in the sequence, in the form of a tuple (position, element).

docs.title: 5.5.5. Deferred Execution
docs.text:
A LINQ query is not executed when it is written, but when its result is iterated over: this is deferred execution. The program [linq-05.cs] demonstrates this using lambdas that display what they are doing:

// LINQ: deferred execution

List<int> nombres = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

// 1 - defining a query does not execute it
Console.WriteLine("[définition de la requête]");
IEnumerable<int> carresPairs = nombres
    .Where(n =>
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"  Where examine {n}");
        return n % 2 == 0;
    })
    .Select(n =>
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"  Select calcule {n}*{n}");
        return n * n;
    });
Console.WriteLine("[la requête est définie, rien n'a encore été exécuté]");

// 2 - It executes as it is traversed, element by element
Console.WriteLine("[foreach]");
foreach (int c in carresPairs)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  foreach reçoit {c}");
}

// 3 - the query is re-evaluated with each pass: it detects changes to the source
IEnumerable<int> grands = nombres.Where(n => n > 4);
Console.WriteLine($"[avant ajout] grands=[{string.Join(", ", grands)}]");
nombres.Add(10);
Console.WriteLine($"[après ajout de 10] grands=[{string.Join(", ", grands)}]");

// 4 - ToList executes the query immediately and stores the result
List<int> instantane = nombres.Where(n => n > 4).ToList();
nombres.Add(20);
Console.WriteLine($"[après ajout de 20] grands=[{string.Join(", ", grands)}], instantane=[{string.Join(", ", instantane)}]");

// 5 - Aggregates (Count, Sum, First...) are also executed immediately
int combien = nombres.Count(n => n > 4);
nombres.Add(30);
Console.WriteLine($"[après ajout de 30] combien={combien}, nouveau Count={nombres.Count(n => n > 4)}");

// 6 - First stops the scan as soon as it finds an element
Console.WriteLine("[First sur une requête]");
int premier = nombres.Where(n =>
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  Where examine {n}");
    return n > 2;
}).First();
Console.WriteLine($"  premier={premier}");

Results:

> dotnet run linq-05.cs
[définition de la requête]
[la requête est définie, rien n'a encore été exécuté]
[foreach]
  Where examine 1
  Where examine 2
  Select calcule 2*2
  foreach reçoit 4
  Where examine 3
  Where examine 4
  Select calcule 4*4
  foreach reçoit 16
  Where examine 5
  Where examine 6
  Select calcule 6*6
  foreach reçoit 36
[avant ajout] grands=[5, 6]
[après ajout de 10] grands=[5, 6, 10]
[après ajout de 20] grands=[5, 6, 10, 20], instantane=[5, 6, 10]
[après ajout de 30] combien=4, nouveau Count=5
[First sur une requête]
  Where examine 1
  Where examine 2
  Where examine 3
  premier=3

Comments:

  • Lines 7–16: A query that selects even numbers and then calculates their squares. The lambdas here are written with a body enclosed in curly braces, which displays a message before returning its value using [return];
  • Line 3 of the results: After the query was defined, nothing was displayed: neither [Where] nor [Select] has examined a single element yet. [carresPairs] does not contain results, but rather a description of a calculation;
  • Lines 4–16: The query runs during the [foreach] loop, element by element: each number passes through [Where], then [Select] if it is even, and then enters the loop before the next number is examined. These are iterators, like [Pairs] within [linq-01.cs];
  • lines 28–31: the query [grands] is re-evaluated on each pass: it takes into account the number 10 added to the list after its definition;
  • line 34: [ToList] executes the query immediately and stores its results: [instantane] is a list that does not see the addition of 20 (line 19);
  • line 39: Methods that return a single value ([Count], [Sum], [First], [Any]…) also iterate through the sequence immediately;
  • lines 45–49: [First] stops iterating as soon as it finds an element: the numbers following 3 are never examined.

Deferred execution has two practical consequences:

  • a query that is traversed multiple times is executed multiple times. If its computation is costly, or if a fixed result is desired, it is converted once and for all using [ToList] or [ToArray];
  • queries can be composed at no cost: chaining [Where], [Select], and [Take] creates no intermediate collection, and only the necessary elements are computed.

We will encounter LINQ throughout the course, and we will see in Chapter 7 how its methods are constructed.

docs.title: 5.6. Text Files
docs.text: The file-reading and file-writing classes are located in the [System.IO] namespace, which is part of the implicit [using] namespace.

docs.title: 5.6.1. The StreamReader class
docs.text:
The [System.IO.StreamReader] class allows you to read the contents of a text file. It is actually capable of handling streams that are not files (a network connection, for example). Here are some of its properties and methods.

Constructors:

constructorrole[public StreamReader(string path)]Creates a read stream from the file at path [path]. The file's content can be encoded in various ways; by default, the UTF-8 encoding is used. Another overload allows you to specify the encoding: [new StreamReader(path, Encoding.Latin1)]

Properties:

propertyrole[public bool EndOfStream { get; }][true] if the feed has been read in its entirety

Methods:

MethodRole[public void Dispose()]Closes the stream and releases the resources allocated for its management. This must be done after the stream has been processed, which is handled by the [using] statement. [Close] does the same thing[public int Peek()]returns the next character from the stream without consuming it; -1 at the end of the stream[public int Read()]returns the next character from the stream and advances by one character; -1 at the end of the stream[public string? ReadLine()]returns the next line from the stream, without the end-of-line character, or [null] if at the end of the stream[public string ReadToEnd()]returns the end of the stream, or "" if at the end of the stream

The program [fichiers-01.cs] is as follows:

// Reading a text file with StreamReader

// the current directory: this is where files specified by a relative path are searched for
Console.WriteLine($"Dossier courant : {Path.GetFileName(Environment.CurrentDirectory)}");
// The file name can be passed as an argument; otherwise, infos.txt
string nomFichier = args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "infos.txt";
try
{
     // Read mode 1: line by line
    Console.WriteLine("Lecture 1----------------");
    using (var flux = new StreamReader(nomFichier))
    {
        string? ligne;
         // ReadLine sets the value to null at the end of the file
        while ((ligne = flux.ReadLine()) != null)
        {
            Console.WriteLine(ligne);
        }
    } // Here, the stream is closed

     // Reading 2: the entire file at once, with a `using` statement
    Console.WriteLine("Lecture 2----------------");
    using var flux2 = new StreamReader(nomFichier);
    Console.Write(flux2.ReadToEnd());
     // stream2 will be closed at the end of the block containing its declaration; here, the try block
}
catch (FileNotFoundException e)
{
     // e.FileName is the full path to the file; only the filename is displayed
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : le fichier [{Path.GetFileName(e.FileName)}] n'existe pas");
}
catch (IOException e)
{
     // other input/output errors
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
}

Comments:

  • line 4: displays the name of the current directory, the one from which the [dotnet run] command was launched. Only the last element of the path is displayed, along with [Path.GetFileName], to avoid cluttering the results with a full path;
  • line 6: The file read is [infos.txt] or the one passed as an argument. Since this is a relative path, it is searched for in the current folder;
  • line 11: The [using (flux = ...) { ... }] structure ensures that the stream is closed when the block ends, even if an exception occurs within the block. This eliminates the need to explicitly call the close method. It applies to any object that implements the [IDisposable] interface—that is, any object with a [Dispose] method that releases resources (file, network connection, database connection, etc.);
  • lines 15–17: The file is read line by line. The assignment [ligne = flux.ReadLine()] is an expression whose value is that of [ligne]: it is compared to [null], which indicates the end of the file. The variable [ligne] is of type [string?]: [ReadLine] can be assigned the value [null];
  • line 23: a using declaration (C# 8). There is no longer a block: the variable [flux2] will be released at the end of the block containing its declaration, in this case the block *[try]*. This more concise syntax is the most common today;
  • line 24: the file is read in one go;
  • lines 27–32: I/O errors are signaled by exceptions derived from [IOException]*. *[FileNotFoundException]* is one such exception; it is therefore caught first. Its property *[FileName] contains the full path of the file being searched for.

The file [infos.txt] is as follows:

12620:0:0
13190:0,05:631
15640:0,1:1290,5

It is located in the [05-classes-dotnet] folder, from which the program is executed:

> dotnet run fichiers-01.cs
Dossier courant : 05-classes-dotnet
Lecture 1----------------
12620:0:0
13190:0,05:631
15640:0,1:1290,5
Lecture 2----------------
12620:0:0
13190:0,05:631
15640:0,1:1290,5

With a nonexistent file:

> dotnet run fichiers-01.cs -- xx.txt
Dossier courant : 05-classes-dotnet
Lecture 1----------------
FileNotFoundException : le fichier [xx.txt] n'existe pas

Selecting the current folder to locate data files is the natural approach for a single-file application that is run from its own folder. For a project, the executable is located in a subfolder named [bin/Debug/net10.0] within the project: we’ll see in the sample application how to copy the data files there and how to locate them.

docs.title: 5.6.2. The StreamWriter class
docs.text:
The [System.IO.StreamWriter] class allows you to write to a text file. Like the [StreamReader] class, it is actually capable of handling streams that are not files. Here are some of its properties and methods.

Constructors:

constructorrole[public StreamWriter(string path)]creates a write stream to the file at path [path]. The file is created, or overwritten if it exists. By default, the text is encoded in UTF-8, without BOM (see below)[public StreamWriter(string path, bool append)]If [append] equals [true], the entries are appended to the end of the existing file

Properties:

propertyrole[public bool AutoFlush { get; set; }]sets the write mode for the file. If [AutoFlush] is equal to [false] (default value), writing to the stream is not immediate: the text is first written to a buffer, then to the file when the buffer is full, when it is explicitly flushed using the [Flush] method, or when the stream is closed. This is the most efficient mode for files because it limits disk access. It is not suitable for all streams, particularly network streams: in a dialogue between two partners, what one writes must be read immediately by the other, and the write stream must be in [AutoFlush=true] mode[public string NewLine { get; set; }]the end-of-line character written by [WriteLine]. By default, this is the system’s end-of-line character: "\r\n" on Windows, "\n" on Linux, and macOS[public Encoding Encoding { get; }]the encoding used

Methods:

Methodrole[public void Dispose()]Closes the stream after writing the buffer's contents to the file. Must be performed after processing the stream; [Close] performs the same action[public void Flush()]writes the contents of the buffer to the file without waiting for it to be full[public void Write(T value)]writes [value] to the file associated with the stream. Here, [T] is not a generic type but symbolizes the fact that the method [Write] accepts different types of parameters ([string], [int], [object]…)[public void WriteLine(T value)]Same as [Write] but with the line-end marker ([NewLine]) added

The program [fichiers-02.cs] is as follows:

// writing a text file with StreamWriter
const string nomFichier = "infos2.txt";
try
{
     // creating the text file (if it already exists, it is overwritten)
    using (var flux = new StreamWriter(nomFichier))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Mode AutoFlush : {flux.AutoFlush}, encodage : {flux.Encoding.WebName}");
         // Loop as long as the entered line is not empty
        while (true)
        {
            Console.Write("ligne (rien pour arrêter) : ");
            string ligne = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "").Trim();
            if (ligne == "")
            {
                break;
            }
             // Write the line to the text file
            flux.WriteLine(ligne);
        }
    } // close the stream: the buffer is written to the file

     // Verification: Reads the created file
    Console.WriteLine($"Contenu de {nomFichier} ({new FileInfo(nomFichier).Length} octets) :");
    using var lecteur = new StreamReader(nomFichier);
    Console.Write(lecteur.ReadToEnd());
}
catch (IOException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"L'erreur suivante s'est produite : {e.Message}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run fichiers-02.cs
Mode AutoFlush : False, encodage : utf-8
ligne (rien pour arrêter) : 1ère ligne
ligne (rien pour arrêter) : 2ième ligne
ligne (rien pour arrêter) : 
Contenu de infos2.txt (25 octets) :
1ère ligne
2ième ligne

Comments:

  • line 6: once again, we use the [using] statement so that we don’t have to explicitly close the stream. This closure occurs automatically at the end of the block (closing curly brace on line 21). It is this closure that writes the text remaining in the buffer to the file; without it, the file might remain incomplete;
  • line 19: writes a line to the text file;
  • line 24: the [FileInfo] class provides information about a file, in this case its size in bytes. The 25 bytes break down as follows: 21 characters, plus 1 additional byte for each of the two [è] (which take up 2 bytes in UTF-8), plus two one-byte line breaks ("\n" on Linux, where the code was run; on Windows, each line break "\r\n" would take up 2 bytes);
  • line 28: why a [try / catch]? We could specify a filename in the form [rep1/rep2/fichier] with a directory [rep1/rep2] that does not exist, making it impossible to create the file. A [DirectoryNotFoundException] exception, derived from [IOException], would then be thrown. There are other possible exception cases (disk full, insufficient permissions, etc.).

docs.title: 5.6.3. The File, Path, and Directory Classes
docs.text:
For common operations, the static class [File] eliminates the need to handle streams: a single method opens the file, reads or writes it in its entirety, and then closes it. The static classes [Path] and [Directory] handle paths and directories, respectively.

methodrole[File.ReadAllText(path)]returns the file’s contents as a string[File.ReadAllLines(path)]Returns the lines of the file in an array [string[]][File.ReadLines(path)]returns the lines of the file as a [IEnumerable<string>] sequence read on demand[File.WriteAllText(path, contents)]creates (or overwrites) the file and writes [contents] to it; [WriteAllLines] writes a collection of lines[File.AppendAllText(path, contents)], [File.AppendAllLines(path, lines)]adds text—lines—to the end of the file (which is created if it does not exist)[File.ReadAllBytes(path)], [File.WriteAllBytes(path, bytes)]reads and writes the file as a byte array[File.Exists(path)], [File.Delete(path)], [File.Copy(source, dest)], [File.Move(source, dest)]checks if a file exists, deletes it, copies it, or moves it[Path.Combine(p1, p2, ...)]constructs a path from its elements, using the system separator[Path.GetFileName(path)], [Path.GetExtension(path)], [Path.GetDirectoryName(path)]extracts the filename, file extension, and folder from a path[Directory.CreateDirectory(path)]creates the folder and its parent folders if they do not exist[Directory.GetFiles(path, pattern)], [Directory.EnumerateFiles(path, pattern)]files in the folder whose names match the pattern ([*.txt]…), in an array or sequence[Directory.Exists(path)], [Directory.Delete(path, recursive)]checks for the existence of a folder and deletes it (along with its contents if [recursive] equals [true])

The program [fichiers-03.cs] uses them:

using System.Text;

// the static classes File, Path, and Directory

// Path.Combine constructs a path using the system separator (\ on Windows, / on Linux)
string dossier = "donnees";
string chemin = Path.Combine(dossier, "villes.txt");
Console.WriteLine($"chemin={chemin}, nom={Path.GetFileName(chemin)}, sans extension={Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(chemin)}, extension={Path.GetExtension(chemin)}");

// Directory.CreateDirectory creates the folder (and its parent folders) if it does not exist
Directory.CreateDirectory(dossier);

// File.WriteAllText: creates (or overwrites) a file with the given text; in UTF-8 without BOM
File.WriteAllText(chemin, "Angers\nNantes\n");
// File.AppendAllLines: adds lines to the end of the file
File.AppendAllLines(chemin, ["Paris", "Lyon"]);
// File.ReadAllLines: all lines in an array
string[] lignes = File.ReadAllLines(chemin);
Console.WriteLine($"ReadAllLines : {lignes.Length} lignes [{string.Join(", ", lignes)}]");
// File.ReadAllText: the entire file in a string
Console.WriteLine($"ReadAllText : {File.ReadAllText(chemin).Length} caractères");
// File.ReadLines: lines are read one by one, on demand (IEnumerable<string>)
foreach (string ville in File.ReadLines(chemin).Where(l => l.StartsWith('N') || l.StartsWith('L')))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"ReadLines + Where : {ville}");
}

// Encoding: by default UTF-8 without BOM; another encoding can be specified
string texte = "élève";
File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dossier, "utf8.txt"), texte);
File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dossier, "utf8bom.txt"), texte, new UTF8Encoding(true));
File.WriteAllText(Path.Combine(dossier, "latin1.txt"), texte, Encoding.Latin1);
foreach (string nom in new[] { "utf8.txt", "utf8bom.txt", "latin1.txt" })
{
    byte[] octets = File.ReadAllBytes(Path.Combine(dossier, nom));
    Console.WriteLine($"{nom,-12}: {octets.Length} octets : {Convert.ToHexString(octets)}");
}
// A Latin-1 file re-encoded in UTF-8: accented characters are lost
Console.WriteLine($"latin1.txt lu en UTF-8 : {File.ReadAllText(Path.Combine(dossier, "latin1.txt"))}");
Console.WriteLine($"latin1.txt lu en Latin-1 : {File.ReadAllText(Path.Combine(dossier, "latin1.txt"), Encoding.Latin1)}");

// File.Exists, Directory.GetFiles
Console.WriteLine($"Exists(villes.txt)={File.Exists(chemin)}, Exists(xx.txt)={File.Exists(Path.Combine(dossier, "xx.txt"))}");
foreach (string fichier in Directory.GetFiles(dossier, "*.txt").Order())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {Path.GetFileName(fichier),-12} {new FileInfo(fichier).Length,3} octets");
}

// cleanup: deletion of the folder and its contents
Directory.Delete(dossier, recursive: true);
Console.WriteLine($"après Delete : Directory.Exists={Directory.Exists(dossier)}");

Results:

> dotnet run fichiers-03.cs
chemin=donnees/villes.txt, nom=villes.txt, sans extension=villes, extension=.txt
ReadAllLines : 4 lignes [Angers, Nantes, Paris, Lyon]
ReadAllText : 25 caractères
ReadLines + Where : Nantes
ReadLines + Where : Lyon
utf8.txt    : 7 octets : C3A96CC3A87665
utf8bom.txt : 10 octets : EFBBBFC3A96CC3A87665
latin1.txt  : 5 octets : E96CE87665
latin1.txt lu en UTF-8 : �l�ve
latin1.txt lu en Latin-1 : élève
Exists(villes.txt)=True, Exists(xx.txt)=False
  latin1.txt     5 octets
  utf8.txt       7 octets
  utf8bom.txt   10 octets
  villes.txt    25 octets
après Delete : Directory.Exists=False

Comments:

  • Line 7: [Path.Combine] uses the system's path separator. The course exercises were run on Linux: the resulting path is [donnees/villes.txt]; on Windows, it would be [donnees\villes.txt]. Constructing paths using [Path.Combine] rather than concatenating strings makes the code portable;
  • line 11: creating the folder [donnees] does not cause an error if it already exists;
  • Lines 14–18: writing, appending, and reading, each in a single statement;
  • line 23: [File.ReadLines] returns a sequence: the lines are read one by one as the loop progresses, like the elements of an iterator. You can apply LINQ to it, and thus process a file several gigabytes in size without loading it into memory—which is what [ReadAllLines] would do. The file is closed at the end of the iteration;
  • lines 29–36: the same text “élève” is written using three encodings, then the bytes of the files are displayed in hexadecimal:
    • In UTF-8, the default encoding of .NET, accented characters take up 2 bytes (é = C3 A9) and the others 1 byte: 7 bytes for 5 characters;
    • in UTF-8 with BOM (Byte Order Mark), the file begins with the 3 bytes EF BB BF, which indicate to software that the file is encoded in UTF-8. [new UTF8Encoding(true)] instructs the system to write this BOM;
    • in Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1), the traditional encoding for Western European texts, each character occupies one byte (é = E9);
  • Line 39: Reading a file with an encoding different from the one used to write it alters accented characters: the byte sequence E9 6C is invalid in UTF-8, and each invalid byte is replaced by the character �. When reading, [File.ReadAllText] and [StreamReader] recognize BOM if it is present; otherwise, they assume UTF-8, unless another encoding is specified (line 40). Today, the rule is simple: text files are written and read in UTF-8;
  • line 44: the names of the text files in the folder. [GetFiles] does not guarantee the order of the names; the method LINQ [Order] (.NET 7) sorts them;
  • line 50: Deletes the folder and its contents. The parameter is passed by name, [recursive: true], which makes the call more readable than a simple [true] (named arguments, Chapter 3).

All of these methods have asynchronous versions ([File.ReadAllTextAsync], [File.ReadAllLinesAsync]…): we’ll use them in Chapter 9, which is devoted to asynchronous programming.

docs.title: 5.7.1. The classes BinaryWriter and BinaryReader
docs.text:
The classes [System.IO.BinaryWriter] and [System.IO.BinaryReader] are used to write and read binary files. In such a file, data is not written as text but in its internal form: a [int] always occupies 4 bytes, regardless of its value.

Consider the following application:

// syntax: dotnet run fichiers-04.cs -- binary text logs
// read a text file (text) and store its contents in a binary file (binary)
// The text file contains lines in the form "name: age," which are written as (string, int)
// (logs) is a text log file

The text file [personnes1.txt] has the following content:

paul : 10
helene : 15

jacques : 11
sylvain : 12
xx : -1

xx: yy : zz
xx : yy

The program [fichiers-04.cs] is as follows:

// Syntax: dotnet run fichiers-04.cs -- text binary logs
// a text file (text) is read, and its contents are stored in a binary file (binary)
// The text file contains lines in the form "name: age," which are written as (string, int)
// (logs) is a text file containing logs

// It requires 3 arguments
if (args.Length != 3)
{
    Console.WriteLine("syntaxe : dotnet run fichiers-04.cs -- texte binaire logs");
    return 1;
}
try
{
     // Open the text file for reading
    using var input = new StreamReader(args[0]);
     // Open the binary file for writing
    using var output = new BinaryWriter(new FileStream(args[1], FileMode.Create, FileAccess.Write));
     // opens the log file for writing
    using var logs = new StreamWriter(args[2]);
     // process the text file
    string? ligne;
    int numLigne = 0, nbPersonnes = 0;
    while ((ligne = input.ReadLine()) != null)
    {
         // one more line
        numLigne++;
         // Empty line? Ignore it
        if (ligne.Trim() == "")
        {
            continue;
        }
         // a line with name: age
        string[] champs = ligne.Split(':', StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries);
         // We need 2 fields
        if (champs.Length != 2)
        {
            logs.WriteLine($"La ligne n° [{numLigne}] du fichier [{args[0]}] a un nombre de champs incorrect");
            continue;
        }
         // The first field must not be empty
        bool erreur = false;
        string nom = champs[0];
        if (nom == "")
        {
            logs.WriteLine($"La ligne n° [{numLigne}] du fichier [{args[0]}] a un nom vide");
            erreur = true;
        }
         // The second field must be an integer >= 0
        if (!int.TryParse(champs[1], out int age) || age < 0)
        {
            logs.WriteLine($"La ligne n° [{numLigne}] du fichier [{args[0]}] a un âge [{champs[1]}] incorrect");
            erreur = true;
        }
         // if there are no errors, write the data to the binary file
        if (!erreur)
        {
            output.Write(nom);
            output.Write(age);
            nbPersonnes++;
        }
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"{numLigne} lignes lues, {nbPersonnes} personnes écrites dans [{args[1]}], erreurs dans [{args[2]}]");
     // End of the `try` block: the three streams are closed here, in the reverse order in which they were opened
}
catch (FileNotFoundException e)
{
     // e.FileName is the full path to the file; only the filename is displayed
    Console.WriteLine($"Le fichier [{Path.GetFileName(e.FileName)}] n'existe pas");
    return 2;
}
catch (IOException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"L'erreur suivante s'est produite : {e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
    return 3;
}
return 0;

Let’s take a closer look at the operations involving the class [BinaryWriter]:

  • Line 17: The object [BinaryWriter] is opened by the operation [new BinaryWriter(new FileStream(args[1], FileMode.Create, FileAccess.Write))]. The constructor’s argument must be a stream ([Stream]). Here, it is a stream created from a file ([FileStream]), for which we specify:
    • the name;
    • the operation to be performed, in this case [FileMode.Create] to create the file (or overwrite it if it exists);
    • the access type, in this case [FileAccess.Write] for write access to the file;
  • lines 57–58: the write operations. The [BinaryWriter] class has overloaded [Write] methods for writing the various types of simple data ([int], [double], [decimal], [bool], [string]...);
  • lines 15–19: The three streams are opened with [using] declarations. They will be closed at the end of the [try] block, in the reverse order in which they were opened. The 2008 course closed them in a [finally] clause after checking that they were not [null]: the [using] declaration does the same thing in a single line;
  • line 10: high-level instructions can end with a [return n]; n is then the program’s exit code, which a script can check (0: success);
  • line 33: the option [TrimEntries] removes spaces around the name and age;
  • line 49: the age must be a positive integer or zero. Thanks to the short-circuit behavior of the [||] operator, the condition [age < 0] is evaluated only if the conversion was successful.

The program’s three arguments are passed after [--] in the [dotnet run] command. The results are as follows:

> dotnet run fichiers-04.cs -- personnes1.txt personnes1.bin logs.txt
9 lignes lues, 4 personnes écrites dans [personnes1.bin], erreurs dans [logs.txt]

The log file [logs.txt] contains the following:

> cat logs.txt
La ligne n° [6] du fichier [personnes1.txt] a un âge [-1] incorrect
La ligne n° [8] du fichier [personnes1.txt] a un nombre de champs incorrect
La ligne n° [9] du fichier [personnes1.txt] a un âge [yy] incorrect

The contents of the binary file [personnes1.bin] can be displayed in hexadecimal using the Linux command [od] (on Windows, the command PowerShell [Format-Hex] produces a similar display):

> od -A d -t x1z personnes1.bin
0000000 04 70 61 75 6c 0a 00 00 00 06 68 65 6c 65 6e 65  >.paul.....helene<
0000016 0f 00 00 00 07 6a 61 63 71 75 65 73 0b 00 00 00  >.....jacques....<
0000032 07 73 79 6c 76 61 69 6e 0c 00 00 00              >.sylvain....<
0000044

This shows how [BinaryWriter] writes the data:

  • a string is written preceded by its length in bytes: the byte 04 followed by the 4 bytes of “paul” (70 61 75 6c);
  • an integer [int] is written over 4 bytes, with the least significant byte first: 10 is written as 0a 00 00 00;
  • the data is written one after another, without any separators or line breaks: the file is 44 bytes long (line 5: with the option [-A d], [od] displays the positions in decimal).

To read this file, you must therefore know the exact order and type of the data that was written. This is what the program [fichiers-05.cs] does; it performs the reverse operation: it reads the binary file to create a text file. If the resulting text file contains the correct data from the original file, you will know that the text → binary → text conversion was successful.

// syntax: dotnet run fichiers-05.cs -- binary to text
// a binary file (binary) is read, and its contents are written to a text file (text)
// The binary file contains (string, int) pairs
// The text file will contain lines in the form name:age

// Two arguments are required
if (args.Length != 2)
{
    Console.WriteLine("syntaxe : dotnet run fichiers-05.cs -- binaire texte");
    return 1;
}
try
{
     // Open the binary file for reading
    using var input = new BinaryReader(new FileStream(args[0], FileMode.Open, FileAccess.Read));
     // Open the text file for writing
    using var output = new StreamWriter(args[1]);
     // Process the binary file until the end of the stream is reached
    int nbPersonnes = 0;
    while (input.BaseStream.Position < input.BaseStream.Length)
    {
         // Read name, then age: in the order they were written
        string nom = input.ReadString();
        int age = input.ReadInt32();
         // Write to the text file
        output.WriteLine($"{nom}:{age}");
        nbPersonnes++;
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"{nbPersonnes} personnes lues dans [{args[0]}] et écrites dans [{args[1]}]");
}
catch (EndOfStreamException)
{
     // The file ends in the middle of a record
    Console.WriteLine($"Le fichier [{args[0]}] est tronqué");
    return 2;
}
catch (FileNotFoundException e)
{
     // e.FileName is the full path to the file; only the filename is displayed
    Console.WriteLine($"Le fichier [{Path.GetFileName(e.FileName)}] n'existe pas");
    return 3;
}
catch (IOException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"L'erreur suivante s'est produite : {e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
    return 4;
}
return 0;

Let’s take a closer look at the operations involving the [BinaryReader] class:

  • line 15: the [BinaryReader] object is opened on a [FileStream] stream using the [FileMode.Open] mode (to open an existing file) and the [FileAccess.Read] access mode (for read-only access);
  • Lines 23–24: Read operations. The [BinaryReader] class provides the [ReadXX] methods to read various types of simple data: [ReadString], [ReadInt32], [ReadDouble], [ReadDecimal], [ReadBoolean]... These must be called in the order of the writes;
  • Line 20: The property [BaseStream] provides the underlying stream, in this case [FileStream]. Reading continues until the current position in the file reaches the end of the file. The 2008 version read indefinitely and detected the end of the file via the [EndOfStreamException] exception: an exception must remain exceptional, and the end of a file is not;
  • line 31: this exception now signals a true anomaly: a file that ends in the middle of a record.

Let’s run the program on the [personnes1.bin] file generated earlier:

> dotnet run fichiers-05.cs -- personnes1.bin personnes2.txt
4 personnes lues dans [personnes1.bin] et écrites dans [personnes2.txt]

The contents of [personnes2.txt] are as follows:

> cat personnes2.txt
paul:10
helene:15
jacques:11
sylvain:12

We find the 4 valid people from the [personnes1.txt] file. With a [tronque.bin] file consisting of the first 30 bytes of [personnes1.bin], reading Jacques’s age fails:

> dotnet run fichiers-05.cs -- tronque.bin tronque.txt
Le fichier [tronque.bin] est tronqué

docs.title: 5.7.2. The JSON serialization
docs.text:
Writing and reading a binary file byte by byte is tedious, and even the slightest discrepancy between writing and reading produces incorrect results. It is generally preferable to serialize objects: automatically convert them into a sequence of bytes or characters, then deserialize them to reconstruct them.

.NET provided the [BinaryFormatter] class for this purpose, which serialized objects into a binary format specific to .NET. It has now been removed: it was declared obsolete in .NET 5, and its implementation was removed in .NET 9, because deserializing data from an untrusted source with [BinaryFormatter] allowed arbitrary code to be executed. Microsoft recommends replacing it with the JSON serialization from the [System.Text.Json] library, which has been integrated into .NET since .NET Core 3.0.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text-based, human-readable, and universal format: it is the exchange format for web services (Chapter 13) and numerous configuration files. An object is written within curly braces in the form of "property":value pairs, with arrays enclosed in square brackets.

The static class [System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer] has two main methods:

methodrole[string Serialize<T>(T value, JsonSerializerOptions? options = null)]returns the text JSON representing the object [value][T? Deserialize<T>(string json, JsonSerializerOptions? options = null)]reconstructs an object of type [T] from the text JSON [json]; throws a [JsonException] if the text is incorrect

The program [fichiers-06.cs] uses them:

#: property PublishAot=false
using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using System.Text.Unicode;

// serialization JSON with System.Text.Json

List<Personne> personnes =
[
    new("paul", 10, ["football"]),
    new("hélène", 15, ["piano", "tennis"]),
    new("jacques", 11, []),
];

// 1 - default serialization: a single line, non-escaped characters ASCII
string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(personnes[1]);
Console.WriteLine($"[par défaut] {json}");

// 2 - options: indentation, accented characters left as is
var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    WriteIndented = true,
    Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All)
};
json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(personnes, options);
// writing to a text file
File.WriteAllText("personnes.json", json);
Console.WriteLine("[personnes.json]");
Console.WriteLine(File.ReadAllText("personnes.json"));

// 3 - deserialization: from JSON text to objects
string texte = File.ReadAllText("personnes.json");
List<Personne>? relues = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<Personne>>(texte);
Console.WriteLine($"[relues] {relues?.Count} personnes");
foreach (Personne p in relues ?? [])
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {p.Nom}, {p.Age} ans, loisirs : [{string.Join(", ", p.Loisirs)}]");
}

// 4 - no attributes: the "Web" options set property names to camelCase
var web = new JsonSerializerOptions(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);
string jsonArticle = JsonSerializer.Serialize(new Article("A12", 12.5m), web);
Console.WriteLine($"[options Web] {jsonArticle}");
// and are case-insensitive when reading
Article? article = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Article>("""{ "CODE": "B7", "prix": 3 }""", web);
Console.WriteLine($"[options Web] {article}");

// 5 - An invalid JSON document causes a JsonException
try
{
    JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Personne>("""{ "nom": "x", "age": "douze" }""");
}
catch (JsonException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"[erreur] {e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
}

// a person; the attributes [JsonPropertyName] define the names of the properties JSON
record Personne(
    [property: JsonPropertyName("nom")] string Nom,
    [property: JsonPropertyName("age")] int Age,
    [property: JsonPropertyName("loisirs")] List<string> Loisirs);

// an item, without attributes
record Article(string Code, decimal Prix);

Results:

> dotnet run fichiers-06.cs
[par défaut] {"nom":"h\u00E9l\u00E8ne","age":15,"loisirs":["piano","tennis"]}
[personnes.json]
[
  {
    "nom": "paul",
    "age": 10,
    "loisirs": [
      "football"
    ]
  },
  {
    "nom": "hélène",
    "age": 15,
    "loisirs": [
      "piano",
      "tennis"
    ]
  },
  {
    "nom": "jacques",
    "age": 11,
    "loisirs": []
  }
]
[relues] 3 personnes
  paul, 10 ans, loisirs : [football]
  hélène, 15 ans, loisirs : [piano, tennis]
  jacques, 11 ans, loisirs : []
[options Web] {"code":"A12","prix":12.5}
[options Web] Article { Code = B7, Prix = 3 }
[erreur] JsonException : The JSON value could not be converted to Personne. Path: $.age | LineNumber: 0 | BytePositionInLine: 28.

Comments:

  • Line 1: A directive for single-file applications. By default, these are configured for native compilation (AOT, "ahead of time"), which produces a standalone executable but disables mechanisms that rely on runtime type discovery (reflection). However, [JsonSerializer] uses reflection by default to discover the properties of objects to be serialized: without this directive, compilation produces warnings and execution fails. A standard [.csproj] project, such as the one in the sample application, does not have this restriction. For a natively compiled application, [System.Text.Json] provides a source generator (a class derived from [JsonSerializerContext]) that generates the serialization code at compile time: we will not cover this here;
  • lines 60–63: the [Personne] record to be serialized. Its properties carry the attribute [JsonPropertyName], which sets the property name in the text JSON to [nom] instead of [Nom]. In a positional record, [property: ...] indicates that the attribute applies to the generated property and not to the constructor parameter;
  • line 17: serialization of an object with default options: the text is written on a single line, and non-ASCII characters are escaped: [é] becomes [\u00E9]. The text remains correct, but it is difficult to read;
  • Lines 21–26: The option [WriteIndented] produces indented text across multiple lines; the option [Encoder] specifies which characters to leave as-is—in this case, all Unicode characters. A list is serialized into an array JSON;
  • line 28: the text JSON is saved to a text file: this is how binary serialization is replaced today;
  • line 34: deserialization reconstructs the list. [Deserialize] creates the [Personne] objects by calling the record’s constructor, whose parameters are associated with the JSON properties of the same name. The result is of type [List<Personne>?]: the text JSON [null] is a valid document that yields [null];
  • line 42: the “Web” options—which are used by default by ASP.NET Core’s web services—write property names in camelCase format (first letter lowercase): [Code] becomes [code], without an attribute. When parsed, they are case-insensitive: [CODE] is accepted (line 31);
  • line 52: an invalid JSON document—in this case, a string where a number is expected—triggers a [JsonException] exception, whose message indicates the location of the error.

We will use JSON in the following example application and throughout the course.

docs.title: 5.8. Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The [System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex] class supports the use of regular expressions. These allow you to validate the format of a string. For example, you can verify that a string representing a date is indeed in the dd/mm/yy format. To do this, you use a pattern and compare the string to that pattern. In this example, d, m, and y must be digits. The pattern for a valid date format is therefore [\d\d/\d\d/\d\d], where the symbol [\d] represents a digit. The symbols that can be used in a pattern are as follows:

characterdescription[\]marks the following character as a special character or literal. For example, [n] corresponds to the character n, [ ] corresponds to a newline character, [\] corresponds to \, and [\(] corresponds to ([^]corresponds to the beginning of the string[$]corresponds to the end of the string[*]matches the preceding element zero or more times. Thus, [zo*] matches z or zoo[+]matches the previous element one or more times. Thus, [zo+] matches "zoo," but not "z"[?]matches the preceding element zero or one time. For example, [a?ve?] matches “ve” in “lever”[.]matches any single character, except for a newline character[(modèle)]searches for the pattern and stores the match (a group). The matching substring can be extracted from the [Groups] collection in the result. To find matches with characters in parentheses, use [\(] or [\)][x|y]matches either x or y. For example, [z|foot] matches z or foot; [(z|f)oo] matches zoo or foo[{n}]n is a non-negative integer. Corresponds exactly n times to the previous element. For example, [o{2}] does not correspond to o in Bob, but to the first two o’s in fooooot[{n,}]matches the previous element at least n times. For example, [o{2,}] does not match the 'o' in 'Bob', but matches all the 'o's in 'fooooot'. [o{1,}] is equivalent to [o+], and [o{0,}] is equivalent to [o*][{n,m}]matches the previous element at least n times and at most m times. For example, [o{1,3}] matches the first three “o”s in “foooooot”; [o{0,1}] is equivalent to [o?][xyz]character set: matches one of the specified characters. For example, [abc] matches the letter “a” in “plat”[^xyz]negative character set: matches any character not listed. For example, [^abc] matches "p" in "plat"[a-z]Character range: matches any character in the specified range, in this case a lowercase unaccented letter[^m-z]negative character range: matches any character not between 'm' and 'z'[ ]matches a word boundary, that is, the position between a word character and a non-word character. For example, [er ] matches "er" in "lever," but not "er" in "verb"[\B]corresponds to a position that is not a word boundary. [en*t\B] corresponds to “ent” in “bien entendu”[\d]corresponds to a digit; is equivalent to [0-9] (along with .NET, also for digits from other Unicode alphabets)[\D]corresponds to a character that is not a digit[ ], [ ], [ ], [ ], [\v]correspond to the characters page break, new line, carriage return, tab, and vertical tab, respectively[\s]corresponds to any whitespace: space, tab, page break, line break… Equivalent to [ \v], plus other Unicode whitespace characters (non-breaking space, etc.)[\S]matches any character that is not a whitespace character[\w]matches any word character: letter (with or without accents), digit, or underscore[\W]matches any character that is not a word character[ um]num is a positive integer: refers to group number num. For example, [(.)\1] matches two consecutive identical characters[\xnn], [\unnnn]corresponds to the hexadecimal character nn (2 digits) or nnnn (4 digits). For example, [\x41] corresponds to A

An element in a template can appear once or multiple times. Let’s look at a few examples using the symbol [\d], which represents a single digit:

templateMeaning[\d]one digit[\d?]0 or 1 digit[\d*]0 or more digits[\d+]1 or more digits[\d{2}]2 digits[\d{3,}]At least 3 digits[\d{5,7}]between 5 and 7 digits

Now let’s imagine a model capable of describing the expected format for a string:

target stringpatterna date in dd/mm/yy format[\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}]a time in the hh:mm:ss format[\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}]an unsigned integer[\d+]a sequence of spaces, which may be empty[\s*]an unsigned integer that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+\s*]an integer that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+\s*]an unsigned real number that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a real number that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a string containing the word "just"[ juste ]

The 2008 course used [+|-] for the sign: enclosed in square brackets, the character [|] has no specific meaning, and this format also accepted the | sign before a number. It also used [(.\d*)] for the decimal part: the unescaped period there represents any character. The patterns above have been corrected.

You can specify where to look for the pattern in the string:

patternmeaning[^modèle]the pattern begins the string[modèle$]Model ends the string[^modèle$]The pattern starts and ends the string[modèle]The pattern is searched for anywhere in the string, starting from the beginning of the string search stringpatterna string ending with an exclamation point[!$]a string ending with a period[\.$]a string beginning with the sequence //[^//]a string consisting of a single word, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s*$]a string consisting of exactly two words, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s+\w+\s*$]a string containing the word "secret"[ secret ]

Sub sets of a pattern can be “extracted.” Thus, not only can we verify that a string matches a particular pattern, but we can also extract from that string the elements corresponding to the pattern’s sub sets that have been enclosed in parentheses. For example, if you are parsing a string containing a date in the dd/mm/yy format and also want to extract the dd, mm, and yy components of that date, you would use the pattern [(\d\d)/(\d\d)/(\d\d)].

In C# code, a pattern is preferably written as a verbatim string [@"..."]: this way, the numerous [] characters in the patterns do not need to be doubled. With a regular string, you would have to write ***["\\d+"] instead of ***[@"\d+"].

docs.title: 5.8.1. Check whether a string matches a given template
docs.text:
An object of type [Regex] is constructed as follows:

constructorrole[public Regex(string pattern)]creates a “regular expression” object from a pattern passed as a parameter ([pattern]). A [ArgumentException] exception is thrown if the pattern is incorrect[public Regex(string pattern, RegexOptions options, TimeSpan matchTimeout)]same as above, with options and a timeout (see below)

Once the regular expression has been constructed, it can be compared to character strings using the [IsMatch] method:

methodrole[public bool IsMatch(string input)]true if the string [input] contains a substring that matches the regular expression pattern

The program [regex-01.cs] is as follows:

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// check whether a string matches a pattern
string modele1 = @"^\s*\d+\s*$";
var regex1 = new Regex(modele1);
// compare instances to the template
foreach (string exemplaire in new[] { "  123  ", "  123a  ", "4567" })
{
    if (regex1.IsMatch(exemplaire))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{exemplaire}] correspond au modèle [{modele1}]");
    }
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{exemplaire}] ne correspond pas au modèle [{modele1}]");
    }
}
// the static method Regex.IsMatch avoids creating the Regex object yourself
Console.WriteLine($"Regex.IsMatch(\"18/05/97\", date) : {Regex.IsMatch("18/05/97", @"^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}$")}");
Console.WriteLine($"Regex.IsMatch(\"5/1/01\", date) : {Regex.IsMatch("5/1/01", @"^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}$")}");

Results:

> dotnet run regex-01.cs
[  123  ] correspond au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[  123a  ] ne correspond pas au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[4567] correspond au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$]
Regex.IsMatch("18/05/97", date) : True
Regex.IsMatch("5/1/01", date) : False

Comments:

  • line 4: the pattern for an unsigned integer, optionally surrounded by spaces, that occupies the entire string (anchors [^] and [$]);
  • line 9: the string “123a,” surrounded by spaces, does not match the pattern: the character “a” cannot be a digit or a space. Without the anchors [^] and [$], the string would match, since it contains a number;
  • line 19: The class [Regex] also has static methods that take the pattern as a parameter. NET stores the most recently used patterns in memory: they can be used in a loop without worrying that the pattern will be parsed on every call.

docs.title: 5.8.2. Find all occurrences of a pattern in a string
docs.text:
The [Matches] method retrieves the elements of a string that match a pattern:

methodrole[public MatchCollection Matches(string input)]returns the collection of elements in the string [input] that match the pattern

The [MatchCollection] class has a property, [Count], which is the number of elements in the collection. If [resultats] is a [MatchCollection] object, then [resultats[i]] is the i-th element of that collection; it is of type [Match]. The class [Match] has various properties, including the following:

  • [Value]: the value of the object [Match], i.e., an element matching the pattern;
  • [Index]: the position where the element was found in the explored string.

The program [regex-02.cs] is as follows:

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// Find all occurrences of a pattern in a string
string modele2 = @"\d+";
var regex2 = new Regex(modele2);
string exemplaire3 = "  123  456  789 ";
MatchCollection resultats = regex2.Matches(exemplaire3);
Console.WriteLine($"Modèle=[{modele2}], exemplaire=[{exemplaire3}]");
Console.WriteLine($"Il y a {resultats.Count} occurrences du modèle dans l'exemplaire");
foreach (Match m in resultats)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"[{m.Value}] trouvé en position {m.Index}");
}
// A MatchCollection is a sequence: LINQ applies to it
int somme = resultats.Sum(m => int.Parse(m.Value));
Console.WriteLine($"somme des nombres trouvés : {somme}");
// Count counts the occurrences without building the collection
Console.WriteLine($"nombre de voyelles de \"anticonstitutionnellement\" : {Regex.Count("anticonstitutionnellement", "[aeiouy]")}");

Results:

> dotnet run regex-02.cs
Modèle=[\d+], exemplaire=[  123  456  789 ]
Il y a 3 occurrences du modèle dans l'exemplaire
[123] trouvé en position 2
[456] trouvé en position 7
[789] trouvé en position 12
somme des nombres trouvés : 1368
nombre de voyelles de "anticonstitutionnellement" : 10

Comments:

  • Line 4: The pattern being searched for is a sequence of digits;
  • line 6: the string in which this pattern is searched for;
  • line 7: all elements of [exemplaire3] that match the pattern [modele2] are retrieved;
  • Lines 10–12: These are displayed. A [MatchCollection] is traversed with [foreach], like a list;
  • line 15: [MatchCollection] implements [IEnumerable<Match>]: LINQ is applied to it. Here, we sum the numbers found;
  • line 18: the method [Count] (.NET 7) counts the occurrences of the pattern without constructing a collection. The pattern [aeiouy] denotes a vowel.

docs.title: 5.8.3. Retrieving Parts of a Pattern
docs.text:
As mentioned earlier, the parts of a pattern enclosed in parentheses are stored: these are the groups. The program [regex-03.cs] uses them:

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// Extract parts of a pattern: the groups
string modele3 = @"(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)";
var regex3 = new Regex(modele3);
string exemplaire4 = "Il est 18:05:49";
// Match returns the first occurrence of the pattern
Match resultat = regex3.Match(exemplaire4);
if (resultat.Success)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"L'exemplaire [{exemplaire4}] correspond au modèle [{modele3}]");
     // Displays parenthesized groups
    for (int i = 0; i < resultat.Groups.Count; i++)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"groupes[{i}]=[{resultat.Groups[i].Value}] trouvé en position {resultat.Groups[i].Index}");
    }
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine($"L'exemplaire [{exemplaire4}] ne correspond pas au modèle [{modele3}]");
}

// Named groups: (?<name>...)
var regexDate = new Regex(@"(?<jour>\d{1,2})/(?<mois>\d{1,2})/(?<annee>\d{4})");
string texte = "Rendez-vous le 3/10/2026, puis le 15/11/2026.";
foreach (Match m in regexDate.Matches(texte))
{
     // A group is identified by its name rather than its number
    int jour = int.Parse(m.Groups["jour"].Value);
    int mois = int.Parse(m.Groups["mois"].Value);
    int annee = int.Parse(m.Groups["annee"].Value);
    var date = new DateOnly(annee, mois, jour);
    Console.WriteLine($"[{m.Value}] : jour={jour}, mois={mois}, année={annee} -> {date:dddd d MMMM yyyy}");
}

// Replace: groups can be reused in the replacement string
string inverse = regexDate.Replace(texte, "${annee}-${mois}-${jour}");
Console.WriteLine($"Replace : {inverse}");

Results:

> dotnet run regex-03.cs
L'exemplaire [Il est 18:05:49] correspond au modèle [(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)]
groupes[0]=[18:05:49] trouvé en position 7
groupes[1]=[18] trouvé en position 7
groupes[2]=[05] trouvé en position 10
groupes[3]=[49] trouvé en position 13
[3/10/2026] : jour=3, mois=10, année=2026 -> samedi 3 octobre 2026
[15/11/2026] : jour=15, mois=11, année=2026 -> dimanche 15 novembre 2026
Replace : Rendez-vous le 2026-10-3, puis le 2026-11-15.

Comments:

  • Line 8: The string [exemplaire4] is compared to the template [regex3] using the method [Match]. This method returns the first occurrence of the template as a [Match] object, which has already been presented. Here, we use two new properties of this class:
    • [Success] (line 9): indicates whether a match was found;
    • [Groups] (line 13): a collection where [Groups[0]] corresponds to the part of the string representing the template, and [Groups[i]] (i >= 1) corresponds to the i-th set of parentheses;
  • if [resultat] is of type [Match], then [resultat.Groups] is of type [GroupCollection] and [resultat.Groups[i]] is of type [Group]. The class [Group] has, like the class [Match], the properties [Value] (the text captured by the group) and [Index] (its position in the parsed string);
  • line 24: a group can be named using the syntax [(?<nom>...)]. Here, the pattern recognizes a date in the d/m/yyyy format, with a one- or two-digit day and month;
  • lines 29–31: a named group is referred to by its name rather than its number: the code is more readable and does not depend on the order of the parentheses;
  • line 32: the type [DateOnly] (.NET 6) represents a date without a time. It is displayed in the format [dddd d MMMM yyyy]: the day of the week appears in French;
  • line 37: the [Replace] method replaces each occurrence of the template with a string in which [${nom}] (or [$1], [$2]… for numbered groups) denotes the value of a group. Dates are thus reformatted into the year-month-day format.

docs.title: 5.8.4. A Learning Program
docs.text:
Finding the regular expression that verifies whether a string matches a certain pattern can sometimes be a real challenge. The program [regex-04.cs] lets you practice. It takes a pattern and a string as input and indicates whether the string matches the pattern or not.

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// a program for learning regular expressions
while (true)
{
     // The pattern is requested
    Console.Write("Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : ");
    string modele = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";
     // Done?
    if (modele.Trim() == "")
    {
        break;
    }
     // Creating the regular expression; an incorrect pattern causes an exception
    Regex regex;
    try
    {
        regex = new Regex(modele, RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
    }
    catch (ArgumentException e)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Erreur : {e.Message}");
        continue;
    }
     // The examples to be compared to the pattern are requested
    while (true)
    {
        Console.Write($"Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [{modele}] ou rien pour arrêter : ");
        string chaine = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";
         // Done?
        if (chaine.Trim() == "")
        {
            break;
        }
        try
        {
             // Performing the comparison
            MatchCollection resultats = regex.Matches(chaine);
            if (resultats.Count == 0)
            {
                Console.WriteLine("Je n'ai pas trouvé de correspondances");
                continue;
            }
             // Display the elements that match the pattern
            foreach (Match m in resultats)
            {
                Console.WriteLine($"J'ai trouvé la correspondance [{m.Value}] en position [{m.Index}]");
                 // and its subelements (groups 1, 2, ...)
                for (int j = 1; j < m.Groups.Count; j++)
                {
                    Console.WriteLine($"\tsous-élément [{m.Groups[j].Value}] en position [{m.Groups[j].Index}]");
                }
            }
        }
        catch (RegexMatchTimeoutException)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("La recherche a été abandonnée : elle durait plus d'une seconde");
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 18: The regular expression is constructed with a one-second timeout: if a search takes longer than that, it is abandoned and a [RegexMatchTimeoutException] exception is thrown (line 55). We’ll see later why this is useful;
  • line 20: an invalid pattern causes a [ArgumentException] exception (more specifically, [RegexParseException], which is derived from it);
  • lines 45–51: For each match, groups #1 and subsequent groups are displayed, if any.

Here is an example of the output:

> dotnet run regex-04.cs
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : \d+
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [\d+] ou rien pour arrêter : 123 456 789
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [123] en position [0]
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [456] en position [4]
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [789] en position [8]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [\d+] ou rien pour arrêter : 
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : (\d{2}):(\d\d)
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] ou rien pour arrêter : 14:15 abcd 17:18 xyzt
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [14:15] en position [0]
    sous-élément [14] en position [0]
    sous-élément [15] en position [3]
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [17:18] en position [11]
    sous-élément [17] en position [11]
    sous-élément [18] en position [14]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] ou rien pour arrêter : 
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : ^\s*\d+\s*$
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter :    1456
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [   1456] en position [0]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*\d+\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter : 
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : ^\s*(\d+)\s*$
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter : 1456
J'ai trouvé la correspondance [1456] en position [0]
    sous-élément [1456] en position [0]
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter : abcd 1456
Je n'ai pas trouvé de correspondances
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] ou rien pour arrêter : 
Tapez le modèle à tester ou rien pour arrêter : (a+)+$
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [(a+)+$] ou rien pour arrêter : aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
La recherche a été abandonnée : elle durait plus d'une seconde
Tapez la chaîne à comparer au modèle [(a+)+$] ou rien pour arrêter :
