Comments:

  • Each command SQL is preceded by a two-line header: the event type ([CommandExecuted]), the execution time, and the command parameters;
  • Line 4: [EnsureDeleted] deleted the database, which already existed (the program had already been run);
  • lines 7–20: [EnsureCreated] created the database, assigned it the character set [utf8mb4] (the full Unicode set of MySQL), then created the table [Articles] from the entity [Article]: the table name is that of the context property [DbSet], the columns are named after the properties, and the column [Id] is the primary key with a generated value ([AUTO_INCREMENT]). All columns are [NOT NULL]: the types [int] and [decimal] do not allow the value [null], nor does the type [string], since nullable types are enabled (we’ll come back to this later);
  • Note the default types: [longtext] for a string (text of any length), and [decimal(65,30)] for a [decimal] (65 digits, 30 of which are after the decimal point). These are rarely the ones we want: the following paragraph shows how to specify them;
  • lines 21–41: [SaveChanges] sent a single command containing three configured [INSERT] commands. Each is followed by a [SELECT] that reads back the primary key generated by MySQL ([LAST_INSERT_ID()]): EF Core copies it to the [Id] property of the inserted object. Parameter values are masked ('?'): these are application data, which may be confidential. During debugging, they can be displayed by adding the [.EnableSensitiveDataLogging()] option to the context configuration;
  • Lines 42–50: The query LINQ [contexte.Articles.OrderBy(a => a.Nom)] was translated into a command [SELECT ... ORDER BY]. EF Core created a [Article] object for each row read.

We did not write any SQL commands or any column-reading code: that is the whole point of a ORM. We can also see that this doesn’t eliminate the need to understand SQL: to determine whether the generated SQL is correct and effective, you need to know how to read it.

docs.title: 11.3. The model
docs.text:
EF Core builds its model from entities in three steps:

  • First, it applies its conventions;
  • it supplements or corrects them using the annotations (attributes) applied to the entities;
  • finally, it applies the configuration written in C# in the [OnModelCreating] method of the context: the API flow.

docs.title: 11.3.1. The Conventions
docs.text:
We saw the essentials of these in the first example:

  • any public property with a [get] getter and a [set] (or [init]) setter is stored in a column of the same name;
  • the property [Id] or [<Entité>Id] is the primary key; if it is an integer, its values are generated by SGBD;
  • the table name is that of the [DbSet] property of the context (or, failing that, that of the class);
  • a property of a nullable type ([int?], [DateOnly?], [string?]) results in a column [NULL]; a property of a non-nullable type ([int], [decimal], [string] when nullable reference types are enabled) results in a [NOT NULL] column;
  • a property that references another entity, or a collection of entities, defines a relationship (we’ll cover this later).

docs.title: 11.3.2. Annotations and the API schema
docs.text:
The [Modele] project defines two entities configured in two different ways. The first is configured using annotations:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace Modele;

// an entity configured by annotations
[Table("produits")]
public class Produit
{
     // The primary key is not named "Id": it must be designated
    [Key]
    public int Code { get; set; }

     // Required string of up to 50 characters
    [Required, MaxLength(50)]
    public string Nom { get; set; } = "";

     // nullable reference type: column NULL allowed
    [MaxLength(200)]
    public string? Description { get; set; }

     // Column name and type (SQL) are enforced
    [Column("prix_ht", TypeName = "decimal(10,2)")]
    public decimal PrixHT { get; set; }

     // nullable value type: NULL column allowed
    public DateOnly? DateRetrait { get; set; }

     // calculated property: no column
    [NotMapped]
    public decimal PrixTTC => PrixHT * 1.2M;
}
  • lines 1–2: the attributes used belong to these two namespaces of .NET. They are not specific to EF Core: the validation attributes ([Required], [MaxLength]) are also used to validate data in ASP.NET Core forms;
  • line 7: the table name;
  • Lines 11–12: The primary key is not named [Id]; the [Key] attribute identifies it;
  • lines 15–16: a required column ([Required]: [NOT NULL]) with a maximum of 50 characters ([MaxLength(50)]: [varchar(50)]). [Required] is redundant here, as the non-nullable type [string] is sufficient to make the column required; it was essential prior to C# 8;
  • lines 19–20: the type *[string?] specifies an optional description: the column will accept the value *[NULL];
  • lines 23–24: [Column] specifies the column name and its type, SQL: [decimal(10,2)], 10 digits, including 2 decimal places;
  • line 27: an optional date. The type [DateOnly] (.NET 6) represents a date without a time: Pomelo associates it with the type SQL [date];
  • lines 30–31: [NotMapped] excludes a property from the model. Here, this is unnecessary: a property without an accessor ([set]) is not registered. The attribute documents the intent.

The second entity has no attributes:

namespace Modele;

// An entity with no annotations: it is configured by the API flow
public class Fournisseur
{
    public int Numero { get; set; }
    public string RaisonSociale { get; set; } = "";
    public string? Telephone { get; set; }
    public DateTime DateCreation { get; set; }
}

It is configured in context by the API flow:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Modele;

// a context used solely to examine the model: it never connects to the server
public class ModeleContext : DbContext
{
    public DbSet<Produit> Produits => Set<Produit>();
    public DbSet<Fournisseur> Fournisseurs => Set<Fournisseur>();

    protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options)
    {
        const string connexion = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=efmodele;User=root;Password=";
        options.UseMySql(connexion, new MySqlServerVersion(new Version(8, 0, 36)));
    }

     // the API fluid: model configuration via code
    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
        modelBuilder.Entity<Fournisseur>(fournisseur =>
        {
            fournisseur.ToTable("fournisseurs");
            fournisseur.HasKey(f => f.Numero);
            fournisseur.Property(f => f.RaisonSociale).IsRequired().HasMaxLength(60);
            fournisseur.HasIndex(f => f.RaisonSociale).IsUnique();
            fournisseur.Property(f => f.Telephone).HasColumnName("tel").HasMaxLength(20);
            fournisseur.Property(f => f.DateCreation).HasDefaultValueSql("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP");
        });
    }
}
  • Line 13: The [efmodele] database will never exist: this context is used solely to examine the model, which does not require a connection (the server version is specified explicitly);
  • line 18: the [OnModelCreating] method receives a [ModelBuilder] object used to describe the model. It is called only once per context type: EF Core caches the model;
  • line 20: [Entity<Fournisseur>(...)] receives a lambda that configures the [Fournisseur] entity. Each method returns the configuration object, which allows calls to be chained together: hence the name “API fluid”;
  • line 22: the table name;
  • line 23: the primary key is the property [Numero];
  • line 24: a required column with a maximum of 60 characters;
  • line 25: a unique index on the company name: no two suppliers can have the same one. There is no equivalent validation attribute; EF Core provides the attribute [Index], placed on the class, which we will use for items;
  • line 26: the property [Telephone] is stored in the column [tel];
  • line 27: the [DateCreation] column has a default value, calculated by SGBD. During an insertion, EF Core will not send a value for this column if the property has the default value for its type, which will allow SGBD to use [CURRENT_TIMESTAMP].

Everything that annotations do can be done with the API Fluid, and the API Fluid allows for even more (indexes, default values, composite keys, complex relationships). Annotations have the advantage of placing the configuration next to the property; the fluid API allows entities to remain independent of EF Core and consolidates the configuration in a single location. The two are often mixed: the fluid API takes precedence in case of a conflict.

The [Program.cs] program displays the model built by EF Core, followed by the SQL script, which would create the tables:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Metadata;
using Modele;

using var contexte = new ModeleContext();

// the model built by EF Core: entities, tables, columns
foreach (IEntityType entite in contexte.Model.GetEntityTypes())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"entité {entite.ClrType.Name} -> table {entite.GetTableName()}");
    foreach (IProperty propriete in entite.GetProperties())
    {
        string cle = propriete.IsPrimaryKey() ? " (clé primaire)" : "";
        string nulle = propriete.IsNullable ? "NULL" : "NOT NULL";
        Console.WriteLine($"  {propriete.Name,-14} -> {propriete.GetColumnName(),-14} {propriete.GetColumnType(),-16} {nulle}{cle}");
    }
}

// the SQL script for creating tables, without executing it
Console.WriteLine("--- script de création");
// (duplicate empty lines are removed)
Console.WriteLine(contexte.Database.GenerateCreateScript().Replace("\n\n\n", "\n\n").Trim());
  • line 8: the [Model] property of the context provides access to the model: its entities ([IEntityType]), and for each one, its properties ([IProperty]);
  • Line 10: [ClrType] is the C# type of the entity, and [GetTableName()] is the name of its table;
  • Lines 13–15: For each property, the column name, its type (SQL), whether it accepts the value [NULL], and whether it is part of the primary key are displayed;
  • line 22: [Database.GenerateCreateScript()] returns the table creation script SQL without executing it. This is the script that [EnsureCreated] would execute.

Results:

> dotnet run
entité Fournisseur -> table fournisseurs
  Numero         -> Numero         int              NOT NULL (clé primaire)
  DateCreation   -> DateCreation   datetime(6)      NOT NULL
  RaisonSociale  -> RaisonSociale  varchar(60)      NOT NULL
  Telephone      -> tel            varchar(20)      NULL
entité Produit -> table produits
  Code           -> Code           int              NOT NULL (clé primaire)
  DateRetrait    -> DateRetrait    date             NULL
  Description    -> Description    varchar(200)     NULL
  Nom            -> Nom            varchar(50)      NOT NULL
  PrixHT         -> prix_ht        decimal(10,2)    NOT NULL
--- creation script
ALTER DATABASE CHARACTER SET utf8mb4;

CREATE TABLE `fournisseurs` (
    `Numero` int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
    `RaisonSociale` varchar(60) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NOT NULL,
    `tel` varchar(20) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NULL,
    `DateCreation` datetime(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT `PK_fournisseurs` PRIMARY KEY (`Numero`)
) CHARACTER SET=utf8mb4;

CREATE TABLE `produits` (
    `Code` int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
    `Nom` varchar(50) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NOT NULL,
    `Description` varchar(200) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NULL,
    `prix_ht` decimal(10,2) NOT NULL,
    `DateRetrait` date NULL,
    CONSTRAINT `PK_produits` PRIMARY KEY (`Code`)
) CHARACTER SET=utf8mb4;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX `IX_fournisseurs_RaisonSociale` ON `fournisseurs` (`RaisonSociale`);
  • Lines 2–6: The [Fournisseur] entity and its columns. The SQL types come from the configuration ([varchar(60)], [varchar(20)]) or from the provider’s choices for a C# type: [int] for [int], [datetime(6)] (microsecond precision) for [DateTime];
  • lines 7–12: the entity [Produit]. Nullable properties ([DateOnly?], [string?]) result in columns [NULL]; the property [PrixTTC] does not appear in the model;
  • Lines 16–33: the creation script. It contains the entire configuration: table and column names, data types ([NOT NULL]), default values, primary keys (with [AUTO_INCREMENT] for integer keys), and unique indexes. Text columns use the [utf8mb4] character set.

docs.title: 11.3.3. Nullable types and columns NULL
docs.text:
Nullable reference types (C# 8, enabled by [<Nullable>enable</Nullable>] in the course projects) have an impact on the model: EF Core reads the nullability annotations generated by the compiler. A [string] property results in a [NOT NULL] column, and a [string?] property results in a [NULL] column. In a project where nullable types are not enabled, all text columns accept [NULL], except those marked [Required].

You must therefore choose the type of each property carefully: it expresses both a C# code rule (“this value may be missing”) and a database constraint. For a required property, two notations are common:

// a default value that satisfies the compiler
public string Nom { get; set; } = "";
// a required member (C# 11): the code that creates the object must assign a value
public required string Nom { get; set; }

The second is safer: the compiler rejects [new Article { Prix = 10 }], where the name has been omitted. EF Core can create entities with [required] members: it does not go through the C# code’s object initializer. For navigation properties to another entity, which EF Core fills in itself, we encounter the notation [= null!]: we’ll look at this when discussing relationships.

docs.title: 11.4. The following examples: two shared libraries
docs.text: The examples in the following paragraphs all use the [efarticles] database and its [articles] table, populated with the six articles from Chapter 10. Rather than repeating the entity and context in each project, we place them in a class library, [Articles.Data], which the projects reference. We also replace the EF Core log, which is too verbose for our examples, with a more compact log, placed in a second library, [Ef.Outils].

docs.title: 11.4.1. The compact log file SQL
docs.text:
using System.Data.Common;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Diagnostics;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

namespace Ef.Outils;

// a compact log of SQL commands executed by EF Core
public static class JournalSql
{
     // an extension member (C# 14) of type DbContextOptionsBuilder
    extension(DbContextOptionsBuilder options)
    {
         // options.AvecJournalSql(): displays each executed SQL command
        public DbContextOptionsBuilder AvecJournalSql() => options.LogTo(Filtre, Afficher);
    }

     // selected events: SQL command executed or failed, start and end of transactions
    private static bool Filtre(EventId id, LogLevel niveau) =>
        id == RelationalEventId.CommandExecuted || id == RelationalEventId.CommandError
        || id == RelationalEventId.TransactionStarted
        || id == RelationalEventId.TransactionCommitted || id == RelationalEventId.TransactionRolledBack;

     // displays an event
    private static void Afficher(EventData donnees)
    {
        switch (donnees)
        {
            case CommandExecutedEventData commande:
                AfficherCommande(commande.Command);
                break;
            case CommandErrorEventData erreur:
                AfficherCommande(erreur.Command);
                Console.WriteLine("    SQL> -- échec de la commande");
                break;
            case TransactionEventData when donnees.EventId == RelationalEventId.TransactionStarted:
                Console.WriteLine("    SQL> -- début de transaction");
                break;
            case TransactionEventData when donnees.EventId == RelationalEventId.TransactionCommitted:
                Console.WriteLine("    SQL> -- transaction validée (COMMIT)");
                break;
            case TransactionEventData:
                Console.WriteLine("    SQL> -- transaction annulée (ROLLBACK)");
                break;
        }
    }

     // Displays the SQL command (indented) followed by its parameters
    private static void AfficherCommande(DbCommand commande)
    {
         // Empty lines are ignored
        foreach (string ligne in commande.CommandText.Split('\n').Select(l => l.TrimEnd()).Where(l => l != ""))
        {
            Console.WriteLine("    SQL> " + ligne);
        }
        if (commande.Parameters.Count > 0)
        {
            var parametres = commande.Parameters.Cast<DbParameter>()
                .Select(p => $"{(p.ParameterName.StartsWith('@') ? "" : "@")}{p.ParameterName}={p.Value}");
            Console.WriteLine($"    SQL> -- paramètres : {string.Join(", ", parametres)}");
        }
    }
}
  • lines 12–15: an extension member (C# 14, see Chapter 4) of type [DbContextOptionsBuilder], the type of the parameter of [OnConfiguring]. We’ll write [options.UseMySql(...).AvecJournalSql()], as if the method had been written by EF Core. It calls another overload of [LogTo], which takes two functions: a filter, which selects the events to log, and a display method, which receives the event itself ([EventData]) rather than preformatted text;
  • lines 19–22: the selected events. Each event in EF Core has an identifier; those for relational operations are constants of the [RelationalEventId] class. We log executed or failed SQL commands, as well as the start, commit, and rollback of transactions;
  • Lines 27–43: Each event type corresponds to a class derived from [EventData], which provides details about it: [CommandExecutedEventData] contains the executed command ADO.NET ([DbCommand], see Chapter 10). The selection is made using a [switch] with filtering by type pattern and [when] clauses;
  • lines 52–54: the command text, line by line, indented and preceded by [SQL>], with empty lines removed;
  • lines 56–60: the command parameters and their values. We read these directly from the command; therefore, our log always displays them, whereas the EF Core log hides them by default. This is acceptable for a course, but not for a production application.

docs.title: 11.4.2. The Entity and the Context of the Articles
docs.text:
The [Article] entity from the [Articles.Data] library uses the annotations from the previous paragraph:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Articles.Data;

// a warehouse item, with annotations specifying its table
[Table("articles")]
[Index(nameof(Nom), IsUnique = true)]
public class Article
{
     // primary key, generated by SGBD (AUTO_INCREMENT)
    public int Id { get; set; }

     // item name: required, up to 30 characters, unique (see [Index])
    [MaxLength(30)]
    public required string Nom { get; set; }

     // Price: 10 digits, including 2 decimal places
    [Column(TypeName = "decimal(10,2)")]
    public decimal Prix { get; set; }

     // Current stock and minimum stock level below which restocking is required
    public int StockActuel { get; set; }
    public int StockMinimum { get; set; }

     // display
    public override string ToString() => $"[{Id}, {Nom}, {Prix}, {StockActuel}, {StockMinimum}]";
}
  • line 8: the table is named [articles], as in Chapter 10;
  • line 9: the attribute [Index] of EF Core (namespace [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore]) creates a unique index on the column [Nom]: No two articles may have the same name, as in the 2008 course database;
  • lines 16–17: a required name of no more than 30 characters. The member is [required]: the code that creates an item must specify its name;
  • lines 20–21: a price in [decimal(10,2)].

The context is as follows:

using Ef.Outils;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Articles.Data;

// database context [efarticles]
public class ArticlesContext : DbContext
{
     // connection string and server version MySQL
    public const string Connexion = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=efarticles;User=root;Password=";
    public static readonly ServerVersion VersionServeur = new MySqlServerVersion(new Version(8, 0, 36));

     // constructor without parameters: configuration is handled by OnConfiguring
    public ArticlesContext() { }

     // constructor receiving a pre-configured object (dependency injection)
    public ArticlesContext(DbContextOptions<ArticlesContext> options) : base(options) { }

     // the item table
    public DbSet<Article> Articles => Set<Article>();

     // default configuration, if the constructor has not received one
    protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options)
    {
        if (!options.IsConfigured)
        {
             // with order display SQL (see project [Ef.Outils])
            options.UseMySql(Connexion, VersionServeur).AvecJournalSql();
        }
    }

     // (re)creation of the database with its six items, without a log
    public static void Initialiser()
    {
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<ArticlesContext>()
            .UseMySql(Connexion, VersionServeur)
            .Options;
        using var contexte = new ArticlesContext(options);
        contexte.Database.EnsureDeleted();
        contexte.Database.EnsureCreated();
        contexte.Articles.AddRange(
            new Article { Nom = "vélo", Prix = 500, StockActuel = 10, StockMinimum = 5 },
            new Article { Nom = "pompe", Prix = 10, StockActuel = 10, StockMinimum = 2 },
            new Article { Nom = "arc", Prix = 600, StockActuel = 4, StockMinimum = 1 },
            new Article { Nom = "flèches - lot de 6", Prix = 100, StockActuel = 12, StockMinimum = 20 },
            new Article { Nom = "combinaison de plongée", Prix = 300, StockActuel = 8, StockMinimum = 2 },
            new Article { Nom = "bouteilles d'oxygène", Prix = 120, StockActuel = 10, StockMinimum = 5 });
        contexte.SaveChanges();
    }
}
  • lines 10–11: the connection string and server version, which are public so that other projects can use them;
  • line 14: a first constructor, with no parameters: the configuration will be handled by [OnConfiguring];
  • line 17: a second constructor, which receives a pre-configured object ([DbContextOptions<ArticlesContext>]) and passes it to the constructor of the [DbContext] class. This is the constructor used by dependency injection (we’ll cover this later);
  • line 25: [OnConfiguring] is called in both cases. [IsConfigured] checks whether the context received a configuration via its constructor. If not, the default configuration is used: MySQL, with the compact log;
  • lines 33–48: a static method that recreates the database with its six articles. It creates a context with a configuration that does not include a log: we do not want to see the SQL from this initialization in the example results. [DbContextOptionsBuilder<T>] is the generic version of the object received by [OnConfiguring]; its property [Options] renders the built configuration. [AddRange] adds multiple entities at once.

The sample projects reference the [Articles.Data] library, which in turn references [Ef.Outils]:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
     <!-- the entity [Article] and the context [ArticlesContext] (including EF Core) -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../Articles.Data/Articles.Data.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

The EF Core and Pomelo packages, referenced by [Articles.Data], are inherited by the projects that reference it.

docs.title: 11.5. Basic operations: add, read, modify, delete
11.5.1. The [Crud] program
docs.text:
The [Crud] project demonstrates the four basic operations (CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete):

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// The database is recreated with its six items
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();
using var contexte = new ArticlesContext();

// 1 - search by primary key
Console.WriteLine("--- Find(1)");
Article? velo = contexte.Articles.Find(1);
Console.WriteLine(velo);
Console.WriteLine("--- Find(1) une seconde fois");
Article? velo2 = contexte.Articles.Find(1);
Console.WriteLine($"même objet : {ReferenceEquals(velo, velo2)}");

// 2 - Add an item
Console.WriteLine("--- Add");
var x = new Article { Nom = "x", Prix = 100, StockActuel = 10, StockMinimum = 1 };
contexte.Articles.Add(x);
Console.WriteLine($"avant SaveChanges : état={contexte.Entry(x).State}, Id={x.Id}");
contexte.SaveChanges();
Console.WriteLine($"après SaveChanges : état={contexte.Entry(x).State}, Id={x.Id}");

// 3 - Update: simply modify the object
Console.WriteLine("--- modification du prix");
x.Prix *= 1.1M;
var prix = contexte.Entry(x).Property(a => a.Prix);
Console.WriteLine($"état={contexte.Entry(x).State}, prix d'origine={prix.OriginalValue}, prix actuel={prix.CurrentValue}");
contexte.SaveChanges();
Console.WriteLine($"après SaveChanges : état={contexte.Entry(x).State}");

// 4 - deletion
Console.WriteLine("--- Remove");
contexte.Articles.Remove(x);
Console.WriteLine($"avant SaveChanges : état={contexte.Entry(x).State}");
contexte.SaveChanges();
Console.WriteLine($"après SaveChanges : état={contexte.Entry(x).State}");

// 5 - Entities tracked by the context
Console.WriteLine("--- les entités suivies");
velo!.StockActuel--;
contexte.ChangeTracker.DetectChanges();
Console.WriteLine(contexte.ChangeTracker.DebugView.LongView);

Results:

> dotnet run
--- Find(1)
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Id` = @__p_0
    SQL> LIMIT 1
    SQL> -- parameters: @__p_0=1
[1, vélo, 500,00, 10, 5]
--- Find(1) a second time
même objet : True
--- Add
avant SaveChanges : état=Added, Id=0
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> INSERT INTO `articles` (`Nom`, `Prix`, `StockActuel`, `StockMinimum`)
    SQL> VALUES (@p0, @p1, @p2, @p3);
    SQL> SELECT `Id`
    SQL> FROM `articles`
    SQL> WHERE ROW_COUNT() = 1 AND `Id` = LAST_INSERT_ID();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p0=x, @p1=100, @p2=10, @p3=1
    SQL> -- Transaction validated (COMMIT)
après SaveChanges : état=Unchanged, Id=7
--- price change
état=Modified, prix d'origine=100, prix actuel=110,0
    SQL> SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1;
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` SET `Prix` = @p0
    SQL> WHERE `Id` = @p1;
    SQL> SELECT ROW_COUNT();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p1=7, @p0=110.0
après SaveChanges : état=Unchanged
--- Remove
avant SaveChanges : état=Deleted
    SQL> SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1;
    SQL> DELETE FROM `articles`
    SQL> WHERE `Id` = @p0;
    SQL> SELECT ROW_COUNT();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p0=7
après SaveChanges : état=Detached
--- Tracked Entities
Article {Id: 1} Modified
    Id: 1 PK
    Nom: 'vélo'
    Prix: 500,00
    StockActuel: 9 Modified Originally 10
    StockMinimum: 5

Comments:

  • Line 10: [Find(1)] searches for the record with primary key 1. The returned type is [Article?]: [Find] returns [null] if the key does not exist. The generated SQL (lines 2–7) is a configured [SELECT], limited to one line;
  • line 13: the second call to [Find(1)] does not send any SQL commands, and returns the same object (line 10). The context stores the entities it has read or added: before querying the database, [Find] checks whether the requested entity is already being tracked. A context never contains two objects for the same row in the database;
  • Lines 18–19: Adding an item. Before [SaveChanges], the item is in state [Added] and its [Id] value is 0 (line 12). [SaveChanges] sends a command to [INSERT], retrieves the generated key, and places it in [x.Id] (line 21). The item transitions to the [Unchanged] state: it is identical to the row in the database;
  • line 26: to modify a row in the database, simply modify the object. No [Update] method is required: the context has retained a copy of the read values (the original values) and compares the current values to them. The item transitions to status [Modified] (line 23);
  • line 27: [contexte.Entry(x)] provides access to the tracking information for the [x] entity: its status ([State]) and, for each property, its original value ([OriginalValue]) and its current value ([CurrentValue]);
  • Line 29: The generated order [UPDATE] (lines 25–28) modifies only the column that has changed, [Prix]. It is followed by a [SELECT ROW_COUNT()]: EF Core verifies that the order has indeed modified a row;
  • lines 34–36: the deletion. [Remove] changes the item’s status to [Deleted]; [SaveChanges] sends the order [DELETE]. The object is then no longer tracked by the context: it is in state [Detached];
  • lines 41–43: the object [contexte.ChangeTracker] (the “change tracking”) manages the tracked entities. [DetectChanges] compares the current values of the entities to their original values (EF Core automatically calls it in [SaveChanges], [Entry], and a few other methods). The property [DebugView.LongView] returns a description of all tracked entities (lines 38–44): the context now tracks only the bicycle, whose inventory has decreased from 10 to 9. The operator [!] in [velo!] tells the compiler that [velo], of type [Article?], is not [null] here.

Two details of the SQL generated by Pomelo:

  • the command [INSERT], followed by [SELECT] from the generated key, is enclosed within a transaction (lines 13–20): the command contains two SQL commands that must succeed together. We’ll come back to transactions later;
  • the isolated commands [UPDATE] and [DELETE] are not enclosed within a transaction. They are preceded by [SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1], a setting for session MySQL (each command is committed as soon as it is executed) that the vendor restores as a precaution. This setting has no effect on an explicitly opened transaction, as we will see.

docs.title: 11.5.2. The States of an Entity
docs.text:
Tracking changes is based on the state of each entity, a value from the [EntityState] enumeration:

StateMeaning[Detached]The object is not tracked by the context (created by [new] and not yet added, or deleted from the database)[Added]The object has been added to the context ([Add]): [SaveChanges] will insert it into the database[Unchanged]The object was read from the database (or saved) and has not been modified since[Modified]At least one property has been modified: [SaveChanges] will send a command [UPDATE][Deleted]The object has been marked for deletion ([Remove]): [SaveChanges] will send a command [DELETE]

Note the work cycle with EF Core: entities are read, modified like ordinary objects, added, and deleted, then [SaveChanges] is called, which sends all necessary commands to the database in a single batch. The context acts as a “unit of work.” A context is a lightweight object designed for a short lifespan: a unit of work, such as a HTTP query in a web application. The same context is not used throughout the entire life of an application, as it would accumulate tracked entities.

docs.title: 11.5.3. Bulk Updates and Reading Without Tracking
docs.text:
Tracking changes comes at a cost: to increase the price of 100 items, you must read all 100 items, modify them one by one, and [SaveChanges] will send 100 [UPDATE] commands. EF Core 7 introduced two methods that directly send a SQL command covering all rows selected by a query: [ExecuteUpdate] and [ExecuteDelete]. The [MajEnMasse] project describes these, as well as read-only operations:

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// The database is recreated with its six items
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();
using var contexte = new ArticlesContext();

// 1 - ExecuteUpdate: a single order UPDATE, no entities loaded into memory
Console.WriteLine("--- réapprovisionnement des articles en rupture");
int nbLignes = contexte.Articles
    .Where(a => a.StockActuel < a.StockMinimum)
    .ExecuteUpdate(s => s.SetProperty(a => a.StockActuel, a => a.StockMinimum * 2));
Console.WriteLine($"{nbLignes} article(s) modifié(s)");

Console.WriteLine("--- hausse de 10 % des prix inférieurs à 150 euros");
nbLignes = contexte.Articles
    .Where(a => a.Prix < 150)
    .ExecuteUpdate(s => s.SetProperty(a => a.Prix, a => a.Prix * 1.1M));
Console.WriteLine($"{nbLignes} article(s) modifié(s)");

// 2 - ExecuteDelete: a single order DELETE
Console.WriteLine("--- suppression des articles de plus de 550 euros");
nbLignes = contexte.Articles.Where(a => a.Prix > 550).ExecuteDelete();
Console.WriteLine($"{nbLignes} article(s) supprimé(s)");

// 3 - read without tracking changes
Console.WriteLine("--- AsNoTracking");
List<Article> articles = contexte.Articles.AsNoTracking().OrderBy(a => a.Id).ToList();
articles.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);
Console.WriteLine($"entités suivies par le contexte : {contexte.ChangeTracker.Entries().Count()}");
// a change to an untracked entity is ignored by SaveChanges
articles[0].Prix = 0;
Console.WriteLine($"SaveChanges : {contexte.SaveChanges()} ligne(s) modifiée(s)");

// 4 - ExecuteUpdate does not modify entities already loaded by the context
Console.WriteLine("--- ExecuteUpdate et entités suivies");
Article velo = contexte.Articles.Single(a => a.Nom == "vélo");
contexte.Articles.Where(a => a.Id == velo.Id).ExecuteUpdate(s => s.SetProperty(a => a.Prix, 450M));
Console.WriteLine($"prix en mémoire : {velo.Prix}");
contexte.Entry(velo).Reload();
Console.WriteLine($"prix après Reload : {velo.Prix}");

Results:

> dotnet run
--- restocking of out-of-stock items
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> SET `a`.`StockActuel` = `a`.`StockMinimum` * 2
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`StockActuel` < `a`.`StockMinimum`
1 article(s) modifié(s)
--- 10% price increase for items under 150 euros
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> SET `a`.`Prix` = `a`.`Prix` * 1.1
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Prix` < 150.0
3 article(s) modifié(s)
--- Removal of items priced over 550 euros
    SQL> DELETE `a`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Prix` > 550.0
1 article(s) supprimé(s)
--- AsNoTracking
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> ORDER BY `a`.`Id`
[1, vélo, 500,00, 10, 5]
[2, pompe, 11,00, 10, 2]
[4, flèches - lot de 6, 110,00, 40, 20]
[5, combinaison de plongée, 300,00, 8, 2]
[6, bouteilles d'oxygène, 132,00, 10, 5]
entités suivies par le contexte : 0
SaveChanges : 0 ligne(s) modifiée(s)
--- ExecuteUpdate and tracked entities
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Nom` = 'vélo'
    SQL> LIMIT 2
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> SET `a`.`Prix` = 450.0
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Id` = @__velo_Id_0
    SQL> -- parameters: @__velo_Id_0=1
prix en mémoire : 500,00
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Id` = @__p_0
    SQL> LIMIT 1
    SQL> -- parameters: @__p_0=1
prix après Reload : 450,00

Comments:

  • Lines 10–12: [ExecuteUpdate] applies to a query ([Where]) and receives a lambda that describes the columns to be modified: [SetProperty(propriété, nouvelle valeur)]. The new value may depend on the row itself ([a => a.StockMinimum * 2]). The SQL statement (lines 3–5) is executed immediately, without [SaveChanges], and returns the number of modified rows;
  • lines 16–18: a 10% increase in low prices. Note that the C# code constants ([150], [1.1M]) are written within the text of the SQL command ([150.0], [1.1]);
  • line 23: [ExecuteDelete] removes the lines selected by the query—in this case, the bow, the only item priced over 550 euros;
  • line 28: [AsNoTracking()] requests a read without tracking: the entities read are not stored by the context (line 26). This is faster and more memory-efficient: it is used for data that is read without being modified (display, calculations). The trade-off is that [SaveChanges] ignores changes to these entities (line 27);
  • lines 37–41: a pitfall. [ExecuteUpdate] operates directly on the database: it does not modify entities already loaded by the context. The bicycle tracked by the context retains its old price (line 37) until it is read again with [contexte.Entry(velo).Reload()]. [Single] returns the single element in the query and throws an exception if there are zero or more elements: this is why the generated SQL requests two lines ([LIMIT 2]).

docs.title: 11.6.1. Queries
docs.text:
Chapter 5 introduced LINQ for in-memory collections. The same operators ([Where], [OrderBy], [Select], [First], [Count], [Sum]...) apply to a [DbSet<T>], but they are not executed by .NET: EF Core translates them into SQL, and it is SGBD that executes them. The [Linq] project provides several examples:

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// the database is recreated with its six items
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();
using var contexte = new ArticlesContext();

// 1 - filtering and sorting
Console.WriteLine("--- les articles à réapprovisionner, par ordre alphabétique");
List<Article> aCommander = contexte.Articles
    .Where(a => a.StockActuel < a.StockMinimum)
    .OrderBy(a => a.Nom)
    .ToList();
aCommander.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);

// 2 - projection: only the relevant columns are retrieved
Console.WriteLine("--- valeur du stock de chaque article");
var valeurs = contexte.Articles
    .Select(a => new { a.Nom, Valeur = a.Prix * a.StockActuel })
    .OrderByDescending(v => v.Valeur)
    .ToList();
foreach (var v in valeurs)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{v.Nom} : {v.Valeur:0.00} euros");
}

// 3 - a single result; the variable [prixMin] becomes a parameter SQL
Console.WriteLine("--- le premier article de plus de 200 euros");
decimal prixMin = 200;
Article? article = contexte.Articles.OrderBy(a => a.Prix).FirstOrDefault(a => a.Prix > prixMin);
Console.WriteLine(article?.ToString() ?? "aucun");

// 4 - Aggregates: the calculation is performed by SGBD
Console.WriteLine("--- agrégats");
int nbArticles = contexte.Articles.Count();
decimal valeurStock = contexte.Articles.Sum(a => a.Prix * a.StockActuel);
Console.WriteLine($"{nbArticles} articles, valeur du stock : {valeurStock:0.00} euros");

// 5 - methods: .NET translated to SQL
Console.WriteLine("--- StartsWith et Contains");
// a list, not an array (see explanations)
List<string> noms = ["arc", "pompe", "raquette"];
var resultats = contexte.Articles
    .Where(a => a.Nom.StartsWith("b") || noms.Contains(a.Nom))
    .Select(a => a.Nom)
    .ToList();
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", resultats));

// 6 - the SQL of a query, without executing it
Console.WriteLine("--- ToQueryString");
IQueryable<Article> requete = contexte.Articles.Where(a => a.Prix < 150).OrderBy(a => a.Prix);
Console.WriteLine(requete.ToQueryString());

// 7 - pagination: the third page of two items, sorted by price in ascending order
Console.WriteLine("--- Skip et Take");
int taillePage = 2, numeroPage = 3;
List<string> page = contexte.Articles
    .OrderBy(a => a.Prix)
    .Skip((numeroPage - 1) * taillePage)
    .Take(taillePage)
    .Select(a => $"{a.Nom} ({a.Prix} euros)")
    .ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"page {numeroPage} : {string.Join(", ", page)}");

// 8 - a C# method that EF Core cannot translate
Console.WriteLine("--- méthode non traduisible");
try
{
    var liste = contexte.Articles.Where(a => Regles.EnRupture(a)).ToList();
}
catch (InvalidOperationException e)
{
     // Only the first sentence of the message is displayed
    int fin = e.Message.IndexOf(" Either");
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : {(fin > 0 ? e.Message[..fin] : e.Message)}");
}
// AsEnumerable: the rest of the query is executed in memory by .NET
var enRupture = contexte.Articles.AsEnumerable().Where(a => Regles.EnRupture(a)).ToList();
enRupture.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);

// a business rule written in C#
static class Regles
{
     // an item is out of stock if its inventory is below the minimum inventory level
    public static bool EnRupture(Article a) => a.StockActuel < a.StockMinimum;
}

Results:

> dotnet run
--- items to be restocked, in alphabetical order
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`StockActuel` < `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> ORDER BY `a`.`Nom`
[4, flèches - lot de 6, 100,00, 12, 20]
--- stock value for each item
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix` * CAST(`a`.`StockActuel` AS decimal(65,30)) AS `Valeur`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> ORDER BY `a`.`Prix` * CAST(`a`.`StockActuel` AS decimal(65,30)) DESC
vélo : 5000,00 euros
arc : 2400,00 euros
combinaison de plongée : 2400,00 euros
flèches - lot de 6 : 1200,00 euros
bouteilles d'oxygène : 1200,00 euros
pompe : 100,00 euros
--- the first item costing more than 200 euros
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Prix` > @__prixMin_0
    SQL> ORDER BY `a`.`Prix`
    SQL> LIMIT 1
    SQL> -- parameters: @__prixMin_0=200
[5, combinaison de plongée, 300,00, 8, 2]
--- aggregates
    SQL> SELECT COUNT(*)
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> SELECT COALESCE(SUM(`a`.`Prix` * CAST(`a`.`StockActuel` AS decimal(65,30))), 0.0)
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
6 articles, valeur du stock : 12300,00 euros
--- StartsWith and Contains
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Nom`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE (`a`.`Nom` LIKE 'b%') OR `a`.`Nom` IN ('arc', 'pompe', 'raquette')
arc, bouteilles d'oxygène, pompe
--- ToQueryString
SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
FROM `articles` AS `a`
WHERE `a`.`Prix` < 150.0
ORDER BY `a`.`Prix`
--- Skip and Take
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> ORDER BY `a`.`Prix`
    SQL> LIMIT @__p_1 OFFSET @__p_0
    SQL> -- parameters: @__p_1=2, @__p_0=4
page 3 : vélo (500,00 euros), arc (600,00 euros)
--- method cannot be translated
InvalidOperationException : The LINQ expression 'DbSet<Article>()
    .Where(a => Regles.EnRupture(a))' could not be translated.
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
[4, flèches - lot de 6, 100,00, 12, 20]

Comments:

  • Lines 10–13: [Where] and [OrderBy] become the clauses [WHERE] and [ORDER BY] (lines 5–6). The query is executed only when its results are requested, in this case by [ToList]: this is the deferred execution of LINQ (Chapter 5);
  • Lines 18–20: a projection. [Select] creates an object of an anonymous type for each item, containing only the name and the inventory value. The generated SQL (line 9) retrieves only the relevant columns and performs the calculation itself. Objects of the anonymous type are not entities: they are not tracked by the context. The provider converts the stock, which is an integer, to [decimal(65,30)] before the multiplication, which explains the many decimal places in the result, which is then formatted using [{v.Valeur:0.00}];
  • line 30: [FirstOrDefault] becomes [LIMIT 1]. The program variable [prixMin] becomes a parameter of the order SQL ([@__prixMin_0], line 21), whereas a constant written in the lambda is copied into the text SQL. Therefore, there is no need to worry about SQL injections: values coming from outside the program are always passed as parameters. This is the rule that Chapter 10 applied manually with parameterized queries;
  • lines 35–36: The aggregates [Count] and [Sum] are calculated by SGBD ([COUNT(*)], [SUM(...)]): only the result is transferred, not the rows. [COALESCE(..., 0.0)] returns 0 if the table is empty, just like [Sum] from LINQ;
  • Lines 42–45: Methods .NET known to EF Core are translated to SQL: [a.Nom.StartsWith("b")] becomes [LIKE 'b%'], and [noms.Contains(a.Nom)], which refers to a memory list, becomes [IN ('arc', 'pompe', 'raquette')] (line 35). There are many translated methods: operations on strings, dates, and mathematical functions;
  • lines 51–52: [ToQueryString()] returns the SQL value of a query without executing it (lines 37–41). This is useful for debugging;
  • lines 57–60: pagination, to display a long list page by page. [Skip] skips the items from previous pages, while [Take] keeps those from the requested page: they become the clauses [OFFSET] and [LIMIT] (line 46). Pagination only makes sense on a sorted list ([OrderBy]);
  • line 61: this projection contains an interpolated string, which EF Core does not translate into SQL. This is not an error: when the untranslatable operation is the final [Select], EF Core requests the necessary columns ([Nom] and [Prix]) from SGBD and performs the projection in memory on each row read. Note that the price is formatted according to the fr-FR locale, using a decimal comma;
  • lines 69–71: EF Core cannot translate the call to any method in the program: it does not know the code for it, and even if it did, it would not necessarily know how to write it in SQL. Executing the query triggers a [InvalidOperationException] (lines 50–51). The message (in English, like all exception messages in .NET), of which the program displays only the first sentence, then offers two solutions: rewrite the query, or explicitly switch to an in-memory evaluation;
  • line 78: [AsEnumerable()] transfers the query from [IQueryable<T>] to [IEnumerable<T>]: the preceding part is translated into SQL (here, reading the entire table), and the following part is executed by LINQ in memory. The result is correct, but the entire table was loaded: with a large table, this should be avoided. It is better to write the condition in the lambda ([a.StockActuel < a.StockMinimum]), as shown on line 11.

docs.title: 11.6.2. IQueryable and expression trees
docs.text:
How can the same lambda be executed in C# on a list and translated to SQL on a [DbSet]? Chapter 7 provided the answer: a [DbSet<T>] implements the [IQueryable<T>] interface, whose methods [Where], [OrderBy], [Select]... receive not delegates ([Func<T, bool>]) but expression trees ([Expression<Func<T, bool>>]). The compiler transforms the lambda [a => a.StockActuel < a.StockMinimum] into a data structure that describes it (“ comparison [<] of property [StockActuel] and property [StockMinimum] of parameter [a]”); EF Core traverses this structure and produces the equivalent SQL. A method such as [Regles.EnRupture] appears in the tree only as a method call, whose code cannot be analyzed: hence the error.

Operators are composed: a query can be built in stages, with each stage returning a new [IQueryable<T>], and only the final execution ([ToList], [First], [Count], [foreach]...) sends a SQL command:

IQueryable<Article> requete = contexte.Articles;
if (prixMax != null)
{
    requete = requete.Where(a => a.Prix <= prixMax);
}
requete = requete.OrderBy(a => a.Nom);
// a single order SELECT, with or without WHERE
List<Article> articles = requete.ToList();

docs.title: 11.6.3. An incompatibility between EF Core 9 and C# 14
docs.text: In the program [Linq], the list [noms] was declared as type [List<string>] rather than [string[]], with a comment referencing this paragraph. With an array, the query [contexte.Articles.Where(a => noms.Contains(a.Nom))] compiles but fails at runtime with a [InvalidOperationException] error (“An exception was thrown while attempting to evaluate a LINQ query parameter expression”). In fact, C# 14 has made the conversion of an array to [ReadOnlySpan<T>] (the type introduced in Chapter 5) an implicit language conversion, which also applies to the object on which an extension method is called. For an array, the call [noms.Contains(...)] therefore now refers to the extension method [MemoryExtensions.Contains(ReadOnlySpan<T>, T)] rather than [Enumerable.Contains(IEnumerable<T>, T)]: This is evident from examining the lambda’s expression tree, and the same program compiled in C# 13 ([<LangVersion>13</LangVersion>]) finds [Enumerable.Contains] and works. EF Core 9, released before C# 14, does not recognize this method: it attempts to evaluate the array conversion to [ReadOnlySpan<string>] to make it a parameter SQL, which fails (the internal exception is a [ArgumentException] thrown by the expression tree interpreter). EF Core 10, released alongside C# 14, supports this syntax. With EF Core 9, you can work around the issue by using a list, as shown here, or by writing [((IEnumerable<string>)noms).Contains(a.Nom)]. This is the only issue encountered in this chapter when using EF Core 9 with .NET 10.

docs.title: 11.7.1. The Store Model
docs.text:
The tables in a database are linked to one another. EF Core represents these links using navigation properties: properties that reference another entity or a collection of entities. The [Relations] project uses a [efboutique] database that describes a small store:

namespace Relations;

// a category includes multiple products (one-to-many relationship)
public class Categorie
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Nom { get; set; } = "";
     // navigation property: products in the category
    public List<Produit> Produits { get; set; } = [];
}

// A product belongs to a category and has multiple tags
public class Produit
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Nom { get; set; } = "";
    public decimal Prix { get; set; }
     // foreign key and navigation property to the category
    public int CategorieId { get; set; }
    public Categorie Categorie { get; set; } = null!;
     // many-to-many relationship with tags
    public List<Etiquette> Etiquettes { get; set; } = [];
}

// A tag (promotion, new item, etc.) is assigned to multiple products
public class Etiquette
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Libelle { get; set; } = "";
    public List<Produit> Produits { get; set; } = [];
}

// a customer places orders
public class Client
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Nom { get; set; } = "";
    public List<Commande> Commandes { get; set; } = [];
}

// a customer order, consisting of order lines
public class Commande
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public DateOnly Date { get; set; }
    public int ClientId { get; set; }
    public Client Client { get; set; } = null!;
    public List<LigneCommande> Lignes { get; set; } = [];
}

// an order line: a quantity of a product
public class LigneCommande
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public int Quantite { get; set; }
    public int CommandeId { get; set; }
    public Commande Commande { get; set; } = null!;
    public int ProduitId { get; set; }
    public Produit Produit { get; set; } = null!;
}
  • a one-to-many relationship between [Categorie] and [Produit]: a category contains multiple products (line 9), and a product belongs to a category (lines 19–20). The property [CategorieId] is the foreign key: by convention, the name of the navigation property followed by [Id]. It is optional in the code (EF Core would create it in the table if it did not exist in the class), but it is convenient: it allows you to determine a product’s category without loading it;
  • a many-to-many relationship between [Produit] and [Etiquette]: a product has multiple labels (line 22), and a label is associated with multiple products (line 30). There is no foreign key: the relationship will be stored in an association table created by EF Core;
  • the one-to-many relationships [Client] - [Commande] and [Commande] - [LigneCommande], and the many-to-one relationship [LigneCommande] - [Produit]: a line item represents a quantity of a product;
  • collections are initialized with an empty collection ([= []], a C# 12 collection expression). Navigation properties pointing to a single entity are initialized with [null!]: the value [null], accompanied by the operator [!], which tells the compiler not to flag a non-nullable property as receiving [null]. This is the conventional notation for a property that EF Core fills in itself during read operations, and which is never [null] in a properly loaded entity. Such a property defines a mandatory relationship (foreign key [NOT NULL]); a property of type [Categorie?] and a key of type [int?] would define an optional relationship.

The context is as follows:

using Ef.Outils;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Relations;

// the database context [efboutique]; [journal]: whether or not to display orders SQL
public class BoutiqueContext(bool journal = true) : DbContext
{
    public DbSet<Categorie> Categories => Set<Categorie>();
    public DbSet<Produit> Produits => Set<Produit>();
    public DbSet<Etiquette> Etiquettes => Set<Etiquette>();
    public DbSet<Client> Clients => Set<Client>();
    public DbSet<Commande> Commandes => Set<Commande>();

    protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options)
    {
        const string connexion = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=efboutique;User=root;Password=";
        options.UseMySql(connexion, new MySqlServerVersion(new Version(8, 0, 36)));
        if (journal)
        {
            options.AvecJournalSql();
        }
    }

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
         // prices with two decimal places
        modelBuilder.Entity<Produit>().Property(p => p.Prix).HasPrecision(10, 2);
    }
}
  • line 7: the context has a primary constructor (C# 12) whose optional parameter [journal] allows the SQL to be omitted;
  • lines 9–13: five [DbSet]. An entity does not need a [DbSet] to be part of the model: [LigneCommande], reached via the navigation property [Commande.Lignes], is in fact part of it;
  • line 19: the compact log is added if requested;
  • line 28: the API fluid sets the price precision.

The tables created by [EnsureCreated] are as follows:

> mysql -uroot efboutique -e "SHOW TABLES; SHOW CREATE TABLE Produits\G SHOW CREATE TABLE EtiquetteProduit\G"
+----------------------+
| Tables_in_efboutique |
+----------------------+
| Categories           |
| Clients              |
| Commandes            |
| EtiquetteProduit     |
| Etiquettes           |
| LigneCommande        |
| Produits             |
+----------------------+
*************************** 1. row ***************************
       Table: Produits
Create Table: CREATE TABLE `Produits` (
  `Id` int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  `Nom` longtext CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci NOT NULL,
  `Prix` decimal(10,2) NOT NULL,
  `CategorieId` int NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (`Id`),
  KEY `IX_Produits_CategorieId` (`CategorieId`),
  CONSTRAINT `FK_Produits_Categories_CategorieId` FOREIGN KEY (`CategorieId`) REFERENCES `Categories` (`Id`) ON DELETE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB AUTO_INCREMENT=5 DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4 COLLATE=utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci
*************************** 1. row ***************************
       Table: EtiquetteProduit
Create Table: CREATE TABLE `EtiquetteProduit` (
  `EtiquettesId` int NOT NULL,
  `ProduitsId` int NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (`EtiquettesId`,`ProduitsId`),
  KEY `IX_EtiquetteProduit_ProduitsId` (`ProduitsId`),
  CONSTRAINT `FK_EtiquetteProduit_Etiquettes_EtiquettesId` FOREIGN KEY (`EtiquettesId`) REFERENCES `Etiquettes` (`Id`) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT `FK_EtiquetteProduit_Produits_ProduitsId` FOREIGN KEY (`ProduitsId`) REFERENCES `Produits` (`Id`) ON DELETE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4 COLLATE=utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci
  • Lines 5–11: one table per entity. The table [LigneCommande] bears the name of the class, in the absence of the [DbSet] property; the table [EtiquetteProduit] is the association table for the many-to-many relationship;
  • Line 22: The foreign key [CategorieId] in table [Produits] references table [Categories]. The option [ON DELETE CASCADE] deletes products from a category when the category is deleted: this is the default behavior of EF Core for a mandatory relationship. EF Core also creates an index on each foreign key (line 21);
  • lines 26–32: the association table has two columns, foreign keys to the two linked tables, which together form its primary key;
  • line 17: we have not limited the length of the names, hence the type [longtext].

docs.title: 11.7.2. The program
docs.text:
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Relations;

// 1 - Create the database and an initial dataset, without a log
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext(journal: false))
{
    contexte.Database.EnsureDeleted();
    contexte.Database.EnsureCreated();
     // two labels
    var promo = new Etiquette { Libelle = "promo" };
    var nouveaute = new Etiquette { Libelle = "nouveauté" };
     // three categories and their products: adding an object graph
    contexte.Categories.AddRange(
        new Categorie
        {
            Nom = "cycles",
            Produits =
            [
                new Produit { Nom = "vélo", Prix = 500, Etiquettes = [promo] },
                new Produit { Nom = "pompe", Prix = 10 },
            ]
        },
        new Categorie
        {
            Nom = "tir à l'arc",
            Produits =
            [
                new Produit { Nom = "arc", Prix = 600, Etiquettes = [nouveaute] },
                new Produit { Nom = "flèches - lot de 6", Prix = 100, Etiquettes = [promo, nouveaute] },
            ]
        },
        new Categorie { Nom = "plongée" });
    contexte.SaveChanges();
     // A customer and their order
    Produit pompe = contexte.Produits.Local.Single(p => p.Nom == "pompe");
    Produit arc = contexte.Produits.Local.Single(p => p.Nom == "arc");
    contexte.Clients.Add(new Client
    {
        Nom = "Martin",
        Commandes =
        [
            new Commande
            {
                Date = new DateOnly(2026, 9, 28),
                Lignes = [new LigneCommande { Produit = pompe, Quantite = 2 }, new LigneCommande { Produit = arc, Quantite = 1 }]
            }
        ]
    });
    contexte.SaveChanges();
}

// 2 - a customer, their order, and its line items, added all at once
Console.WriteLine("--- ajout d'un client, d'une commande et de ses deux lignes");
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext())
{
    Produit velo = contexte.Produits.Single(p => p.Nom == "vélo");
    Produit fleches = contexte.Produits.Single(p => p.Nom == "flèches - lot de 6");
    var client = new Client
    {
        Nom = "Dupont",
        Commandes =
        [
            new Commande
            {
                Date = new DateOnly(2026, 10, 1),
                Lignes = [new LigneCommande { Produit = velo, Quantite = 1 }, new LigneCommande { Produit = fleches, Quantite = 3 }]
            }
        ]
    };
    contexte.Clients.Add(client);
    contexte.SaveChanges();
    Console.WriteLine($"client n° {client.Id}, commande n° {client.Commandes[0].Id}");
}

// 3 - Navigation properties are not loaded automatically
Console.WriteLine("--- une commande sans Include");
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext())
{
    Commande commande = contexte.Commandes.First();
    Console.WriteLine($"commande n° {commande.Id} : client={commande.Client?.Nom ?? "non chargé"}, {commande.Lignes.Count} ligne(s)");
}

// 4 - Loading relationships with Include and ThenInclude
Console.WriteLine("--- Include et ThenInclude");
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext())
{
    List<Commande> commandes = contexte.Commandes
        .Include(c => c.Client)
        .Include(c => c.Lignes).ThenInclude(l => l.Produit)
        .ToList();
    foreach (Commande commande in commandes)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"commande n° {commande.Id} du {commande.Date} pour {commande.Client.Nom}");
        foreach (LigneCommande ligne in commande.Lignes)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"  {ligne.Quantite} x {ligne.Produit.Nom} à {ligne.Produit.Prix} euros");
        }
    }
}

// 5 - Explicitly loading a collection
Console.WriteLine("--- chargement explicite");
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext())
{
    Categorie categorie = contexte.Categories.Single(c => c.Nom == "tir à l'arc");
    contexte.Entry(categorie).Collection(c => c.Produits).Load();
    Console.WriteLine($"{categorie.Nom} : {string.Join(", ", categorie.Produits.Select(p => p.Nom))}");
}

// 6 - The many-to-many relationship in a query
Console.WriteLine("--- les produits en promotion");
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext())
{
    var enPromo = contexte.Produits
        .Where(p => p.Etiquettes.Any(e => e.Libelle == "promo"))
        .Select(p => new { p.Nom, Categorie = p.Categorie.Nom })
        .ToList();
    enPromo.ForEach(p => Console.WriteLine($"{p.Nom} ({p.Categorie})"));
}

// 7 - a calculation across relationships, performed by SGBD
Console.WriteLine("--- montant des commandes");
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext())
{
    var montants = contexte.Commandes
        .Select(c => new { c.Id, Client = c.Client.Nom, Montant = c.Lignes.Sum(l => l.Quantite * l.Produit.Prix) })
        .ToList();
    montants.ForEach(m => Console.WriteLine($"commande n° {m.Id} ({m.Client}) : {m.Montant:0.00} euros"));
}

// 8 - a grouping: number of products and average price by category
Console.WriteLine("--- produits par catégorie");
using (var contexte = new BoutiqueContext())
{
    var parCategorie = contexte.Produits
        .GroupBy(p => p.Categorie.Nom)
        .Select(g => new { Categorie = g.Key, Nombre = g.Count(), PrixMoyen = g.Average(p => p.Prix) })
        .OrderBy(g => g.Categorie)
        .ToList();
    parCategorie.ForEach(g => Console.WriteLine($"{g.Categorie} : {g.Nombre} produit(s), prix moyen {g.PrixMoyen:0.00} euros"));
}

Comments:

  • Lines 13–32: Three categories are added, along with their products and product tags: a graph of objects. EF Core iterates through the navigation properties and adds all encountered entities to the context. [SaveChanges] inserts them in the correct order (categories before the products that reference them) and populates the foreign keys and the association table. This initialization is performed without logging;
  • lines 35–36: The property [Local] of a [DbSet] provides access to the entities already tracked by the context, without querying the database;
  • lines 56–71: a customer, their order, and its two line items are added in a single call to [Add]. The SQL (lines 11–35) shows the order of insertions: the customer, then the order—whose foreign key ([ClientId]) receives the key generated for the customer ([@p1=2])—and finally the line items, whose foreign key ([CommandeId]) receives the key from the order;
  • Lines 79–80: By default, EF Core loads only the requested entity. The navigation properties [Client] and [Lignes] of the read command were not populated (line 41): [Client] is equal to [null] (despite the non-nullable declaration, hence the [?.] operator), and the list of lines is empty. EF Core supports lazy loading: the navigation property is loaded automatically upon its first read. It must be explicitly enabled (package [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Proxies], navigation properties [virtual]); we do not use it because it hides database access;
  • Lines 87–89: eager loading. [Include(c => c.Client)] instructs the system to load the customer for each order; [Include(c => c.Lignes)] loads the order lines, and [ThenInclude(l => l.Produit)] loads the product for each line. Everything is loaded by a single query [SELECT], using joins (lines 45–51). The display shows both orders and their lines;
  • line 106: the explicit load. We load the collection of products from a category that has already been read: a second query, [SELECT], reads the products whose foreign key matches that of the category. For a navigation property to a single entity, we write [contexte.Entry(produit).Reference(p => p.Categorie).Load()];
  • Lines 114–116: Navigation properties are used in the queries LINQ, without [Include]: [p.Etiquettes.Any(...)] becomes a subquery [EXISTS] on the association table (lines 72–76), and [p.Categorie.Nom] becomes a join;
  • lines 125–126: a calculation across two relations—the amount of each order—entirely performed by SGBD using a subquery (lines 81–84);
  • lines 135–138: a group by. [GroupBy] groups products by category name; for each group ([g]), the key ([g.Key]), the number of products ([Count]), and the average price ([Average]) are calculated by SGBD: the query becomes a [GROUP BY] (lines 90–93). The category [plongée], which has no products, does not appear: the join with the category table is an inner join ([INNER JOIN]).

The so-called “N+1 query” problem is a risk for any user of a ORM. Suppose we want to display the customer name for each order, and we read the orders without [Include], then retrieve the customer for each one via an explicit load (or a deferred load, which amounts to the same thing without us realizing it): we execute one query for the N orders, then N queries, one per order. With a thousand orders, this results in a thousand and one round trips to the server, whereas a single round trip would have sufficed. The solutions are those shown in the example: [Include], or better yet, a projection ([Select]) that retrieves only the relevant data. The log entry SQL helps identify the problem: the same query repeated numerous times.

docs.title: 11.8.1. The Principle
docs.text:
So far, the database has been created by [EnsureCreated], after being deleted by [EnsureDeleted]. This is impossible for a live application: its database contains data that must be preserved when the model evolves (a new column, a new table). Furthermore, [EnsureCreated] can only create a database that does not exist: if the database already exists with tables, it does nothing, even if the model has changed.

Migrations address this need. A migration is a C# class, generated by the [dotnet ef] tool, that describes the transition from one version of the model to the next: its [Up] method applies the change (create a table, add a column), while its [Down] method reverts it. The database contains a table named [__EFMigrationsHistory], where EF Core records the migrations that have been applied to it; this allows it to know which ones still need to be applied.

docs.title: 11.8.2. The project
docs.text:
The [Clients] project uses the [efclients] database. Its project file adds the [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design] package, which is required by the [dotnet ef] tool:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
     <!-- EF Core and its provider MySQL (Pomelo) -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore" Version="9.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql" Version="9.0.0" />
     <!-- the code used by the tool [dotnet ef] (migrations): not required at runtime -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design" Version="9.0.0">
      <PrivateAssets>all</PrivateAssets>
      <IncludeAssets>runtime; build; native; contentfiles; analyzers; buildtransitive</IncludeAssets>
    </PackageReference>
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
  • Lines 15–18: The element [PrivateAssets] (“all”) indicates that this package is intended for development only: it is not distributed to projects that reference it and is not required for execution. This is what the [dotnet add package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design] command outputs.

The entity is a client:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace Clients;

// a client
public class Client
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    [MaxLength(50)]
    public string Nom { get; set; } = "";
    [MaxLength(100)]
    public string Email { get; set; } = "";
    [MaxLength(20)]
    public string? Telephone { get; set; }
}

In the first version of the application, the client does not have a phone number: lines 13–14 do not yet exist. We will add them in the second version.

The [dotnet ef] tool must be able to create a context to determine the model and, for certain commands, connect to the database. To do this, it uses, in order: a class from the project that implements the [IDesignTimeDbContextFactory<T>] interface, or the dependency injection container of a ASP.NET Core application, or, failing that, a parameterless constructor for the context. We’re writing a factory:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design;

namespace Clients;

// the context receives its configuration from its constructor (primary constructor)
public class ClientsContext(DbContextOptions<ClientsContext> options) : DbContext(options)
{
    public DbSet<Client> Clients => Set<Client>();
}

// the context factory used by the [dotnet ef] tool (and by our program)
public class ClientsContextFactory : IDesignTimeDbContextFactory<ClientsContext>
{
    public ClientsContext CreateDbContext(string[] args)
    {
        const string connexion = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=efclients;User=root;Password=";
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<ClientsContext>()
            .UseMySql(connexion, new MySqlServerVersion(new Version(8, 0, 36)))
            .Options;
        return new ClientsContext(options);
    }
}
  • line 7: the context receives its configuration via a primary constructor (C# 12), which it passes to the constructor of *[DbContext]. It does not have a *[OnConfiguring] method: it does not know its base; the entity that creates it chooses it;
  • Lines 13–21: the factory. Its [CreateDbContext] method builds the configuration ([DbContextOptionsBuilder<T>]) and creates the context. The parameter [args] receives any arguments passed to the tool; we do not use it.

docs.title: 11.8.3. The First Migration
docs.text:
The commands for the [dotnet ef] tool are entered in the project folder. The first migration, which we call [Initiale], is created by the [dotnet ef migrations add] command:

> dotnet ef migrations add Initiale
Build started...
Build succeeded.
Done. To undo this action, use 'ef migrations remove'

The tool compiled the project, created a context with the factory, compared the model to that of the last migration (there isn’t one yet), and generated three files in a folder named [Migrations]:

Clients/
  Clients.csproj
  Client.cs
  ClientsContext.cs
  Program.cs
  Migrations/
    20261003100720_Initiale.cs              la migration
    20261003100720_Initiale.Designer.cs     le modèle à la date de la migration
    ClientsContextModelSnapshot.cs          l'instantané du modèle actuel

The file names begin with the date and time the migration was created (year, month, day, hour, minute, second): migrations are applied in this order. The file [ClientsContextModelSnapshot.cs] contains a description of the model as it stands after the last migration: the tool uses this file to compare against the current model in order to generate the next migration. These files are part of the application’s source code: they are stored and managed along with the rest of the code (in a Git repository, for example).

The generated migration is as follows:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Metadata;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Migrations;

#nullable disable

namespace Clients.Migrations
{
     /// <inheritdoc />
    public partial class Initiale : Migration
    {
         /// <inheritdoc />
        protected override void Up(MigrationBuilder migrationBuilder)
        {
            migrationBuilder.AlterDatabase()
                .Annotation("MySql:CharSet", "utf8mb4");

            migrationBuilder.CreateTable(
                name: "Clients",
                columns: table => new
                {
                    Id = table.Column<int>(type: "int", nullable: false)
                        .Annotation("MySql:ValueGenerationStrategy", MySqlValueGenerationStrategy.IdentityColumn),
                    Nom = table.Column<string>(type: "varchar(50)", maxLength: 50, nullable: false)
                        .Annotation("MySql:CharSet", "utf8mb4"),
                    Email = table.Column<string>(type: "varchar(100)", maxLength: 100, nullable: false)
                        .Annotation("MySql:CharSet", "utf8mb4")
                },
                constraints: table =>
                {
                    table.PrimaryKey("PK_Clients", x => x.Id);
                })
                .Annotation("MySql:CharSet", "utf8mb4");
        }

         /// <inheritdoc />
        protected override void Down(MigrationBuilder migrationBuilder)
        {
            migrationBuilder.DropTable(
                name: "Clients");
        }
    }
}
  • line 9: a migration derives from the [Migration] class;
  • lines 12–32: the [Up] method describes the operations to be performed, using a [MigrationBuilder] object: modify the database character set ([AlterDatabase]), create the table [Clients] ([CreateTable]) with its columns and primary key. The annotations [MySql:...] contain information specific to the Pomelo vendor;
  • lines 36–39: The method [Down] reverses the migration by deleting the table.

The code for a migration can be modified manually, for example, to add operations that the tool cannot deduce from the model ([migrationBuilder.Sql("...")] executes any SQL command).

docs.title: 11.8.4. Apply a migration
docs.text:
The command [dotnet ef database update] applies any migrations to the database that have not yet been applied, or, if given the name of a migration, all migrations up to and including that one:

> dotnet ef database update Initiale
Build started...
Build succeeded.
Acquiring an exclusive lock for migration application. See https://aka.ms/efcore-docs-migrations-lock for more information if this takes too long.
Applying migration '20261003100720_Initiale'.
Done.

The database [efclients] did not exist: it was created. The client [mysql] of MySQL shows its tables:

> mysql -uroot -t efclients -e "SHOW TABLES; DESCRIBE Clients;"
+-----------------------+
| Tables_in_efclients   |
+-----------------------+
| Clients               |
| __EFMigrationsHistory |
+-----------------------+
+-------+--------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+
| Field | Type         | Null | Key | Default | Extra          |
+-------+--------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+
| Id    | int          | NO   | PRI | NULL    | auto_increment |
| Nom   | varchar(50)  | NO   |     | NULL    |                |
| Email | varchar(100) | NO   |     | NULL    |                |
+-------+--------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+

It contains the model table [Clients] and the table [__EFMigrationsHistory], which contains one row per applied migration.

docs.title: 11.8.5. A second migration
docs.text:
The application is evolving: the property [Telephone], of type [string?] and limited to 20 characters, is added to the entity [Client] (this is the version of the file [Client.cs] shown above). A new migration is created:

> dotnet ef migrations add AjoutTelephone
Build started...
Build succeeded.
Done. To undo this action, use 'ef migrations remove'

The tool compared the current model to the snapshot and generated the following migration:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Migrations;

#nullable disable

namespace Clients.Migrations
{
     /// <inheritdoc />
    public partial class AjoutTelephone : Migration
    {
         /// <inheritdoc />
        protected override void Up(MigrationBuilder migrationBuilder)
        {
            migrationBuilder.AddColumn<string>(
                name: "Telephone",
                table: "Clients",
                type: "varchar(20)",
                maxLength: 20,
                nullable: true)
                .Annotation("MySql:CharSet", "utf8mb4");
        }

         /// <inheritdoc />
        protected override void Down(MigrationBuilder migrationBuilder)
        {
            migrationBuilder.DropColumn(
                name: "Telephone",
                table: "Clients");
        }
    }
}
  • Lines 13–18: [Up] adds the column [Telephone], which is optional since the property is of type [string?]. The existing rows in the table will be assigned the value [NULL]. If the property had been required ([string]), a value would have had to be assigned to the existing rows: the migration would have done so using the empty string, which is the column’s default value ([defaultValue: ""]);
  • rows 25–27: [Down] deletes the column.

The model snapshot has also been updated. Here are the key changes:

    [DbContext(typeof(ClientsContext))]
    partial class ClientsContextModelSnapshot : ModelSnapshot
    {
        protected override void BuildModel(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
        {
#pragma warning disable 612, 618
            modelBuilder
                .HasAnnotation("ProductVersion", "9.0.0")
                .HasAnnotation("Relational:MaxIdentifierLength", 64);

            MySqlModelBuilderExtensions.AutoIncrementColumns(modelBuilder);

            modelBuilder.Entity("Clients.Client", b =>
                {
                    b.Property<int>("Id")
                        .ValueGeneratedOnAdd()
                        .HasColumnType("int");

                    MySqlPropertyBuilderExtensions.UseMySqlIdentityColumn(b.Property<int>("Id"));

                    b.Property<string>("Email")
                        .IsRequired()
                        .HasMaxLength(100)
                        .HasColumnType("varchar(100)");

                    b.Property<string>("Nom")
                        .IsRequired()
                        .HasMaxLength(50)
                        .HasColumnType("varchar(50)");

                    b.Property<string>("Telephone")
                        .HasMaxLength(20)
                        .HasColumnType("varchar(20)");

                    b.HasKey("Id");

                    b.ToTable("Clients");
                });
  • line 12: the attribute [DbContext] associates the snapshot with the context [ClientsContext];
  • lines 24–48: the description of the entity [Client], written using the API fluid: each property, its type (SQL), its length, its required status ([IsRequired]), the primary key, and the table. The property [Telephone] is included here (lines 42–44). By comparing this model to the current model in the code, the tool will determine the operations for the next migration. This file should never be modified manually; to undo the last migration (if it has not been applied), use [dotnet ef migrations remove], which deletes its files and restores the snapshot to its previous state.

The command [dotnet ef migrations list] lists the project’s migrations and those that have not yet been applied to the database:

> dotnet ef migrations list
Build started...
Build succeeded.
20261003100720_Initiale
20261003100726_AjoutTelephone (Pending)

The [dotnet ef migrations script] command generates the SQL script for a migration—or a series of migrations—without executing it. It is used when the production database is not updated by the developer, but by an administrator who wants to review and execute the SQL script themselves:

> dotnet ef migrations script Initiale AjoutTelephone
Build started...
Build succeeded.
START TRANSACTION;
ALTER TABLE `Clients` ADD `Telephone` varchar(20) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NULL;

INSERT INTO `__EFMigrationsHistory` (`MigrationId`, `ProductVersion`)
VALUES ('20261003100726_AjoutTelephone', '9.0.0');

COMMIT;
  • Lines 4–10: The migration is executed within a transaction: the schema modification and the addition of the migration to the history table either succeed or fail together. Warning: Under MySQL, a schema modification command ([ALTER TABLE], [CREATE TABLE]) implicitly commits the current transaction.
