If an error occurs in the middle of a migration, the database may remain in an intermediate state;
  • Line 7: The migration is logged in the history table, along with the version of EF Core that applied it.

docs.title: 11.8.6. Applying Migrations from the Application
docs.text:
An application can also apply migrations itself at startup. This is what the program in the [Clients] project does:

using Clients;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// The context is created by the same factory as that of the [dotnet ef] tool
using ClientsContext contexte = new ClientsContextFactory().CreateDbContext(args);

// the migration status
Console.WriteLine($"migrations appliquées : {string.Join(", ", contexte.Database.GetAppliedMigrations())}");
Console.WriteLine($"migrations en attente : {string.Join(", ", contexte.Database.GetPendingMigrations())}");

// Pending migrations
contexte.Database.Migrate();
Console.WriteLine("Migrate() : la base est à jour");

// The new column is ready for use
contexte.Clients.Add(new Client { Nom = "Dupont", Email = "dupont@example.com", Telephone = "01 23 45 67 89" });
contexte.SaveChanges();
foreach (Client client in contexte.Clients.AsNoTracking())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"[{client.Id}, {client.Nom}, {client.Email}, {client.Telephone ?? "pas de téléphone"}]");
}
  • line 5: the context is created using the factory provided by the tool;
  • lines 8–9: the migrations applied to the database (read from the history table) and those that remain to be applied;
  • line 12: [Migrate] applies the pending migrations (creating the database if necessary). This is equivalent to [dotnet ef database update];
  • Lines 16–20: The new column is used.

Results:

> dotnet run
migrations appliquées : 20261003100720_Initiale
migrations en attente : 20261003100726_AjoutTelephone
Migrate() : la base est à jour
[1, Dupont, dupont@example.com, 01 23 45 67 89]

The second migration was applied by the program. The history table now contains both migrations:

> mysql -uroot -t efclients -e "SELECT * FROM __EFMigrationsHistory"
+-------------------------------+----------------+
| MigrationId                   | ProductVersion |
+-------------------------------+----------------+
| 20261003100720_Initiale       | 9.0.0          |
| 20261003100726_AjoutTelephone | 9.0.0          |
+-------------------------------+----------------+

Applying migrations at startup is convenient for a small application or during development. For a large application deployed across multiple servers, it is preferable to apply them as a separate step in the deployment process (script SQL, or migration executable generated by [dotnet ef migrations bundle]). Note the following:

  • [EnsureCreated]: for examples, tests, and prototypes, when the database can be deleted and recreated;
  • migrations: as soon as the database contains data that needs to be retained. The two should not be mixed: a database created by [EnsureCreated] does not have a history table, and migrations cannot be applied to it.

docs.title: 11.9. Asynchrony
docs.text:
A database query is an I/O operation: while the server is working, the waiting thread does nothing. Chapter 9 showed how to free up this thread using [async] and [await]. EF Core provides an asynchronous version of all methods that access the database: [ToListAsync], [FirstOrDefaultAsync], [SingleAsync], [CountAsync], [SumAsync], [FindAsync], [SaveChangesAsync], etc. They are defined in the [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore] namespace (not [System.Linq]). The [Asynchrone] project uses them:

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// The database is recreated with its six articles
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();
// the context is released asynchronously (using await)
await using var contexte = new ArticlesContext();

// 1 - asynchronous requests
Console.WriteLine("--- ToListAsync");
List<Article> articles = await contexte.Articles.Where(a => a.Prix < 200).OrderBy(a => a.Prix).ToListAsync();
articles.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);
Console.WriteLine("--- FirstOrDefaultAsync et CountAsync");
Article? arc = await contexte.Articles.FirstOrDefaultAsync(a => a.Nom == "arc");
int nbEnRupture = await contexte.Articles.CountAsync(a => a.StockActuel < a.StockMinimum);
Console.WriteLine($"{arc}, {nbEnRupture} article(s) en rupture");

// 2 - asynchronous save
Console.WriteLine("--- SaveChangesAsync");
arc!.Prix = 550;
int nbLignes = await contexte.SaveChangesAsync();
Console.WriteLine($"{nbLignes} ligne(s) modifiée(s)");

// 3 - an asynchronous stream: rows are processed as they are read
Console.WriteLine("--- await foreach");
await foreach (Article article in contexte.Articles.AsNoTracking().Where(a => a.Prix >= 300).AsAsyncEnumerable())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"lu : {article.Nom}");
}

// 4 - Cancellation
Console.WriteLine("--- annulation");
using var annulation = new CancellationTokenSource();
annulation.Cancel();
try
{
    await contexte.Articles.ToListAsync(annulation.Token);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run
--- ToListAsync
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Prix` < 200.0
    SQL> ORDER BY `a`.`Prix`
[2, pompe, 10,00, 10, 2]
[4, flèches - lot de 6, 100,00, 12, 20]
[6, bouteilles d'oxygène, 120,00, 10, 5]
--- FirstOrDefaultAsync and CountAsync
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Nom` = 'arc'
    SQL> LIMIT 1
    SQL> SELECT COUNT(*)
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`StockActuel` < `a`.`StockMinimum`
[3, arc, 600,00, 4, 1], 1 article(s) en rupture
--- SaveChangesAsync
    SQL> SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1;
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` SET `Prix` = @p0
    SQL> WHERE `Id` = @p1;
    SQL> SELECT ROW_COUNT();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p1=3, @p0=550
1 ligne(s) modifiée(s)
--- await foreach
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Prix` >= 300.0
lu : vélo
lu : arc
lu : combinaison de plongée
--- cancellation
OperationCanceledException : The operation was canceled.

Comments:

  • Line 7: A [DbContext] implements [IAsyncDisposable]: [await using] (C# 8, Chapter 9) releases it asynchronously;
  • line 11: [ToListAsync] executes the query and returns a [Task<List<Article>>]. The query itself ([Where], [OrderBy]) is written as before: only the method that executes it changes;
  • lines 14–15: the asynchronous versions of [FirstOrDefault] and [Count];
  • line 21: the asynchronous save;
  • line 26: [AsAsyncEnumerable()] returns the query as an asynchronous stream ([IAsyncEnumerable<T>], Chapter 9), which is iterated over using [await foreach]. Entities are processed as they are read, without forming a list: this is useful for processing a large number of lines;
  • lines 33–39: Asynchronous methods accept a [CancellationToken] (Chapter 9). Here, the token is canceled before the call: [ToListAsync] immediately launches a [OperationCanceledException] (line 34). In a web application, the token from the HTTP request is passed: if the client aborts the request, the current read operation is interrupted.

An important rule: a context is not thread-safe and accepts only one operation at a time. Do not launch two simultaneous requests on the same context (for example, with [Task.WhenAll]): you must wait ([await]) for one operation to finish before starting another. EF Core often detects this error and triggers a [InvalidOperationException] (“A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed”), but not always. For truly parallel requests, one context is used per task.

In a console application like our examples, asynchrony offers no visible benefit. It becomes particularly valuable in a server application (Chapters 12 and 13), where a thread freed up during a SQL request can serve other clients. This is why ASP.NET Core applications consistently use the asynchronous methods of EF Core.

docs.title: 11.10.1. Transactions
docs.text:
Chapter 10 introduced transactions: a set of operations that either all succeed or all fail. With EF Core, there are two key points to note:

  • [SaveChanges] is transactional: if it sends multiple commands, it executes them within a transaction. If any one of them fails, none are committed, and [SaveChanges] initiates a [DbUpdateException];
  • To group multiple calls to [SaveChanges] (or commands such as [ExecuteUpdate], [ExecuteSql]...) into a single transaction, you open an explicit transaction with [contexte.Database.BeginTransaction()] (or its asynchronous version), commit it with [Commit], and roll it back with [Rollback].

The [Transactions] project illustrates both cases:

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// The database is recreated with its six items
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();

// 1 - SaveChanges is transactional: all or nothing
Console.WriteLine("--- SaveChanges : deux ajouts dont le second viole l'unicité du nom");
using (var contexte = new ArticlesContext())
{
    contexte.Articles.Add(new Article { Nom = "raquette", Prix = 80, StockActuel = 5, StockMinimum = 2 });
    contexte.Articles.Add(new Article { Nom = "vélo", Prix = 450, StockActuel = 3, StockMinimum = 1 });
    try
    {
        contexte.SaveChanges();
    }
    catch (DbUpdateException e)
    {
         // The error in SGBD is the internal exception
        Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : {e.InnerException?.Message}");
    }
}
await AfficherAsync("raquette");

// 2 - an explicit transaction that encompasses multiple SaveChanges
Console.WriteLine("--- transaction explicite annulée");
await using (var contexte = new ArticlesContext())
{
    await using var transaction = await contexte.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
    try
    {
         // sale of two bicycles
        Article velo = await contexte.Articles.SingleAsync(a => a.Nom == "vélo");
        velo.StockActuel -= 2;
        await contexte.SaveChangesAsync();
         // Adding an item with a name that already exists: error
        contexte.Articles.Add(new Article { Nom = "pompe", Prix = 12, StockActuel = 5, StockMinimum = 1 });
        await contexte.SaveChangesAsync();
         // validation of the entire set (this cannot be done here)
        await transaction.CommitAsync();
    }
    catch (DbUpdateException e)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : {e.InnerException?.Message}");
         // canceling all operations in the transaction
        await transaction.RollbackAsync();
    }
}
// The sale of the bicycles has been canceled
await AfficherAsync("vélo");

// Displaying an item retrieved from the database, with a new context
static async Task AfficherAsync(string nom)
{
    await using var contexte = new ArticlesContext();
    Article? article = await contexte.Articles.AsNoTracking().SingleOrDefaultAsync(a => a.Nom == nom);
    Console.WriteLine($"article [{nom}] dans la base : {article?.ToString() ?? "absent"}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run
--- SaveChanges: two additions, the second of which violates the uniqueness of the name
    SQL> -- transaction start
    SQL> INSERT INTO `articles` (`Nom`, `Prix`, `StockActuel`, `StockMinimum`)
    SQL> VALUES (@p0, @p1, @p2, @p3);
    SQL> SELECT `Id`
    SQL> FROM `articles`
    SQL> WHERE ROW_COUNT() = 1 AND `Id` = LAST_INSERT_ID();
    SQL> INSERT INTO `articles` (`Nom`, `Prix`, `StockActuel`, `StockMinimum`)
    SQL> VALUES (@p4, @p5, @p6, @p7);
    SQL> SELECT `Id`
    SQL> FROM `articles`
    SQL> WHERE ROW_COUNT() = 1 AND `Id` = LAST_INSERT_ID();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p0=racket, @p1=80, @p2=5, @p3=2, @p4=bike, @p5=450, @p6=3, @p7=1
DbUpdateException : Duplicate entry 'vélo' for key 'articles.IX_articles_Nom'
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Nom` = @__nom_0
    SQL> LIMIT 2
    SQL> -- parameters: @__nom_0=racket
article [raquette] dans la base : absent
--- explicit transaction canceled
    SQL> -- transaction start
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Nom` = 'vélo'
    SQL> LIMIT 2
    SQL> SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1;
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` SET `StockActuel` = @p0
    SQL> WHERE `Id` = @p1;
    SQL> SELECT ROW_COUNT();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p1=1, @p0=8
    SQL> INSERT INTO `articles` (`Nom`, `Prix`, `StockActuel`, `StockMinimum`)
    SQL> VALUES (@p0, @p1, @p2, @p3);
    SQL> SELECT `Id`
    SQL> FROM `articles`
    SQL> WHERE ROW_COUNT() = 1 AND `Id` = LAST_INSERT_ID();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p0=pump, @p1=12, @p2=5, @p3=1
    SQL> -- command failed
DbUpdateException : Duplicate entry 'pompe' for key 'articles.IX_articles_Nom'
    SQL> -- transaction canceled (ROLLBACK)
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Nom` = @__nom_0
    SQL> LIMIT 2
    SQL> -- parameters: @__nom_0=bike
article [vélo] dans la base : [1, vélo, 500,00, 10, 5]

Comments:

  • Lines 11–15: Two items are added, the second of which has the same name as an existing item. [SaveChanges] opens a transaction (line 3) and sends both [INSERT] messages. The second one violates the unique index on the [Nom] column: MySQL rejects the insertion, and [SaveChanges] triggers a [DbUpdateException], whose internal exception is the error from SGBD (line 15). The transaction was not committed: it is abandoned, and its operations are rolled back by MySQL. The racket, which had been successfully inserted, is not in the database (line 21);
  • line 29: an explicit transaction. The returned object ([IDbContextTransaction]) is released by [await using]: if it has not been committed, the transaction is rolled back at this point;
  • Lines 33–35: The first entry, [SaveChangesAsync], records the sale of two bicycles. Since a transaction is already in progress, [SaveChanges] does not start a new one; instead, it is included in the existing one. The order [SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1], which precedes [UPDATE] (line 28), does not validate the current transaction: the subsequent lines show that the sale will indeed be canceled;
  • lines 37–38: the second record fails (lines 38–40);
  • line 40: validation is never reached;
  • line 46: in [catch], the transaction is rolled back (line 41). The sale of the bicycles, although recorded by the first [SaveChangesAsync], is canceled: the bicycle inventory remains at 10 (line 47);
  • Lines 53–57: An asynchronous local function that re-reads an item with a new context to view the actual state of the database rather than the entities tracked by the working context.

docs.title: 11.10.2. Optimistic Concurrency
docs.text:
Two users read the same item, which has a stock of 10. The first user sells one item and updates the stock to 9. The second user, who read the stock before this update, sells three items and updates the stock to 7: the first user’s sale is lost. This is the problem of lost updates.

One solution would be to lock the row for the entire duration of each user’s operation (“pessimistic” concurrency): this blocks other users, sometimes for a long time. EF Core implements optimistic concurrency: nothing is locked, but at the time of the commit, the system verifies that the row has not been modified since it was read. To do this, one or more properties are designated as concurrency tokens: EF Core adds the condition “the token still has the value read” to the [WHERE] clause for the [UPDATE] and [DELETE] statements. If the command does not modify any rows, it means another user has already processed them: EF Core initiates a [DbUpdateConcurrencyException].

The [Concurrence] project turns the stock into a concurrency token. Rather than modifying the [Article] entity shared by the other examples, it derives the context and supplements the model with the API fluid:

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Concurrence;

// the item context, where inventory becomes a concurrency token
public class ArticlesConcurrenceContext : ArticlesContext
{
    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
        base.OnModelCreating(modelBuilder);
         // The read stock value will be verified during each UPDATE or DELETE
        modelBuilder.Entity<Article>().Property(a => a.StockActuel).IsConcurrencyToken();
    }
}
  • line 11: the parent class configuration is retained;
  • line 13: the property [StockActuel] becomes a concurrency token. The equivalent annotation is the [ConcurrencyCheck] attribute applied to the property.

The program simulates the two users with two contexts:

using Articles.Data;
using Concurrence;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// The database is recreated with its six items
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();

// Two users, two contexts: each reads the same item
using var contexte1 = new ArticlesConcurrenceContext();
using var contexte2 = new ArticlesConcurrenceContext();
Console.WriteLine("--- les deux utilisateurs lisent le vélo");
Article velo1 = contexte1.Articles.Single(a => a.Nom == "vélo");
Article velo2 = contexte2.Articles.Single(a => a.Nom == "vélo");

// User 1 sells 1 bicycle
Console.WriteLine("--- l'utilisateur 1 vend 1 vélo");
velo1.StockActuel -= 1;
contexte1.SaveChanges();
Console.WriteLine($"stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 1 : {velo1.StockActuel}");

// User 2 sells 3 bicycles based on outdated data (stock = 10)
Console.WriteLine("--- l'utilisateur 2 vend 3 vélos");
velo2.StockActuel -= 3;
try
{
    contexte2.SaveChanges();
}
catch (DbUpdateConcurrencyException e)
{
     // Only the first sentence of the message is displayed
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message[..(e.Message.IndexOf('.') + 1)]}");
     // Solution: Retrieve the item from the database and process the sale again
    Console.WriteLine("--- l'utilisateur 2 relit le vélo et recommence");
    foreach (var entree in e.Entries)
    {
        entree.Reload();
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"stock relu : {velo2.StockActuel}");
    velo2.StockActuel -= 3;
    contexte2.SaveChanges();
    Console.WriteLine($"stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 2 : {velo2.StockActuel}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run
--- Both users view the bicycle
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Nom` = 'vélo'
    SQL> LIMIT 2
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Nom` = 'vélo'
    SQL> LIMIT 2
--- User 1 sells 1 bike
    SQL> SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1;
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` SET `StockActuel` = @p0
    SQL> WHERE `Id` = @p1 AND `StockActuel` = @p2;
    SQL> SELECT ROW_COUNT();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p1=1, @p0=9, @p2=10
stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 1 : 9
--- User 2 sells 3 bikes
    SQL> SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1;
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` SET `StockActuel` = @p0
    SQL> WHERE `Id` = @p1 AND `StockActuel` = @p2;
    SQL> SELECT ROW_COUNT();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p1=1, @p0=7, @p2=10
DbUpdateConcurrencyException : The database operation was expected to affect 1 row(s), but actually affected 0 row(s); data may have been modified or deleted since entities were loaded.
--- User 2 returns the bike and starts over
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM `articles` AS `a`
    SQL> WHERE `a`.`Id` = @__p_0
    SQL> LIMIT 1
    SQL> -- parameters: @__p_0=1
stock relu : 9
    SQL> SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1;
    SQL> UPDATE `articles` SET `StockActuel` = @p0
    SQL> WHERE `Id` = @p1 AND `StockActuel` = @p2;
    SQL> SELECT ROW_COUNT();
    SQL> -- parameters: @p1=1, @p0=6, @p2=9
stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 2 : 6

Comments:

  • lines 12–13: each user reads the bike in their own context;
  • lines 17–18: The first user’s order [UPDATE] contains the condition [StockActuel = @p2], with the value read, 10 (lines 13–16). The line is modified;
  • lines 23–26: The second user’s order contains the same condition, with the value they read, 10, while the database inventory is now 9. No rows are modified: [SELECT ROW_COUNT()] returns 0, and EF Core triggers a [DbUpdateConcurrencyException] (line 24);
  • lines 34–36: The [Entries] property of the exception lists the conflicting entities. The resolution depends on the application: abort, warn the user, or, as here, re-read the entity from the database ([Reload]) and repeat the operation. The re-read inventory is 9 (line 31), and the sale of the three bicycles results in an inventory of 6, with the condition [StockActuel = 9] (line 36).

The most common concurrency token is not business data but a dedicated column that is modified with each update to the row: a version number or a modification date. Under SQL Server, a property of type [byte[]] marked with the attribute [Timestamp] is associated with type [rowversion], which SGBD modifies automatically; Under MySQL, an integer or a date is often used that the application—or a trigger—modifies with each update.

docs.title: 11.11. The raw SQL
docs.text:
EF Core generates SQL from LINQ, but it is still possible to write the SQL for a query yourself, to use a feature specific to SGBD or to optimize a complex query. The [SqlBrut] project presents the available methods:

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

// The database is recreated with its six items
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();
using var contexte = new ArticlesContext();

// 1 - FromSql: a handwritten SQL query that returns entities
Console.WriteLine("--- FromSql");
decimal prixMin = 200;
List<Article> chers = contexte.Articles
    .FromSql($"SELECT * FROM articles WHERE Prix > {prixMin}")
    .OrderBy(a => a.Nom)
    .ToList();
chers.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);

// 2 - Interpolation produces a parameter: no SQL injection possible
Console.WriteLine("--- tentative d'injection SQL avec FromSql");
string nom = "x' OR '1'='1";
int nb = contexte.Articles.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM articles WHERE Nom = {nom}").Count();
Console.WriteLine($"{nb} article(s) trouvé(s)");
// the same query constructed by concatenation: never do this
Console.WriteLine("--- la même tentative avec FromSqlRaw et une concaténation");
nb = contexte.Articles.FromSqlRaw("SELECT * FROM articles WHERE Nom = '" + nom + "'").Count();
Console.WriteLine($"{nb} article(s) trouvé(s)");

// 3 - SqlQuery: results that are not entities (the column is named "Value")
Console.WriteLine("--- SqlQuery");
List<string> noms = contexte.Database
    .SqlQuery<string>($"SELECT Nom AS Value FROM articles WHERE StockActuel < StockMinimum")
    .ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"en rupture : {string.Join(", ", noms)}");
decimal valeur = contexte.Database
    .SqlQuery<decimal>($"SELECT SUM(Prix * StockActuel) AS Value FROM articles")
    .Single();
Console.WriteLine($"valeur du stock : {valeur} euros");

// 4 - ExecuteSql: an update order
Console.WriteLine("--- ExecuteSql");
decimal coefficient = 0.9M;
string article = "arc";
int nbLignes = contexte.Database.ExecuteSql($"UPDATE articles SET Prix = Prix * {coefficient} WHERE Nom = {article}");
Console.WriteLine($"{nbLignes} ligne(s) modifiée(s)");

Results:

> dotnet run
--- FromSql
    SQL> SELECT `a`.`Id`, `a`.`Nom`, `a`.`Prix`, `a`.`StockActuel`, `a`.`StockMinimum`
    SQL> FROM (
    SQL>     SELECT * FROM articles WHERE Prix > @p0
    SQL> ) AS `a`
    SQL> ORDER BY `a`.`Nom`
    SQL> -- parameters: @p0=200
[3, arc, 600,00, 4, 1]
[5, combinaison de plongée, 300,00, 8, 2]
[1, vélo, 500,00, 10, 5]
--- Attempt to inject SQL with FromSql
    SQL> SELECT COUNT(*)
    SQL> FROM (
    SQL>     SELECT * FROM articles WHERE Nom = @p0
    SQL> ) AS `a`
    SQL> -- parameters: @p0=x' OR '1'='1
0 article(s) trouvé(s)
--- the same attempt with FromSqlRaw and a concatenation
    SQL> SELECT COUNT(*)
    SQL> FROM (
    SQL>     SELECT * FROM articles WHERE Nom = 'x' OR '1'='1'
    SQL> ) AS `a`
6 article(s) trouvé(s)
--- SqlQuery
    SQL> SELECT Nom AS Value FROM articles WHERE StockActuel < StockMinimum
en rupture : flèches - lot de 6
    SQL> SELECT `s`.`Value`
    SQL> FROM (
    SQL>     SELECT SUM(Prix * StockActuel) AS Value FROM articles
    SQL> ) AS `s`
    SQL> LIMIT 2
valeur du stock : 12300,00 euros
--- ExecuteSql
    SQL> UPDATE articles SET Prix = Prix * @p0 WHERE Nom = @p1
    SQL> -- parameters: @p0=0.9, @p1=arc
1 ligne(s) modifiée(s)

Comments:

  • Lines 11–13: [FromSql] executes a query SQL that returns rows from an entity’s table and instantiates entities (followed by the context). Its parameter is an interpolated string: EF Core does not convert it to text; instead, it receives a [FormattableString] object that contains the text and the values to be inserted separately, and converts each value into a SQL parameter ([@p0], line 5). The result of [FromSql] is a [IQueryable<T>]: it can be completed with LINQ. The order [OrderBy] was added by EF Core around our query, which became a subquery;
  • lines 19–20: an attempt at injection using SQL. The value of [nom] is passed as a parameter: it is compared as-is to the [Nom] column, and no record matches (line 18);
  • line 24: the same query constructed by concatenation and passed to [FromSqlRaw], which executes the text provided to it. The value of [nom] becomes the code SQL, the condition remains true, and the query returns all six items (line 24): this is a successful SQL injection. [FromSqlRaw] should only be used with constant text, with values passed as parameters ([FromSqlRaw("... WHERE Nom = {0}", nom)]);
  • lines 29–31: [Database.SqlQuery<T>] (EF Core 7 for simple types, EF Core 8 for others) executes a query that returns values of any type, in this case strings. For a simple type, the returned column must be named [Value] (alias [AS Value]): this is the name that EF Core uses when it constructs the query with LINQ, as with the following [Single] (lines 28–32). [SqlQuery] also accepts any class, whose properties are assigned the columns of the same name;
  • lines 40–42: [Database.ExecuteSql] executes an update command, also configured via interpolation, and returns the number of modified rows.

All of these methods have an asynchronous version ([ToListAsync] on the result of [FromSql], [ExecuteSqlAsync]).

docs.title: 11.12. Context and Dependency Injection
docs.text:
The previous examples created their contexts using [new]. In a layered application, and in all ASP.NET Core applications, contexts are created by the dependency injection container introduced in Chapter 6. EF Core provides two extension methods of [IServiceCollection] for this purpose:

  • [AddDbContext<T>(options => ...)] registers the [T] context with a “scoped” lifetime: the container creates a context per scope, provides it to all services within that scope that request it, and releases it at the end of the scope. In a web application, a scope is created for each request HTTP: each request has its own context, which corresponds to the context’s unit of work;
  • [AddDbContextFactory<T>(options => ...)] registers a context factory, [IDbContextFactory<T>], whose method [CreateDbContext] creates a new context on each call. It is used in long-running services (singletons), which cannot maintain the same context throughout the application’s lifetime, and in parallel processing, which requires one context per task.

In both cases, the lambda receives a *[DbContextOptionsBuilder] and configures the context as *[OnConfiguring]* did; the context must have a constructor that accepts a *[DbContextOptions<T>], such as the one in the *[ArticlesContext]* class.

The [Injection] project references the [Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection] package (version 10.0.12, as in Chapter 6). It defines two services:

using Articles.Data;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Injection;

// a service that receives the context via injection: its lifetime is that of the context
public class ArticlesDao(ArticlesContext contexte)
{
     // items to be restocked
    public List<string> ArticlesEnRupture() =>
        contexte.Articles.Where(a => a.StockActuel < a.StockMinimum).Select(a => a.Nom).ToList();
}

// a long-running service: it receives a context factory
public class StatistiquesService(IDbContextFactory<ArticlesContext> fabrique)
{
     // Each call uses a new context, which is released immediately
    public async Task<decimal> ValeurStockAsync()
    {
        await using ArticlesContext contexte = await fabrique.CreateDbContextAsync();
        return await contexte.Articles.SumAsync(a => a.Prix * a.StockActuel);
    }
}
  • line 7: a service that receives the context via its (primary) constructor. It must be registered with the same lifetime as the context (scoped);
  • line 15: a service that receives a context factory;
  • line 20: each call to the method creates a context and immediately releases it.

The program is as follows:

using Articles.Data;
using Injection;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;

// the database is recreated with its six items
ArticlesContext.Initialiser();

// 1 - AddDbContext: the context is saved with a “scoped” lifetime
var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddDbContext<ArticlesContext>(options =>
    options.UseMySql(ArticlesContext.Connexion, ArticlesContext.VersionServeur));
services.AddScoped<ArticlesDao>();
using ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();

ArticlesContext contexteDeLaPortee1;
using (IServiceScope portee = provider.CreateScope())
{
     // Within the same scope, the same context is always obtained
    contexteDeLaPortee1 = portee.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ArticlesContext>();
    var contexte = portee.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ArticlesContext>();
    Console.WriteLine($"portée 1 : même contexte = {ReferenceEquals(contexte, contexteDeLaPortee1)}");
     // The service [ArticlesDao] received this context
    var dao = portee.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ArticlesDao>();
    Console.WriteLine($"portée 1 : en rupture = {string.Join(", ", dao.ArticlesEnRupture())}");
}
using (IServiceScope portee = provider.CreateScope())
{
     // a different scope: a different context
    var contexte = portee.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ArticlesContext>();
    Console.WriteLine($"portée 2 : même contexte qu'en portée 1 = {ReferenceEquals(contexte, contexteDeLaPortee1)}");
}
// At the end of its scope, the context was released
try
{
    contexteDeLaPortee1.Articles.Count();
}
catch (ObjectDisposedException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message[..(e.Message.IndexOf('.') + 1)]}");
}

// 2 - AddDbContextFactory: a context factory for a long-running service
var services2 = new ServiceCollection();
services2.AddDbContextFactory<ArticlesContext>(options =>
    options.UseMySql(ArticlesContext.Connexion, ArticlesContext.VersionServeur));
services2.AddSingleton<StatistiquesService>();
using ServiceProvider provider2 = services2.BuildServiceProvider();
var statistiques = provider2.GetRequiredService<StatistiquesService>();
Console.WriteLine($"valeur du stock : {await statistiques.ValeurStockAsync():0.00} euros");

Results:

> dotnet run
portée 1 : même contexte = True
portée 1 : en rupture = flèches - lot de 6
portée 2 : même contexte qu'en portée 1 = False
ObjectDisposedException : Cannot access a disposed context instance.
valeur du stock : 12300,00 euros

Comments:

  • Lines 11–12: Context registration. The configuration given here is the one received by the context builder: [OnConfiguring] therefore evaluates [options.IsConfigured] as true and does not add the log SQL. It could be added here along with [AvecJournalSql];
  • line 13: the service [ArticlesDao], which is also scoped;
  • line 17: [CreateScope()] creates a scope. “Scoped” services are obtained from the scope’s service provider ([portee.ServiceProvider]);
  • lines 20–22: two requests for the context within the same scope return the same object (line 2);
  • line 24: the container creates the service [ArticlesDao] by passing it the scope’s context;
  • lines 27–31: another scope receives a different context (line 4);
  • lines 36–38: at the end of its scope, the context was released by the container; using it triggers a [ObjectDisposedException]. This is the classic error of a long-running service that retained a context received within a scope;
  • lines 45–47: the context factory and a singleton service that uses it. The service can live as long as the application: it does not hold onto a context; it creates a new one for each calculation.

Keep in mind the rules for a context’s lifetime: short-lived (one unit of work), never shared among multiple threads, and always released ([using], or the container).

docs.title: 11.13.1. The Architecture
docs.text:
Version 6 of the tax calculation application (Chapter 10) read the tax brackets from a MySQL database using ADO.NET. Version 7 does the same using EF Core. As with version 6, only the [dao] layer changes: the [metier] and [ui] layers from version 5 (Chapter 6) are reused as-is via project references.

The solution includes two new projects in the [11-efcore/ImpotsV7] folder:

ImpotsV7/
  Impots.Dao.Ef/                 bibliothèque : la couche [dao] EF Core
    Impots.Dao.Ef.csproj
    TrancheImpotEntity.cs        l'entité de persistance
    ImpotsContext.cs             le contexte, avec les données d'amorçage
    ImpotsContextFactory.cs      la fabrique utilisée par [dotnet ef]
    EfImpot.cs                   l'implémentation de IImpotDao
    Migrations/
      20261003100850_Initiale.cs
      20261003100850_Initiale.Designer.cs
      ImpotsContextModelSnapshot.cs
  Impots.Ui.Ef/                  exécutable : intégration des couches
    Impots.Ui.Ef.csproj
    Program.cs
    impots-ef.json
    impots-ef-erreur.json

docs.title: 11.13.2. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [Impots.Dao.Ef] project references the [dao] layer from version 5, which contains the entities ([TrancheImpot], [ImpotException]) and the interface [IImpotDao]:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
     <!-- The [dao] layer in version 5: entities, IImpotDao interface, HardwiredImpot -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/ImpotsV5/Impots.Dao/Impots.Dao.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
     <!-- EF Core and its provider MySQL -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore" Version="9.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql" Version="9.0.0" />
     <!-- for the [dotnet ef] tool (migrations) -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design" Version="9.0.0">
      <PrivateAssets>all</PrivateAssets>
      <IncludeAssets>runtime; build; native; contentfiles; analyzers; buildtransitive</IncludeAssets>
    </PackageReference>
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
  • line 11: the reference to the [Impots.Dao] project in version 5, using a relative path;
  • lines 16–19: EF Core, Pomelo, and the package required for the [dotnet ef] tool.

The [Entites.TrancheImpot] structure in version 5 cannot be a EF Core entity: it is a [readonly record struct], which is unmodifiable and has no primary key. It is not modified because it is part of the contract between the layers, shared by all versions. A persistence entity specific to the [dao] layer is created, whose role is to represent a row in the table:

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace Dao;

// a tax bracket as recorded in the database: a EF Core entity
[Table("tranches")]
public class TrancheImpotEntity
{
     // the primary key, which does not exist in Entites.TrancheImpot
    public int Id { get; set; }

    [Column("limite", TypeName = "decimal(10,2)")]
    public decimal Limite { get; set; }

    [Column("coeffr", TypeName = "decimal(6,4)")]
    public decimal CoeffR { get; set; }

    [Column("coeffn", TypeName = "decimal(10,2)")]
    public decimal CoeffN { get; set; }
}
  • row 6: the table [tranches], as in version 7 of the 2008 course;
  • row 10: the primary key, which is also used to sort the ranges;
  • lines 12–19: the three columns, with appropriate [decimal] data types: the limit and the coefficient [coeffN] are amounts with two decimal places, and [coeffR] is a rate with four decimal places.

Context:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Dao;

// the context of the database [efimpots]: it is configured by its creator
public class ImpotsContext(DbContextOptions<ImpotsContext> options) : DbContext(options)
{
     // the tax bracket table
    public DbSet<TrancheImpotEntity> Tranches => Set<TrancheImpotEntity>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
         // initialization data: the brackets in class HardwiredImpot (version 5),
         // numbered starting at 1; they will be inserted by the migration
        TrancheImpotEntity[] tranches = new HardwiredImpot().TranchesImpot
            .Select((t, i) => new TrancheImpotEntity { Id = i + 1, Limite = t.Limite, CoeffR = t.CoeffR, CoeffN = t.CoeffN })
            .ToArray();
        modelBuilder.Entity<TrancheImpotEntity>().HasData(tranches);
    }
}
  • line 6: the context is configured by its constructor: the main program will choose the database;
  • lines 15–17: the seed data. To avoid rewriting the scale brackets, we reuse those from class [HardwiredImpot] in version 5, which we number starting from 1 with the overloading of [Select], which provides the element index;
  • Line 18: [HasData] declares rows that are part of the model. Migrations insert them into the table, and if they change, the next migration will contain the necessary commands [UPDATE], [INSERT], or [DELETE]. Primary keys must be specified explicitly so that the tool can compare data across versions.

The factory used by tool [dotnet ef]:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design;

namespace Dao;

// the factory used by the [dotnet ef] tool to create the context (migrations)
public class ImpotsContextFactory : IDesignTimeDbContextFactory<ImpotsContext>
{
    public ImpotsContext CreateDbContext(string[] args)
    {
         // the development database; at runtime, the string comes from the configuration
        const string connexion = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=efimpots;User=root;Password=";
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<ImpotsContext>()
            .UseMySql(connexion, new MySqlServerVersion(new Version(8, 0, 36)))
            .Options;
        return new ImpotsContext(options);
    }
}

It is used only by the tool during development: the connection string for the development database is hard-coded there. At runtime, the connection string comes from the application's configuration file.

The [EfImpot] class implements the [IImpotDao] interface:

using System.Data.Common;
using Entites;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace Dao;

// a [dao] layer that reads tax brackets from a database using EF Core
public class EfImpot : IImpotDao
{
     // error codes specific to this implementation
    public enum CodeErreurs { Acces = 1, TableVide = 2 }

     // tax brackets
    public TrancheImpot[] TranchesImpot { get; }

     // constructor: the context factory is injected
    public EfImpot(IDbContextFactory<ImpotsContext> fabrique)
    {
        try
        {
             // a short-lived context, just long enough to read the table
            using ImpotsContext contexte = fabrique.CreateDbContext();
             // Persistence entities are mapped to application entities
            TranchesImpot = contexte.Tranches
                .AsNoTracking()
                .OrderBy(t => t.Id)
                .Select(t => new TrancheImpot(t.Limite, t.CoeffR, t.CoeffN))
                .ToArray();
        }
        catch (DbException e)
        {
             // SGBD error: encapsulated in a ImpotException
            throw new ImpotException("Erreur lors de la lecture des tranches d'impôt dans la base de données", e)
            {
                Code = (int)CodeErreurs.Acces
            };
        }
         // The [metier] layer requires at least one slice
        if (TranchesImpot.Length == 0)
        {
            throw new ImpotException("La table des tranches d'impôt est vide") { Code = (int)CodeErreurs.TableVide };
        }
    }
}
  • line 11: the error codes for this implementation, as for [FileImpot] and [JsonImpot];
  • line 17: the [dao] layer receives a context factory. It will be a singleton: it reads the slices once and for all in its constructor, using a short-lived context that is released immediately (line 22);
  • lines 24–28: reading the table, without tracking (the slices will not be modified), in primary key order. The [Select] projection transforms each persistence entity into a [Entites.TrancheImpot]: the rest of the application never sees the [TrancheImpotEntity] entity. EF Core requests only the three relevant columns from SGBD;
  • lines 30–35: an error in SGBD (database inaccessible, table missing, etc.) manifests as an exception derived from [DbException], the base class for ADO.NET connector exceptions (Chapter 10): [MySqlException] for MySqlConnector. As in other implementations, it is encapsulated in a [ImpotException];
  • lines 39–41: an empty table is also an error: the [metier] layer requires at least one slice.

docs.title: 11.13.3. The database
docs.text:
The [efimpots] database is created by the [Initiale] migration, generated by the [dotnet ef migrations add Initiale] command entered in the [Impots.Dao.Ef] project folder. The tool accepted a class library as the starter project because it contains the [ImpotsContextFactory] factory and the [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design] package (otherwise, an executable project is specified using the [--startup-project] option). The migration is as follows:

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Metadata;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Migrations;

#nullable disable

#pragma warning disable CA1814 // Prefer jagged arrays over multidimensional

namespace Impots.Dao.Ef.Migrations
{
     /// <inheritdoc />
    public partial class Initiale : Migration
    {
         /// <inheritdoc />
        protected override void Up(MigrationBuilder migrationBuilder)
        {
            migrationBuilder.AlterDatabase()
                .Annotation("MySql:CharSet", "utf8mb4");

            migrationBuilder.CreateTable(
                name: "tranches",
                columns: table => new
                {
                    Id = table.Column<int>(type: "int", nullable: false)
                        .Annotation("MySql:ValueGenerationStrategy", MySqlValueGenerationStrategy.IdentityColumn),
                    limite = table.Column<decimal>(type: "decimal(10,2)", nullable: false),
                    coeffr = table.Column<decimal>(type: "decimal(6,4)", nullable: false),
                    coeffn = table.Column<decimal>(type: "decimal(10,2)", nullable: false)
                },
                constraints: table =>
                {
                    table.PrimaryKey("PK_tranches", x => x.Id);
                })
                .Annotation("MySql:CharSet", "utf8mb4");

            migrationBuilder.InsertData(
                table: "tranches",
                columns: new[] { "Id", "coeffn", "coeffr", "limite" },
                values: new object[,]
                {
                    { 1, 0m, 0m, 4962m },
                    { 2, 291.09m, 0.068m, 8382m },
                    { 3, 1322.92m, 0.191m, 14753m },
                    { 4, 2668.39m, 0.283m, 23888m },
                    { 5, 4846.98m, 0.374m, 38868m },
                    { 6, 6883.66m, 0.426m, 47932m },
                    { 7, 9505.54m, 0.481m, 0m }
                });
        }

         /// <inheritdoc />
        protected override void Down(MigrationBuilder migrationBuilder)
        {
            migrationBuilder.DropTable(
                name: "tranches");
        }
    }
}
  • lines 19–31: table creation;
  • lines 35–46: insertion of seed data, one line per slice;
  • line 6: the generated code disables a code analyzer warning regarding multidimensional tables ([new object[,]]).

The migration script SQL shows the commands that will be executed:

> dotnet ef migrations script
Build started...
Build succeeded.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS `__EFMigrationsHistory` (
    `MigrationId` varchar(150) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NOT NULL,
    `ProductVersion` varchar(32) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT `PK___EFMigrationsHistory` PRIMARY KEY (`MigrationId`)
) CHARACTER SET=utf8mb4;

START TRANSACTION;
ALTER DATABASE CHARACTER SET utf8mb4;

CREATE TABLE `tranches` (
    `Id` int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
    `limite` decimal(10,2) NOT NULL,
    `coeffr` decimal(6,4) NOT NULL,
    `coeffn` decimal(10,2) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT `PK_tranches` PRIMARY KEY (`Id`)
) CHARACTER SET=utf8mb4;

INSERT INTO `tranches` (`Id`, `coeffn`, `coeffr`, `limite`)
VALUES (1, 0.0, 0.0, 4962.0),
(2, 291.09, 0.068, 8382.0),
(3, 1322.92, 0.191, 14753.0),
(4, 2668.39, 0.283, 23888.0),
(5, 4846.98, 0.374, 38868.0),
(6, 6883.66, 0.426, 47932.0),
(7, 9505.54, 0.481, 0.0);

INSERT INTO `__EFMigrationsHistory` (`MigrationId`, `ProductVersion`)
VALUES ('20261003100850_Initiale', '9.0.0');

COMMIT;

The table [__EFMigrationsHistory] is created if it does not exist (lines 4–8), and then the migration is applied in a transaction. Apply the migration:

> dotnet ef database update
Build started...
Build succeeded.
Acquiring an exclusive lock for migration application. See https://aka.ms/efcore-docs-migrations-lock for more information if this takes too long.
Applying migration '20261003100850_Initiale'.
Done.

and the table’s contents are verified:

> mysql -uroot -t efimpots -e "SELECT * FROM tranches"
+----+----------+--------+---------+
| Id | limite   | coeffr | coeffn  |
+----+----------+--------+---------+
|  1 |  4962.00 | 0.0000 |    0.00 |
|  2 |  8382.00 | 0.0680 |  291.09 |
|  3 | 14753.00 | 0.1910 | 1322.92 |
|  4 | 23888.00 | 0.2830 | 2668.39 |
|  5 | 38868.00 | 0.3740 | 4846.98 |
|  6 | 47932.00 | 0.4260 | 6883.66 |
|  7 |     0.00 | 0.4810 | 9505.54 |
+----+----------+--------+---------+

The pay scale brackets are present, with the last one having a zero limit (it is not used by the [metier] layer, which selects the last bracket when no other is suitable).

To set up the database on your end: the [Initiale] migration is already included with the course codes in the [11-efcore/ImpotsV7/Impots.Dao.Ef/Migrations] folder. Therefore, you do not need to re-enter the [dotnet ef migrations add Initiale] command (it was used to generate the migration, so that step is already complete). Simply:

  • run MySQL (in Laragon; see the appendix; user [root] with no password);
  • install the [dotnet-ef] tool if you haven’t already: [dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef --version 9.0.0];
  • navigate to the [11-efcore/ImpotsV7/Impots.Dao.Ef] folder and enter the single command [dotnet ef database update].

The [efimpots] database is then created, with its [tranches] table populated with the seed data. If the command fails, verify that MySQL is running and that the connection string for the [ImpotsContextFactory] factory matches your server (port 3306, username [root], blank password).

docs.title: 11.13.4. Layer Integration
docs.text:
The executable project [Impots.Ui.Ef] consists of the following layers:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
     <!-- the [metier] and [ui] layers from version 5, unchanged -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/ImpotsV5/Impots.Metier/Impots.Metier.csproj" />
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/ImpotsV5/Impots.Ui/Impots.Ui.csproj" />
     <!-- the new layer [dao] -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../Impots.Dao.Ef/Impots.Dao.Ef.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
     <!-- dependency injection container and configuration JSON -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="10.0.12" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Json" Version="10.0.12" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
     <!-- the configuration files are copied next to the executable -->
    <None Update="impots-ef*.json" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
  • lines 12–13: layers [metier] and [ui] from version 5. The [Impots.Ui] project is an executable: it can be referenced as a library to use its [Ui.Dialogue] class;
  • Line 15: the new layer [dao];
  • line 26: the configuration files. They are not named [appsettings.json]: the referenced project [Impots.Ui] already copies its own files [appsettings*.json] to the output folder, and two files with the same name would conflict.

The configuration file [impots-ef.json] contains the connection string:

{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "Impots": "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=efimpots;User=root;Password="
  }
}

The section [ConnectionStrings] is the usual location for connection strings in the .NET configuration: the method [config.GetConnectionString("Impots")] reads the key [ConnectionStrings:Impots]. The file [impots-ef-erreur.json] refers to a database named [efimpotsabsente], which does not exist.

The main program is the one from version 5, in which only the composition of the [dao] layer changes:

using Dao;
using Entites;
using Metier;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Ui;

// the configuration file: impots-ef.json by default, or the one passed as an argument
string fichierConfig = args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "impots-ef.json";

// integration of layers
IImpotMetier metier;
try
{
     // reads the configuration file, located next to the executable
    IConfiguration config = new ConfigurationBuilder()
        .SetBasePath(AppContext.BaseDirectory)
        .AddJsonFile(fichierConfig, optional: false)
        .Build();
    string connexion = config.GetConnectionString("Impots")
        ?? throw new ImpotException($"Chaîne de connexion [Impots] absente du fichier {fichierConfig}");

     // saving layers to the container
    var services = new ServiceCollection();
     // a EF Core context factory, configured for MySQL
    services.AddDbContextFactory<ImpotsContext>(options =>
        options.UseMySql(connexion, new MySqlServerVersion(new Version(8, 0, 36))));
     // the [dao] layer: EfImpot will receive the factory
    services.AddSingleton<IImpotDao, EfImpot>();
     // the [metier] layer: it will receive the [dao] layer
    services.AddSingleton<IImpotMetier, ImpotMetier>();

     // creation of the container, followed by the layer [metier] (and therefore the layer [dao])
    ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
    metier = provider.GetRequiredService<IImpotMetier>();
}
catch (Exception e)
{
     // display the error and terminate the program
    Dialogue.AfficherErreur(e);
    return 1;
}

// user dialog, the one from version 5
Dialogue.Run(metier);
return 0;
  • lines 21–22: the connection string read from the configuration. A [throw] (C# 7) expression to the right of [??] throws an exception if it is missing;
  • lines 27–28: a context factory [ImpotsContext], configured with the connection string from the configuration;
  • line 30: the [dao] layer is a [EfImpot]: the container will pass the context factory to it. A singleton [dao] layer cannot directly receive a context, which is “scoped”—hence the factory;
  • line 32: the [metier] layer from version 5;
  • line 46: the dialog box from version 5.

docs.title: 11.13.5. Executions
docs.text:
> dotnet run
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : o 2 60000
Impôt=4282 euros
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : o 3 60000
Impôt=2959 euros
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter : n 0 60000
Impôt=11519 euros
Paramètres du calcul de l'impôt au format : Marié (o/n) NbEnfants Salaire ou rien pour arrêter :

The threshold values from previous versions are retained: 4,282 euros for a married couple with two children and a combined income of 60,000 euros, 2,959 euros for a family with three children, and 11,519 euros for a single person without children.

With the configuration file [impots-ef-erreur.json], which refers to a nonexistent database:

> dotnet run -- impots-ef-erreur.json
Chaîne des exceptions :
----------------------------------------
Entites.ImpotException: Erreur lors de la lecture des tranches d'impôt dans la base de données
----------------------------------------
MySqlConnector.MySqlException: Unknown database 'efimpotsabsente'
----------------------------------------
  • line 6: the original exception, thrown by the MySqlConnector connector, via EF Core;
  • line 4: the [dao] layer encapsulated it within a [ImpotException], which was displayed by the main program.

The 2008 course demonstrated, in version 7, that the [dao] layer could switch from SGBD (from MySQL to SQL Server Compact) simply by modifying the configuration file, thanks to the generic connector in ADO.NET. With EF Core, switching from SGBD is equivalent to switching providers: replacing the Pomelo package with that of another SGBD (for example, [Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer]) and the [UseMySql] call with the corresponding call ([UseSqlServer]), then regenerate the migrations, which contain provider-specific information. The code for class [EfImpot], written as LINQ, remains unchanged.

docs.title: 11.14. Conclusion: ADO.NET, Dapper, or EF Core?
docs.text:
We now have two ways to access a database: ADO.NET (Chapter 10) and EF Core (this chapter). There is a third, intermediate method that is widely used: Dapper, a small library (a “micro-ORM”) that adds extension methods to the ADO.NET connection. These methods execute a hand-written SQL query and automatically convert the rows in the result into objects: [connexion.Query<Article>("SELECT * FROM articles WHERE Prix > @prix", new { prix = 200 })]. You write the SQL, and Dapper handles mapping the columns to properties.

StrengthsWeaknessesADO.NETFull control over SQL; performance; no dependenciesa lot of repetitive code (parameters, reading columns); SQL in strings, not checked by the compilerDapperSQL hand-written but without copy code; performance similar to ADO.NETNo change tracking or generation of [INSERT]/[UPDATE]; no migrationsEF CoreLINQ queries verified by the compiler; change tracking; relationships; migrations; independent of SGBDan additional layer to understand; SQL generated to be monitored; less suitable for complex bulk processing

The following guidelines can be proposed:

  • EF Core is suitable for most management applications: a model of interconnected entities, operations for reading and updating entities, and a schema that evolves with the application. It is the default choice for ASP.NET Core applications;
  • ADO.NET, or Dapper, is suitable when you want precise control over the SQL executed: complex reporting queries, stored procedures, processing very large volumes, or an existing database with a schema poorly suited to an object-oriented model;
  • These approaches can be combined: an application can use EF Core for the most part and hand-written SQL code—using [FromSql], [SqlQuery], or Dapper—for a few critical queries. EF Core also provides access to the ADO.NET connection it uses ([contexte.Database.GetDbConnection()]).

In any case, knowing about ORM does not eliminate the need to understand SQL and how SGBD works: the log of executed SQL commands, which we have displayed throughout this chapter, is the primary tool for verifying what EF Core actually does.

For further information, Microsoft’s documentation is comprehensive and available in French: Entity Framework Core. The Pomelo provider is documented on its repository: Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql.

docs.title: 8. Execution Threads
docs.text:
This chapter introduces the simultaneous execution of multiple pieces of code within a single program: threads (execution threads) and the tools used to synchronize them. In 2008, most machines had only one processor, and parallelism was largely an illusion maintained by the operating system. Today, even the most basic laptop has multiple cores: multiple threads actually run at the same time, making the synchronization issues discussed here even more prevalent.

The examples are single-file applications ([dotnet run threads-01.cs]) located in the [08-threads] folder. Note that the implicit directives [using] for these applications include [System.Threading] and [System.Threading.Tasks]: the classes [Thread], [Lock], [Mutex], [Monitor], [Interlocked], [Task]… can be used without the [using] directive.

A word of caution before you begin: the results of a multithreaded program vary from one execution to the next. The order in which threads are assigned the processor depends on the operating system, the number of processors, and the machine’s load. The results shown in this chapter were obtained on a dual-processor Linux machine shared with other programs. If you run the examples, you will get similar results, but they will rarely be identical.

docs.title: 8.1. The Thread Class
docs.text:
When an application is launched, it runs in an execution flow called a thread. The class .NET that models a thread is the [System.Threading.Thread] class. Its main constructors, properties, and methods are as follows:

MemberRole[Thread(ThreadStart start)]creates a thread that will execute the [start] method. The [ThreadStart] delegate refers to a method with no parameters and no return value: [void M()][Thread(ParameterizedThreadStart start)]same as above, but with a method that has a parameter of type [object?]: [void M(object? obj)][static Thread CurrentThread]the thread executing the code that requested this property[string? Name]the thread name, useful for tracking[int ManagedThreadId]A unique numeric identifier for the thread[bool IsBackground]Indicates whether the thread is a background thread (see below)[bool IsAlive]indicates whether the thread is currently running[void Start()], [void Start(object? obj)]starts the thread's execution, optionally passing it information of type [object][void Join()], [bool Join(TimeSpan délai)]The thread T1, which executes [T2.Join()], is blocked until the thread T2 has finished. The second form limits the duration of the wait[static void Sleep(int ms)]The thread executing the method is suspended for [ms] milliseconds. It loses the CPU, which is given to another thread

The 2008 course also covered the [Abort] method, which forcibly terminated a thread. It no longer exists in practice: since .NET Core, it throws the [PlatformNotSupportedException] exception. Abruptly stopping a thread could leave the data it was handling in an inconsistent state. Today, a thread is asked to stop cooperatively, using a cancellation token ([CancellationToken]) that the thread checks regularly: we’ll see this in the next chapter.

Here is an initial application demonstrating the existence of a main execution thread—the one that executes the program’s high-level instructions (the equivalent of the [Main] method). The [threads-01.cs] program is as follows:

// the main thread of a program

// the thread that executes this code
Thread principal = Thread.CurrentThread;
// Initially, it has no name
Console.WriteLine($"Nom du thread courant : [{principal.Name}]");
// it is given a name
principal.Name = "Main";
Console.WriteLine($"Nom du thread courant : [{principal.Name}]");
// some properties
Console.WriteLine($"Identifiant (ManagedThreadId) : {principal.ManagedThreadId}");
Console.WriteLine($"Thread d'arrière-plan (IsBackground) : {principal.IsBackground}");
Console.WriteLine($"Thread du pool (IsThreadPoolThread) : {principal.IsThreadPoolThread}");
Console.WriteLine($"Priorité (Priority) : {principal.Priority}");
Console.WriteLine($"État (ThreadState) : {principal.ThreadState}");
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre de processeurs : {Environment.ProcessorCount}");

// a display every second
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{principal.Name} : {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss}");
     // the thread is suspended for 1 second
    Thread.Sleep(1000);
}

Results:

> dotnet run threads-01.cs
Nom du thread courant : []
Nom du thread courant : [Main]
Identifiant (ManagedThreadId) : 1
Thread d'arrière-plan (IsBackground) : False
Thread du pool (IsThreadPoolThread) : False
Priorité (Priority) : Normal
État (ThreadState) : Running
Nombre de processeurs : 2
Main : 11:35:54
Main : 11:35:55
Main : 11:35:56
Main : 11:35:57
Main : 11:35:58

Comments:

  • Line 4: A reference to the thread executing the program is retrieved;
  • Lines 5–9: We display its name, modify it, and then display it again. Initially, the main thread has no name (line 2 of the results);
  • lines 11–15: some thread properties. The main thread has the ID 1; it is a foreground thread ([IsBackground] equals [False]) that does not belong to the thread pool (we’ll discuss these two concepts later); it is currently running ([Running]);
  • Line 16: The machine that ran the example has 2 processors;
  • lines 19–23: a loop that displays a message every second. [Thread.Sleep(1000)] suspends the main thread for one second. The 2008 course used an infinite loop here that was terminated by Ctrl-C; we are limiting ourselves to five displays. Note the format [HH:mm:ss] (hours from 0 to 23): the 2008 course used [hh], which displays hours from 1 to 12.

docs.title: 8.2. Creating Execution Threads
docs.text:
It is possible to have applications where pieces of code execute “simultaneously” in different execution threads. If the machine has fewer processors than there are threads ready to execute, the threads share the processors: each one takes turns using a processor for a short time (a few milliseconds). On a multiprocessor machine, multiple threads actually execute at the same time. The amount of time allocated to a thread depends on various factors, including its priority, which has a default value but can be set programmatically (property [Priority]). A thread that has the processor may release it early:

  • by waiting for an event (completion of another thread with [Join], waiting for a signal);
  • by entering a sleep state for a specified duration ([Sleep]).

A thread T is first created using one of the constructors presented above, for example:

Thread t = new Thread(Afficher);

where [Afficher] is a method with one of the following two signatures:

void Afficher();
void Afficher(object? obj);

Creating a thread does not start it:

  • the execution of thread T is initiated by [T.Start()]: the method passed to the constructor of T is then executed by thread T. The code that executes the instruction [T.Start()] does not wait for thread T to finish; it immediately moves on to the next instruction. We then have two threads running in parallel. They often need to communicate with each other to track the progress of the shared work: this is the problem of thread synchronization;
  • Once started, thread T runs autonomously. It stops when the method it is executing is complete;
  • we can wait for it to finish executing using [T.Join()]. This is a blocking instruction: the thread executing it is blocked until thread T has finished its work. This is a basic method of synchronization.

The program [threads-02.cs] is as follows:

// creating execution threads

// the main thread is named
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";

// creating 5 threads
var taches = new Thread[5];
for (int i = 0; i < taches.Length; i++)
{
     // Thread No. i will execute the Display method
    taches[i] = new Thread(Affiche);
     // Assigning a name to it
    taches[i].Name = i.ToString();
     // We start its execution (non-blocking operation)
    taches[i].Start();
}

// End of the main thread
Console.WriteLine($"Fin du thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} à {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");

// the method executed by the threads
static void Affiche()
{
     // the thread executing the method
    Thread courant = Thread.CurrentThread;
    Console.WriteLine($"Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread {courant.Name} (id {courant.ManagedThreadId}) : {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");
     // Suspended for 1 second
    Thread.Sleep(1000);
    Console.WriteLine($"Fin d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread {courant.Name} : {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");
}

Comments:

  • line 4: we give the main thread a name;
  • lines 7–15: 5 threads are created and started. Their references are stored in an array so they can be retrieved later. Each thread executes the [Affiche] method on lines 22–29;
  • line 11: the name of the method [Affiche] is automatically converted to a delegate of type [ThreadStart] (delegates were introduced in the previous chapter);
  • line 15: thread No. i is launched. This operation is non-blocking: thread No. i runs in parallel with the main thread that launched it;
  • line 19: the main thread reaches the end of the program;
  • lines 22–29: the method [Affiche] displays the name and ID of the thread executing it, as well as the start and end times (to the millisecond) of execution;
  • line 28: any thread executing the [Affiche] method pauses for 1 second. The processor is then handed over to another thread waiting for the processor. At the end of the 1-second pause, the paused thread becomes eligible for the processor again. It will obtain it when its turn comes.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-02.cs
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 2 (id 6) : 11:36:01.725
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 4 (id 8) : 11:36:01.725
Fin du thread Main à 11:36:01.725
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 0 (id 4) : 11:36:01.725
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 1 (id 5) : 11:36:01.725
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 3 (id 7) : 11:36:01.725
Fin d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 1 : 11:36:02.779
Fin d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 0 : 11:36:02.778
Fin d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 4 : 11:36:02.779
Fin d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 2 : 11:36:02.779
Fin d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 3 : 11:36:02.779

These results are very informative:

  • First, we see that launching a thread is not blocking. The main thread launched 5 threads and reached the end of the program (line 4) even though three of the launched threads had not yet displayed their first message;
  • the order in which the threads execute is unpredictable: in this run, threads 2 and 4 displayed their start messages before thread 0. The operating system has 6 threads and 2 processors here; it allocates the processors to these threads according to its own rules;
  • We also note that the order of the displays does not always follow the order of the displayed times: the time is calculated before it is displayed, and in the meantime, another thread may have written to the console. [Console.WriteLine] is thread-safe: two lines written by two threads do not get mixed up, but their order is not guaranteed;
  • each thread pauses for one second with [Sleep], then completes execution of the [Affiche] method;
  • Finally, the program did not stop when the main thread finished its work: the process waited for all 5 threads to finish. This is because these threads are foreground threads: a .NET process terminates when all of its foreground threads have finished.

Conversely, a thread can be declared a background thread by setting its [IsBackground] property to [true] before launching it. Background threads do not prevent the process from terminating: when the last foreground thread terminates, they are stopped. The program [threads-03.cs] is as follows:

// background threads

// the main thread is named
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";

// creation of 5 background threads
var taches = new Thread[5];
for (int i = 0; i < taches.Length; i++)
{
    taches[i] = new Thread(Affiche)
    {
        Name = i.ToString(),
         // A background thread does not prevent the process from terminating
        IsBackground = true
    };
    taches[i].Start();
}

// We'll give the threads time to start up
Thread.Sleep(100);
// End of the main thread, and thus of the process
Console.WriteLine($"Fin du thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} à {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");

// the method executed by the threads
static void Affiche()
{
    Thread courant = Thread.CurrentThread;
    Console.WriteLine($"Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread {courant.Name} : {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");
     // sleep for 1 s
    Thread.Sleep(1000);
    Console.WriteLine($"Fin d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread {courant.Name} : {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");
}

Comments:

  • line 14: the 5 threads are background threads. The properties [Name] and [IsBackground] are set using an object initializer;
  • line 20: the main thread waits 100 ms to give the threads time to start, then it terminates.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-03.cs
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 4 : 11:36:04.770
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 3 : 11:36:04.764
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 1 : 11:36:04.766
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 0 : 11:36:04.764
Début d'exécution de la méthode Affiche dans le thread 2 : 11:36:04.766
Fin du thread Main à 11:36:04.872

All 5 threads began execution, then the main thread terminated (line 7). The background threads were then stopped during their one-second sleep: no end message is displayed. The 2008 course achieved the same result by ending [Main] with [Environment.Exit(0)], an instruction that stops all threads in the application, not just the thread executing it. The threads in the thread pool, which we’ll discuss later, are background threads.

If the main thread wants to wait for the threads it created to finish, it uses the [Join] method. The program [threads-04.cs] also demonstrates another way to specify the code a thread should execute: a lambda.

// Wait for a thread to finish using Join—threads created with a lambda

// The main thread is named
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";

// creation of 5 threads
var taches = new Thread[5];
for (int i = 0; i < taches.Length; i++)
{
     // local copy of i, captured by the lambda
    int numero = i;
     // The thread executes the lambda, which calls `Affiche` with a typed parameter
    taches[i] = new Thread(() => Affiche(numero, 1000 + 100 * numero)) { Name = i.ToString() };
    taches[i].Start();
}

// waiting for all threads to finish
foreach (Thread tache in taches)
{
     // the main thread is blocked until the thread [tache] finishes
    tache.Join();
}
// main thread ends
Console.WriteLine($"Fin du thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} à {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");

// the method executed by the threads
static void Affiche(int numero, int duree)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Début d'exécution de la tâche {numero} dans le thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} : {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");
     // Suspended for [duree] milliseconds
    Thread.Sleep(duree);
    Console.WriteLine($"Fin d'exécution de la tâche {numero} dans le thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} : {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}");
}

Comments:

  • Line 13: The thread executes the lambda [() => Affiche(numero, 1000 + 100 * numero)]. A lambda with no parameters and no return value is compatible with the delegate [ThreadStart]. This syntax allows you to call a method with typed parameters (in this case, two [int]) instead of the imposed signature [void M(object? obj)];
  • Line 11: The lambda uses a copy of the loop variable [i]. This is essential: a lambda captures the variable, not its value. In a [for] loop, the variable [i] is unique across all iterations; if the lambda used [i], a thread that starts late could read the value of [i] from a subsequent iteration, or even the final value 5. The variable [numero], declared within the loop body, is, on the other hand, a new variable for each iteration (a loop variable [foreach] is also new for each iteration, as of C# 5);
  • lines 18–21: the main thread waits for each of the threads. It is first blocked waiting for thread 0, then for thread 1, and so on. When it exits the loop, the 5 threads it launched have finished;
  • line 31: task #i sleeps for 1,000 + 100 × i milliseconds, so that the threads finish in a known order.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-04.cs
Début d'exécution de la tâche 1 dans le thread 1 : 11:36:06.779
Début d'exécution de la tâche 3 dans le thread 3 : 11:36:06.779
Début d'exécution de la tâche 0 dans le thread 0 : 11:36:06.779
Début d'exécution de la tâche 4 dans le thread 4 : 11:36:06.779
Début d'exécution de la tâche 2 dans le thread 2 : 11:36:06.779
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 0 dans le thread 0 : 11:36:07.828
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 1 dans le thread 1 : 11:36:07.928
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 2 dans le thread 2 : 11:36:08.029
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 3 dans le thread 3 : 11:36:08.128
Fin d'exécution de la tâche 4 dans le thread 4 : 11:36:08.228
Fin du thread Main à 11:36:08.229

The last line shows that the main thread finished after the threads it had launched, at the moment the last of them finished.

docs.title: 8.3. The Benefits of Threads
docs.text:
Now that we’ve highlighted the existence of a default thread—the one that executes the main program—and we know how to create additional ones, let’s consider the benefits of threads. They have two main uses:

  • to utilize all the machine’s processors for a time-consuming calculation: the work is divided into chunks assigned to different threads. We’ll do this using the [Parallel] library at the end of this chapter;
  • to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, particularly when some of them primarily involve waiting (for a network response, a disk read, or user input). This is the case with client/server Internet applications, which we’ll cover in a later chapter.

In a client-server Internet application, a server located on a machine named S1 responds to requests from clients located on remote machines C1, C2, ..., Cn:

We use Internet applications that follow this pattern every day: web services, email, file transfers, and so on. In the diagram above, the server S1 must serve clients Ci simultaneously. If we take the example of a file server, we know that a transfer can sometimes take several minutes. It is out of the question for a single client to monopolize the server for such a long period of time. A common solution is for the server to create as many execution threads as there are clients. Each thread is then responsible for handling a specific client:

In practice, the server uses a thread pool with a limited number of threads, as described later. Modern servers go a step further: while a client is waiting for a response from the network, no thread is reserved for it. This is made possible by asynchronous programming, which is the subject of the next chapter.

docs.title: 8.4. Information Exchange Between Threads
docs.text:
In the previous examples, the threads executed a method with no parameters. The [Thread(ParameterizedThreadStart)] constructor accepts a method with the signature [void M(object? obj)]. This allows information to be passed to the launched thread:

t.Start(obj1);

launches the thread [t], which then executes the method associated with it by construction, passing it the actual parameter [obj1]. The program [threads-05.cs] is as follows:

// information exchange between threads

// The main thread is named
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";

// creation of 5 threads
var taches = new Thread[5];
var donnees = new Donnees[5];
for (int i = 0; i < taches.Length; i++)
{
     // Thread No. i will execute the Sleep(object?) method
    taches[i] = new Thread(Dormir) { Name = i.ToString() };
     // The object exchanged with the thread: the launching thread sets StartTime and Duration
    donnees[i] = new Donnees { Debut = DateTime.Now, Duree = i + 1 };
     // The thread is launched by passing it this object
    taches[i].Start(donnees[i]);
}

// We wait for the threads one after another
for (int i = 0; i < taches.Length; i++)
{
     // Wait for thread #i to finish
    taches[i].Join();
     // Thread No. i has set the "End" property of its object
    Donnees d = donnees[i];
    Console.WriteLine($"Thread {taches[i].Name} terminé : début {d.Debut:HH:mm:ss}, durée programmée {d.Duree} s, fin {d.Fin:HH:mm:ss}, durée effective {(d.Fin - d.Debut).TotalSeconds:F3} s");
}
// End of the main thread
Console.WriteLine($"Fin du thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} à {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss}");

// The method executed by the threads: signature void (object?)
static void Dormir(object? infos)
{
     // the parameter is retrieved with its actual type
    if (infos is not Donnees data)
    {
        return;
    }
     // suspended for Duree seconds
    Thread.Sleep(data.Duree * 1000);
     // The launched thread returns a result to the launching thread
    data.Fin = DateTime.Now;
}

// Information exchanged between the calling thread and the called thread
class Donnees
{
     // set by the calling thread
    public DateTime Debut { get; init; }
    public int Duree { get; init; }
     // set by the launched thread
    public DateTime Fin { get; set; }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 46–52: The information passed to the threads is a [Donnees] object. There is a two-way exchange of information between the launching thread and the launched thread. [Debut] and [Duree] are properties of [init]: they can only be set when the object is created:
    • [Debut]: the thread’s execution start time, set by the launching thread;
    • [Duree]: duration in seconds of the launched thread’s sleep, set by the launching thread;
    • [Fin]: thread execution end time, set by the launched thread;
  • line 12: each thread is associated with the [Dormir] method in lines 32–42, whose signature [void Dormir(object? infos)] corresponds to the delegate [ParameterizedThreadStart];
  • lines 14–16: a [Donnees] object is created, stored in the [donnees] array, and then passed to the [Start] method, which launches the thread;
  • lines 20–26: The main thread waits for each of the threads it has launched to finish, then retrieves the [donnees[i]] object from thread No. i and displays its contents;
  • line 35: the received parameter is of type [object?]; the pattern filter [infos is not Donnees data] checks its actual type and stores it in the typed variable [data]. The 2008 course performed a type cast to [(Data)infos], which throws an exception if the object is not of the expected type;
  • line 40: the parameter’s property [Duree] sets the sleep duration;
  • line 42: the [Fin] property of the parameter is set.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-05.cs
