docs.title: 8.7. Concurrent Collections
docs.text:
The previous examples protected very simple shared data (a counter, an array). When threads share a collection (list, dictionary, queue), one could protect each access with a [lock]. But ordinary collections ([List<T>], [Dictionary<TKey,TValue>], [Queue<T>]) are not designed to be modified by multiple threads simultaneously: unprotected use can result in the loss of elements, trigger unexpected exceptions, or even corrupt the collection’s internal structure. Starting with .NET 4, the [System.Collections.Concurrent] namespace offers collections designed to be shared between threads without explicit locking:

CollectionRole[ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue>]a dictionary whose operations, including conditional updates, are safe[ConcurrentQueue<T>]a queue (first-in, first-out)[ConcurrentStack<T>]a stack (last-in, first-out)[ConcurrentBag<T>]a bag: an unordered collection[BlockingCollection<T>]an envelope of the previous collections that blocks the consumer when the collection is empty and, possibly, the producer when it is full

docs.title: 8.7.1. ConcurrentDictionary and ConcurrentQueue
docs.text:
In the program [threads-18.cs], four threads generate random numbers and count the number of times each number appears in a shared dictionary:

// Concurrent collections: ConcurrentDictionary and ConcurrentQueue

using System.Collections.Concurrent;

// the shared dictionary: cipher -> number of draws
var tirages = new ConcurrentDictionary<int, int>();
// the shared queue for thread reports
var comptesRendus = new ConcurrentQueue<string>();

// 4 threads each generate 100,000 random digits
const int nbTirages = 100_000;
var threads = new Thread[4];
for (int i = 0; i < threads.Length; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(() =>
    {
        for (int j = 0; j < nbTirages; j++)
        {
            int chiffre = Random.Shared.Next(0, 10);
             // Add a key with the value 1 or perform an atomic update of the existing value
            tirages.AddOrUpdate(chiffre, 1, (cle, ancienneValeur) => ancienneValeur + 1);
        }
         // report placed in the queue
        comptesRendus.Enqueue($"le thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} a terminé ses {nbTirages:N0} tirages");
    })
    { Name = $"T{i}" };
    threads[i].Start();
}
foreach (Thread thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}

// The reports, in the order they were received
while (comptesRendus.TryDequeue(out string? compteRendu))
{
    Console.WriteLine(compteRendu);
}
// the results of the draws
foreach (var (chiffre, nombre) in tirages.OrderBy(paire => paire.Key))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"chiffre {chiffre} : {nombre,6:N0} tirages");
}
Console.WriteLine($"total : {tirages.Values.Sum():N0} tirages (attendu : {threads.Length * nbTirages:N0})");
// GetOrAdd: returns the value associated with the key, after adding it if it did not exist
Console.WriteLine($"GetOrAdd(10, 0) = {tirages.GetOrAdd(10, 0)}, nombre de clés : {tirages.Count}");

Comments:

  • line 3: the namespace for concurrent collections;
  • line 6: the shared dictionary associates each digit with its number of occurrences;
  • line 8: a queue where each thread deposits a report at the end of its work;
  • line 21: the method [AddOrUpdate] adds the key [chiffre] with the value 1 if it does not exist, and otherwise replaces its value with the one calculated by the function [(cle, ancienneValeur) => ancienneValeur + 1]. The operation is atomic. We could not write [tirages[chiffre]++]: this expression reads the value and then writes the new one, in two operations, and two threads could lose an update as in the example [threads-07.cs];
  • line 24: each thread places its report in the queue;
  • lines 35–37: the main thread empties the queue. [TryDequeue] returns [false] when the queue is empty. Concurrent collections only offer “Try…” methods that combine the check and the operation: a check for [Count > 0] followed by a removal would not be safe, since another thread could empty the queue in between;
  • line 40: the dictionary is traversed in key order; each key/value pair is split into two variables;
  • line 46: the [GetOrAdd] method returns the value associated with the key, after adding the key with the provided value if it did not exist.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-18.cs
le thread T0 a terminé ses 100 000 tirages
le thread T2 a terminé ses 100 000 tirages
le thread T1 a terminé ses 100 000 tirages
le thread T3 a terminé ses 100 000 tirages
chiffre 0 : 40 168 tirages
chiffre 1 : 39 980 tirages
chiffre 2 : 39 982 tirages
chiffre 3 : 39 856 tirages
chiffre 4 : 40 170 tirages
chiffre 5 : 40 271 tirages
chiffre 6 : 40 081 tirages
chiffre 7 : 39 704 tirages
chiffre 8 : 39 722 tirages
chiffre 9 : 40 066 tirages
total : 400 000 tirages (attendu : 400 000)
GetOrAdd(10, 0) = 0, nombre de clés : 11

The total number of runs is correct: no updates were lost. The reports appear in the order in which the threads completed their work.

docs.title: 8.7.2. Producers and Consumers: BlockingCollection
docs.text:
The reader-writer problem is a variant of the classic producer-consumer problem: threads produce data that other threads consume. The [BlockingCollection<T>] class solves it without any explicit synchronization tools:

  • [Add(élément)] adds an element. If the collection has a limited capacity and is full, the producer is blocked until a spot becomes available;
  • [CompleteAdding()] signals that no more elements will be added;
  • [GetConsumingEnumerable()] returns an enumeration that removes elements one by one. If the collection is empty, the consumer is blocked until an element arrives; the enumeration ends when the collection is empty and [CompleteAdding] has been called.

The program [threads-19.cs] is as follows:

// producers/consumers with BlockingCollection<T>

using System.Collections.Concurrent;

//: a queue of at most 3 elements
using var file = new BlockingCollection<int>(boundedCapacity: 3);

// the producer adds 8 numbers and then signals that they are done
var producteur = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (int i = 1; i <= 8; i++)
    {
         // blocks if the queue is full
        file.Add(i);
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff} : P a déposé {i} (éléments en attente : {file.Count})");
        Thread.Sleep(100);
    }
     // no more elements will be added
    file.CompleteAdding();
    Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff} : P a terminé");
});

// two consumers take numbers as long as there are any left
var consommateurs = new Thread[2];
for (int i = 0; i < consommateurs.Length; i++)
{
    consommateurs[i] = new Thread(() =>
    {
        string nom = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
         // The enumeration waits for elements and stops when the queue is empty and finished
        foreach (int nombre in file.GetConsumingEnumerable())
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff} : {nom} a pris {nombre}");
             // processing the number
            Thread.Sleep(600);
        }
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff} : {nom} a terminé");
    })
    { Name = $"C{i + 1}" };
}

// launch and wait for all threads
producteur.Start();
foreach (Thread consommateur in consommateurs)
{
    consommateur.Start();
}
producteur.Join();
foreach (Thread consommateur in consommateurs)
{
    consommateur.Join();
}

Comments:

  • line 6: a queue (the default underlying collection is a [ConcurrentQueue<int>]) containing at most 3 elements. The parameter is passed by name, which makes the call more readable;
  • Lines 9–20: The producer deposits the numbers 1 through 8, one every tenth of a second, then signals that it is finished;
  • lines 24–37: two consumers retrieve the numbers and spend 0.6 seconds processing each one. They consume the numbers more slowly than the producer generates them;
  • line 31: the blocking enumeration. Each number is retrieved by only one of the two consumers.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-19.cs
11:37:27.216 : C2 a pris 1
11:37:27.213 : P a déposé 1 (éléments en attente : 0)
11:37:27.366 : P a déposé 2 (éléments en attente : 1)
11:37:27.366 : C1 a pris 2
11:37:27.466 : P a déposé 3 (éléments en attente : 1)
11:37:27.566 : P a déposé 4 (éléments en attente : 2)
11:37:27.666 : P a déposé 5 (éléments en attente : 3)
11:37:27.866 : C2 a pris 3
11:37:27.866 : P a déposé 6 (éléments en attente : 3)
11:37:27.966 : C1 a pris 4
11:37:27.966 : P a déposé 7 (éléments en attente : 3)
11:37:28.466 : C2 a pris 5
11:37:28.466 : P a déposé 8 (éléments en attente : 3)
11:37:28.566 : C1 a pris 6
11:37:28.567 : P a terminé
11:37:29.066 : C2 a pris 7
11:37:29.167 : C1 a pris 8
11:37:29.667 : C2 a terminé
11:37:29.767 : C1 a terminé

We see the producer quickly enqueue the first numbers, then—as soon as the queue contains 3 elements—only enqueue a number when a consumer dequeues one: it is blocked by [Add] when the queue is full. The consumers share the numbers and stop when the queue is empty and the process is complete. Note that the consumer C2 displayed the retrieval of the number 1 before the producer displayed its insertion: the insertion did indeed occur earlier, but the producer was interrupted between [Add] and its display.

The class [Channel<T>] in the namespace [System.Threading.Channels] provides the same service for asynchronous programming: a consumer waiting for an element does not block any threads. We’ll cover this in the next chapter.

docs.title: 8.8. The thread pool
docs.text:
Until now, to manage threads, we have created them using [new Thread(...)] and then executed them using [Start()]. Creating a thread is a relatively costly operation: in particular, the system must allocate a stack for it, and each thread occupies memory as long as it exists. We’ll see in the chapter on databases that connection pools exist: open connections are kept in reserve and lent to threads that request them, since opening a connection is costly. A similar system exists for threads: the thread pool (ThreadPool) of .NET.

  • As long as the number of threads in the pool is below a minimum threshold, the pool immediately creates a new thread for each task that cannot find a free thread. By default, this minimum is the number of processors; it can be read using [ThreadPool.GetMinThreads(out min1, out min2)] and changed using [ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(min1, min2)]. The pool manages two types of threads: work threads (min1), which execute the jobs assigned to them, and asynchronous I/O threads (min2);
  • if this number is insufficient, the pool creates additional threads incrementally, up to a maximum that can be read using [ThreadPool.GetMaxThreads(out max1, out max2)] and changed using [ThreadPool.SetMaxThreads(max1, max2)]. When the maximum is reached, the jobs assigned to the pool are queued until a thread becomes available;
  • A thread that has completed a task is not destroyed: it is returned to the pool and used for the next task.

The thread pool offers two advantages: it saves time spent creating threads (a few threads can handle hundreds of requests), and by limiting the number of threads, it prevents the application from becoming overwhelmed by too many requests.

To assign a task to the pool, use the [ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(WaitCallback callback, object? etat)] method, where [WaitCallback] is a delegate of signature [void M(object? etat)]. The task will be executed by a thread in the pool, with the parameter [etat]. The program [threads-20.cs] is as follows:

// the thread pool

// the main thread
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";

// minimum number of threads in the pool
ThreadPool.GetMinThreads(out int min1, out int min2);
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre minimum de threads de travail dans le pool : {min1}");
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre minimum de threads d'E/S asynchrones dans le pool : {min2}");
ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(3, min2);
ThreadPool.GetMinThreads(out min1, out _);
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre minimum de threads de travail après changement : {min1}");
// Maximum number of threads in the pool
ThreadPool.GetMaxThreads(out int max1, out int max2);
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre maximum de threads de travail dans le pool : {max1}");
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre maximum de threads d'E/S asynchrones dans le pool : {max2}");
bool ok = ThreadPool.SetMaxThreads(5, max2);
ThreadPool.GetMaxThreads(out max1, out _);
Console.WriteLine($"Nombre maximum de threads de travail après changement : {max1} (SetMaxThreads a rendu {ok})");

// 7 jobs are assigned to the pool; the counter ensures they are completed
using var travauxRestants = new CountdownEvent(7);
for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++)
{
    var data = new Donnees { Numero = i, Debut = DateTime.Now, Duree = 3 };
    ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(Dormir, data);
}
Console.WriteLine($"À {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.ff}, le thread Main a confié les 7 travaux au pool et attend leur fin");
// waiting for the 7 jobs to finish
travauxRestants.Wait();
Console.WriteLine($"À {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.ff}, fin du thread Main");

// the job executed by a thread in the pool
void Dormir(object? infos)
{
    if (infos is not Donnees data)
    {
        return;
    }
     // pool status
    ThreadPool.GetAvailableThreads(out int disponibles, out _);
    Console.WriteLine($"À {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.ff}, le travail n° {data.Numero} commence dans le thread {Thread.CurrentThread.ManagedThreadId} pour {data.Duree} s (threads de travail disponibles : {disponibles})");
     // Suspended for Duration seconds
    Thread.Sleep(data.Duree * 1000);
    DateTime fin = DateTime.Now;
    Console.WriteLine($"À {fin:HH:mm:ss.ff}, le travail n° {data.Numero} se termine : programmé pour {data.Duree} s, il a duré {(fin - data.Debut).TotalSeconds:F2} s depuis sa demande");
     // one less job
    travauxRestants.Signal();
}

// Information passed to each job
class Donnees
{
    public int Numero { get; init; }
    public DateTime Debut { get; init; }
    public int Duree { get; init; }
}

Comments:

  • lines 7–12: We read and display the current minimum number of both types of threads in the pool, then set the minimum number of worker threads to 3. The parameter [out _] is an “ignored parameter”: we are not interested in the returned value;
  • lines 14–19: We do the same to set the maximum number of worker threads to 5. [SetMaxThreads] returns [false] if the requested value is rejected, for example, if it is less than the number of processors;
  • line 22: A [CountdownEvent] object acts as a countdown timer: each call to its [Signal] method decrements it, and its [Wait] method blocks the calling thread until it reaches 0. Here, it allows the main thread to wait for the 7 jobs to finish: you cannot call [Join] on a thread from the pool, since you do not own it. The 2008 course asked the user to call [Entrée] once the jobs were completed;
  • lines 23–26: We assign 7 tasks, each lasting 3 seconds, to the pool, even though the pool will never have more than 5 worker threads. Each task receives a [Donnees] object;
  • line 30: the main thread waits for the 7 jobs to finish;
  • lines 34–48: the task executed by a thread in the pool. This is a non-static local function because it uses the local variable [travauxRestants];
  • line 41: the number of worker threads still available (the maximum minus the number of busy threads);
  • line 48: the counter is decremented at the end of each job.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-20.cs
Nombre minimum de threads de travail dans le pool : 2
Nombre minimum de threads d'E/S asynchrones dans le pool : 1
Nombre minimum de threads de travail après changement : 3
Nombre maximum de threads de travail dans le pool : 32767
Nombre maximum de threads d'E/S asynchrones dans le pool : 1000
Nombre maximum de threads de travail après changement : 5 (SetMaxThreads a rendu True)
À 11:37:31.85, le thread Main a confié les 7 travaux au pool et attend leur fin
À 11:37:31.85, le travail n° 1 commence dans le thread 6 pour 3 s (threads de travail disponibles : 2)
À 11:37:31.85, le travail n° 0 commence dans le thread 4 pour 3 s (threads de travail disponibles : 2)
À 11:37:31.85, le travail n° 2 commence dans le thread 7 pour 3 s (threads de travail disponibles : 2)
À 11:37:32.85, le travail n° 3 commence dans le thread 8 pour 3 s (threads de travail disponibles : 1)
À 11:37:33.85, le travail n° 4 commence dans le thread 9 pour 3 s (threads de travail disponibles : 0)
À 11:37:34.85, le travail n° 0 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,04 s depuis sa demande
À 11:37:34.85, le travail n° 1 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,00 s depuis sa demande
À 11:37:34.85, le travail n° 2 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 3,00 s depuis sa demande
À 11:37:34.85, le travail n° 5 commence dans le thread 7 pour 3 s (threads de travail disponibles : 0)
À 11:37:34.85, le travail n° 6 commence dans le thread 4 pour 3 s (threads de travail disponibles : 0)
À 11:37:35.85, le travail n° 3 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 4,00 s depuis sa demande
À 11:37:36.85, le travail n° 4 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 5,00 s depuis sa demande
À 11:37:37.85, le travail n° 6 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 6,00 s depuis sa demande
À 11:37:37.85, le travail n° 5 se termine : programmé pour 3 s, il a duré 6,00 s depuis sa demande
À 11:37:37.85, fin du thread Main
  • On this dual-processor machine, the pool initially had a minimum of 2 worker threads and a maximum of 32,767;
  • jobs 0, 1, and 2 started immediately: the pool has a minimum of 3 threads;
  • jobs 3 and 4 started with delays of one and two seconds, respectively: there were no free threads left, and the pool—once it exceeds its minimum—creates new threads only gradually as long as jobs are waiting. The maximum of 5 threads is then reached: no threads remain available;
  • Jobs 5 and 6 had to wait for a thread to become available after jobs 0, 1, and 2 finished. We can see that they reused threads 7 and 4, which had executed the first jobs;
  • In total, jobs 5 and 6 took 6 seconds from the time they were requested: 3 seconds of waiting and 3 seconds of execution.

It is rarely necessary to change the pool limits: its default values are suitable for most applications. In fact, [QueueUserWorkItem] is rarely used directly: we work through tasks, which are described below.

docs.title: 8.9.1. Task.Run
docs.text:
Since .NET 4, the [System.Threading.Tasks.Task] class represents a job (a task) that runs asynchronously. [Task.Run(action)] assigns a job to the thread pool, just like [QueueUserWorkItem], but returns a [Task] object that allows you to track this job: check if it’s finished, wait for it, retrieve its result, or the exception it threw. A task that returns a result of type T is of type [Task<T>]. The program [threads-21.cs] is as follows:

// Task.Run: Assign a job to the thread pool and retrieve its result

Console.WriteLine($"Thread principal : id {Thread.CurrentThread.ManagedThreadId}, thread du pool : {Thread.CurrentThread.IsThreadPoolThread}");

// three tasks, each returning an int result
var taches = new Task<int>[3];
for (int i = 0; i < taches.Length; i++)
{
    int numero = i;
    taches[i] = Task.Run(() =>
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff} : la tâche {numero} s'exécute dans le thread {Thread.CurrentThread.ManagedThreadId} (thread du pool : {Thread.CurrentThread.IsThreadPoolThread})");
         // task
        Thread.Sleep(500 * (numero + 1));
         // the task’s result
        return numero * 10;
    });
}
// waiting for the three tasks to complete (blocking)
Task.WaitAll(taches);
// the results
for (int i = 0; i < taches.Length; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"tâche {i} : état {taches[i].Status}, résultat {taches[i].Result}");
}

// a task that throws an exception
Task tacheEnErreur = Task.Run(Echouer);
try
{
     // the task's exception is rethrown by Wait, wrapped in a AggregateException
    tacheEnErreur.Wait();
}
catch (AggregateException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} contenant {e.InnerException?.GetType().Name} : {e.InnerException?.Message}");
}
Console.WriteLine($"tâche en erreur : état {tacheEnErreur.Status}");

// the work of the task that failed
static void Echouer() => throw new InvalidOperationException("test....");

Comments:

  • Lines 10–16: Each task executes a lambda that displays the thread executing it, sleeps for 0.5, 1, or 1.5 seconds, and then returns a result of type [int]. [Task.Run] therefore returns a [Task<int>];
  • line 20: the main thread waits for the three tasks to finish. This is a blocking wait, like [Join];
  • line 24: the property [Status] indicates the task’s status; [RanToCompletion] means it completed normally;
  • line 24: the property [Result] is the result of the task. If the task had not completed, reading [Result] would block the thread until it finished;
  • line 28: a task that executes the [Echouer] method, which throws an exception;
  • line 32: the exception thrown in the task is not lost: it is stored in the object [Task], then rethrown in the thread waiting for the task. [Wait] wraps it in a [AggregateException] exception (a task can group several of these together), whose [InnerException] property is the original exception;
  • line 41: the method that throws the exception. We could have passed the lambda [() => throw new InvalidOperationException(...)] directly to [Task.Run].

Results:

> dotnet run threads-21.cs
Thread principal : id 1, thread du pool : False
11:37:39.970 : la tâche 0 s'exécute dans le thread 4 (thread du pool : True)
11:37:39.969 : la tâche 1 s'exécute dans le thread 6 (thread du pool : True)
11:37:40.516 : la tâche 2 s'exécute dans le thread 4 (thread du pool : True)
tâche 0 : état RanToCompletion, résultat 0
tâche 1 : état RanToCompletion, résultat 10
tâche 2 : état RanToCompletion, résultat 20
AggregateException contenant InvalidOperationException : test....
tâche en erreur : état Faulted
  • The tasks run in threads from the pool (line 3);
  • Task 2 did not start until Task 0 had finished, in the thread that Task 0 had freed up: the pool had only 2 threads (the default minimum on this machine) and did not create a third one in time;
  • the results are retrieved after the tasks have finished;
  • the exception from the task that failed was caught by the main thread, and the task’s status is [Faulted].

This example also replaces the one for the [BackgroundWorker] class from the 2008 course, which demonstrated how to run a job in the background, retrieve its result or exception, and cancel it. [BackgroundWorker] was designed for Windows Forms graphical user interfaces; it has now been replaced by tasks, with cancellation handled by [CancellationToken] and progress tracking by the [IProgress<T>] interface, which are presented in the following chapter along with [async] / [await], which allow you to wait for a task without blocking a thread.

docs.title: 8.9.2. Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach
docs.text:
The [System.Threading.Tasks.Parallel] class (.NET 4) automatically distributes the iterations of a loop among multiple threads in the pool:

  • [Parallel.For(début, fin, i => ...)] executes the loop body for i ranging from [début] to [fin] - 1;
  • [Parallel.ForEach(collection, élément => ...)] executes the loop body for each element in the collection;
  • a parameter [ParallelOptions] allows you to limit the number of iterations executed simultaneously (property [MaxDegreeOfParallelism]);
  • both methods do not yield control until all iterations are complete. The thread that calls them participates in the work itself.

These loops are only suitable if the iterations are independent: their order of execution is undefined, and if they update shared data, that data must be protected. The program [threads-22.cs] is as follows:

// the parallel library: Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach

using System.Collections.Concurrent;
using System.Diagnostics;

// 1 - Count the prime numbers less than N
const int N = 5_000_000;
// sequential version
var chrono = Stopwatch.StartNew();
int nbSequentiel = 0;
for (int i = 2; i < N; i++)
{
    if (EstPremier(i))
    {
        nbSequentiel++;
    }
}
Console.WriteLine($"for séquentiel    : {nbSequentiel:N0} nombres premiers en {chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");

// parallel version #1: iterations are distributed across multiple threads
chrono.Restart();
int nbParallele1 = 0;
Parallel.For(2, N, i =>
{
    if (EstPremier(i))
    {
         // the counter is shared: atomic increment
        Interlocked.Increment(ref nbParallele1);
    }
});
Console.WriteLine($"Parallel.For n° 1 : {nbParallele1:N0} nombres premiers en {chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");

// parallel version #2: each thread counts in a local variable,
//, which is added to the shared total only once, at the end
chrono.Restart();
int nbParallele2 = 0;
// the threads that ran and the number of prime numbers found by each
var threads = new ConcurrentDictionary<int, int>();
Parallel.For(2, N,
     // initialization of the local counter
    () => 0,
     // the body of the loop sets the new value of the local counter
    (i, etat, local) => EstPremier(i) ? local + 1 : local,
     // End of a thread’s work: add its local counter to the total
    local =>
    {
        Interlocked.Add(ref nbParallele2, local);
        threads.AddOrUpdate(Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId, local, (_, n) => n + local);
    });
Console.WriteLine($"Parallel.For n° 2 : {nbParallele2:N0} nombres premiers en {chrono.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");
foreach (var (id, nb) in threads.OrderBy(paire => paire.Key))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  thread {id} : {nb:N0} nombres premiers trouvés");
}

// 2 - Process a collection with at most 2 concurrent processes
string[] fichiers = ["a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt", "d.txt", "e.txt"];
var options = new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 2 };
Parallel.ForEach(fichiers, options, fichier =>
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff} : traitement de {fichier} dans le thread {Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId}");
     // Simulated processing
    Thread.Sleep(500);
});
Console.WriteLine("Parallel.ForEach terminé");

// prime number test (intentionally simple)
static bool EstPremier(int n)
{
    if (n < 2)
    {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++)
    {
        if (n % d == 0)
        {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Comments:

  • lines 7–18: We count the prime numbers less than 5,000,000 using a standard [for] loop. The function [EstPremier] (lines 68–81) tests divisors up to the square root of the number: this is a time-consuming process, and the iterations are independent;
  • lines 22–31: the same loop using [Parallel.For]. The counter [nbParallele1] is shared by all threads: it is incremented by [Interlocked.Increment] (a local variable captured by a lambda can be passed by reference);
  • Lines 36–50: An overloaded version of [Parallel.For] allows you to work with a local variable: [Parallel.For] breaks the loop down into tasks, each executed by a single thread, and each task has its own counter. The first lambda (41) initializes a task’s counter; the second (43) is the body of the loop, which takes the counter and returns its new value; the third (45) is executed once per task, at the end of its work: it adds the task’s counter to the shared total. This significantly reduces the number of atomic operations;
  • line 48: for each thread that participated, we record the number of prime numbers it found;
  • lines 57–65: [Parallel.ForEach] processes a collection of filenames (the processing is simulated by a half-second pause), with at most 2 simultaneous processes.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-22.cs
for séquentiel    : 348 513 nombres premiers en 2061 ms
Parallel.For n° 1 : 348 513 nombres premiers en 2161 ms
Parallel.For n° 2 : 348 513 nombres premiers en 1928 ms
  thread 1 : 112 640 nombres premiers trouvés
  thread 4 : 118 169 nombres premiers trouvés
  thread 5 : 36 754 nombres premiers trouvés
  thread 7 : 80 950 nombres premiers trouvés
11:37:50.239 : traitement de c.txt dans le thread 7
11:37:50.239 : traitement de a.txt dans le thread 1
11:37:50.776 : traitement de d.txt dans le thread 7
11:37:50.776 : traitement de b.txt dans le thread 1
11:37:51.277 : traitement de e.txt dans le thread 7
Parallel.ForEach terminé
  • All three loops find the same number of prime numbers;
  • several threads participated in the parallel loop, including the main thread (ID 1);
  • the processing of [Parallel.ForEach] occurs in pairs, half a second apart, and in an order that does not match that of the list;
  • The time savings in this run are disappointing: there are only 2 processors, which our program’s threads were sharing with other very active programs at the time of the capture. On a lightly loaded machine with n processors, a parallel loop like this one can be nearly n times faster than the sequential loop. You should always measure before drawing conclusions: parallelization comes at a cost (work distribution, synchronization) that is only worthwhile if each iteration involves enough computation.

docs.title: 8.10.1. The Principle
docs.text:
Consider a three-layer application:

Suppose the application is multi-user, such as a web application. Each user request is handled by a thread. The thread’s lifecycle is as follows:

  • the thread is created or retrieved from the thread pool to fulfill a user’s request;
  • if this request requires data, the thread executes a method in the [ui] layer, which calls a method in the [metier] layer, which in turn calls a method in the [dao] layer;
  • the thread returns the response to the user. It then either terminates or is returned to the thread pool.

During the second step, it may be useful for the thread to have its own data—that is, data not shared with other threads. This data could, for example, belong to the specific user the thread is serving and be used in the various [ui, metier, dao] layers without being passed as a parameter to each method.

The 2008 course used the methods [Thread.SetData] and [Thread.GetData] for this purpose, which manage a sort of private dictionary for the thread. They still exist but are rarely used; two simpler and more efficient tools are preferred:

  • the [[ThreadStatic]] attribute applied to a static field: each thread has its own instance of the field;
  • the [ThreadLocal<T>] class: an object whose [Value] property has a different value for each thread. A function passed to the constructor provides the initial value for each thread.

The program [threads-23.cs] compares a regular static field with these two tools:

// Thread-specific local data: [ThreadStatic] and ThreadLocal<T>

Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";
// The main thread writes its own values
Contexte.Partage = 100;
Contexte.ParThread = 100;
Contexte.Utilisateur.Value = "admin";

// Three threads write and then read the three data items
var threads = new Thread[3];
for (int i = 0; i < threads.Length; i++)
{
    int numero = i;
    threads[i] = new Thread(() =>
    {
         // write
        Contexte.Partage = numero;
        Contexte.ParThread = numero;
         // The T2 thread does not specify a user: it will use the default value
        if (numero != 2)
        {
            Contexte.Utilisateur.Value = $"utilisateur{numero}";
        }
         // We let the other threads write in turn
        Thread.Sleep(200);
         // read
        Afficher();
    })
    { Name = $"T{i}" };
    threads[i].Start();
}
foreach (Thread thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}
// re-read by the main thread
Afficher();

// displays the data as seen by the current thread
static void Afficher()
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{Thread.CurrentThread.Name,-4} : Partage={Contexte.Partage,-3} ParThread={Contexte.ParThread,-3} AvecInitialiseur={Contexte.AvecInitialiseur,-2} Utilisateur={Contexte.Utilisateur.Value}");
}

// the program's data
static class Contexte
{
     // a regular static field: a single instance, shared by all threads
    public static int Partage;
     // one instance per thread
    [ThreadStatic]
    public static int ParThread;
     // Caution: the initializer is executed only for the first thread that uses the class
    [ThreadStatic]
    public static int AvecInitialiseur = 5;
     // one instance per thread, initialized for each thread by the factory passed to the constructor
    public static readonly ThreadLocal<string> Utilisateur = new(() => $"anonyme (thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name})");
}

Comments:

  • line 49: a regular static field. There is only one instance of it, shared by all threads;
  • lines 51–52: the attribute *[[ThreadStatic]]* gives each thread an instance of the field;
  • lines 54–55: a classic pitfall. The initializer [= 5] is executed by the class’s static constructor, just once, in the thread that uses the class first. For the other threads, the field has the default value of its type, which is 0 in this case;
  • line 57: a [ThreadLocal<string>] object. The lambda passed to the constructor is executed the first time a thread reads [Value] without having written to it; it provides the initial value for that thread;
  • Lines 5–7: The main thread writes its own values;
  • lines 17–22: Each thread writes its own values, except for the thread T2, which does not set a user;
  • line 25: each thread waits for the others to write before reading the values again.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-23.cs
T0   : Partage=2   ParThread=0   AvecInitialiseur=0  Utilisateur=utilisateur0
T2   : Partage=2   ParThread=2   AvecInitialiseur=0  Utilisateur=anonyme (thread T2)
T1   : Partage=2   ParThread=1   AvecInitialiseur=0  Utilisateur=utilisateur1
Main : Partage=2   ParThread=100 AvecInitialiseur=5  Utilisateur=admin
  • the ordinary field [Partage] has the same value for all threads: the last value written (in this execution, that of thread T2);
  • the field [ParThread] retained, in each thread, the value that thread had written to it;
  • the field [AvecInitialiseur] is 5 for the main thread and 0 for the others;
  • the property [Utilisateur.Value] has the value written by each thread; the thread T2, which had not written to it, received the initial value provided by the constructor’s lambda.

Thread-local data has a limitation: it is scoped to the thread, not the process. With asynchronous programming, as discussed in the next chapter, a single process can start in one thread and continue in another after a wait. In this case, we use the [AsyncLocal<T>] class, whose value persists across threads.

docs.title: 8.10.2. Application: A Transaction Shared Across Layers
docs.text:
Consider the following three-tier application, in which the [dao] layer manages a table of items:

Suppose that the interface of the [dao] layer is initially as follows:

interface IDao
{
    int InsertArticle(Article article);
    List<Article> GetAllArticles();
    void DeleteAllArticles();
}

Later, the need arises to insert a table of items within a transaction, because the system must operate on an all-or-nothing basis: either all items are inserted, or none are. A method named [InsertArticles(Article[] articles)] can be added to the interface. Then, for another application, the need arises to delete a list of items, again within a transaction… To meet different business requirements, the [dao] layer will grow. We can take a different approach:

  • include only the basic operations (insert, update, delete, read an item) in the [dao] layer;
  • move operations that simultaneously update multiple items to the [metier] layer. These operations use the basic operations from the [dao] layer.

The advantage of this solution is that the same [dao] layer can be used without modification with different [metier] layers. It introduces a challenge in managing the transaction that groups the updates to be performed atomically:

  • the transaction must be started by the [metier] layer before it calls the methods of the [dao] layer;
  • the methods in the [dao] layer must be aware of the transaction’s existence in order to participate in it;
  • the transaction must be completed (committed or rolled back) by the [metier] layer.

To ensure that the methods of the [dao] layer are aware of any ongoing transaction, the transaction could be added as a parameter to each method of the [dao] layer. This parameter would then appear in the signature of the interface’s methods, which would bind the interface to a specific data source. Thread-local data provides a more elegant solution: the [metier] layer places the transaction in the thread-local data, and that is where the [dao] layer retrieves it. The method signatures of the [dao] layer do not need to be changed. Multiple threads (multiple users) can work simultaneously: each has its own transaction.

The 2008 course used a SQL Server Compact database, a product that has since been discontinued. Databases will be covered in the chapters on ADO.NET and Entity Framework Core. To keep the focus on threads, we’ll use an in-memory table and a simulated transaction here. The [threads-24.cs] program combines all the layers into a single file. The entities are as follows:

// an item
record Article(int Id, string Nom, decimal Prix, int StockActuel, int StockMinimum);

// A simulated transaction: it records how to roll back each update
class Transaction
{
    private static int compteur;
    private readonly Stack<Action> annulations = new();
    public int Numero { get; } = Interlocked.Increment(ref compteur);

     // records the operation that rolls back an update
    public void Journaliser(Action annulation) => annulations.Push(annulation);
     // commits the transaction: the updates are retained
    public void Commit() => annulations.Clear();
     // rolls back the transaction: updates are rolled back, from the last to the first
    public void Rollback()
    {
        while (annulations.TryPop(out Action? annulation))
        {
            annulation();
        }
    }
}

// thread-local data shared by the layers
static class ContexteThread
{
     // the thread’s current transaction (null if there is none)
    public static readonly ThreadLocal<Transaction?> Transaction = new();
}
  • line 60: an article is a [record] whose identifier [Id] is set by the [dao] layer;
  • lines 63–78: a simulated transaction. Each update made within the transaction records the operation needed to undo it (method [Journaliser]); [Commit] commits the transaction while ignoring these operations; [Rollback] rolls it back by executing the rollback operations, from the last to the first (hence the stack [Stack<Action>]). A real database operates in a similar manner, using a transaction log;
  • line 67: Each transaction is assigned a unique number. Since transactions can be created by multiple threads simultaneously, the counter is incremented atomically;
  • lines 84–87: the thread-local data shared by the layers: the thread’s current transaction, or [null] if there is none.

The [dao] layer is as follows:

// the [dao] layer: an in-memory item table with a uniqueness constraint on the name
interface IDao
{
    int InsertArticle(Article article);
    List<Article> GetAllArticles();
    void DeleteAllArticles();
}

class Dao : IDao
{
     // the table, shared by all threads, and its lock
    private readonly List<Article> table = [];
    private readonly Lock verrou = new();
    private int prochainId = 1;

    public int InsertArticle(Article article)
    {
         // Is there a transaction in progress in the current thread?
        Transaction? transaction = ContexteThread.Transaction.Value;
        lock (verrou)
        {
            if (table.Any(a => a.Nom == article.Nom))
            {
                throw new InvalidOperationException($"un article nommé [{article.Nom}] existe déjà");
            }
            Article insere = article with { Id = prochainId++ };
            table.Add(insere);
             // Within a transaction, we note how to roll back the insertion
            transaction?.Journaliser(() =>
            {
                lock (verrou)
                {
                    table.Remove(insere);
                }
            });
            string mode = transaction is null ? "hors transaction" : $"dans la transaction {transaction.Numero}";
            Console.WriteLine($"[{Thread.CurrentThread.Name}] [dao] insertion de {insere.Nom} (id {insere.Id}) {mode}");
            return 1;
        }
    }

    public List<Article> GetAllArticles()
    {
        lock (verrou)
        {
            return [.. table];
        }
    }

    public void DeleteAllArticles()
    {
        lock (verrou)
        {
            table.Clear();
        }
    }
}
  • line 101: the item table, shared by all threads. Access to it is protected by the lock on line 102;
  • line 108: the method [InsertArticle] retrieves any transaction that the [metier] layer has placed in the current thread’s local data;
  • Lines 111–113: The table has a unique constraint on item names: inserting an item with a name that already exists throws an exception;
  • Line 115: The inserted item is a copy of the received item, with an identifier assigned by the [dao] layer. The expression [with] creates a copy of a [record] by modifying certain properties;
  • Lines 118–122: If a transaction occurs, the [dao] layer participates by recording how to undo the insertion. The operator [?.] calls [Journaliser] only if [transaction] is not [null];
  • line 125: a trace message displays the thread, the inserted item, and the transaction, if any;
  • lines 131–135: The list of items returned is a copy of the table (collection expression [.. table]), so that the caller does not iterate over it while another thread is modifying it.

The [metier] layer is as follows:

// the [metier] layer
interface IMetier
{
    void InsertArticlesInTransaction(Article[] articles);
    void InsertArticlesOutOfTransaction(Article[] articles);
    List<Article> GetAllArticles();
    void DeleteAllArticles();
}

class Metier(IDao dao) : IMetier
{
     // Inserting an array of items: all or nothing
    public void InsertArticlesInTransaction(Article[] articles)
    {
         // Start of the transaction, recorded in the thread’s local data
        var transaction = new Transaction();
        ContexteThread.Transaction.Value = transaction;
        try
        {
            foreach (Article article in articles)
            {
                 // The [dao] layer will retrieve the transaction from the thread
                dao.InsertArticle(article);
                 // Simulated processing, allowing other threads time to intervene
                Thread.Sleep(200);
            }
            transaction.Commit();
            Console.WriteLine($"[{Thread.CurrentThread.Name}] [metier] transaction {transaction.Numero} validée");
        }
        catch
        {
            transaction.Rollback();
            Console.WriteLine($"[{Thread.CurrentThread.Name}] [metier] transaction {transaction.Numero} annulée");
            throw;
        }
        finally
        {
             // the thread no longer has any active transactions
            ContexteThread.Transaction.Value = null;
        }
    }

     // insertion of an item table without a transaction
    public void InsertArticlesOutOfTransaction(Article[] articles)
    {
        foreach (Article article in articles)
        {
            dao.InsertArticle(article);
        }
    }

    public List<Article> GetAllArticles() => dao.GetAllArticles();
    public void DeleteAllArticles() => dao.DeleteAllArticles();
}
  • line 157: the [dao] layer is injected by the main constructor;
  • lines 163–164: the [InsertArticlesInTransaction] method starts a transaction and saves it to the thread’s local data;
  • line 170: the insertion method of the [dao] layer is called for each item, without passing the transaction to it;
  • line 172: a pause simulates processing, in order to give another thread time to intervene during the transaction (third part of the test program);
  • line 174: if the program reaches this point, no exception has occurred: the transaction is committed;
  • lines 177–181: if an exception occurs, the transaction is rolled back and the exception is rethrown to the caller;
  • line 186: In any case, the thread no longer has an active transaction. This is important if the thread is reused (pooled thread);
  • line 191: the same insertion, without a transaction.

The test program is as follows:

// data local to a thread: the [metier] layer places the transaction there; the [dao] layer retrieves it from there

// The application layers
IDao dao = new Dao();
IMetier metier = new Metier(dao);
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";

// Two items with the same name: the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the name
Article[] articles = [new(0, "article", 100, 10, 1), new(0, "article", 100, 10, 1)];

// 1 - insertion outside a transaction
Console.WriteLine("Insertion des articles hors transaction...");
Executer(() => metier.InsertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles));
AfficherArticles(metier);

// 2 - insertion within a transaction
metier.DeleteAllArticles();
Console.WriteLine("Insertion des articles dans une transaction...");
Executer(() => metier.InsertArticlesInTransaction(articles));
AfficherArticles(metier);

// 3 - two concurrent threads: Thread A’s transaction is not visible to Thread B
metier.DeleteAllArticles();
Console.WriteLine("Deux threads simultanés...");
Article[] articlesA = [new(0, "clavier", 20, 5, 1), new(0, "souris", 10, 5, 1), new(0, "clavier", 20, 5, 1)];
Article[] articlesB = [new(0, "écran", 150, 2, 1)];
var threadA = new Thread(() => Executer(() => metier.InsertArticlesInTransaction(articlesA))) { Name = "A" };
var threadB = new Thread(() => Executer(() => metier.InsertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articlesB))) { Name = "B" };
threadA.Start();
Thread.Sleep(100);
threadB.Start();
threadA.Join();
threadB.Join();
AfficherArticles(metier);

// performs an action while displaying any exceptions
static void Executer(Action action)
{
    try
    {
        action();
    }
    catch (Exception e)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{Thread.CurrentThread.Name}] {e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
    }
}

// displays the list of items
static void AfficherArticles(IMetier metier)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Liste des articles :");
    foreach (Article article in metier.GetAllArticles())
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"  {article}");
    }
}
  • Line 9: We create an array of two items with the same name. The insertion of the second item will be rejected. If the insertion is performed outside a transaction, the first item is inserted and remains in the array. If it is performed within a transaction, the first item is inserted and then removed when the transaction is rolled back;
  • Lines 11–14: Insert the table outside a transaction, then display the table;
  • Lines 16–20: Same process within a transaction;
  • lines 22–34: Two threads are working simultaneously. Thread A inserts three items within a transaction (the third violates the uniqueness constraint); meanwhile, Thread B inserts an item outside a transaction;
  • lines 37–45: The function [Executer] performs an action and displays any exception, preceded by the thread name.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-24.cs
Insertion des articles hors transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion de article (id 1) hors transaction
[Main] InvalidOperationException : un article nommé [article] existe déjà
Liste des articles :
  Article { Id = 1, Nom = article, Prix = 100, StockActuel = 10, StockMinimum = 1 }
Insertion des articles dans une transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion de article (id 2) dans la transaction 1
[Main] [metier] transaction 1 annulée
[Main] InvalidOperationException : un article nommé [article] existe déjà
Liste des articles :
Deux threads simultanés...
[A] [dao] insertion de clavier (id 3) dans la transaction 2
[B] [dao] insertion de écran (id 4) hors transaction
[A] [dao] insertion de souris (id 5) dans la transaction 2
[A] [metier] transaction 2 annulée
[A] InvalidOperationException : un article nommé [clavier] existe déjà
Liste des articles :
  Article { Id = 4, Nom = écran, Prix = 150, StockActuel = 2, StockMinimum = 1 }
  • The insertion outside the transaction left the first record in the table (line 6);
  • the insertion made within a transaction left no records in the table: the record with ID 2 was removed by the rollback;
  • In the third part, thread B inserted the monitor while thread A’s transaction 2 was in progress: it did so outside the transaction, since the transaction is a local variable of thread A. The rollback of transaction 2 removed the keyboard and mouse inserted by A, but not the monitor inserted by B.

docs.title: 8.10.3. Conclusion
docs.text: The previous example demonstrated the value of thread-local data for transaction management. It should not be replicated as-is. .NET provides this mechanism out of the box with the [System.Transactions.TransactionScope] class: an “ambient” transaction, accessible via [Transaction.Current], in which database connections automatically participate. Frameworks such as Entity Framework Core also manage transactions without the [dao] layer code having to handle them. And in today’s web applications, which are asynchronous, this context information is carried by [AsyncLocal<T>] rather than by thread-local data.

docs.title: 8.11. Further Reading
docs.text:
Thread synchronization is a challenging field. This chapter has introduced the main tools; to learn more:

  • Microsoft’s documentation, chapter “Threading in .NET”: Managed threading, particularly the “Overview of synchronization primitives” page;
  • Microsoft’s documentation, chapter “Parallel Programming”: Parallel Programming in .NET, which covers the [Parallel] library, tasks, and concurrent collections;
  • the “Threading” chapter from Joseph Albahari’s book, [C# in a Nutshell], for which the 2008 course already recommended the C# 3.0 edition. An older but still informative version of this chapter is available online: Threading in C#.

In modern code, [Thread] objects are rarely manipulated directly. Instead, tasks ([Task]) are preferred, as they run in the thread pool, and especially asynchronous programming using the keywords [async] and [await], which allows you to wait for a long-running operation (network, database, or file access) without blocking a thread. This is the subject of the next chapter. Nevertheless, the concepts covered in this chapter remain essential: tasks run in threads, and the data they share must be protected using the same tools ([lock], [Interlocked], concurrent collections).

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The PDF in the document is ICI.

The code in this document is ICI.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It is a rewrite, for C# 14 and the .NET 10 platform, of the course “Learning C# Version 3.0 with the .NET 3.5 framework, written by Serge Tahé in May 2008. It retains the course outline, examples, and central theme, while updating the language, libraries, and tools:

  • the 2008 course used C# 3.0 and the .NET 3.5 framework on Windows with Visual C# 2008 Express. Since then, C# has seen eleven major versions (from C# 4.0 in 2010 to C# 14 in 2025), and the .NET platform has been completely rewritten: it is now open-source, cross-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS), and released annually. This document uses .NET 10 (November 2025, long-term support version) and C# 14;
  • the chapter on Windows Forms graphical user interfaces has been removed: today, business applications are most often written with web interfaces. The “User Events” chapter, which followed it, has been reworked into a chapter on delegates, lambda expressions, and events, without forms;
  • Two chapters are new: asynchronous programming ([Task] tasks and the [async] / [await], introduced in 2012 with C# 5) and Entity Framework Core, the object-relational mapping tool for .NET. The chapter on commonly used .NET classes now covers LINQ (the 2008 course explicitly stated that it did not cover this);
  • the tools have changed: the [VS Code] editor (or the IDE and [Visual Studio 2026]) and the [dotnet] command replace Visual C# 2008 Express; the [MSTest] testing framework replaces [NUnit 2]; the dependency injection provided by [Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection] replaces [Spring.NET]; SGBD, [MySQL] (provided by [Laragon]) and the [MySqlConnector] connector replace SQL Server 2005 Express; the [HttpClient] class replaces [WebClient] and [WebRequest], which have been deprecated; the REST / JSON web services written with ASP.NET Core replace the SOAP and [ASMX] web services;
  • anything that has become obsolete has been removed or marked as such, and each chapter presents the latest features of the language and platform as of the time of writing.

This document is not a comprehensive course. Like the 2008 edition, it is intended for readers who already have programming experience and want to learn the basics of C#. It uses examples: more than two hundred programs (nearly three hundred C# files), most of them short, with line-by-line comments.

docs.title: 1.1. C# and .NET from 2002 to 2026
docs.text:
C# was released in February 2002, alongside Microsoft’s .NET 1.0 platform, to which it is tied. The .NET platform is a runtime environment similar to the Java Virtual Machine: the compilers for the .NET languages (C#, F#, VB.NET) generate intermediate code (IL, “Intermediate Language”) that the .NET virtual machine (the CLR, “Common Language Runtime”) compiles on the fly into machine code. All classes on the platform are available to all .NET languages.

In 2008, the course stated that .NET ran only on Windows and that the Mono project allowed it to be used, to a limited extent, on Unix and Linux. The situation has changed significantly:

  • 2016: .NET Core 1.0. Microsoft has released a new implementation of .NET, which is open source (MIT license, code available on GitHub) and cross-platform: Windows, Linux, and macOS. The old “.NET” framework (.NET Framework 4.x) remains supported for legacy Windows applications but is no longer being developed;
  • 2020: .NET 5. .NET Core becomes simply “.NET”: a single platform for all uses (console, web, desktop, mobile, cloud);
  • Since 2020: A new version of .NET is released every year in November. Even-numbered versions (.NET 6, 8, 10) have extended support (LTS, three years); odd-numbered versions (.NET 7, 9) have standard support (STS: eighteen months, extended to two years starting with .NET 9). Each version of .NET introduces a new version of C#;
  • November 2025: .NET 10 (LTS) and C# 14, which are used in this document. .NET 10 is supported through November 2028.

The 2008 course also noted that in 2002, C# was largely a copy of Java and that it was easy to switch between the two, but that the two languages had since developed their own distinct characteristics. The gap has widened: Over the course of its various versions, C# has incorporated concepts from functional languages (lambda expressions, LINQ, pattern matching, records, immutable types), asynchronous programming ([async] / [await], which JavaScript, Python, and Rust have since adopted), and a type system that detects null references at compile time.

The following table summarizes the main new features of the language since C# 3.0 and indicates the chapter of this document where they are discussed:

VersionYearMajor New FeaturesChapterC# 4.02010named and optional parameters (the [dynamic] type and generic variance, which also appeared in C# 4, are not covered)3C# 52012Asynchronous methods [async] / [await]9C# 62015interpolated strings [$"..."], [nameof], operator [?.], exception filters [when], expression-bodied members3, 4C# 7.0–7.32017–2018tuples and destructuring, [out var], local functions, pattern matching, binary literals and separators [_], parameters [in]3, 4C# 82019nullable reference types, expressions [switch], indexes [^1], and ranges [1..3], [??=], declarations [using], default interface methods, asynchronous streams [await foreach]3 through 9C# 92020high-level statements, [record], properties [init], [new()] to target type, relational and logical patterns3, 4C# 102021[global using], file-scope namespaces, [record struct], natural type of lambdas3, 4, 7C# 112022raw strings ["""], members [required], list patterns, abstract static interface members3, 4, 5, 12C# 122023primary constructors, collection expressions [1, 2, 3], aliases for any type, default lambda parameters3–7C# 132024collections [params], type [System.Threading.Lock]3, 8C# 142025extension members ([extension] blocks), [field] keyword, [a?.B = x] conditional assignment, user-defined compound assignment operators, untyped lambda parameter modifiers4, 7

On the platform side, the new features introduced include: the [dotnet] command and single-file applications (.NET 10), the [.slnx] solution format, LINQ, modern generic collections, [System.Text.Json], compile-time-generated regular expressions, dependency injection, tasks and the parallel library, channels [Channel<T>], [HttpClient], ASP.NET Core and Entity Framework Core.

docs.title: 1.3. The Common Thread: Tax Calculation
docs.text:
As in 2008, the same problem is revisited throughout the document: calculating the income tax for a taxpayer who has only their salary to report. The tax bracket used is that of the original course (2003 income): it is no longer current, but it suffices for our purpose, which is to write the same application in several different ways. It is implemented in nine versions:

VersionChapterContent13A single program: validated input, calculation, display24Classes and interfaces: [TrancheImpot], [IImpot], [AbstractImpot], [HardwiredImpot]35calculation data read from a text file or a JSON file46A layered architecture ([dao], [metier], [ui]) within a single project56One library per layer, unit tests, and integration of layers via dependency injection610A [dao] layer that reads data from a MySQL database using ADO.NET711a [dao] layer written with Entity Framework Core812A TCP tax calculation server and its client913a REST web service for tax calculation, a console client, and a web client

Starting with version 5, subsequent versions reuse the layers from version 5 and replace only the layer that has changed: this is the whole point of the layered architecture presented in Chapter 6.

docs.text:
The code in this document is organized in a single folder named [csharp-oct-2026], with one subfolder per chapter:

csharp-oct-2026/

The small programs are single-file applications: a single file named [.cs], executed by the command [dotnet run fichier.cs] (Chapter 2). Multi-file programs are projects ([.csproj]) grouped into a solution ([.slnx]) by chapter.

All programs in this document were compiled without errors or warnings using SDK .NET 10, and then executed. The results reproduced in the document are those from these executions. They were obtained in the French locale (fr-FR), as on a French Windows workstation: real numbers are displayed with a decimal point, and dates are in French. Two notes:

  • error messages from the .NET platform (exception messages) are in English: .NET does not provide French translations for these messages;
  • the examples were run on Linux. For the most part, this makes no difference: .NET is cross-platform. The few differences (file paths with / instead of \, line endings) are noted where they occur.

The results of multithreaded, asynchronous, or network programs, as well as the measured execution times, may vary from one run to another: the comments focus on what is reproducible.

docs.text:
The 2008 course cited the books that helped in writing it: “Professional C# Programming” (Wrox), “C# and .NET” by Gérard Leblanc (Eyrolles), and “C# 3.0 in a Nutshell” by Joseph and Ben Albahari (O’Reilly), “one of the best programming books I’ve ever read.” For the 2026 edition, the primary sources are:
